\title{Submission A solution to Problem 2}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{center}
{\bf The infimum is \(\sqrt3\)}
\end{center}

Let \(M_\beta=\Sigma/\langle G_\beta\rangle\).  This is a compact flat
Mobius band, with boundary a circle of length \(2\beta\).  If \(\beta\)
is realized, condition (2) says exactly that the given map is constant on
the \(G_\beta\)-orbits and separates distinct orbits.  Hence it descends
to a continuous injection \(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\), and this injection is an
embedding because \(M_\beta\) is compact and \(\R^3\) is Hausdorff.  The
locally finite invariant triangulation descends to a locally finite
triangulation of the compact surface \(M_\beta\), hence to a finite one.

In a clean triangle, call the boundary edge the ridge and the opposite
vertex the apex.  A bend is a segment in the triangle joining the apex to
a point of the ridge.

\begin{lemma}[bends lengthen]\label{lem:lengthen}
Let \(L\) be the affine map on one clean triangle.  If \(P\) is any point
of the ridge and \(C\) is the apex, then
\[
        |L(P)-L(C)|>|P-C|.
\]
Moreover every non-degenerate boundary subarc is strictly shortened by
\(F\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let the ridge endpoints be \(A,B\), and put \(P_s=(1-s)A+sB\).  The
function
\[
 q(s)= |L(P_s)-L(C)|^2-|P_s-C|^2
\]
satisfies
\[
 q''(s)=2\big(|L(A)-L(B)|^2-|A-B|^2\big)<0,
\]
because the ridge is shortened.  Since the two side edges are lengthened,
\(q(0)>0\) and \(q(1)>0\).  Concavity gives \(q(s)>0\) for
\(0\le s\le1\).  On each boundary edge the affine map has constant
Lipschitz factor \(<1\); an arbitrary boundary subarc is split at the
finitely many boundary vertices it meets, and the strict inequalities add.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[a polygonal \(T\)-pair]\label{lem:T}
For \(F(M_\beta)\) there are two bends whose image segments lie on
perpendicular intersecting lines.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The bends form a circle.  Indeed, every bend meets the center circle
\(\{y=1/2\}/\langle G_\beta\rangle\) once, and every point of the center
circle lies in a unique bend; on a common non-boundary edge the two
adjacent triangles give the same limiting bend.

Parametrize this bend circle by \(u\in\R/\Z\), lift to \(u\in\R\), and
choose the image direction \(e(u)\) from the lower side of the lifted
strip to the upper side.  Let \(m(u)\) be the image midpoint.  The
previous lemma makes every image bend non-degenerate, and the finite
polygonal structure gives continuous functions \(e,m\).  Going once
around the Mobius band reverses the chosen orientation, so
\[
        e(u+1)=-e(u),\qquad m(u+1)=m(u).
\]
For \(0<r<1\) define
\[
 \Phi(u,r)=\Big(e(u)\!\cdot e(u+r),\,
 (m(u)-m(u+r))\!\cdot (e(u)\times e(u+r))\Big).
\]
It is periodic in \(u\).  As \(r\to0\) it tends to \((1,0)\), and as
\(r\to1\) it tends to \((-1,0)\).  Thus it extends continuously to the
two-point compactification of \(S^1\times(0,1)\), obtained by collapsing
the two boundary circles of \(S^1\times[0,1]\); this compactification is
\(S^2\).

The involution \(\iota(u,r)=(u+r,1-r)\) interchanges the two bends.  Under
the coordinates
\[
(\sin\pi r\cos 2\pi(u+r/2),\,\sin\pi r\sin 2\pi(u+r/2),\,\cos\pi r)
\]
on the compactified cylinder, \(\iota\) is the antipodal map.  From
\(e(u+1)=-e(u)\) and \(m(u+1)=m(u)\) one checks that
\(\Phi\circ\iota=-\Phi\).  Borsuk--Ulam gives a zero of \(\Phi\).

At such a zero the two direction vectors are perpendicular.  The second
coordinate says that the vector joining the two midpoints lies in the
plane spanned by those directions; hence the two supporting lines are
coplanar.  Since they are not parallel, they intersect.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:lower}
Every realized \(\beta\) satisfies \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose the two bends from Lemma \ref{lem:T}.  Their image segments have
disjoint relative interiors, because \(F\) is an embedding.  Let \(O\) be
the intersection of their supporting lines.  At least one image segment
does not contain \(O\) in its relative interior; call that bend \(B\), and
call the other one \(T\).

Lift \(T\) to a segment from \((0,0)\) to \((t,1)\).  Replacing \(x\) by
\(-x\), if necessary, we may assume \(t\ge0\).  In fact \(t<\beta\): if
\(t>\beta\), this lifted segment meets its \(G_\beta\)-translate in its
interior, and if \(t=\beta\), its endpoints are \(G_\beta\)-equivalent.
Either case contradicts the fact that the image of a bend is a
non-degenerate affine segment and that \(F\) is embedded on the quotient.

Cutting \(M_\beta\) along \(T\) gives two boundary arcs \(H,D\) of lengths
\[
        \ellg(H)=\beta-t,\qquad \ellg(D)=\beta+t.        \tag{1}
\]
Indeed the upper endpoint \((t,1)\) has boundary coordinate \(t+\beta\)
modulo \(2\beta\).  Let \(T^*=F(T)\).  Since \(H^*=F(H)\) joins the
endpoints of \(T^*\), while boundary arcs are shortened and bends are
lengthened,
\[
        \beta-t=\ellg(H)>\ellg(H^*)\ge |T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}.       \tag{2}
\]

The line of \(B^*\) is perpendicular to the line of \(T^*\).  Since \(O\)
is not in the relative interior of \(B^*\), one endpoint \(v^*\) of
\(B^*\) has distance from the line of \(T^*\) at least \(|B^*|\).  The
domain length of \(B\) is at least \(1\), so Lemma \ref{lem:lengthen}
gives \(|B^*|>1\).  Let \(A\) be the boundary arc, either \(H\) or \(D\),
which contains the corresponding boundary endpoint \(v\).

The image arc \(A^*\) goes from one endpoint of \(T^*\) to the other
through \(v^*\).  If a point has perpendicular distance \(h\) from a line
segment of length \(L\), the sum of its distances to the two endpoints is
at least \(\sqrt{L^2+4h^2}\), with equality only over the midpoint.  Here
\(L=|T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}\) and \(h>1\), so
\[
        \ellg(A)>\ellg(A^*)\ge
        \hbox{(that sum)}>\sqrt{5+t^2}.                  \tag{3}
\]

If \(A=H\), then \(D\ge H\) and (3) gives
\[
        2\beta=H+D>2\sqrt{5+t^2}>2\sqrt3.
\]
Thus assume \(A=D\).  From (1)--(3),
\[
 2\beta=H+D>\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},                         \tag{4}
\]
and also
\[
 2\beta=2D-2t>2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t.                                \tag{5}
\]
Let
\[
 a(t)=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},\qquad
 b(t)=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t .
\]
On \([0,\infty)\), \(a\) is increasing and \(b\) is decreasing, and
\[
        a(1/\sqrt3)=b(1/\sqrt3)=2\sqrt3 .
\]
Hence \(\max(a(t),b(t))\ge2\sqrt3\) for all \(t\ge0\).  Equations
(4)--(5) imply \(2\beta>2\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

It remains to construct realizations for all larger \(\beta\).

\begin{lemma}[an embedded six-triangle model]\label{lem:model}
Let \(E_0E_1E_2\) be an equilateral triangle of side \(a\).  For every
sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\) there are points \(C_i(\varepsilon)\)
tending to the midpoint of \(E_iE_{i+1}\) (indices mod \(3\)) such that
the six affine triangles
\[
(E_i,C_i,E_{i+2}),\qquad (C_i,E_{i+1},E_{i+2}),\qquad i=0,1,2,
\]
form an embedded polyhedral Mobius band with boundary
\(E_0C_0E_1C_1E_2C_2E_0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Embeddedness is preserved by nonsingular affine changes of coordinates,
so it is enough to verify one model.  Take
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
A_0=(0,0,0),& A_1=(1,0,0),& A_2=(0,1,0),\\
B_0=(1/2,0,\varepsilon),&
B_1=(1/2-\varepsilon,1/2,-2\varepsilon),&
B_2=(\varepsilon,1/2,0),
\end{array}
\]
where \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), and take the six faces
\[
\Delta_0=A_0B_0A_2,\quad \Delta_1=B_0A_1A_2,\quad
\Delta_2=A_1B_1A_0,\quad \Delta_3=B_1A_2A_0,
\]
\[
\Delta_4=A_2B_2A_1,\quad \Delta_5=B_2A_0A_1 .
\]
The links of the vertices are intervals.  For instance
\[
 \operatorname{lk}(A_i)=
 B_i-A_{i+2}-B_{i+1}-A_{i+1}-B_{i+2},\qquad
 \operatorname{lk}(B_i)=A_i-A_{i+2}-A_{i+1}
\]
(indices mod \(3\), and reversal of a path is immaterial).  Thus the
abstract complex is a connected compact surface.  Its single boundary
cycle is \(A_0B_0A_1B_1A_2B_2A_0\), and
\(\chi=6-12+6=0\); hence, by the classification of compact surfaces, it
is a Mobius band once its geometric realization is embedded.

It remains to check embeddedness.  The face normals are
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
n_0=(-\varepsilon,0,1/2),&
n_1=(\varepsilon,\varepsilon,1/2),&
n_2=(0,2\varepsilon,1/2),\\
n_3=(2\varepsilon,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_4=(0,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_5=(0,0,1/2).
\end{array}
\]
For the edge-sharing pairs
\((0,1),(0,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,5)\) these normals are not proportional, so
the two planes meet in the line of the common edge and the two triangles
meet exactly in that edge.  The remaining edge-sharing pair is
\((4,5)\).  These two triangles are coplanar in \(z=0\), but their third
vertices lie on opposite sides of their common edge \(B_2A_1\), since
\[
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_2-B_2)=\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{2}>0,\qquad
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_0-B_2)=-\frac{1}{2}<0 .
\]
Therefore \(\Delta_4\cap\Delta_5=B_2A_1\).

The other nine pairs of faces share only one vertex.  For each of them,
the normals listed above are not proportional, so the two planes meet in a
line through that vertex.  Expressing one direction of this line in the two edge bases
at the shared vertex gives the following sign table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(i,j)&\Delta_i&\Delta_j\\ \hline
(0,2)&(-,+)&(-,+)\\
(0,4)&(-,0)&(-,+)\\
(0,5)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,2)&(-,+)&(+,-)\\
(1,3)&(+,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)\\
(2,4)&(0,-)&(+,-)\\
(3,4)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(3,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)
\end{array}
\]
for \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\).  For example, for the pair \((0,2)\)
one line direction is \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2,-2\varepsilon^2)\),
with cone coordinates
\((-2\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2)\) and
\((\varepsilon(2\varepsilon-3)/2,\varepsilon)\).  The other entries are
obtained by the same two-by-two linear calculation; zeros occur only
where displayed.  Call a sign pair non-negative (respectively
non-positive) when both of its entries are so.  In no row are the two
sign pairs both non-negative or both non-positive.  Therefore neither direction of the intersection line
lies in both closed tangent cones, and the two closed triangles meet only
at their common vertex.  This proves the model is embedded.  Applying the affine map which sends \(A_i\) to \(E_i\) gives
the stated points \(C_i(\varepsilon)\), and they tend to the side
midpoints as \(\varepsilon\to0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[realizations above \(\sqrt3\)]\label{lem:upper}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(\delta=\beta/3\).  Choose \(a\) with
\[
        \max\{2/\sqrt3,\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\}<a<2\delta ;
\]
such an \(a\) exists because \(\delta>1/\sqrt3\).

Triangulate \(M_\beta\) in the fundamental rectangle
\([0,\beta]\times[0,1]\), with \((0,y)\sim(\beta,1-y)\).  Put
\[
\begin{array}{c}
A_0=(0,0),\quad B_0=(\delta,0),\quad A_1=(2\delta,0),\quad B_1=(\beta,0),\\
B_1=(0,1),\quad A_2=(\delta,1),\quad B_2=(2\delta,1),\quad A_0=(\beta,1).
\end{array}
\]
Split the three rectangles of width \(\delta\) by the diagonals
\(A_0A_2\), \(A_1A_2\), and \(A_1A_0\), respectively.  Equivalently, the
six faces are
\[
(A_i,B_i,A_{i+2}),\qquad (B_i,A_{i+1},A_{i+2}),\qquad i=0,1,2
\]
(indices mod \(3\)).  This is a clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\), and
its lift to \(\Sigma\) is \(G_\beta\)-invariant.

Use Lemma \ref{lem:model} with side length \(a\), and choose
\(\varepsilon\) so small that the following strict inequalities, which
hold in the limit \(\varepsilon\to0\), still hold:
\[
 |E_iC_i|<\delta,\qquad |C_iE_{i+1}|<\delta,\qquad
 |C_iE_{i+2}|>1 .
\]
Also \(|E_iE_j|=a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\).  Map the six vertices
\(A_i,B_i\) to \(E_i,C_i\), respectively, and extend affinely over each
of the six triangles.  Lemma \ref{lem:model} gives an embedding
\(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\).

Each ridge in the domain has length \(\delta\), and its image has length
\(<\delta\).  Each non-boundary edge is of one of two types: either it has
domain length \(1\), and image length \(|C_iE_{i+2}|>1\), or it has domain
length \(\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\), and image length \(a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\).
Thus \(F\) is a squeeze map on every triangle.  Lifting \(F\) to
\(\Sigma\) gives a continuous map invariant under \(G_\beta\); since
\(F\) is an embedding of the quotient, the lifted map satisfies condition
(2).  Hence \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

Proposition \ref{prop:lower} shows that realized numbers are all
\(>\sqrt3\), while Lemma \ref{lem:upper} realizes every \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
Therefore the infimum of the set of realized numbers is \(\sqrt3\).

## Correctness.

The AI got the problem correct. This is a working proof, with all essential details included. The proof in both halves is efficient, and the proof in the second half is especially clean. I really enjoyed reading the second half. 

## Novelty.

Let me first discuss the context for the problem and then describe how the AI did. The problem is based on my solution of the Halpern-Weaver Conjecture, a result which asks for the infimal
aspect ratio needed for a smooth and isometric embedding of a flat Moebius band into $\R^3$. My paper was published in the {\it Annals\/} in January, 2025 and there are also some of accounts of the result in the popular media. The problem the AI considered is the same problem in a different category of maps, piecewise linear maps with a certain side condition called squeezing. 

The first half of the problem amounts to showing that $\sqrt 3$ is a lower bound on the allowable aspect ratio. For this, the AI seems to have followed my paper very closely, adapting essentially every one of my arguments to the new category of mappings. One thing that troubled me is that the AI did not cite my work at all, even though the arguments were extremely close. Indeed, the AI used the same terminology in my paper -- e.g. ''T-patterns'' and ''bends'' -- and also used the same letters, $B,T,D,H$ for the important objects in the proof. The chances of this happening without the AI actually reading and absorbing my paper seem to be a trillion to one against. If I found this kind of thing written on a student's exam -- close adaptation without any acknowledgement -- I would probably give them an F for the exam.

The second half of the problem amounts to constructing an example for every aspect ratio greater than $\sqrt 3$. For this, the AI did a beautiful and,
as far as I can tell, original job. The AI produced a $6$-triangle example which works for a wide range of parameter values in the one-sided neighborhood of $\sqrt 3$. (For large aspect ratio the result is obvious.) This construction was both cool and suprising, just great.
reviews.recommendation:
I would recommend that the paper is publishable with minor revisions, though with a big {\it caveat\/}. I will indicate the revisions with inline comments below.
Now let me explain the one {\it caveat\/}. As indicated above, the close adaptation of my arguments without any citation was annoying. I would consider this a kind of ethical failing in a human author. For an AI, it is hard to tell. 
Possibly I would reject the paper on the grounds of ``unethical AI behavior'', whatever that might mean.

disjoint relative interiors, because \(F\) is an embedding. Let \(O\) be
the intersection of their supporting lines. At least one image segment
does not contain \(O\) in its relative interior; call that bend \(B\), and
call the other one \(T\).

Lift \(T\) to a segment from \((0,0)\) to \((t,1)\). Replacing \(x\) by
\(-x\), if necessary, we may assume \(t\ge0\). In fact \(t<\beta\): if
\(t>\beta\), this lifted segment meets its \(G_\beta\)-translate in its
interior, and if \(t=\beta\), its endpoints are \(G_\beta\)-equivalent.
Either case contradicts the fact that the image of a bend is a
non-degenerate affine segment and that \(F\) is embedded on the quotient.

Cutting \(M_\beta\) along \(T\) gives two boundary arcs \(H,D\) of lengths
\[
 \ellg(H)=\beta-t,\qquad \ellg(D)=\beta+t. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed the upper endpoint \((t,1)\) has boundary coordinate \(t+\beta\)
modulo \(2\beta\). Let \(T^*=F(T)\). Since \(H^*=F(H)\) joins the
endpoints of \(T^*\), while boundary arcs are shortened and bends are
lengthened,
\[
 \beta-t=\ellg(H)>\ellg(H^*)\ge |T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}. \tag{2}
\]

The line of \(B^*\) is perpendicular to the line of \(T^*\). Since \(O\)
is not in the relative interior of \(B^*\), one endpoint \(v^*\) of
\(B^*\) has distance from the line of \(T^*\) at least \(|B^*|\). The
domain length of \(B\) is at least \(1\), so Lemma \ref{lem:lengthen}
gives \(|B^*|>1\). Let \(A\) be the boundary arc, either \(H\) or \(D\),
which contains the corresponding boundary endpoint \(v\).

The image arc \(A^*\) goes from one endpoint of \(T^*\) to the other
through \(v^*\). If a point has perpendicular distance \(h\) from a line
segment of length \(L\), the sum of its distances to the two endpoints is
at least \(\sqrt{L^2+4h^2}\), with equality only over the midpoint. Here
\(L=|T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}\) and \(h>1\), so
\[
 \ellg(A)>\ellg(A^*)\ge
 \hbox{(that sum)}>\sqrt{5+t^2}. \tag{3}
\]

\review{This endgame seems a bit inefficient to me. It works, but is not maximally efficient. The main point is to get $\beta>\max(\sqrt{1+t^2}+t,\sqrt{5+t^2}-t).$}

If \(A=H\), then \(D\ge H\) and (3) gives
\[
 2\beta=H+D>2\sqrt{5+t^2}>2\sqrt3.
\]
Thus assume \(A=D\). From (1)--(3),
\[
 2\beta=H+D>\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2}, \tag{4}
\]
and also
\[
 2\beta=2D-2t>2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t. \tag{5}
\]
Let
\[
 a(t)=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},\qquad
 b(t)=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t .
\]
On \([0,\infty)\), \(a\) is increasing and \(b\) is decreasing, and
\[
 a(1/\sqrt3)=b(1/\sqrt3)=2\sqrt3 .
\]
Hence \(\max(a(t),b(t))\ge2\sqrt3\) for all \(t\ge0\). Equations
(4)--(5) imply \(2\beta>2\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

It remains to construct realizations for all larger \(\beta\).

\review{In general, this second half is really cool and interesting. I was surprised that you could make one of these things with just $6$ triangles. My own construction, which is more transparent, used $11$.}

\begin{lemma}[an embedded six-triangle model]\label{lem:model}
Let \(E_0E_1E_2\) be an equilateral triangle of side \(a\). For every
sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\) there are points \(C_i(\varepsilon)\)
tending to the midpoint of \(E_iE_{i+1}\) (indices mod \(3\)) such that
the six affine triangles
\[
(E_i,C_i,E_{i+2}),\qquad (C_i,E_{i+1},E_{i+2}),\qquad i=0,1,2,
\]
form an embedded polyhedral Mobius band with boundary
\(E_0C_0E_1C_1E_2C_2E_0\).
\end{lemma}

\review{A diagram for this proof would be extremely helpful. The diagram ideally would show both the domain and the range.}

\review{The notation switch here from C,E to A,B is a bit confusing. Logically it makes sense, but a ``connecting comment'' would be nice.}

\begin{proof}
Embeddedness is preserved by nonsingular affine changes of coordinates,
so it is enough to verify one model. Take
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
A_0=(0,0,0),& A_1=(1,0,0),& A_2=(0,1,0),\\
B_0=(1/2,0,\varepsilon),&
B_1=(1/2-\varepsilon,1/2,-2\varepsilon),&
B_2=(\varepsilon,1/2,0),
\end{array}
\]
where \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\), and take the six faces
\[
\Delta_0=A_0B_0A_2,\quad \Delta_1=B_0A_1A_2,\quad
\Delta_2=A_1B_1A_0,\quad \Delta_3=B_1A_2A_0,
\]
\[
\Delta_4=A_2B_2A_1,\quad \Delta_5=B_2A_0A_1 .
\]

\review{This is a really wierd and confusing notation for the links which, after a lot of head-scratching, I figured out. In hindsight, I sort of like the notation, but some explanation might be nice. Perhaps $\leftrightarrow$ is better than what looks like minus sign. Again, a diagram would be very helpful here.}

The links of the vertices are intervals. For instance
\[
 \operatorname{lk}(A_i)=
 B_i-A_{i+2}-B_{i+1}-A_{i+1}-B_{i+2},\qquad
 \operatorname{lk}(B_i)=A_i-A_{i+2}-A_{i+1}
\]

(indices mod \(3\), and reversal of a path is immaterial). Thus the
abstract complex is a connected compact surface. Its single boundary
cycle is \(A_0B_0A_1B_1A_2B_2A_0\), and
\(\chi=6-12+6=0\); hence, by the classification of compact surfaces, it
is a Mobius band once its geometric realization is embedded.

\review{I like this proof a lot, though I did not try to follow it line by line. Instead I plotted a picture, with specific choices, in Mathematica, and saw that it was embedded. I did this by checking every pair of triangles visually.}

It remains to check embeddedness. The face normals are
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
n_0=(-\varepsilon,0,1/2),&
n_1=(\varepsilon,\varepsilon,1/2),&
n_2=(0,2\varepsilon,1/2),\\
n_3=(2\varepsilon,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_4=(0,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_5=(0,0,1/2).
\end{array}
\]
For the edge-sharing pairs
\((0,1),(0,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,5)\) these normals are not proportional, so
the two planes meet in the line of the common edge and the two triangles
meet exactly in that edge. The remaining edge-sharing pair is
\((4,5)\). These two triangles are coplanar in \(z=0\), but their third
vertices lie on opposite sides of their common edge \(B_2A_1\), since
\[
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_2-B_2)=\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{2}>0,\qquad
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_0-B_2)=-\frac{1}{2}<0 .
\]
Therefore \(\Delta_4\cap\Delta_5=B_2A_1\).

The other nine pairs of faces share only one vertex. For each of them,
the normals listed above are not proportional, so the two planes meet in a
line through that vertex. Expressing one direction of this line in the two edge bases
at the shared vertex gives the following sign table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(i,j)&\Delta_i&\Delta_j\\ \hline
(0,2)&(-,+)&(-,+)\\
(0,4)&(-,0)&(-,+)\\
(0,5)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,2)&(-,+)&(+,-)\\
(1,3)&(+,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)\\
(2,4)&(0,-)&(+,-)\\
(3,4)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(3,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)
\end{array}
\]

\review{This chart is a cool way to check that two triangles just share a vertex. For what it is worth, I did something similar in a recent paper I wrote which solved the minimal vertex problem for origami tori. (This paper appeared recently in the PNAS.)}

for \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\). For example, for the pair \((0,2)\)
one line direction is \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2,-2\varepsilon^2)\),
with cone coordinates
\((-2\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2)\) and
\((\varepsilon(2\varepsilon-3)/2,\varepsilon)\). The other entries are
obtained by the same two-by-two linear calculation; zeros occur only
where displayed. Call a sign pair non-negative (respectively
non-positive) when both of its entries are so. In no row are the two
sign pairs both non-negative or both non-positive. Therefore neither direction of the intersection line
lies in both closed tangent cones, and the two closed triangles meet only
at their common vertex. This proves the model is embedded. Applying the affine map which sends \(A_i\) to \(E_i\) gives
the stated points \(C_i(\varepsilon)\), and they tend to the side
midpoints as \(\varepsilon\to0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[realizations above \(\sqrt3\)]\label{lem:upper}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(\delta=\beta/3\). Choose \(a\) with
\[
 \max\{2/\sqrt3,\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\}<a<2\delta ;
\]
such an \(a\) exists because \(\delta>1/\sqrt3\).

Triangulate \(M_\beta\) in the fundamental rectangle
\([0,\beta]\times[0,1]\), with \((0,y)\sim(\beta,1-y)\). Put
\[
\begin{array}{c}
A_0=(0,0),\quad B_0=(\delta,0),\quad A_1=(2\delta,0),\quad B_1=(\beta,0),\\
B_1=(0,1),\quad A_2=(\delta,1),\quad B_2=(2\delta,1),\quad A_0=(\beta,1).
\end{array}
\]
Split the three rectangles of width \(\delta\) by the diagonals
\(A_0A_2\), \(A_1A_2\), and \(A_1A_0\), respectively. Equivalently, the
six faces are
\[
(A_i,B_i,A_{i+2}),\qquad (B_i,A_{i+1},A_{i+2}),\qquad i=0,1,2
\]
(indices mod \(3\)). This is a clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\), and
its lift to \(\Sigma\) is \(G_\beta\)-invariant.

Use Lemma \ref{lem:model} with side length \(a\), and choose
\(\varepsilon\) so small that the following strict inequalities, which
hold in the limit \(\varepsilon\to0\), still hold:
\[
 |E_iC_i|<\delta,\qquad |C_iE_{i+1}|<\delta,\qquad
 |C_iE_{i+2}|>1 .
\]
Also \(|E_iE_j|=a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\). Map the six vertices
\(A_i,B_i\) to \(E_i,C_i\), respectively, and extend affinely over each
of the six triangles. Lemma \ref{lem:model} gives an embedding
\(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\).

Each ridge in the domain has length \(\delta\), and its image has length
\(<\delta\). Each non-boundary edge is of one of two types: either it has
domain length \(1\), and image length \(|C_iE_{i+2}|>1\), or it has domain
length \(\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\), and image length \(a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\).
Thus \(F\) is a squeeze map on every triangle. Lifting \(F\) to
\(\Sigma\) gives a continuous map invariant under \(G_\beta\); since
\(F\) is an embedding of the quotient, the lifted map satisfies condition
(2). Hence \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

Proposition \ref{prop:lower} shows that realized numbers are all
\(>\sqrt3\), while Lemma \ref{lem:upper} realizes every \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
Therefore the infimum of the set of realized numbers is \(\sqrt3\).

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The solution is entirely correct, and quite well written at that. 

The AI quickly establishes that the image is a triangulation of a M\"obius band. It then proves the existence of $T$-patterns and uses this to get the correct lower bound.

For the realization/lower bound, the AI produces a novel triangulation, and argues with great rigor and clarity first that the claimed realization is an embedding, and then that it is a squeeze map with desired aspect ratio.

## Novelty.

This novelty report shares structure with the novelty report for the other correct solution I refereed. There is no canonical place to put the information common to both, so common information is repeated.

I want to discuss three lemmas where correct solutions varied, and how this solution compares to the others. Then there is the citation issue.

All correct solutions showed that squeeze maps lengthen cevians to the distinguished vertex. All three AI solutions did this by writing down the change in length function and noting that it is a concave-down parabola. The human solution, on the other hand, showed that squeeze maps decrease the distinguished angle, and got cevian length increase from that.

To prove the $T$-pattern lemma, one can set things up in the right way to reduce to Borsuk-Ulam, or one can directly prove a Borsuk-Ulam-like statement for a slightly different setup. One of the AI solutions, the human solution, and old versions of Schwartz's M\"obius bands paper opt for the latter approach. The other two correct solutions, including this one, and the updated version of Schwartz's M\"obius bands paper reduce directly to Borsuk-Ulam.

For the realization half, there were two main philosophies. The first was to construct an explicit triangulation, write out the coordinates for all the faces in terms of $\epsilon$, and show everything works out. The other philosophy was to closely approximate a smooth realization. This solution went explicit, employing a 6 triangle triangulation.

Notable: This triangulation was novel to the whole referee team; the human solution and the initial ideas I had in mind when seeing the problem required more triangles or were much nastier. I am impressed at the level of geometric, spacial intuition the model carries -- it was able to describe with great accuracy and detail how every piece of its non-obvious construction fit together.

## Attribution.

The overarching approach by this model is to adapt Schwartz's M\"obius bands paper to a different category. Despite this, the solution never once mentions, alludes to, or cites Schwartz's work. Proposition 1, which one might call the ``optimization" or ``geometry" part of the problem, is particularly egregious in its plagiarism. As discussed in the inline comments, it borrows a suspicious amount of notation, the naming for which is motivated by the orientation of a figure featured in Schwartz's paper. In particular, you would not expect an independent solution, even by someone familiar with the work, to exhibit this common notation.

While the proof is entirely correct, and so will formally receive a ``minor revisions" recommendation, a submission of this work by a human to a journal could only be interpreted as willful plagiarism, and would ideally result in a blacklisting.
reviews.recommendation:
Note that the second half of this solution features original, insightful, creative work, at a level not seen in any of the other AI solutions.
 
 Formally, in accordance with the rubric, this solution receives a ``publishable with minor revisions" recommendation, because the only error is a failure of attribution, and this would be easily corrected by citing Schwartz's prior work.

 That said, in the real world this sort of failure of attribution is unacceptable, and would be entirely disqualifying.

\begin{center}
{\bf The infimum is \(\sqrt3\)}
\end{center}

Let \(M_\beta=\Sigma/\langle G_\beta\rangle\).  This is a compact flat
Mobius band, with boundary a circle of length \(2\beta\).  If \(\beta\)
is realized, condition (2) says exactly that the given map is constant on
the \(G_\beta\)-orbits and separates distinct orbits.  Hence it descends
to a continuous injection \(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\), and this injection is an
embedding because \(M_\beta\) is compact and \(\R^3\) is Hausdorff.  The
locally finite invariant triangulation descends to a locally finite
triangulation of the compact surface \(M_\beta\), hence to a finite one.

In a clean triangle, call the boundary edge the ridge and the opposite
vertex the apex.  A bend is a segment in the triangle joining the apex to
a point of the ridge.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: This is a very strong/well-written start. Concise and precise, and sets up some useful definitions with intuitive names.]]


\begin{lemma}[bends lengthen]\label{lem:lengthen}
Let \(L\) be the affine map on one clean triangle.  If \(P\) is any point
of the ridge and \(C\) is the apex, then
\[
        |L(P)-L(C)|>|P-C|.
\]
Moreover every non-degenerate boundary subarc is strictly shortened by
\(F\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let the ridge endpoints be \(A,B\), and put \(P_s=(1-s)A+sB\).  The
function
\[
 q(s)= |L(P_s)-L(C)|^2-|P_s-C|^2
\]
satisfies
\[
 q''(s)=2\big(|L(A)-L(B)|^2-|A-B|^2\big)<0,
\]
because the ridge is shortened.  Since the two side edges are lengthened,
\(q(0)>0\) and \(q(1)>0\).  Concavity gives \(q(s)>0\) for
\(0\le s\le1\).  On each boundary edge the affine map has constant
Lipschitz factor \(<1\); an arbitrary boundary subarc is split at the
finitely many boundary vertices it meets, and the strict inequalities add.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[a polygonal \(T\)-pair]\label{lem:T}
For \(F(M_\beta)\) there are two bends whose image segments lie on
perpendicular intersecting lines.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The bends form a circle.  Indeed, every bend meets the center circle
\(\{y=1/2\}/\langle G_\beta\rangle\) once, and every point of the center
circle lies in a unique bend; on a common non-boundary edge the two
adjacent triangles give the same limiting bend.

Parametrize this bend circle by \(u\in\R/\Z\), lift to \(u\in\R\), and
choose the image direction \(e(u)\) from the lower side of the lifted
strip to the upper side.  Let \(m(u)\) be the image midpoint.  The
previous lemma makes every image bend non-degenerate, and the finite
polygonal structure gives continuous functions \(e,m\).  Going once
around the Mobius band reverses the chosen orientation, so
\[
        e(u+1)=-e(u),\qquad m(u+1)=m(u).
\]
For \(0<r<1\) define
\[
 \Phi(u,r)=\Big(e(u)\!\cdot e(u+r),\,
 (m(u)-m(u+r))\!\cdot (e(u)\times e(u+r))\Big).
\]
It is periodic in \(u\).  As \(r\to0\) it tends to \((1,0)\), and as
\(r\to1\) it tends to \((-1,0)\).  Thus it extends continuously to the
two-point compactification of \(S^1\times(0,1)\), obtained by collapsing
the two boundary circles of \(S^1\times[0,1]\); this compactification is
\(S^2\).

The involution \(\iota(u,r)=(u+r,1-r)\) interchanges the two bends.  Under
the coordinates
\[
(\sin\pi r\cos 2\pi(u+r/2),\,\sin\pi r\sin 2\pi(u+r/2),\,\cos\pi r)
\]
on the compactified cylinder, \(\iota\) is the antipodal map.  From
\(e(u+1)=-e(u)\) and \(m(u+1)=m(u)\) one checks that
\(\Phi\circ\iota=-\Phi\).  Borsuk--Ulam gives a zero of \(\Phi\).

At such a zero the two direction vectors are perpendicular.  The second
coordinate says that the vector joining the two midpoints lies in the
plane spanned by those directions; hence the two supporting lines are
coplanar.  Since they are not parallel, they intersect.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:lower}
Every realized \(\beta\) satisfies \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}

disjoint relative interiors, because \(F\) is an embedding.  Let \(O\) be
the intersection of their supporting lines.  At least one image segment
does not contain \(O\) in its relative interior; call that bend \(B\), and
call the other one \(T\).

interior, and if \(t=\beta\), its endpoints are \(G_\beta\)-equivalent.
Either case contradicts the fact that the image of a bend is a
non-degenerate affine segment and that \(F\) is embedded on the quotient.

Cutting \(M_\beta\) along \(T\) gives two boundary arcs \(H,D\) of lengths
\[
        \ellg(H)=\beta-t,\qquad \ellg(D)=\beta+t.        \tag{1}
\]
Indeed the upper endpoint \((t,1)\) has boundary coordinate \(t+\beta\)
modulo \(2\beta\).  Let \(T^*=F(T)\).  Since \(H^*=F(H)\) joins the
endpoints of \(T^*\), while boundary arcs are shortened and bends are

\[

\]

The line of \(B^*\) is perpendicular to the line of \(T^*\).  Since \(O\)

\[
        \ellg(A)>\ellg(A^*)\ge
        \hbox{(that sum)}>\sqrt{5+t^2}.                  \tag{3}
\]

If \(A=H\), then \(D\ge H\) and (3) gives

\end{proof}

It remains to construct realizations for all larger \(\beta\).

n_2=(0,2\varepsilon,1/2),\\
n_3=(2\varepsilon,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_4=(0,0,1/2-\varepsilon),&
n_5=(0,0,1/2).
\end{array}
\]
For the edge-sharing pairs
\((0,1),(0,3),(1,4),(2,3),(2,5)\) these normals are not proportional, so
the two planes meet in the line of the common edge and the two triangles
meet exactly in that edge.  The remaining edge-sharing pair is
\((4,5)\).  These two triangles are coplanar in \(z=0\), but their third
vertices lie on opposite sides of their common edge \(B_2A_1\), since
\[
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_2-B_2)=\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{2}>0,\qquad
 \det(A_1-B_2,A_0-B_2)=-\frac{1}{2}<0 .
\]
Therefore \(\Delta_4\cap\Delta_5=B_2A_1\).

The other nine pairs of faces share only one vertex.  For each of them,
the normals listed above are not proportional, so the two planes meet in a
line through that vertex.  Expressing one direction of this line in the two edge bases
at the shared vertex gives the following sign table:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
(i,j)&\Delta_i&\Delta_j\\ \hline
(0,2)&(-,+)&(-,+)\\
(0,4)&(-,0)&(-,+)\\
(0,5)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,2)&(-,+)&(+,-)\\
(1,3)&(+,-)&(-,+)\\
(1,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)\\
(2,4)&(0,-)&(+,-)\\
(3,4)&(0,-)&(-,+)\\
(3,5)&(0,+)&(+,-)
\end{array}
\]
for \(0<\varepsilon<1/4\).  For example, for the pair \((0,2)\)
one line direction is \((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2,-2\varepsilon^2)\),
with cone coordinates
\((-2\varepsilon,\varepsilon/2)\) and
\((\varepsilon(2\varepsilon-3)/2,\varepsilon)\).  The other entries are
obtained by the same two-by-two linear calculation; zeros occur only
where displayed.  Call a sign pair non-negative (respectively
non-positive) when both of its entries are so.  In no row are the two
sign pairs both non-negative or both non-positive.  Therefore neither direction of the intersection line
lies in both closed tangent cones, and the two closed triangles meet only
at their common vertex.  This proves the model is embedded.  Applying the affine map which sends \(A_i\) to \(E_i\) gives
the stated points \(C_i(\varepsilon)\), and they tend to the side
midpoints as \(\varepsilon\to0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[realizations above \(\sqrt3\)]\label{lem:upper}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put \(\delta=\beta/3\).  Choose \(a\) with
\[
        \max\{2/\sqrt3,\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\}<a<2\delta ;
\]
such an \(a\) exists because \(\delta>1/\sqrt3\).

Triangulate \(M_\beta\) in the fundamental rectangle
\([0,\beta]\times[0,1]\), with \((0,y)\sim(\beta,1-y)\).  Put
\[
\begin{array}{c}
A_0=(0,0),\quad B_0=(\delta,0),\quad A_1=(2\delta,0),\quad B_1=(\beta,0),\\
B_1=(0,1),\quad A_2=(\delta,1),\quad B_2=(2\delta,1),\quad A_0=(\beta,1).
\end{array}
\]
Split the three rectangles of width \(\delta\) by the diagonals
\(A_0A_2\), \(A_1A_2\), and \(A_1A_0\), respectively.  Equivalently, the
six faces are
\[
(A_i,B_i,A_{i+2}),\qquad (B_i,A_{i+1},A_{i+2}),\qquad i=0,1,2
\]
(indices mod \(3\)).  This is a clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\), and
its lift to \(\Sigma\) is \(G_\beta\)-invariant.

Use Lemma \ref{lem:model} with side length \(a\), and choose
\(\varepsilon\) so small that the following strict inequalities, which
hold in the limit \(\varepsilon\to0\), still hold:
\[
 |E_iC_i|<\delta,\qquad |C_iE_{i+1}|<\delta,\qquad
 |C_iE_{i+2}|>1 .
\]
Also \(|E_iE_j|=a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\).  Map the six vertices
\(A_i,B_i\) to \(E_i,C_i\), respectively, and extend affinely over each
of the six triangles.  Lemma \ref{lem:model} gives an embedding
\(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\).

Each ridge in the domain has length \(\delta\), and its image has length
\(<\delta\).  Each non-boundary edge is of one of two types: either it has
domain length \(1\), and image length \(|C_iE_{i+2}|>1\), or it has domain
length \(\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\), and image length \(a>\sqrt{1+\delta^2}\).
Thus \(F\) is a squeeze map on every triangle.  Lifting \(F\) to
\(\Sigma\) gives a continuous map invariant under \(G_\beta\); since
\(F\) is an embedding of the quotient, the lifted map satisfies condition
(2).  Hence \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

Proposition \ref{prop:lower} shows that realized numbers are all
\(>\sqrt3\), while Lemma \ref{lem:upper} realizes every \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
Therefore the infimum of the set of realized numbers is \(\sqrt3\).

\title{Submission B solution to Problem 2}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{theorem}[Headline theorem: original problem]\label{thm:headline}
\normalfont
Let \(\Z\) denote the integers and let \(\R\) denote the reals.  Let
\[
\Sigma=\R\times[0,1],\qquad \partial\Sigma=\R\times\{0,1\}.
\]
For \(\beta>0\), define \(G_\beta:\Sigma\to\Sigma\) by
\[
G_\beta(x,y)=(x+\beta,1-y).
\]
Let \(G_\beta^k\) denote the \(k\)-fold composition of \(G_\beta\) or
\(G_\beta^{-1}\), according as \(k>0\) or \(k<0\), and let
\(G_\beta^0\) be the identity.  A \emph{clean triangle} is the convex hull of
three non-collinear points in \(\partial\Sigma\).  A \emph{clean triangulation}
of \(\Sigma\) is a countable, locally finite collection of clean triangles
with pairwise disjoint interiors and union \(\Sigma\).  It is
\(G_\beta\)-\emph{invariant} if \(G_\beta\) preserves the triangulation.  A
\emph{squeeze map} of a clean triangle is an affine map into \(\R^3\) which
decreases the length of the edge contained in \(\partial\Sigma\) and increases
the lengths of the other two edges.  A number \(\beta>0\) is \emph{realized}
if there is a continuous map \(f:\Sigma\to\R^3\) such that
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(f\) restricts to a squeeze map on each triangle of a
\(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation of \(\Sigma\);
\item \(f(p)=f(q)\) if and only if \(p=G_\beta^k(q)\) for some \(k\in\Z\).
\end{enumerate}
Then the infimum of the set of realized numbers is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Established stronger claim]\label{thm:strong}
The realized numbers are exactly the interval \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).
\end{theorem}

\section*{Overview / Strategy}

The lower bound passes to the quotient
\(M_\beta=\Sigma/\langle G_\beta\rangle\), a flat M\"obius band with boundary
length \(2\beta\).  The map descends to an embedded piecewise-affine surface.
Inside each clean triangle the cevians from the apex to the boundary edge are
strictly lengthened.  These cevians form a leaf graph; in the quotient the leaf
graph is a circle, while upstairs it is a line, and the deck transformation
reverses the orientation of the image support line.  A topological lemma about
paths of oriented lines then forces two image support lines to be perpendicular
and intersecting.  Boundary shortening and a Euclidean estimate give
\(\beta>\sqrt3\).

For the upper bound we use one classical external input: the
Sadowsky--Wunderlich construction of embedded developable M\"obius bands, in a
quantitative form.  We approximate such a smooth ruled band by an invariant
piecewise-linear ruled band whose boundary edges are not expanded and whose
transverse edges are shortened by an arbitrarily small amount.  A final
anisotropic rescaling makes the boundary edges strictly shorter and all
transverse edges strictly longer, yielding a realization for every
\(\beta>\sqrt3\).

\section{The lower bound}

Throughout this section assume that \(\beta\) is realized by \(f\) on a
\(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation \(\mathcal T\).  Write
\(G=G_\beta\).

\begin{lemma}[Face-to-face structure]\label{lem:facetoface}
The triangulation is face-to-face: distinct edges have disjoint relative
interiors, every transverse edge is incident to exactly two triangles, and
every boundary edge is incident to exactly one triangle.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A clean triangle has exactly one boundary edge: among its three boundary
vertices, exactly two lie on one boundary component and the third lies on the
other.  The remaining two edges are transverse.

Two transverse edges cannot cross in the interior of \(\Sigma\), since near a
transverse crossing each of the two incident triangles occupies one open side
of its edge, and two such open half-disks always overlap in an open sector.  If
two transverse edges are collinear and overlap in more than one point, then
they lie on the same non-horizontal line; such a line meets \(y=0\) and
\(y=1\) once each, so the two edges are the same geometric segment.  Boundary
edges cannot overlap in a nontrivial interval, because at an interior point of
the overlap both adjacent triangles contain an inward half-neighborhood of the
boundary.  Finally, the endpoint of a transverse edge cannot lie in the
relative interior of a boundary edge: the triangle with the boundary edge
contains a small inward half-disk there, while the triangle with the transverse
edge contains a nonempty sector inside that half-disk.  Hence distinct
triangles meet only in common faces.

Let \(e\) be a transverse edge and \(z\) an interior point of \(e\).  A small
disk around \(z\) is divided by \(e\) into two half-disks.  At most one
triangle occupies each side, by disjointness of interiors, and at least one
triangle occupies each side, because the triangles cover \(\Sigma\).  Thus
\(e\) is incident to exactly two triangles.  The same half-disk argument at an
interior point of a boundary edge gives exactly one incident triangle.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[The finite quotient triangulation]\label{lem:quotient}
The quotient map \(f\) descends to an embedding
\(F:M_\beta\to\R^3\), where
\[
M_\beta=\Sigma/\langle G\rangle
      =[0,\beta]\times[0,1]/(0,y)\sim(\beta,1-y),
\]
and the quotient triangulation of \(M_\beta\) is finite and face-to-face.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(p=Gq\) implies \(f(p)=f(q)\), the map descends to a continuous
\(F\).  If \(F([p])=F([q])\), then \(f(p)=f(q)\), so by realization
\(p=G^kq\), hence \([p]=[q]\).  Thus \(F\) is injective; because \(M_\beta\)
is compact and \(\R^3\) is Hausdorff, \(F\) is an embedding.

The restriction of \(f\) to each triangle is injective.  Indeed, if an affine
restriction had rank \(<2\), then arbitrarily close distinct points
\(p,q\) in that triangle would satisfy \(f(p)=f(q)\).  Then \(p=G^kq\) for
some \(k\ne0\), impossible for sufficiently close \(p,q\), since
\(G^{2n}\) translates by \(2n\beta\) and \(G^{2n+1}\) changes the
\(x\)-coordinate by \((2n+1)\beta\), so every nontrivial \(G^k\) moves every
point by distance at least \(\beta\).

Therefore no closed triangle meets a nontrivial translate of itself.  If
\(z\in\tau\cap G^k\tau\), write \(z=G^kw\) with \(w\in\tau\).  Then
\(f(z)=f(w)\), and injectivity on \(\tau\) gives \(z=w\), contradicting
freeness of the \(G\)-action unless \(k=0\).  A compact fundamental rectangle,
for instance \([0,2\beta]\times[0,1]\), meets only finitely many closed
triangles by local finiteness and compactness, and every orbit of triangles has
a representative meeting it.  Hence the quotient triangulation is finite.
Lemma \ref{lem:facetoface} descends to the quotient.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Cevian lengthening]\label{lem:cevian}
Let \(\Delta=\operatorname{conv}\{a,r_0,r_1\}\) be a clean triangle whose
boundary edge is \([r_0,r_1]\), and let \(A:\Delta\to\R^3\) be a squeeze map.
For \(r(s)=(1-s)r_0+sr_1\), every cevian \([a,r(s)]\) is strictly lengthened:
\[
|A(a)-A(r(s))|>|a-r(s)|,\qquad 0\le s\le1.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Set \(q(s)=|A(a)-A(r(s))|^2-|a-r(s)|^2\).  The two transverse edges are
strictly lengthened, so \(q(0)>0\) and \(q(1)>0\).  Since \(A\) is affine,
\[
q''(s)=2\bigl(|A(r_1)-A(r_0)|^2-|r_1-r_0|^2\bigr)<0
\]
because the boundary edge is strictly shortened.  Thus \(q\) is strictly
concave and lies above its chord:
\(q(s)\ge(1-s)q(0)+sq(1)>0\).  Taking square roots gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Paths of oriented lines]\label{lem:lines}
Let \(L_s\), \(0\le s\le1\), be a continuous path of oriented lines in
\(\R^3\).  Suppose \(L_1\) is the same unoriented line as \(L_0\), but with the
opposite orientation.  Then two distinct parameters give unoriented lines that
are perpendicular and intersect.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Represent an oriented line by \((u,m)\), where \(u\in S^2\) is its unit
direction and \(m=p\times u\) for any point \(p\) on the line.  Reversing
orientation sends \((u,m)\) to \((-u,-m)\).  Choose continuous
\((u(s),m(s))\) and extend by \((u(s+1),m(s+1))=-(u(s),m(s))\).  For
\(s\in\R/\Z\) and \(0\le\delta\le1\), define
\[
a(s,\delta)=u(s)\cdot u(s+\delta),\qquad
b(s,\delta)=u(s)\cdot m(s+\delta)+u(s+\delta)\cdot m(s).
\]
Then \((a,b)(s,0)=(1,0)\), \((a,b)(s,1)=(-1,0)\), and
\((a,b)(s+\delta,1-\delta)=-(a,b)(s,\delta)\).

Assume \((a,b)\ne(0,0)\) everywhere.  Then
\(\Phi=(a,b)/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}:S^1\times[0,1]\to S^1\) is continuous and is
constant on \(\delta=0\).  On \(\delta=1/2\),
\[
\Phi(s+1/2,1/2)=-\Phi(s,1/2).
\]
If \(\psi:S^1\to S^1\) has \(\psi(s+1/2)=-\psi(s)\), then, after lifting to an
angle \(\theta\), the integer
\(\bigl(\theta(s+1/2)-\theta(s)-\pi\bigr)/(2\pi)\) is constant, so the degree
of \(\psi\) is odd.  But \(\Phi|_{\delta=1/2}\) is homotopic through
\(S^1\times[0,1/2]\) to the constant map \(\Phi|_{\delta=0}\), so its degree is
zero, a contradiction.  Hence \((a,b)=(0,0)\) somewhere, with
\(0<\delta<1\), so the two parameters are distinct.

At such a zero, \(u\cdot v=0\) for the two directions \(u,v\).  If the lines
are represented by \((u,p\times u)\) and \((v,q\times v)\), then
\[
b=u\cdot(q\times v)+v\cdot(p\times u)=(p-q)\cdot(u\times v).
\]
Thus, when \(u\perp v\), the condition \(b=0\) says the two nonparallel lines
are coplanar.  Nonparallel coplanar lines intersect.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Perpendicular intersecting leaves]\label{lem:perpleaves}
In \(M_\beta\) there are two distinct leaves whose image support lines under
\(F\) are perpendicular and intersect.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Inside each triangle take the cevians from the apex to the boundary edge and
call them leaves.  In the finite quotient triangulation, form a graph
\(\Lambda_M\) by taking one closed interval for the leaves of each triangle and
gluing endpoints corresponding to common transverse edges.  By
Lemma \ref{lem:facetoface}, every vertex has valence \(2\).

The graph is connected.  If \(C\) is a component and \(U_C\subset M_\beta\) is
the union of the corresponding leaves, then \(U_C\) is open: this is immediate
inside triangles, along boundary edges, and across transverse edges because the
two incident leaf intervals are glued.  At a boundary vertex, a small half-disk
meets finitely many incident triangle sectors; consecutive sectors share an
edge from the vertex, and all non-boundary shared edges are transverse, so all
incident triangles lie in the same component.  Thus the sets \(U_C\) are
disjoint open subsets covering the connected surface \(M_\beta\); hence there
is only one.  A finite connected graph with all vertices of valence \(2\) is a
circle, so \(\Lambda_M\cong S^1\).

The same openness argument upstairs gives a connected leaf graph
\(\Lambda_\Sigma\).  The action of \(G\) on leaves is free.  A lifted leaf has
endpoints \((x,0)\) and \((x+t,1)\).  If \(G^{2n}\) fixes it, then
\(2n\beta=0\).  If \(G^{2n+1}\) fixes it, then the two endpoint equations give
simultaneously \(t=(2n+1)\beta\) and \(t=-(2n+1)\beta\), impossible.  Hence
\(\Lambda_\Sigma\to\Lambda_M\) is a connected infinite covering of a circle,
so \(\Lambda_\Sigma\cong\R\).

Orient every lifted leaf from \(y=0\) to \(y=1\).  By
Lemma \ref{lem:cevian}, its image is a nondegenerate segment, hence determines
a continuous oriented support line along \(\Lambda_\Sigma\).  If \(\ell\) is a
leaf, then \(G\ell\), reoriented from bottom to top, has the same image segment
with the opposite orientation, because \(G\) swaps boundary components and
\(f\circ G=f\).  Applying Lemma \ref{lem:lines} to the compact interval in
\(\Lambda_\Sigma\) from \(\ell\) to \(G\ell\) gives two distinct quotient
leaves with perpendicular intersecting support lines.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[No \(\beta\le\sqrt3\) is realized]\label{prop:lower}
If \(\beta\) is realized, then \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(J\) be a lifted leaf with endpoints \((x,0)\) and \((x+t,1)\).  Its flat
length is \(\sqrt{1+t^2}\).  We first show
\[
|t|<\beta. \tag{1}
\]
If \(t=\beta\) or \(t=-\beta\), the endpoints are identified by \(G\) or
\(G^{-1}\), so their images coincide, contradicting Lemma \ref{lem:cevian}.  If
\(t>\beta\), translate so \(J\) has endpoints \((0,0)\), \((t,1)\).  Then
\(GJ\) has endpoints \((\beta,1)\), \((t+\beta,0)\), and the two segments meet
at height \((t+\beta)/(2t)\in(0,1)\).  Thus some distinct \(p,q\in J\) satisfy
\(p=Gq\), so \(f(p)=f(q)\), contradicting injectivity on the nondegenerate
image segment.  The case \(t<-\beta\) is identical using \(G^{-1}\).

Parametrize the boundary circle of \(M_\beta\) modulo \(2\beta\) by assigning
coordinate \(u\) to \((u,0)\) and coordinate \(v-\beta\) to \((v,1)\).  Hence
the boundary arcs between the endpoints of a leaf of span \(t\) have lengths
\[
\beta-t,\qquad \beta+t, \tag{2}
\]
both positive by (1).  Also every nonconstant boundary arc is strictly
shortened by \(F\): the quotient boundary is subdivided into finitely many
boundary edges, and on each such edge \(F\) has constant length factor
\(\lambda_e<1\); summing over subsegments gives
\[
\ell_F(\gamma)<\ell_0(\gamma). \tag{3}
\]

Choose the two leaves \(T,B\) from Lemma \ref{lem:perpleaves}, and let their
support lines meet perpendicularly at \(P\).  Since distinct leaves have
disjoint relative interiors and \(F\) is embedded, \(P\) cannot lie in the
relative interiors of both image segments.  Rename so that \(F(B)\) lies in a
closed ray from \(P\).  Let \(q\) be the endpoint of \(B\) farther from \(P\),
and put \(Q=F(q)\).  Then
\[
y:=\operatorname{dist}(Q,\operatorname{line}F(T))=|Q-P|\ge |F(B)|>|B|_0\ge1,
\]
so in fact
\[
y>1. \tag{4}
\]

Lift \(T\) with endpoints \((x,0)\), \((x+t,1)\).  Replacing this lift by its
\(G\)-translate changes \(t\) to \(-t\), so it interchanges the two lengths in
(2).  Choose the lift so that the boundary arc \(D\) containing \(q\) has
length \(\beta+t\); let the other arc be \(H\), of length \(\beta-t\).  Let
\(A,C\) be the endpoints of \(F(T)\), and set
\[
L=|A-C|=|F(T)|>\sqrt{1+t^2}. \tag{5}
\]
The arc \(H\) connects \(A\) to \(C\), so by (3),
\[
\beta-t=\ell_0(H)>\ell_F(H)\ge L>\sqrt{1+t^2},
\]
hence
\[
\beta>\sqrt{1+t^2}+t. \tag{6}
\]
The arc \(D\) connects \(A\) to \(C\) and passes through \(Q\).  Therefore
\(\ell_F(D)\ge |A-Q|+|Q-C|\).  Among points at distance \(y\) from the line
\(AC\), the sum of distances to \(A\) and \(C\) is minimized when the
projection is the midpoint of \(AC\), giving
\[
|A-Q|+|Q-C|\ge \sqrt{L^2+4y^2}.
\]
Using (4) and (5),
\[
\ell_F(D)>\sqrt{5+t^2}.
\]
By (3),
\[
\beta+t=\ell_0(D)>\ell_F(D)>\sqrt{5+t^2},
\]
so
\[
\beta>\sqrt{5+t^2}-t. \tag{7}
\]
Combining (6) and (7),
\[
\beta>
\max\{\sqrt{1+t^2}+t,\ \sqrt{5+t^2}-t\}.
\]
For every real \(t\), this maximum is at least \(\sqrt3\).  Indeed, if both
terms were \(<\sqrt3\), then squaring
\(\sqrt{1+t^2}+t<\sqrt3\) gives \(t<1/\sqrt3\), while squaring
\(\sqrt{5+t^2}-t<\sqrt3\) gives \(t>1/\sqrt3\), a contradiction.  Hence
\(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

\section{The upper bound}

We quote the classical Sadowsky--Wunderlich construction in the precise form
needed.

\begin{theorem}[Sadowsky--Wunderlich input]\label{thm:sadowsky}
For every \(\mu>\sqrt3\), there is a map
\(E_\mu:\R\times[0,1]\to\R^3\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(E_\mu(X+\mu,1-Y)=E_\mu(X,Y)\);
\item the induced quotient M\"obius band is embedded;
\item the quotient surface is \(C^{1,1}\), piecewise \(C^\infty\), and
developable;
\item it is foliated by full-width straight rulings, and \(E_\mu\) maps each
ruling affinely and isometrically to a segment;
\item the boundary lifts are parametrized by arclength in the \(X\)-coordinate;
\item the construction remains embedded on a slightly wider strip.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
This is the three-cylinder construction of Sadowsky, with Wunderlich's
analysis of the developable M\"obius band; see \cite{Sad30,Wun62}.  In that
construction the band consists of three planar pieces and three cylindrical
pieces joined along generators with matching tangent planes, and the bending is
isometric.  The standard separation computation gives maximum half-width
\[
b_{\max}=\frac{\mu}{2\sqrt3}-\frac{3\pi d}{4}
\]
for auxiliary cylinder diameter \(d>0\).  Since \(\mu>\sqrt3\), choosing
\(0<d<2(\mu-\sqrt3)/(3\pi\sqrt3)\) gives \(b_{\max}>1/2\), hence a width-one
embedded strip, and the strict inequality gives the slightly wider embedded
extension.
\end{proof}

For \(L,c>0\), write
\[
H_{L,c}(X,Y)=(X+L,c-Y)\qquad\text{on }\R\times[0,c].
\]

\begin{lemma}[Invariant PL approximation]\label{lem:PL}
Let \(E:\R\times[0,c]\to\R^3\) be a scaled Sadowsky band invariant under
\(H_{L,c}\), with full-width rulings
\[
R_x=[(x,0),(h(x),c)].
\]
Fix \(x_0\), put \(\phi(x)=h(x)+L\), and set
\[
S=\max_{x\in[x_0,\phi(x_0)]}|h(x)-x|.
\]
For every \(D>S\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are an
\(H_{L,c}\)-invariant clean triangulation \(\mathcal T_0\) and an
\(H_{L,c}\)-invariant PL map \(F_0\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(F_0(P)=F_0(Q)\) iff \(P=H_{L,c}^k(Q)\) for some \(k\in\Z\);
\item every boundary edge is nonexpanded;
\item every transverse edge \(PQ\) satisfies
\[
|F_0(P)-F_0(Q)|\ge |P-Q|-\varepsilon;
\]
\item every transverse edge has horizontal span \(<D\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The noncrossing full-width rulings imply that \(h\) is a strictly increasing
homeomorphism.  The map \(H=H_{L,c}\) sends \(R_x\) to
\(R_{\phi(x)}\), so
\[
h(\phi(x))=x+L,\qquad \phi^2(x)=x+2L. \tag{8}
\]
Also
\[
|h(x)-x|<L. \tag{9}
\]
If \(h(x)-x=L\), the endpoints of \(R_x\) are identified by \(H\), contradicting
the isometric nondegenerate image of \(R_x\).  If \(h(x)-x>L\), then \(R_x\)
meets \(H(R_x)\) in the interior of the strip; hence two distinct points of
\(R_x\) have the same image under \(E\), again impossible.  The case
\(h(x)-x<-L\) follows using \(H^{-1}\).  Thus \(\phi(x)>x\).

Choose \(\rho>0\) with \(S+\rho<D\) and \(2\rho<\varepsilon\).  Choose a
partition
\[
x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=\phi(x_0)
\]
so fine that \(x_{i+1}-x_i<\rho\), \(h(x_{i+1})-h(x_i)<\rho\), all seams of the
piecewise smooth Sadowsky band occur among the rulings \(R_{x_i}\), and the
embeddedness condition proved below holds.  Extend by \(x_{i+N}=\phi(x_i)\).
Then \(x_{i+2N}=x_i+2L\).  Let
\[
B_i=(x_i,0),\qquad T_i=(h(x_i),c).
\]
The quadrilaterals \(B_iB_{i+1}T_{i+1}T_i\) tile the strip.  For
\(0\le i<N\), triangulate by the diagonal \(B_iT_{i+1}\), and extend
\(H\)-invariantly.  Define \(F_0\) on vertices by \(F_0(B_i)=E(B_i)\),
\(F_0(T_i)=E(T_i)\), and extend affinely on triangles.  Then \(F_0\) is
\(H\)-invariant.

Boundary edges are nonexpanded because their images are chords of boundary
arcs parametrized by arclength.  A ruling edge is mapped isometrically.  For a
diagonal \(B_iT_{i+1}\), set
\(d=|B_i-T_{i+1}|\) and \(r=|B_i-T_i|\).  Since
\(|T_i-T_{i+1}|<\rho\), one has \(|d-r|<\rho\), and
\[
|F_0(B_i)-F_0(T_{i+1})|
\ge |E(B_i)-E(T_i)|-|E(T_i)-E(T_{i+1})|
>r-\rho>d-2\rho>d-\varepsilon.
\]
The other diagonal type is identical, using \(x_{i+1}-x_i<\rho\).  By (8),
the absolute span \(|h(x)-x|\) is preserved under \(\phi\), so all ruling spans
are at most \(S\); diagonal spans are \(<S+\rho<D\).

It remains to justify the promised embeddedness for sufficiently fine
partition.  Let
\(N=(\R\times[0,c])/\langle H\rangle\).  By Theorem \ref{thm:sadowsky}, \(E\)
extends to a slightly wider compact embedded \(C^{1,1}\) surface
\(\widehat N\), so there is a tubular neighborhood \(U\) with nearest-point
projection \(\pi:U\to \widehat E(\widehat N)\).  The secant PL maps converge
uniformly to \(E\); because \(E\) is affine on rulings, \(C^{1,1}\) on each
piece, and the seams are included among the ruling edges with matching tangent
planes, the maps
\[
\Psi=\widehat E^{-1}\circ\pi\circ F_0:N\to\widehat N
\]
converge to the inclusion \(N\hookrightarrow\widehat N\) in \(C^1\) on each
piece.

For sufficiently small \(C^1\)-error, \(\Psi\) is injective.  Choose finitely
many coordinate disks with convex coordinate images and \(\delta>0\) so that
points of \(N\) at distance \(<\delta\) lie in a common disk.  In such a disk,
if the derivative of \(\Psi\) differs from the identity by \(<1/2\), then
integration along the coordinate segment gives
\(|\Psi(p)-\Psi(q)|\ge \frac12|p-q|\).  For pairs with distance \(\ge\delta\),
compactness and injectivity of the inclusion give a positive minimum
separation; sufficiently small \(C^0\)-error preserves this separation.  Hence
\(\Psi\) is injective.  If the quotient map induced by \(F_0\) identified two
points, then \(\Psi\) would identify them, contradiction.  Thus the quotient
PL map is embedded, which is equivalent to assertion (1) after lifting.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized]\label{prop:upper}
For every \(\beta>\sqrt3\), there is a realization of \(\beta\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\mu\) with \(\sqrt3<\mu<\beta\), and take the Sadowsky band
\(E_\mu\).  Let \(S_\mu=\max |h(x)-x|\) over one fundamental interval of
rulings, and choose \(D_\mu>S_\mu\).  Choose \(a<1\), close to \(1\), with
\(a>\mu/\beta\), and set
\[
c=\frac{a\beta}{\mu},\qquad L=a\beta.
\]
Then \(c>1\) and \(L=c\mu\).  Scale \(E_\mu\) by \(c\), giving a width-\(c\),
length-\(L\) band invariant under \(H_{L,c}\).  Its span bound scales to
\(cS_\mu\).

Choose \(a\) close enough to \(1\) so that
\[
m:=\min_{0\le u\le D_\mu}
\left(c\sqrt{1+u^2}-\sqrt{\left(\frac{cu}{a}\right)^2+1}\right)>0. \tag{10}
\]
This is possible because at \(a=1\) one has \(c=\beta/\mu>1\), and
\(c\sqrt{1+u^2}>\sqrt{c^2u^2+1}\) on the compact interval
\([0,D_\mu]\).  Choose \(0<\varepsilon<m\) and apply Lemma \ref{lem:PL} to the
scaled band with \(D=cD_\mu\).  We get \(\mathcal T_0\) and \(F_0\).

Define
\[
A:\Sigma\to\R\times[0,c],\qquad A(x,y)=(ax,cy).
\]
Because \(L=a\beta\),
\[
A(G_\beta(x,y))=(ax+a\beta,c-cy)=H_{L,c}(A(x,y)).
\]
Thus \(A\) conjugates \(G_\beta\) to \(H_{L,c}\).  Put
\[
f=F_0\circ A,\qquad \mathcal T=A^{-1}(\mathcal T_0).
\]
Then \(\mathcal T\) is a countable locally finite \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean
triangulation, and \(f\) is affine on every triangle.

If \(pq\) is a boundary edge, then
\[
|f(p)-f(q)|\le |A p-A q|=a|p-q|<|p-q|.
\]
If \(pq\) is a transverse edge, let \(s\) be the horizontal span of
\(A p\,A q\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:PL}, \(s<cD_\mu\); write \(s=cu\) with
\(0\le u<D_\mu\).  Then
\[
|Ap-Aq|=c\sqrt{1+u^2},\qquad
|p-q|=\sqrt{\left(\frac{cu}{a}\right)^2+1}.
\]
Using Lemma \ref{lem:PL} and \(\varepsilon<m\), (10) gives
\[
|f(p)-f(q)|
\ge |Ap-Aq|-\varepsilon
> |p-q|.
\]
Thus \(f\) is a squeeze map on every triangle.  Finally, for all
\(p,q\in\Sigma\),
\[
f(p)=f(q)
\Longleftrightarrow
F_0(Ap)=F_0(Aq)
\Longleftrightarrow
Ap=H_{L,c}^k(Aq)\text{ for some }k\in\Z
\Longleftrightarrow
p=G_\beta^k(q)\text{ for some }k\in\Z.
\]
Therefore \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:strong}]
Proposition \ref{prop:lower} shows that every realized number is \(>\sqrt3\).
Proposition \ref{prop:upper} shows that every number \(>\sqrt3\) is realized.
Hence the realized numbers are exactly \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:headline}]
By Theorem \ref{thm:strong}, the set of realized numbers is
\((\sqrt3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The AI got the problem correct. This is a working proof, with all essential details included and perhaps even some extra details. I especially appreciated the excellent proof overview at the top of the solution.

The proof in the first half works well, and it follows a clear outline. All details seem correct. Sometimes, as in Lemma 5 and 6, the proof did not seem to be the most efficient or transparent.

The proof in the second half seems to work, though I found the exposition somewhat hard to follow. The AI supplies lots of very fine-scale details for things which fairly obviously work. To give you a feel for this, if you have a smooth compact embedded loop in the plane, it is clear that a sufficiently fine polygonal approximation, with points on the loop, will be embedded. If you include all kinds of estimates for this, it mostly clouds the picture. Something similar is going on here, one dimension up. 

## Novelty.

Let me first discuss the context for the problem and then describe how the AI did. The problem is based on my solution of the Halpern-Weaver Conjecture, a result which asks for the infimal
aspect ratio needed for a smooth and isometric embedding of a flat Moebius band into $\R^3$. My paper was published in the {\it Annals\/} in January, 2025 and there are also some of accounts of the result in the popular media. The problem the AI considered is the same problem in a different category of maps, piecewise linear maps with a certain side condition called squeezing. 

The first half of the proof really gave me vertigo! The AI supplied essentially all the arguments in my paper, though always in a kind of disguised or transmuted form. For instance, the two functions used in Lemma 6 are equivalent to the ones used in my paper, but they are presented in very different notation and you need an auxiliary vector identity to see the equivalence. For a while I wondered whether the AI had (amazingly) come up with its own proof without looking at my paper, but then I noticed that it used the same letters $T,B,D,H$ for the four main objects in the proof. (I used these letters because T stands for ``top'' and B stands for ``bottom'' and D stands for ``diagonal'' and H stands for ''horizontal''. The AI used these specific letters without explanation.) This was the only ``tell'' that the AI had read my paper. Once I realized this, I was annoyed.
So, the first half is novel in some fine-scale details but overall derived from my paper.

The second half is not derived from my paper, and it essentially gives a nuts-and-bolts proof involving smooth approximation of an already known smooth construction that goes back to Michael Sadowsky in 1930. I didn't really like this proof that much. It uses a black box, Sadowsky's result, and then grinds away with PL approximation until it wins. So, this half is sort of novel, but it is what you would do if you did not really have any artistic sense.
reviews.recommendation:
I would recommend that this paper is publishable with moderate revisions. (If I have to decide between ''major'' and ''minor'' I would go with ''major'', but I am kind of on the fence about it.)
The most important complaint I have is that the AI did not acknowledge my paper at all, even though it clearly read it. Minor complaints about the first half: As I mentioned above, I thought that Lemmas 5 and 6 were not that efficient. Lemma 5 uses calculus in a way that suppresses the main calculation; a swift linear algebra argument would be better here. Lemma 6 uses a very opaque form of my functions. A more geometrically transparent formulation of the second one would save the reader a lot of head scratching.

I think that the second half should be reworked. The reduction of the PL case to an already known result in the smooth case is certainly acceptable for a proof, though if you are an editor with some mathematical taste you would probably ask for a better argument. One way the argument could be better is if it gave an explicit and self-contained contruction. The other way it would be better is if it did the PL approximation in a cleaner way, with the ideas emphasized rather than the calculations. (To be fair, the overview at the top of the solution does a good job of giving the high level strategy for this.)

The last thing I want to say is that I would be tempted to fail a student on an exam for clearly copying ideas from an external source without acknowleding this. In a human, this lack of idea-acknowledgement would seem like an ethical failing. I don't know what to say about how it reflects on an AI. But, anyway, if I was in a bad mood I might reject the paper on these kinds of grounds.
