\subsection{The upper bound}

We quote the classical Sadowsky--Wunderlich construction in the precise form
needed.

\begin{theorem}[Sadowsky--Wunderlich input]\label{thm:sadowsky}
For every \(\mu>\sqrt3\), there is a map
\(E_\mu:\R\times[0,1]\to\R^3\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(E_\mu(X+\mu,1-Y)=E_\mu(X,Y)\);
\item the induced quotient M\"obius band is embedded;
\item the quotient surface is \(C^{1,1}\), piecewise \(C^\infty\), and
developable;
\item it is foliated by full-width straight rulings, and \(E_\mu\) maps each
ruling affinely and isometrically to a segment;
\item the boundary lifts are parametrized by arclength in the \(X\)-coordinate;
\item the construction remains embedded on a slightly wider strip.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
This is the three-cylinder construction of Sadowsky, with Wunderlich's
analysis of the developable M\"obius band; see \cite{Sad30,Wun62}.  In that
construction the band consists of three planar pieces and three cylindrical
pieces joined along generators with matching tangent planes, and the bending is
isometric.  The standard separation computation gives maximum half-width
\[
b_{\max}=\frac{\mu}{2\sqrt3}-\frac{3\pi d}{4}
\]
for auxiliary cylinder diameter \(d>0\).  Since \(\mu>\sqrt3\), choosing
\(0<d<2(\mu-\sqrt3)/(3\pi\sqrt3)\) gives \(b_{\max}>1/2\), hence a width-one
embedded strip, and the strict inequality gives the slightly wider embedded
extension.
\end{proof}

For \(L,c>0\), write
\[
H_{L,c}(X,Y)=(X+L,c-Y)\qquad\text{on }\R\times[0,c].
\]

\begin{lemma}[Invariant PL approximation]\label{lem:PL}
Let \(E:\R\times[0,c]\to\R^3\) be a scaled Sadowsky band invariant under
\(H_{L,c}\), with full-width rulings
\[
R_x=[(x,0),(h(x),c)].
\]
Fix \(x_0\), put \(\phi(x)=h(x)+L\), and set
\[
S=\max_{x\in[x_0,\phi(x_0)]}|h(x)-x|.
\]
For every \(D>S\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there are an
\(H_{L,c}\)-invariant clean triangulation \(\mathcal T_0\) and an
\(H_{L,c}\)-invariant PL map \(F_0\) such that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \(F_0(P)=F_0(Q)\) iff \(P=H_{L,c}^k(Q)\) for some \(k\in\Z\);
\item every boundary edge is nonexpanded;
\item every transverse edge \(PQ\) satisfies
\[
|F_0(P)-F_0(Q)|\ge |P-Q|-\varepsilon;
\]
\item every transverse edge has horizontal span \(<D\).
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The noncrossing full-width rulings imply that \(h\) is a strictly increasing
homeomorphism.  The map \(H=H_{L,c}\) sends \(R_x\) to
\(R_{\phi(x)}\), so
\[
h(\phi(x))=x+L,\qquad \phi^2(x)=x+2L. \tag{8}
\]
Also
\[
|h(x)-x|<L. \tag{9}
\]
If \(h(x)-x=L\), the endpoints of \(R_x\) are identified by \(H\), contradicting
the isometric nondegenerate image of \(R_x\).  If \(h(x)-x>L\), then \(R_x\)
meets \(H(R_x)\) in the interior of the strip; hence two distinct points of
\(R_x\) have the same image under \(E\), again impossible.  The case
\(h(x)-x<-L\) follows using \(H^{-1}\).  Thus \(\phi(x)>x\).

Choose \(\rho>0\) with \(S+\rho<D\) and \(2\rho<\varepsilon\).  Choose a
partition
\[
x_0<x_1<\cdots<x_N=\phi(x_0)
\]
so fine that \(x_{i+1}-x_i<\rho\), \(h(x_{i+1})-h(x_i)<\rho\), all seams of the
piecewise smooth Sadowsky band occur among the rulings \(R_{x_i}\), and the
embeddedness condition proved below holds.  Extend by \(x_{i+N}=\phi(x_i)\).
Then \(x_{i+2N}=x_i+2L\).  Let
\[
B_i=(x_i,0),\qquad T_i=(h(x_i),c).
\]
The quadrilaterals \(B_iB_{i+1}T_{i+1}T_i\) tile the strip.  For
\(0\le i<N\), triangulate by the diagonal \(B_iT_{i+1}\), and extend
\(H\)-invariantly.  Define \(F_0\) on vertices by \(F_0(B_i)=E(B_i)\),
\(F_0(T_i)=E(T_i)\), and extend affinely on triangles.  Then \(F_0\) is
\(H\)-invariant.

Boundary edges are nonexpanded because their images are chords of boundary
arcs parametrized by arclength.  A ruling edge is mapped isometrically.  For a
diagonal \(B_iT_{i+1}\), set
\(d=|B_i-T_{i+1}|\) and \(r=|B_i-T_i|\).  Since
\(|T_i-T_{i+1}|<\rho\), one has \(|d-r|<\rho\), and
\[
|F_0(B_i)-F_0(T_{i+1})|
\ge |E(B_i)-E(T_i)|-|E(T_i)-E(T_{i+1})|
>r-\rho>d-2\rho>d-\varepsilon.
\]
The other diagonal type is identical, using \(x_{i+1}-x_i<\rho\).  By (8),
the absolute span \(|h(x)-x|\) is preserved under \(\phi\), so all ruling spans
are at most \(S\); diagonal spans are \(<S+\rho<D\).

It remains to justify the promised embeddedness for sufficiently fine
partition.  Let
\(N=(\R\times[0,c])/\langle H\rangle\).  By Theorem \ref{thm:sadowsky}, \(E\)
extends to a slightly wider compact embedded \(C^{1,1}\) surface
\(\widehat N\), so there is a tubular neighborhood \(U\) with nearest-point
projection \(\pi:U\to \widehat E(\widehat N)\).  The secant PL maps converge
uniformly to \(E\); because \(E\) is affine on rulings, \(C^{1,1}\) on each
piece, and the seams are included among the ruling edges with matching tangent
planes, the maps
\[
\Psi=\widehat E^{-1}\circ\pi\circ F_0:N\to\widehat N
\]
converge to the inclusion \(N\hookrightarrow\widehat N\) in \(C^1\) on each
piece.

For sufficiently small \(C^1\)-error, \(\Psi\) is injective.  Choose finitely
many coordinate disks with convex coordinate images and \(\delta>0\) so that
points of \(N\) at distance \(<\delta\) lie in a common disk.  In such a disk,
if the derivative of \(\Psi\) differs from the identity by \(<1/2\), then
integration along the coordinate segment gives
\(|\Psi(p)-\Psi(q)|\ge \frac12|p-q|\).  For pairs with distance \(\ge\delta\),
compactness and injectivity of the inclusion give a positive minimum
separation; sufficiently small \(C^0\)-error preserves this separation.  Hence
\(\Psi\) is injective.  If the quotient map induced by \(F_0\) identified two
points, then \(\Psi\) would identify them, contradiction.  Thus the quotient
PL map is embedded, which is equivalent to assertion (1) after lifting.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized]\label{prop:upper}
For every \(\beta>\sqrt3\), there is a realization of \(\beta\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Choose \(\mu\) with \(\sqrt3<\mu<\beta\), and take the Sadowsky band
\(E_\mu\).  Let \(S_\mu=\max |h(x)-x|\) over one fundamental interval of
rulings, and choose \(D_\mu>S_\mu\).  Choose \(a<1\), close to \(1\), with
\(a>\mu/\beta\), and set
\[
c=\frac{a\beta}{\mu},\qquad L=a\beta.
\]
Then \(c>1\) and \(L=c\mu\).  Scale \(E_\mu\) by \(c\), giving a width-\(c\),
length-\(L\) band invariant under \(H_{L,c}\).  Its span bound scales to
\(cS_\mu\).

Choose \(a\) close enough to \(1\) so that
\[
m:=\min_{0\le u\le D_\mu}
\left(c\sqrt{1+u^2}-\sqrt{\left(\frac{cu}{a}\right)^2+1}\right)>0. \tag{10}
\]
This is possible because at \(a=1\) one has \(c=\beta/\mu>1\), and
\(c\sqrt{1+u^2}>\sqrt{c^2u^2+1}\) on the compact interval
\([0,D_\mu]\).  Choose \(0<\varepsilon<m\) and apply Lemma \ref{lem:PL} to the
scaled band with \(D=cD_\mu\).  We get \(\mathcal T_0\) and \(F_0\).

Define
\[
A:\Sigma\to\R\times[0,c],\qquad A(x,y)=(ax,cy).
\]
Because \(L=a\beta\),
\[
A(G_\beta(x,y))=(ax+a\beta,c-cy)=H_{L,c}(A(x,y)).
\]
Thus \(A\) conjugates \(G_\beta\) to \(H_{L,c}\).  Put
\[
f=F_0\circ A,\qquad \mathcal T=A^{-1}(\mathcal T_0).
\]
Then \(\mathcal T\) is a countable locally finite \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean
triangulation, and \(f\) is affine on every triangle.

If \(pq\) is a boundary edge, then
\[
|f(p)-f(q)|\le |A p-A q|=a|p-q|<|p-q|.
\]
If \(pq\) is a transverse edge, let \(s\) be the horizontal span of
\(A p\,A q\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:PL}, \(s<cD_\mu\); write \(s=cu\) with
\(0\le u<D_\mu\).  Then
\[
|Ap-Aq|=c\sqrt{1+u^2},\qquad
|p-q|=\sqrt{\left(\frac{cu}{a}\right)^2+1}.
\]
Using Lemma \ref{lem:PL} and \(\varepsilon<m\), (10) gives
\[
|f(p)-f(q)|
\ge |Ap-Aq|-\varepsilon
> |p-q|.
\]
Thus \(f\) is a squeeze map on every triangle.  Finally, for all
\(p,q\in\Sigma\),
\[
f(p)=f(q)
\Longleftrightarrow
F_0(Ap)=F_0(Aq)
\Longleftrightarrow
Ap=H_{L,c}^k(Aq)\text{ for some }k\in\Z
\Longleftrightarrow
p=G_\beta^k(q)\text{ for some }k\in\Z.
\]
Therefore \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:strong}]
Proposition \ref{prop:lower} shows that every realized number is \(>\sqrt3\).
Proposition \ref{prop:upper} shows that every number \(>\sqrt3\) is realized.
Hence the realized numbers are exactly \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:headline}]
By Theorem \ref{thm:strong}, the set of realized numbers is
\((\sqrt3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

\begin{abstract}
We prove the stronger statement that a number \(\beta>0\) is realized in the sense of the question if and only if \(\beta>\sqrt 3\).  Hence the infimum of the set of realized numbers is \(\sqrt 3\).
\end{abstract}

\section{Preliminaries}

Let
\[
M_\beta=\Sigma/\langle G_\beta\rangle .
\]
Thus \(M_\beta\) is the flat Mobius band obtained from the rectangle
\([0,\beta]\times[0,1]\) by identifying \((0,y)\sim(\beta,1-y)\).  Its boundary is a circle of flat length \(2\beta\).  We use the boundary coordinate
\[
s(x,0)=x\pmod {2\beta},\qquad s(x,1)=x+\beta\pmod {2\beta}.
\]

\begin{lemma}[quotient and boundary contraction]
Suppose \(\beta\) is realized.  Then the map \(f\) descends to a topological embedding
\[
\bar f:M_\beta\longrightarrow \R^3 .
\]
Moreover, the \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation descends to a finite clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\), and every nondegenerate boundary arc \(A\subset \partial M_\beta\) satisfies
\[
\len(\bar f(A))<\len_0(A),
\]
where \(\len_0\) denotes flat boundary length.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Condition (2) gives \(f\circ G_\beta=f\), so \(f\) descends to \(\bar f\).  The same condition says precisely that \(\bar f\) is injective.  Since \(M_\beta\) is compact and \(\R^3\) is Hausdorff, \(\bar f\) is an embedding.

A compact fundamental domain in \(\Sigma\) meets only finitely many triangles by local finiteness, so only finitely many \(G_\beta\)-orbits of triangles occur.  Thus the quotient triangulation is finite.

Finally, on each boundary edge of the triangulation, \(f\) is affine and strictly shortens that edge.  Hence it strictly shortens every subsegment of every boundary edge.  Since every boundary arc is a finite union of such subsegments, its image has strictly smaller length.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[the squeeze cone]
Let \(\tau\) be a clean triangle with boundary edge \(AB\) and opposite vertex \(C\).  If an affine map \(L:\tau\to \R^3\) decreases the length of \(AB\) and increases the lengths of \(AC\) and \(BC\), then \(L\) increases the length of every segment joining \(C\) to a point of \(AB\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write \(u=C-A\), \(v=C-B\), so \(u-v=B-A\).  Let
\[
q(w)=|Lw|^2-|w|^2 .
\]
The hypotheses are
\[
q(u)>0,\qquad q(v)>0,\qquad q(u-v)<0.
\]
For \(0\le t\le 1\),
\[
q((1-t)u+tv)
=(1-t)q(u)+tq(v)-t(1-t)q(u-v)>0.
\]
Thus every cevian from \(C\) to the base \(AB\) is strictly lengthened.
\end{proof}

\section{The canonical ruling and a \(T\)-pattern}

For every clean triangle, foliate it by the straight segments joining the vertex opposite the boundary edge to points of the boundary edge.  Adjacent clean triangles share a nonboundary edge, and that edge is one of the leaves in both triangles.  Therefore these local foliations glue.

\begin{lemma}[canonical ruling]
The quotient clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\) carries a continuous circle-family \(\mathcal L=\{L_t\}_{t\in S^1}\) of straight clean segments with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Each \(L_t\) is contained in a single clean triangle and joins the two boundary components in the universal cover.
\item The relative interiors of distinct leaves are disjoint and the leaves cover \(M_\beta\).
\item The image \(\bar f(L_t)\) is a straight segment in \(\R^3\), and
\[
|\bar f(L_t)|>|L_t|_0\ge 1.
\]
\item A continuous orientation of the leaves reverses after one circuit of the parameter circle.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal T\) be the finite clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Form the dual graph whose vertices are triangles and whose edges correspond to shared nonboundary edges.  Every triangle has exactly two nonboundary edges, and every nonboundary edge is shared by two triangles, so the dual graph is \(2\)-regular.  It is connected: at each boundary vertex the link is an interval, so the triangles incident to that vertex are connected through shared nonboundary edges; since the triangulation is connected, the dual graph is connected.  Hence the dual graph is a single cycle.

On a triangle \(\tau\), the family of cevians from the opposite vertex to the boundary edge is parametrized by an interval; its two endpoint leaves are the two nonboundary edges of \(\tau\).  Gluing these intervals according to the cyclic dual graph gives a parameter circle \(S^1\).  This proves the existence and continuity of the family \(\{L_t\}\), and the relative interiors are plainly disjoint.

Each leaf is contained in a clean triangle, and by the preceding squeeze-cone lemma its image is strictly longer than its flat length.  Since every clean segment crosses from \(y=0\) to \(y=1\) in the universal cover, its flat length is at least \(1\).

Finally, the leaf family is an interval-bundle structure on the Mobius band away from finitely many boundary vertices.  Since \(M_\beta\) is the nontrivial \(I\)-bundle over a circle, the orientation line of the fibers is nontrivial.  Equivalently, in the universal cover, going once around the leaf circle applies the deck transformation \(G_\beta\), which exchanges the two boundary components.  Hence any continuous orientation of the leaves is reversed after one circuit.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\(T\)-pattern]
There are two distinct leaves \(L_s,L_t\) such that the two straight segments
\[
\bar f(L_s),\qquad \bar f(L_t)
\]
lie in perpendicular coplanar lines.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Lift the parameter circle to \(\R\).  Choose continuously oriented unit direction vectors \(u(r)\) for the image segments and let \(m(r)\) denote their midpoints.  By the orientation-reversal property,
\[
u(r+2\pi)=-u(r),\qquad m(r+2\pi)=m(r).
\]

Let
\[
\Upsilon=\{(r,s): r<s<r+2\pi\}/(r,s)\sim(r+2\pi,s+2\pi).
\]
Compactify \(\Upsilon\) by adding two points: \(\partial_+\), corresponding to \(s\to r\), and \(\partial_-\), corresponding to \(s\to r+2\pi\).  This compactification is a \(2\)-sphere, and the swap involution
\[
(r,s)\longmapsto (s,r+2\pi)
\]
extends to the antipodal map on that sphere.

Define
\[
F(r,s)=\left(u(r)\cdot u(s),\ (m(r)-m(s))\cdot (u(r)\times u(s))\right).
\]
Then \(F\) extends continuously to the compactification with
\[
F(\partial_+)=(1,0),\qquad F(\partial_-)=(-1,0),
\]
and satisfies
\[
F(s,r+2\pi)=-F(r,s).
\]
By the Borsuk--Ulam theorem, \(F\) has a zero.  At such a zero, the two direction vectors are perpendicular, and the vector joining the midpoints is orthogonal to the normal \(u(r)\times u(s)\).  Therefore the two supporting lines are coplanar.  This gives the desired pair of leaves.
\end{proof}

\section{The lower bound}

\begin{lemma}[geometry of a squeezed \(T\)-pattern]
If \(\beta\) is realized, then \(\beta>\sqrt 3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(T\) and \(B\) be the two leaves supplied by the preceding lemma.  Write
\[
T^*=\bar f(T),\qquad B^*=\bar f(B).
\]
Their supporting lines are perpendicular and coplanar.  Interchange \(T\) and \(B\), if necessary, so that the line supporting \(T^*\) does not meet the relative interior of \(B^*\).  Otherwise the two embedded segments would have an interior intersection.

Let \(u\) be the endpoint of \(B\) whose image is farthest from the line supporting \(T^*\).  Since \(B^*\) is perpendicular to that line and the line does not meet the relative interior of \(B^*\), the distance \(h\) from \(\bar f(u)\) to the line supporting \(T^*\) satisfies
\[
h\ge |B^*|>|B|_0\ge 1.
\]

Let the endpoints of \(T\) divide \(\partial M_\beta\) into two boundary arcs \(H\) and \(D\), with \(u\in D\).  Choose the signed horizontal displacement \(t\) of \(T\) so that
\[
\len_0(H)=\beta-t,\qquad \len_0(D)=\beta+t.
\]
Then
\[
|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Because \(T\) is a leaf, it is lengthened:
\[
|T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Since \(H\) is a boundary path joining the endpoints of \(T\),
\[
\sqrt{1+t^2}<|T^*|\le \len(\bar f(H))<\beta-t. \tag{1}
\]

Now consider the planar triangle \(\Delta\) whose base is \(T^*\) and whose third vertex is \(\bar f(u)\).  Its base has length \(>|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}\), and its height is \(h>1\).  If \(\vee\) denotes the union of the two nonbase sides of \(\Delta\), the elementary reflection argument gives
\[
\len(\vee)>\sqrt{5+t^2}.
\]
Indeed, among all triangles with base length \(b\) and height \(h\), the sum of the two nonbase sides is at least \(\sqrt{b^2+4h^2}\).

The boundary arc \(D\) runs from one endpoint of \(T\) to the other through \(u\).  Hence the two sides of \(\vee\) are no longer than the two corresponding subarcs of \(\bar f(D)\).  Therefore
\[
\sqrt{5+t^2}<\len(\vee)\le \len(\bar f(D))<\beta+t. \tag{2}
\]
From (1) and (2),
\[
2\beta>\alpha(t):=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},
\]
and also
\[
2\beta>\gamma(t):=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t.
\]
Let \(t_0=1/\sqrt3\).  Then
\[
\alpha(t_0)=\gamma(t_0)=2\sqrt3.
\]
Moreover, \(\alpha\) is increasing for \(t>0\), and \(\gamma\) is strictly decreasing on \(\R\).  Thus for every real \(t\),
\[
\max\{\alpha(t),\gamma(t)\}\ge 2\sqrt3.
\]
Consequently \(2\beta>2\sqrt3\), so \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

\section{Realization for every \(\beta>\sqrt3\)}

We use the classical existence theorem for paper Mobius bands: for every width \(w>0\) and every length \(\lambda\) with \(\lambda/w>\sqrt3\), there exists a smooth embedded isometric Mobius band of width \(w\) and length \(\lambda\), obtained by smoothing the triangular Mobius band.  Moreover, it has a continuous ruling by straight bends whose preimages are straight segments joining the two boundary components.  This is the standard Sadowsky--Wunderlich construction; see Sadowsky \cite{Sadowsky}, the translation by Hinz--Fried \cite{HinzFried}, and the modern discussion in Schwartz \cite{Schwartz}.

\begin{proposition}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  Choose numbers \(w,\lambda\) such that
\[
1<w,\qquad \sqrt3\,w<\lambda<\beta,\qquad
w^2-1>\beta^2-\lambda^2.
\]
This is possible by taking \(\lambda\) sufficiently close to \(\beta\) and then \(w>1\) sufficiently close to \(1\).

Let \(\rho=\lambda/\beta<1\).  Let
\[
P_{\lambda,w}=([0,\lambda]\times[0,w])/(0,y)\sim(\lambda,w-y),
\]
and let
\[
I:P_{\lambda,w}\longrightarrow \R^3
\]
be a smooth embedded paper Mobius band with a ruling by straight bends.  Define
\[
A:M_\beta\longrightarrow P_{\lambda,w},\qquad A[x,y]=[\rho x,wy].
\]
This is well-defined because
\[
A(x+\beta,1-y)=(\rho x+\lambda,w-wy),
\]
which is the defining Mobius identification in \(P_{\lambda,w}\).  Put
\[
F=I\circ A:M_\beta\longrightarrow \R^3.
\]
Then \(F\) is an embedding.

Let \(\{C_s\}_{s\in S^1}\) be the pulled-back bend ruling on \(M_\beta\).  Each \(C_s\) is a clean straight segment.  If \(C_s\) has signed horizontal displacement \(d\), with \(|d|\le \beta\), then
\[
|F(C_s)|^2=\rho^2d^2+w^2.
\]
Hence
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2
=\rho^2d^2+w^2-(d^2+1)
=(w^2-1)-(1-\rho^2)d^2.
\]
Since \(|d|\le\beta\),
\[
(1-\rho^2)d^2\le (1-\rho^2)\beta^2=\beta^2-\lambda^2,
\]
so
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2\ge w^2-1-(\beta^2-\lambda^2)>0. \tag{3}
\]
Thus every pulled-back bend is strictly lengthened by \(F\).

Choose finitely many bends \(C_{s_0},\dots,C_{s_{N-1}}\) in cyclic order, with mesh sufficiently small.  Consecutive bends bound clean quadrilaterals in \(M_\beta\).  Split each such quadrilateral by one of its diagonals.  This gives a finite clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Define a piecewise-affine map \(\bar f\) by setting \(\bar f=F\) on all vertices and extending affinely over each triangle.

For sufficiently small mesh, \(\bar f\) is an embedding.  Indeed, in bend coordinates the smooth map \(F\) has the form
\[
F(s,r)=(1-r)a(s)+r b(s),
\]
with \(a,b\) \(C^1\) boundary curves.  The above piecewise-affine maps are the usual secant approximations to this ruled embedding; they converge to \(F\) in \(C^1\).  A \(C^1\)-small perturbation of a compact \(C^1\)-embedded surface is again embedded.

Now check the squeeze inequalities.  If \(e\) is a boundary edge of flat length \(\ell\), then the boundary arc of \(F\) between its endpoints has length \(\rho\ell\), so the chord \(\bar f(e)\) has length at most \(\rho\ell<\ell\).  Hence boundary edges are strictly shortened.

The nonboundary edges are of two types: selected bends and diagonals between two sufficiently close selected bends.  Selected bends are strictly lengthened by (3).  For the diagonals, the relevant squared length difference depends continuously on the two adjacent bend parameters and agrees, when the parameters coincide, with the positive quantity in (3).  Compactness of the parameter circle gives a uniform positive margin, so for sufficiently small mesh every diagonal is also strictly lengthened.

Therefore \(\bar f\) restricts to a squeeze map on every triangle of the clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Lifting the triangulation and the map to \(\Sigma\) gives a \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation and a continuous map
\[
f:\Sigma\to\R^3
\]
with \(f=\bar f\circ \pi\), where \(\pi:\Sigma\to M_\beta\) is the quotient map.  Since \(\bar f\) is an embedding,
\[
f(p)=f(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \pi(p)=\pi(q)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=G_\beta^k(q)\text{ for some }k\in\Z.
\]
Thus \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
The set of realized numbers is exactly \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).  In particular, its infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower-bound lemma shows that every realized \(\beta\) satisfies \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  The proposition shows that every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.  Hence the set of realized numbers is \((\sqrt3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The AI got the problem correct. This is a working proof, with all essential details included. 

The proof in the first half works well, and it follows a clear outline. All details seem correct. 

The proof in the second half seems to work, though the exposition seemed a bit heavy on calculations and light on conceptual explanation. In particular, there was a statement about $C^1$-convergence of the approximation which needed to be interpreted generously. See inline comment below. I did not check the calculations line by line but it was clear to me that this approach works.

## Novelty.

Let me first discuss the context for the problem and then describe how the AI did. The problem is based on my solution of the Halpern-Weaver Conjecture, a result which asks for the infimal
aspect ratio needed for a smooth and isometric embedding of a flat Moebius band into $\R^3$. My paper was published in the {\it Annals\/} in January, 2025 and there are also some of accounts of the result in the popular media. The problem the AI considered is the same problem in a different category of maps, piecewise linear maps with a certain side condition called squeezing. 

The first half of the problem amounts to showing that $\sqrt 3$ is a lower bound on the allowable aspect ratio. For this, the AI seems to have followed my paper very closely, adapting essentially every one of my arguments to the new category of mappings. While the AI did cite my paper (just as context for the second half) it did not acknowledge that it was following the arguments in my paper very closely. I know the AI read my paper because 
it used the same terminology and notation from my paper -- e.g.
``T-patterns'' and ``bends'', and the letters $T,zb,D,H$ for the main objects in the geometric part of the proof.

The second half is not derived from my paper, and it essentially gives a nuts-and-bolts proof involving smooth approximation of an already known smooth construction that goes back to Michael Sadowsky in 1930. I didn't really like this proof that much. It uses a black box, Sadowsky's result, and then 
does PL approximation until it wins. So, this half is sort of novel, but it is what you would do if you did not really have any artistic sense.
reviews.recommendation:
I think that this paper is publishable with minor revisions.
First, I think that the paper should make completely clear
that it is getting the main ideas from my paper. Second, I
think that the paper should clean up the second half. I think
it is acceptable as a solution to use a smooth result as a
black box, but it would be nice to have an explicit and
self-contained exposition. I would not insist on this, however. The PL approximation approach here
is not too bad -- better than a similar argument that one of the other AIs did -- so
I wouldn't insist on a total overhaul. In case, the author really wants to use the PL approach, I might just try for a
more conceptual argument that follows a similar outline.
inline_comments: This is really the same as Lemma T in my paper on the optimal paper Moebius band. It is the main point.

This lemma is the main geometric construction. It is pretty much the same as what I have in my optimal paper Moebius band paper. Also, it could use a picture! For geometry solutions it would be very useful to have the AI do this.

The various citations here are rather confused. The best reference would be the existence of smooth isometric embeddings of aspect ratio converting to $\sqrt 3$ using the {\it pseudofold\/} construction in the 1977 paper by Halpern and Weaver. My own paper doesn't really discuss this existence result at all, though it does sketch a proof of the existence of the bend foliation.
Right at the beginning of this proof it would be nice to discuss the strategy briefly, to explain the roles of $w$ and $\lambda$.
I have some question about the $C^1$-convergence. Technically the PL map is not $C^1$ in the ordinary sense. However, this fine point seems like it can be easily tightened up.
I like that this argument is conceptual and does not get bogged down in two much fine-scale detail.

Let \(\tau\) be a clean triangle with boundary edge \(AB\) and opposite vertex \(C\).  If an affine map \(L:\tau\to \R^3\) decreases the length of \(AB\) and increases the lengths of \(AC\) and \(BC\), then \(L\) increases the length of every segment joining \(C\) to a point of \(AB\).

\begin{proof}
Write \(u=C-A\), \(v=C-B\), so \(u-v=B-A\).  Let
\[
q(w)=|Lw|^2-|w|^2 .
\]
The hypotheses are
\[
q(u)>0,\qquad q(v)>0,\qquad q(u-v)<0.
\]
For \(0\le t\le 1\),
\[
q((1-t)u+tv)
=(1-t)q(u)+tq(v)-t(1-t)q(u-v)>0.
\]
Thus every cevian from \(C\) to the base \(AB\) is strictly lengthened.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The canonical ruling and a \(T\)-pattern}

For every clean triangle, foliate it by the straight segments joining the vertex opposite the boundary edge to points of the boundary edge.  Adjacent clean triangles share a nonboundary edge, and that edge is one of the leaves in both triangles.  Therefore these local foliations glue.

The quotient clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\) carries a continuous circle-family \(\mathcal L=\{L_t\}_{t\in S^1}\) of straight clean segments with the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Each \(L_t\) is contained in a single clean triangle and joins the two boundary components in the universal cover.
\item The relative interiors of distinct leaves are disjoint and the leaves cover \(M_\beta\).
\item The image \(\bar f(L_t)\) is a straight segment in \(\R^3\), and
\[

\]

\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}

Every triangle has exactly two nonboundary edges, and every nonboundary edge is shared by two triangles, so the dual graph is \(2\)-regular.  It is connected: at each boundary vertex the link is an interval, so the triangles incident to that vertex are connected through shared nonboundary edges; since the triangulation is connected, the dual graph is connected.  Hence the dual graph is a single cycle.

On a triangle \(\tau\), the family of cevians from the opposite vertex to the boundary edge is parametrized by an interval; its two endpoint leaves are the two nonboundary edges of \(\tau\).  Gluing these intervals according to the cyclic dual graph gives a parameter circle \(S^1\).  This proves the existence and continuity of the family \(\{L_t\}\), and the relative interiors are plainly disjoint.

Each leaf is contained in a clean triangle, and by the preceding squeeze-cone lemma its image is strictly longer than its flat length.  Since every clean segment crosses from \(y=0\) to \(y=1\) in the universal cover, its flat length is at least \(1\).

\begin{lemma}[\(T\)-pattern]
There are two distinct leaves \(L_s,L_t\) such that the two straight segments
\[

\]
lie in perpendicular coplanar lines.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Lift the parameter circle to \(\R\).  Choose continuously oriented unit direction vectors \(u(r)\) for the image segments and let \(m(r)\) denote their midpoints.  By the orientation-reversal property,
\[
u(r+2\pi)=-u(r),\qquad m(r+2\pi)=m(r).
\]

Let
\[
\Upsilon=\{(r,s): r<s<r+2\pi\}/(r,s)\sim(r+2\pi,s+2\pi).
\]
Compactify \(\Upsilon\) by adding two points: \(\partial_+\), corresponding to \(s\to r\), and \(\partial_-\), corresponding to \(s\to r+2\pi\).  This compactification is a \(2\)-sphere, and the swap involution
\[
(r,s)\longmapsto (s,r+2\pi)
\]
extends to the antipodal map on that sphere.

Define
\[
F(r,s)=\left(u(r)\cdot u(s),\ (m(r)-m(s))\cdot (u(r)\times u(s))\right).
\]
Then \(F\) extends continuously to the compactification with
\[
F(\partial_+)=(1,0),\qquad F(\partial_-)=(-1,0),
\]
and satisfies
\[

\]
By the Borsuk--Ulam theorem, \(F\) has a zero.  At such a zero, the two direction vectors are perpendicular, and the vector joining the midpoints is orthogonal to the normal \(u(r)\times u(s)\).  Therefore the two supporting lines are coplanar.  This gives the desired pair of leaves.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The lower bound}

\begin{lemma}[geometry of a squeezed \(T\)-pattern]
If \(\beta\) is realized, then \(\beta>\sqrt 3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(T\) and \(B\) be the two leaves supplied by the preceding lemma.  Write
\[
T^*=\bar f(T),\qquad B^*=\bar f(B).
\]
Their supporting lines are perpendicular and coplanar.  Interchange \(T\) and \(B\), if necessary, so that the line supporting \(T^*\) does not meet the relative interior of \(B^*\).  Otherwise the two embedded segments would have an interior intersection.

Let \(u\) be the endpoint of \(B\) whose image is farthest from the line supporting \(T^*\).  Since \(B^*\) is perpendicular to that line and the line does not meet the relative interior of \(B^*\), the distance \(h\) from \(\bar f(u)\) to the line supporting \(T^*\) satisfies
\[
h\ge |B^*|>|B|_0\ge 1.
\]

Let the endpoints of \(T\) divide \(\partial M_\beta\) into two boundary arcs \(H\) and \(D\), with \(u\in D\).  Choose the signed horizontal displacement \(t\) of \(T\) so that
\[
\len_0(H)=\beta-t,\qquad \len_0(D)=\beta+t.
\]
Then
\[
|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Because \(T\) is a leaf, it is lengthened:
\[
|T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Since \(H\) is a boundary path joining the endpoints of \(T\),
\[
\sqrt{1+t^2}<|T^*|\le \len(\bar f(H))<\beta-t. \tag{1}
\]

Now consider the planar triangle \(\Delta\) whose base is \(T^*\) and whose third vertex is \(\bar f(u)\).  Its base has length \(>|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}\), and its height is \(h>1\).  If \(\vee\) denotes the union of the two nonbase sides of \(\Delta\), the elementary reflection argument gives
\[
\len(\vee)>\sqrt{5+t^2}.
\]
Indeed, among all triangles with base length \(b\) and height \(h\), the sum of the two nonbase sides is at least \(\sqrt{b^2+4h^2}\).

The boundary arc \(D\) runs from one endpoint of \(T\) to the other through \(u\).  Hence the two sides of \(\vee\) are no longer than the two corresponding subarcs of \(\bar f(D)\).  Therefore
\[
\sqrt{5+t^2}<\len(\vee)\le \len(\bar f(D))<\beta+t. \tag{2}
\]
From (1) and (2),
\[
2\beta>\alpha(t):=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},
\]
and also
\[
2\beta>\gamma(t):=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t.
\]
Let \(t_0=1/\sqrt3\).  Then
\[
\alpha(t_0)=\gamma(t_0)=2\sqrt3.
\]
Moreover, \(\alpha\) is increasing for \(t>0\), and \(\gamma\) is strictly decreasing on \(\R\).  Thus for every real \(t\),
\[
\max\{\alpha(t),\gamma(t)\}\ge 2\sqrt3.
\]
Consequently \(2\beta>2\sqrt3\), so \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{Realization for every \(\beta>\sqrt3\)}



[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The various citations here are rather confused. We use the classical existence theorem for paper Mobius bands: for every width \(w>0\) and every length \(\lambda\) with \(\lambda/w>\sqrt3\), there exists a smooth embedded isometric Mobius band of width \(w\) and length \(\lambda\), obtained by smoothing the triangular Mobius band. \begin{proposition}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{proposition}



[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Right at the beginning of this proof it would be nice to discuss the strategy briefly, to explain the roles of $w$ and $\lambda$.]]




\begin{proof}
Fix \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  Choose numbers \(w,\lambda\) such that
\[
1<w,\qquad \sqrt3\,w<\lambda<\beta,\qquad
w^2-1>\beta^2-\lambda^2.
\]
This is possible by taking \(\lambda\) sufficiently close to \(\beta\) and then \(w>1\) sufficiently close to \(1\).

Let \(\rho=\lambda/\beta<1\).  Let
\[
P_{\lambda,w}=([0,\lambda]\times[0,w])/(0,y)\sim(\lambda,w-y),
\]
and let
\[
I:P_{\lambda,w}\longrightarrow \R^3
\]
be a smooth embedded paper Mobius band with a ruling by straight bends.  Define
\[
A:M_\beta\longrightarrow P_{\lambda,w},\qquad A[x,y]=[\rho x,wy].
\]
This is well-defined because
\[
A(x+\beta,1-y)=(\rho x+\lambda,w-wy),
\]
which is the defining Mobius identification in \(P_{\lambda,w}\).  Put
\[
F=I\circ A:M_\beta\longrightarrow \R^3.
\]
Then \(F\) is an embedding.

Let \(\{C_s\}_{s\in S^1}\) be the pulled-back bend ruling on \(M_\beta\).  Each \(C_s\) is a clean straight segment.  If \(C_s\) has signed horizontal displacement \(d\), with \(|d|\le \beta\), then
\[
|F(C_s)|^2=\rho^2d^2+w^2.
\]
Hence
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2
=\rho^2d^2+w^2-(d^2+1)
=(w^2-1)-(1-\rho^2)d^2.
\]
Since \(|d|\le\beta\),
\[
(1-\rho^2)d^2\le (1-\rho^2)\beta^2=\beta^2-\lambda^2,
\]
so
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2\ge w^2-1-(\beta^2-\lambda^2)>0. \tag{3}
\]
Thus every pulled-back bend is strictly lengthened by \(F\).

Choose finitely many bends \(C_{s_0},\dots,C_{s_{N-1}}\) in cyclic order, with mesh sufficiently small.  Consecutive bends bound clean quadrilaterals in \(M_\beta\).  Split each such quadrilateral by one of its diagonals.  This gives a finite clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Define a piecewise-affine map \(\bar f\) by setting \(\bar f=F\) on all vertices and extending affinely over each triangle.

For sufficiently small mesh, \(\bar f\) is an embedding. 


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I have some question about the $C^1$-convergence.  Technically the PL map is not $C^1$ in the ordinary sense. However, this fine point seems like it can be easily tightened up.]]



Indeed, in bend coordinates the smooth map \(F\) has the form
\[
F(s,r)=(1-r)a(s)+r b(s),
\]
with \(a,b\) \(C^1\) boundary curves.  The above piecewise-affine maps are the usual secant approximations to this ruled embedding; they converge to \(F\) in \(C^1\).  A \(C^1\)-small perturbation of a compact \(C^1\)-embedded surface is again embedded.

Now check the squeeze inequalities.  If \(e\) is a boundary edge of flat length \(\ell\), then the boundary arc of \(F\) between its endpoints has length \(\rho\ell\), so the chord \(\bar f(e)\) has length at most \(\rho\ell<\ell\).  Hence boundary edges are strictly shortened.



[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I like that this argument is conceptual and does not get bogged down in two much fine-scale detail.]]



The nonboundary edges are of two types: selected bends and diagonals between two sufficiently close selected bends.  Selected bends are strictly lengthened by (3).  For the diagonals, the relevant squared length difference depends continuously on the two adjacent bend parameters and agrees, when the parameters coincide, with the positive quantity in (3).  Compactness of the parameter circle gives a uniform positive margin, so for sufficiently small mesh every diagonal is also strictly lengthened.

Therefore \(\bar f\) restricts to a squeeze map on every triangle of the clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Lifting the triangulation and the map to \(\Sigma\) gives a \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation and a continuous map
\[
f:\Sigma\to\R^3
\]
with \(f=\bar f\circ \pi\), where \(\pi:\Sigma\to M_\beta\) is the quotient map.  Since \(\bar f\) is an embedding,
\[
f(p)=f(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \pi(p)=\pi(q)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=G_\beta^k(q)\text{ for some }k\in\Z.
\]
Thus \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
The set of realized numbers is exactly \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).  In particular, its infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower-bound lemma shows that every realized \(\beta\) satisfies \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  The proposition shows that every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.  Hence the set of realized numbers is \((\sqrt3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

Similer to Submission B, this solution provides a correct argument both for the lower bound $\beta \geq \sqrt{3}$ and for the realizability of every $\beta > \sqrt{3}$. It accomplishes the first goal by adapting Schwartz's argument, which shows that a smoothly isometrically embedded M\"obius strip has aspect ratio greater than $\sqrt{3}$, to the PL setting in which the triangles in the triangulation satisfy the ``squeeze map'' hypothesis. This adaptation is carried out without any major logical flaws.

For the second goal, the solution starts with the piecewise smooth ruled isometric embeddings of the M\"obius band due to Sadowsky and Halpern--Weaver, approximates these embeddings by PL embeddings, and then carefully chooses scaling factors for the domain M\"obius band so that the resulting PL embedding satisfies the squeeze property. This part of the argument is also supported by justifications, including detailed inequalities, and a verification that the chosen scaling achieves the squeeze property on each triangle. However, the argument involving embeddedness of PL approximations of the smooth embedding is confusing. See the inline comment for Proposition 6. Nevertheless, I believe that the statement is salvagable using perhaps a slightly different strategy, such as working directly with the explicit construction. 

## Novelty.

Similar to Submission B, for both parts of the argument, the strategies implemented by this solution are essentially the same as the expected strategy for this problem, the strategy followed by the human solution, and the strategies pursued by some of the other AI models. Therefore, this approach should not be considered novel.

For the first part, the solution identifies that the proof strategy underlying Schwartz's theorem can be modified to prove the lower bound $\beta > \sqrt{3}$ in the setting of the problem statement. However, given access to Schwartz's result, adapting the argument to the PL category is a relatively routine task. In particular, Lemmas 4 and 5 use proof strategies that are very similar to those of corresponding lemmas in Schwartz's paper. The solution however fails to cite Schwartz's work explicitly in this part of the argument.

For the second part, the solution uses PL approximations of a known construction in the smooth setting. This is also a standard strategy, provided the necessary background from the existing literature is available.
reviews.recommendation: I consider this solution to be publishable after minor revisions. There are some minor errors in the statement of Lemma 3(i), but these do not affect the overall proof. There are also some inaccuracies in the discussion of the relevant literature, but these can likewise be corrected.
inline_comments: (Minor comment) Lemma 3(i) is not true as stated. Some of the $L_t$'s are boundary edges shared by two adjacent clean triangles, and hence are contained in both clean triangles. This issue can nevertheless be resolved by modifying condition (i) to account for this edge case. Moreover, it does not appear to affect the later argument that invokes Lemma 3.

(Minor comment) The proofs of Lemmas 4 and 5 appear to implement essentially the same strategies as those given or outlined in Schwartz's paper for similar lemmas. The solution should therefore cite Schwartz's work explicitly in this part of the argument, rather than presenting these proof strategies as if they were novel.

(Major comment) The solution claims that there exists a ``smooth embedded isometric Mobius band...'' and cites Sadowsky's 1930 work, together with a modern English translation by Hinz--Fried. However, the isometric embedding constructed by Sadowsky is not smooth; rather, it is piecewise smooth and globally $C^1$. The first construction of a globally smooth isometric embedding is due to Halpern--Weaver in their 1977 paper Inverting a cylinder through isometric immersions and embeddings. This misattribution suggests that the solution does not accurately reflect the relevant literature.

(Major comment) The argument that the secant approximations converge in $C^1$ is confusing as written. First, the PL embeddings themselves are only piecewise $C^1$, rather than globally $C^1$, so the phrase ``$C^1$ embedding'' is not appropriate in this context without further clarification. I believe that the intended statement is likely true, but it requires a much clearer argument. One possible approach would be to prove embeddedness directly from the explicit Sadowsky construction using the geometry of planar equilateral triangles and half-cylinders.
Not sure how much the argument here for diagonal stretching needs to be elaborated, but I nevertheless believe that the statement is still true.

|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Because \(T\) is a leaf, it is lengthened:
\[
|T^*|>\sqrt{1+t^2}.
\]
Since \(H\) is a boundary path joining the endpoints of \(T\),
\[
\sqrt{1+t^2}<|T^*|\le \len(\bar f(H))<\beta-t. \tag{1}
\]

Now consider the planar triangle \(\Delta\) whose base is \(T^*\) and whose third vertex is \(\bar f(u)\).  Its base has length \(>|T|_0=\sqrt{1+t^2}\), and its height is \(h>1\).  If \(\vee\) denotes the union of the two nonbase sides of \(\Delta\), the elementary reflection argument gives
\[
\len(\vee)>\sqrt{5+t^2}.
\]
Indeed, among all triangles with base length \(b\) and height \(h\), the sum of the two nonbase sides is at least \(\sqrt{b^2+4h^2}\).

The boundary arc \(D\) runs from one endpoint of \(T\) to the other through \(u\).  Hence the two sides of \(\vee\) are no longer than the two corresponding subarcs of \(\bar f(D)\).  Therefore
\[
\sqrt{5+t^2}<\len(\vee)\le \len(\bar f(D))<\beta+t. \tag{2}
\]
From (1) and (2),
\[
2\beta>\alpha(t):=\sqrt{1+t^2}+\sqrt{5+t^2},
\]
and also
\[
2\beta>\gamma(t):=2\sqrt{5+t^2}-2t.
\]
Let \(t_0=1/\sqrt3\).  Then
\[
\alpha(t_0)=\gamma(t_0)=2\sqrt3.
\]
Moreover, \(\alpha\) is increasing for \(t>0\), and \(\gamma\) is strictly decreasing on \(\R\).  Thus for every real \(t\),
\[
\max\{\alpha(t),\gamma(t)\}\ge 2\sqrt3.
\]
Consequently \(2\beta>2\sqrt3\), so \(\beta>\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: (Minor comment) The proofs of Lemmas 4 and 5 appear to implement essentially the same strategies as those given or outlined in Schwartz's paper for similar lemmas. The solution should therefore cite Schwartz's work explicitly in this part of the argument, rather than presenting these proof strategies as if they were novel.]]


\subsection{Realization for every \(\beta>\sqrt3\)}

We use the classical existence theorem for paper Mobius bands: for every width \(w>0\) and every length \(\lambda\) with \(\lambda/w>\sqrt3\), there exists a smooth embedded isometric Mobius band of width \(w\) and length \(\lambda\), obtained by smoothing the triangular Mobius band.  Moreover, it has a continuous ruling by straight bends whose preimages are straight segments joining the two boundary components.  This is the standard Sadowsky--Wunderlich construction; see Sadowsky \cite{Sadowsky}, the translation by Hinz--Fried \cite{HinzFried}, and the modern discussion in Schwartz \cite{Schwartz}.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: (Major comment) The solution claims that there exists a ``smooth embedded isometric Mobius band...'' and cites Sadowsky's 1930 work, together with a modern English translation by Hinz--Fried. However, the isometric embedding constructed by Sadowsky is not smooth; rather, it is piecewise smooth and globally $C^1$. The first construction of a globally smooth isometric embedding is due to Halpern--Weaver in their 1977 paper \emph{Inverting a cylinder through isometric immersions and embeddings}. This misattribution suggests that the solution does not accurately reflect the relevant literature.]]


\begin{proposition}
Every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  Choose numbers \(w,\lambda\) such that
\[
1<w,\qquad \sqrt3\,w<\lambda<\beta,\qquad
w^2-1>\beta^2-\lambda^2.
\]
This is possible by taking \(\lambda\) sufficiently close to \(\beta\) and then \(w>1\) sufficiently close to \(1\).

Let \(\rho=\lambda/\beta<1\).  Let
\[
P_{\lambda,w}=([0,\lambda]\times[0,w])/(0,y)\sim(\lambda,w-y),
\]
and let
\[
I:P_{\lambda,w}\longrightarrow \R^3
\]
be a smooth embedded paper Mobius band with a ruling by straight bends.  Define
\[
A:M_\beta\longrightarrow P_{\lambda,w},\qquad A[x,y]=[\rho x,wy].
\]
This is well-defined because
\[
A(x+\beta,1-y)=(\rho x+\lambda,w-wy),
\]
which is the defining Mobius identification in \(P_{\lambda,w}\).  Put
\[
F=I\circ A:M_\beta\longrightarrow \R^3.
\]
Then \(F\) is an embedding.

Let \(\{C_s\}_{s\in S^1}\) be the pulled-back bend ruling on \(M_\beta\).  Each \(C_s\) is a clean straight segment.  If \(C_s\) has signed horizontal displacement \(d\), with \(|d|\le \beta\), then
\[
|F(C_s)|^2=\rho^2d^2+w^2.
\]
Hence
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2
=\rho^2d^2+w^2-(d^2+1)
=(w^2-1)-(1-\rho^2)d^2.
\]
Since \(|d|\le\beta\),
\[
(1-\rho^2)d^2\le (1-\rho^2)\beta^2=\beta^2-\lambda^2,
\]
so
\[
|F(C_s)|^2-|C_s|_0^2\ge w^2-1-(\beta^2-\lambda^2)>0. \tag{3}
\]
Thus every pulled-back bend is strictly lengthened by \(F\).

Choose finitely many bends \(C_{s_0},\dots,C_{s_{N-1}}\) in cyclic order, with mesh sufficiently small.  Consecutive bends bound clean quadrilaterals in \(M_\beta\).  Split each such quadrilateral by one of its diagonals.  This gives a finite clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Define a piecewise-affine map \(\bar f\) by setting \(\bar f=F\) on all vertices and extending affinely over each triangle.

For sufficiently small mesh, \(\bar f\) is an embedding.  Indeed, in bend coordinates the smooth map \(F\) has the form
\[
F(s,r)=(1-r)a(s)+r b(s),
\]
with \(a,b\) \(C^1\) boundary curves.  The above piecewise-affine maps are the usual secant approximations to this ruled embedding; they converge to \(F\) in \(C^1\).  A \(C^1\)-small perturbation of a compact \(C^1\)-embedded surface is again embedded.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: (Major comment) The argument that the secant approximations converge in $C^1$ is confusing as written. First, the PL embeddings themselves are only piecewise $C^1$, rather than globally $C^1$, so the phrase ``$C^1$ embedding'' is not appropriate in this context without further clarification. I believe that the intended statement is likely true, but it requires a much clearer argument. One possible approach would be to prove embeddedness directly from the explicit Sadowsky construction using the geometry of planar equilateral triangles and half-cylinders.]]


Now check the squeeze inequalities.  If \(e\) is a boundary edge of flat length \(\ell\), then the boundary arc of \(F\) between its endpoints has length \(\rho\ell\), so the chord \(\bar f(e)\) has length at most \(\rho\ell<\ell\).  Hence boundary edges are strictly shortened.

The nonboundary edges are of two types: selected bends and diagonals between two sufficiently close selected bends.  Selected bends are strictly lengthened by (3).  For the diagonals, the relevant squared length difference depends continuously on the two adjacent bend parameters and agrees, when the parameters coincide, with the positive quantity in (3).  Compactness of the parameter circle gives a uniform positive margin, so for sufficiently small mesh every diagonal is also strictly lengthened.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Not sure how much the argument here for diagonal stretching needs to be elaborated, but I nevertheless believe that the statement is still true.]]


Therefore \(\bar f\) restricts to a squeeze map on every triangle of the clean triangulation of \(M_\beta\).  Lifting the triangulation and the map to \(\Sigma\) gives a \(G_\beta\)-invariant clean triangulation and a continuous map
\[
f:\Sigma\to\R^3
\]
with \(f=\bar f\circ \pi\), where \(\pi:\Sigma\to M_\beta\) is the quotient map.  Since \(\bar f\) is an embedding,
\[
f(p)=f(q)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \pi(p)=\pi(q)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=G_\beta^k(q)\text{ for some }k\in\Z.
\]
Thus \(\beta\) is realized.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
The set of realized numbers is exactly \((\sqrt3,\infty)\).  In particular, its infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The lower-bound lemma shows that every realized \(\beta\) satisfies \(\beta>\sqrt3\).  The proposition shows that every \(\beta>\sqrt3\) is realized.  Hence the set of realized numbers is \((\sqrt3,\infty)\), whose infimum is \(\sqrt3\).
\end{proof}

## Correctness.

This solution is incorrect. The solutions acknowledges as much, calling itself a partial solution and suggesting the gaps in its own arguments. 

For the upper bound, the AI system correctly argues (somewhat sloppily) that a squeeze map increases the lengths of cevians of clean triangles. It then tries to apply the result of Schwartz on smooth locally isometric embeddings of paper M\"obius bands. While Schwartz's result is in spirit quite similar to the desired result, it cannot be directly applied in any serious way. The AI response acknowledges this, discussing the smooth vs PL distinction and the issue of squeeze maps resulting in a M\"obius band that, if cut open and laid flat, would no longer be a trapezoid, but instead some many-sided polygon.

There is a subtlety within this result that was alluded to in the AI response, but is worth making explicit. The lower bound is false if one simply requires a continuous or piecewise linear embedding into $\mathbb{R}^3$. The idea is that one can ``fold over folds" to get as small an aspect ratio as one wishes. The AI miscites Schwartz's theorem in a rather particular way: ``any embedded ruled Moebius band" must have aspect ratio at least $\sqrt{3}$. The ruling is the key property, guarenteed both by smoothness and the setup in this problem, that allows Schwartz's proof strategy to go through. Unfortunately for the model, the core of this problem was to demonstrate that, and the model did not.

For the realization half of the question, the AI solution makes some vague suggestion for how to do the realization. It unclearly and incorrectly describes the limiting shape it hopes to approximate. The AI assessment of the gap in its proof points out how it did not give an explicit family of examples and rigorously show the clean mapping property for each triangle. ``This step acts merely as a heuristic." This is too generous. A heuristic or idea for how to proceed would be something like ``Our codomain will be three equilateral triangles, normally translated by small amounts. We then connect them in a cyclic order using small rectangles that we triangulate." The AI's solution does not, as far as I can see, include any clear or promising idea for a construction.

## Novelty.

This solution has the most compressed formatting out of the bunch. 

## Attribution.

This is the only AI solution to adequately cite Schwartz's work, although the result it claimed to cite was not proven in the paper.
reviews.recommendation: This work falls into the ``should be rejected" category. It has minimal correct math, and the proof sketch it does offer shows minimal promise. The realization section in particular seems to demonstrate poor understanding.
inline_comments: The ``limit M\"obius band" consists of three equilateral triangles, not six. It is unclear what construction the author is describing.

## Correctness.

The solution attempts to address the stated problem in two steps, but neither step is carried out with the rigor required for proof-based mathematics. As a result, the solution does not provide a correct resolution of the problem.

In Step 1, the solution attempts to establish the lower bound $\beta > \sqrt{3}$ by appealing directly to an existing result of Schwartz on the lower bound for the aspect ratio of piecewise smooth isometrically embedded Möbius bands. However, as noted in the editor’s note and the inline comment, this argument contains a significant gap. The embeddings described in the problem statement are obtained by an affine squeeze map and, in particular, are not isometric on the individual triangles. Therefore, Schwartz’s result does not immediately apply to the setting of the problem statement. The solution does not recognize or address this discrepancy, leaving the argument for Step 1 incomplete.

In Step 2, the solution attempts to describe a method for constructing continuous embeddings realizing every $\beta > \sqrt{3}$, but the argument only contains a verbal description of a realization map for each $\beta > \sqrt{3}$ without any mathematical justification. Throughout this step, the solution makes several nontrivial claims about the properties of the proposed construction without proving them. Therefore, Step 2 should be regarded as an informal heuristic rather than a rigorous mathematical argument.

## Novelty.

The solution does not demonstrate substantial novelty in its approach. In Step 1, it attempts to implement a strategy similar to that used in the human solution, but it does not carry out this strategy successfully. In Step 2, the level of novelty is difficult to assess, since the proposed construction is not described in a mathematically precise way.
reviews.recommendation:
The arguments given in the solution contain significant gaps. First, the solution claims that Step 1 follows directly from a result of Schwartz. However, that result does not seem to apply directly in the present setting, since the hypotheses in Schwartz’s theorem differ in crucial ways from the assumptions made here. The solution does not address this discrepancy, and as a result Step 1 remains unproved.

There is a similar issue in Step 2. The author gives a heuristic description of the construction of a family of geometric objects, but the discussion is not sufficiently precise to constitute a rigorous proof. In particular, the solution does not verify that the constructed family satisfies the properties required for the argument. Thus, the discussion in Step 2 should be regarded as informal motivation rather than as a complete mathematical proof.

Because the arguments for both steps currently lack the necessary mathematical rigor, I recommend rejecting the solution for publication in its present form.
inline_comments: (Minor comment) I am confused by the sentence ``let the map $f$ have directional vectors $\vec X$ and $\vec Y$.'' It is not standard practice to say that a map has two directional vectors. I suspect that the author intends $\vec X$ and $\vec Y$ to denote two sides of the image triangle, but this should be made explicit.

(Major comment) The statement ``Applying this to our polyhedral Moebius band ...'' is incorrect as written. Schwartz's theorem does not automatically apply in this setting. In particular, Schwartz's theorem assumes that the embedding is piecewise isometric. However, the map described here restricts on the clean triangles to affine squeeze maps, which are not isometric embeddings. This is a significant discrepancy between the hypotheses of Schwartz's theorem and the setting considered here, and it is not addressed in the solution.

(Major comment) The claim ``a sequence of $6$ equilateral triangles ...'' is incorrect. In Sadowsky's construction of a nearly optimal paper Moebius band, the relevant configuration consists of $3$, rather than $6$, equilateral triangles. Nevertheless, the stated ruling length and perimeter are correct, although the computation leading to them is flawed.

(Major comment) The solution does not justify several nontrivial claims about the properties of the proposed construction. For example, it is not mathematically clear what it means in this context to ```open up' the flat equilateral triangle.'' The solution also claims that the embedding can be scaled so that ``the boundary strictly contracts to a length ...'' and that ``internal thickness pushes out to ensure all cross-edges strictly exceed their domain lengths,'' but these assertions are not accompanied by any mathematical justification. As written, this is only a heuristic description of a construction, rather than a mathematically rigorous argument.
