\begin{comment}
\end{comment}

The submission claims that the inequality holds for $p \in [0, 1/3] \cup \{1/2, 1\}$. The submitted proof crucially relies on two results. First, it reduces the inequality from arbitrary convex combinations to the uniform convex combination $w_1 = \ldots = w_m = \frac{1}{m}$ by way of a comparison theorem. This reduces the inequality to the well-studied problem of bounding the probability that a binomial random variable exceeds its mean. Second, it claims that this inequality is true and follows from results in the literature. 

## Correctness.

The submission fails to provide enough justification for both crucial steps. For the comparison theorem (Lemma 3), the submission cites a paper of Hoeffding. But it is unclear how to translate Hoeffding's results into Lemma 3. Moreover, as stated, Lemma 3 cannot hold and we provide a counter-example below. The claimed result might be true if one replaces i.i.d real-valued random variables with Bernoulli random variables, but it is still not obvious how to prove this. 

For the second fact, the submission cites a paper of Samuels and a paper of Jogdeo-Samuels to claim that 
\[
 \Pr[\text{Binom}(n, p) \geq np] \geq p \quad \text{ for } 0 \leq p \leq \frac{1}{3}. 
\]
However, it is unclear how this result comes from these two papers. 

The submission correctly prove that the inequality does not universally hold for any of the values outside of $[0, 1/3] \cup \{1/2, 1\}$. 

## Novelty.

The submission does not propose any new approaches or ideas not already known in the literature.
reviews.recommendation: The submission should be rejected. The proposed proof strategy is very natural, but the submission makes no meaningful progress towards this strategy.

\date{}


\subsection*{Overview / Strategy}

The problem is to determine for which probabilities \(p\) the displayed inequality holds uniformly over all finite convex weight vectors. The main positive argument has two reductions. First, Hoeffding's extremal theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables reduces the weighted problem to the special case of equal weights. In the Bernoulli case, equal weights give binomial averages. Second, a classical binomial mean-tail estimate of Jogdeo--Samuels type says that for \(0\le p\le 1/3\), every binomial average is at least its mean with probability at least \(p\). These two facts are stated precisely in Section~1 and used in Proposition~\ref{prop:smallp}.

The remaining cases are elementary. At \(p=1/2\), the Bernoulli subset is uniformly distributed over all subsets, and pairing every subset with its complement gives probability at least \(1/2\). At \(p=1\), the assertion is immediate. To show that there are no other probabilities, equal weights on three variables give counterexamples for every \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), and equal weights on two variables give counterexamples for every \(p\in(1/2,1)\).

\begin{definition}
A Bernoulli\((p)\) random variable is a random variable taking value \(1\) with probability \(p\) and value \(0\) with probability \(1-p\). For \(p\in[0,1]\), let \(\mathcal P(p)\) denote the following assertion:
for every integer \(m\ge1\), every choice of nonnegative real numbers
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and every family \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) of i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables, one has
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Headline theorem: the original problem]\label{thm:main}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds exactly for
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]
Equivalently, the complete set of probabilities \(p\) for which
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p
\]
holds for every finite convex weight vector \((w_1,\ldots,w_m)\) and every i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) family \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) is
\[
\boxed{[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Classical one-dimensional inputs}

The proof uses two standard one-dimensional results. They are quoted in the precise forms needed below. The first is Hoeffding's reduction theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables; the second is the binomial mean-tail estimate used to evaluate the equal-weight case.

\begin{lemma}[Hoeffding's reduction for convex combinations]\label{lem:hoeffding}
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. real-valued random variables. For \(t\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
L(t):=\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right].
\]
Then for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every choice of weights
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
one has
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} w_iX_i\ge t\right]\ge L(t).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
This is the one-dimensional half-line form of Hoeffding's extremal theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables; see Hoeffding \cite{Hoeffding1955}. To make explicit that the closed-tail convention used here causes no ambiguity, we record the standard passage from the open-tail formulation.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It is unclear how the paper of Hoeffding gives the open-tail bound. Moreover, as stated, this result is incorrect. For a counter-example, consider the distribution $\Pr(X = 0) = \Pr(X = 1) = 0.1$ and $\Pr(X = 2) = 0.8$. Then 
\begin{align*}
    \Pr \left [0.1 X_1 + 0.1 X_2 + 0.8 X_3 > 0.8 \right ] &= 0.899, \\
    \inf_{N \geq 1} \Pr \left [ \frac{X_1 + \ldots + X_N}{N} \geq t\right ] & = 0.9
\end{align*}
It might be true that the result holds for Bernoulli random variables, but this is not obvious and is equivalent to Csóka's conjecture.]]

Hoeffding's theorem gives, for every real \(u\),
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>u\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>u\right].
\]
Fix \(t\in\mathbb R\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), apply the preceding inequality with \(u=t-\varepsilon\). For each \(N\),
\[
\left\{\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right\}
\subseteq
\left\{\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>t-\varepsilon\right\},
\]
and therefore
\[
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>t-\varepsilon\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right]
=L(t).
\]
Thus
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>t-\varepsilon\right]\ge L(t)
\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
\]
As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the events
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>t-\varepsilon\right\}
\]
decrease to
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i\ge t\right\}.
\]
By continuity of probability from above,
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i\ge t\right]\ge L(t).
\]
This is the desired closed-tail statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Binomial mean-tail inequality]\label{lem:binomial}
Let
\[
X_{N,p}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p).
\]
Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(0\le p\le \frac13\), then for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p.
\]
Equivalently, since \(X_{N,p}\) is integer-valued,
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil]\ge p.
\]

\item If \(p=\frac12\), then for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]\ge \frac12.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, in the first assertion equality occurs for \(N=1\) and \(0<p\le1/3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(p=0\), \(X_{N,0}=0\) almost surely, so
\[
\Pr[X_{N,0}\ge0]=1\ge0.
\]
For \(0<p\le1/3\), the first assertion is the classical binomial mean-tail estimate of Samuels and Jogdeo--Samuels; see \cite{Samuels1965,JogdeoSamuels1968}. 


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It is not clear how the cited papers imply $\Pr[X_{N, p} \geq Np] \geq p$. There are papers of Greenberg–Mohri, Pelekis–Ramon, Doerr, Rigolett-Tong which study the question of bounding this quantity. It is unclear if this inequality follows from their works. For example, from Rigolett-Tong, we get 
\[
    \Pr[X_{N, p} \geq Np] \geq \min \left \{ \frac{1}{4}, p \right \}
\]
but this is not enough.]]


In the form needed here, that estimate states exactly that for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil]\ge p.
\]
Because \(X_{N,p}\) is integer-valued, the events
\[
\{X_{N,p}\ge Np\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\{X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil\}
\]
are identical. This proves the first assertion.

For \(p=1/2\), the binomial distribution is symmetric:
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=j]=\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=N-j]
\qquad (0\le j\le N).
\]
If \(N=2r+1\) is odd, then the values \(0,\ldots,r\) pair with the values \(2r+1,\ldots,r+1\), and exactly one member of each pair is at least \(N/2=r+\frac12\). Hence
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]=\frac12.
\]
If \(N=2r\) is even, then the values \(0,\ldots,r-1\) pair with \(2r,\ldots,r+1\), while \(r\) is the central value and is included in the event \(\{X_{N,1/2}\ge r\}\). Therefore
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]
=
\frac12\bigl(1-\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]\bigr)
+\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]
=
\frac12+\frac12\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]
\ge\frac12.
\]
This proves the second assertion.

Finally, if \(N=1\) and \(0<p\le1/3\), then
\[
\{X_{1,p}\ge p\}=\{X_{1,p}=1\},
\]
so
\[
\Pr[X_{1,p}\ge p]=p.
\]
Thus equality is possible in the first assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The positive cases}

\begin{proposition}[The interval \(0\le p\le1/3\)]\label{prop:smallp}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds for every
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13].
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in[0,1/3]\). Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables.

Extend \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\), if necessary, to an infinite i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) with \(X_i=v_i\) for \(1\le i\le m\). Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} with \(t=p\) gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i X_i\ge p\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge p\right].
\]
For each \(N\), the sum \(X_1+\cdots+X_N\) has binomial distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)\). Hence, writing \(X_{N,p}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)\),
\[
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np].
\]
Therefore
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np].
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}, since \(0\le p\le1/3\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p
\qquad\text{for every }N\ge1.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(N\) gives
\[
\inf_{N\ge1}\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p.
\]
Since \(m\), the weights, and the Bernoulli\((p)\) family were arbitrary, \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds.
\end{proof}


\begin{proposition}[The point \(p=1/2\)]\label{prop:halfp}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((1/2)\) random variables.

Let
\[
A=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}: v_i=1\}.
\]
Because the \(v_i\) are independent and each is \(1\) with probability \(1/2\), the random set \(A\) is uniformly distributed over all \(2^m\) subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). For a subset \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), write
\[
w(B)=\sum_{i\in B}w_i.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i=w(A),
\]
so the desired event is
\[
\{w(A)\ge1/2\}.
\]

Pair every subset \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with its complement \(B^c\). These pairs partition the \(2^m\) subsets into \(2^{m-1}\) unordered pairs. Since
\[
w(B)+w(B^c)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
at least one of \(B\) and \(B^c\) has weight at least \(1/2\). Thus at least one subset in each complementary pair belongs to the event \(\{w(A)\ge1/2\}\).

Every subset has probability \(2^{-m}\). Since at least \(2^{m-1}\) subsets satisfy \(w(B)\ge1/2\), we obtain
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge\frac12\right]
=
\Pr[w(A)\ge1/2]
\ge
2^{m-1}\cdot 2^{-m}
=
\frac12.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The point \(p=1\)]\label{prop:onep}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((1)\) random variables. A Bernoulli\((1)\) random variable equals \(1\) almost surely, so
\[
v_i=1\qquad\text{almost surely for every }i.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i
=
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i
=
1
\]
almost surely. Hence
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge1\right]=1\ge1.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Counterexamples outside the claimed set}
\begin{proposition}[Failure for \(1/3<p<1/2\)]\label{prop:countermiddle}
For every
\[
p\in\left(\frac13,\frac12\right),
\]
the assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\). Take
\[
m=3,\qquad w_1=w_2=w_3=\frac13,
\]
and let \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables. Put
\[
N=v_1+v_2+v_3.
\]
Then \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,p)\) and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i=\frac{N}{3}.
\]

Because \(p>1/3\), one success is not enough:
\[
\frac13<p.
\]
Because \(p<1/2<2/3\), two successes are enough:
\[
\frac23\ge p.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right\}
=
\{N\ge2\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[N\ge2].
\]
Since \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,p)\),
\[
\Pr[N\ge2]
=
\binom{3}{2}p^2(1-p)+p^3
=
3p^2(1-p)+p^3
=
p^2(3-2p).
\]
Now
\[
p-p^2(3-2p)
=
p(1-3p+2p^2)
=
p(1-p)(1-2p).
\]
For \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), the factors \(p\), \(1-p\), and \(1-2p\) are all positive. Hence
\[
p-p^2(3-2p)>0,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
p^2(3-2p)<p.
\]
Thus this choice of weights gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right]<p.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Failure for \(1/2<p<1\)]\label{prop:counterlarge}
For every
\[
p\in\left(\frac12,1\right),
\]
the assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in(1/2,1)\). Take
\[
m=2,\qquad w_1=w_2=\frac12,
\]
and let \(v_1,v_2\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables. Put
\[
N=v_1+v_2.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i=\frac{N}{2}.
\]
Because \(p>1/2\), one success is not enough:
\[
\frac12<p.
\]
Since \(N\) can only take the values \(0,1,2\), the event
\[
\left\{\frac{N}{2}\ge p\right\}
\]
occurs only when \(N=2\), that is, when both \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) equal \(1\). Hence
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[v_1=1,\ v_2=1].
\]
By independence,
\[
\Pr[v_1=1,\ v_2=1]=p^2.
\]
Since \(0<p<1\),
\[
p^2<p.
\]
Thus this choice of weights gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i\ge p\right]<p.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the classification}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Proposition~\ref{prop:smallp} proves that \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds for every
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13].
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:halfp} proves that \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds, and Proposition~\ref{prop:onep} proves that \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds. Hence
\[
\mathcal P(p)\quad\text{holds for every}\quad
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]

It remains to show that no other probability works. Since \(p\) is a probability, \(p\in[0,1]\). The complement of
\[
[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}
\]
inside \([0,1]\) is
\[
\left(\frac13,\frac12\right)\cup\left(\frac12,1\right).
\]
For every \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), Proposition~\ref{prop:countermiddle} gives an explicit choice of weights for which the desired inequality fails. For every \(p\in(1/2,1)\), Proposition~\ref{prop:counterlarge} gives an explicit choice of weights for which the desired inequality fails.

Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds exactly for
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]
This proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

## Correctness.

My recommendation is that the submission should be rejected. The proof attempt relies on two key inequalities, Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} and Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}.

The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} is based on a false claim. This constitutes a fundamental flaw in the proof. Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}, meanwhile, is not stated in the cited sources. The submission claims that it is a classical result following from \cite{Samuels1965} and \cite{JogdeoSamuels1968}, but neither paper contains the lemma in the form stated here. While it is plausible that a result of this type could be derived from those works, such a derivation is not immediate, and no justification is provided.

The remainder of the argument, which reduces the main claim to these two lemmas, appears to be correct. 

## Novelty.

I would say that the novelty of this solution is low. Even assuming that Lemmas were correct, the main argument consists essentially of an immediate reduction to these auxiliary results.

\date{}

\subsection*{Overview / Strategy}

The problem is to determine for which probabilities \(p\) the displayed inequality holds uniformly over all finite convex weight vectors. The main positive argument has two reductions. First, Hoeffding's extremal theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables reduces the weighted problem to the special case of equal weights. In the Bernoulli case, equal weights give binomial averages. Second, a classical binomial mean-tail estimate of Jogdeo--Samuels type says that for \(0\le p\le 1/3\), every binomial average is at least its mean with probability at least \(p\). These two facts are stated precisely in Section~1 and used in Proposition~\ref{prop:smallp}.

The remaining cases are elementary. At \(p=1/2\), the Bernoulli subset is uniformly distributed over all subsets, and pairing every subset with its complement gives probability at least \(1/2\). At \(p=1\), the assertion is immediate. To show that there are no other probabilities, equal weights on three variables give counterexamples for every \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), and equal weights on two variables give counterexamples for every \(p\in(1/2,1)\).

\begin{definition}
A Bernoulli\((p)\) random variable is a random variable taking value \(1\) with probability \(p\) and value \(0\) with probability \(1-p\). For \(p\in[0,1]\), let \(\mathcal P(p)\) denote the following assertion:
for every integer \(m\ge1\), every choice of nonnegative real numbers
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and every family \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) of i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables, one has
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Headline theorem: the original problem]\label{thm:main}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds exactly for
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]
Equivalently, the complete set of probabilities \(p\) for which
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p
\]
holds for every finite convex weight vector \((w_1,\ldots,w_m)\) and every i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) family \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) is
\[
\boxed{[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\subsection{Classical one-dimensional inputs}

The proof uses two standard one-dimensional results. They are quoted in the precise forms needed below. The first is Hoeffding's reduction theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables; the second is the binomial mean-tail estimate used to evaluate the equal-weight case.

\begin{lemma}[Hoeffding's reduction for convex combinations]\label{lem:hoeffding}
Let \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) be i.i.d. real-valued random variables. For \(t\in\mathbb R\), define
\[
L(t):=\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right].
\]
Then for every integer \(m\ge1\) and every choice of weights
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
one has
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m} w_iX_i\ge t\right]\ge L(t).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
This is the one-dimensional half-line form of Hoeffding's extremal theorem for convex combinations of i.i.d. random variables; see Hoeffding \cite{Hoeffding1955}. To make explicit that the closed-tail convention used here causes no ambiguity, we record the standard passage from the open-tail formulation.

Hoeffding's theorem gives, for every real \(u\),
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>u\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>u\right].
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: No such statement appears in Hoeffding  \cite{Hoeffding1955}. In fact, the claim is wrong as stated. It has a counterexample already for $m = 2$.]]


Fix \(t\in\mathbb R\). For every \(\varepsilon>0\), apply the preceding inequality with \(u=t-\varepsilon\). For each \(N\),
\[
\left\{\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right\}
\subseteq
\left\{\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>t-\varepsilon\right\},
\]
and therefore
\[
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}>t-\varepsilon\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge t\right]
=L(t).
\]
Thus
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>t-\varepsilon\right]\ge L(t)
\qquad\text{for every }\varepsilon>0.
\]
As \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), the events
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i>t-\varepsilon\right\}
\]
decrease to
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i\ge t\right\}.
\]
By continuity of probability from above,
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_iX_i\ge t\right]\ge L(t).
\]
This is the desired closed-tail statement.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Binomial mean-tail inequality]\label{lem:binomial}
Let
\[
X_{N,p}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p).
\]
Then the following hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(0\le p\le \frac13\), then for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p.
\]
Equivalently, since \(X_{N,p}\) is integer-valued,
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil]\ge p.
\]

\item If \(p=\frac12\), then for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]\ge \frac12.
\]
\end{enumerate}
Moreover, in the first assertion equality occurs for \(N=1\) and \(0<p\le1/3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(p=0\), \(X_{N,0}=0\) almost surely, so
\[
\Pr[X_{N,0}\ge0]=1\ge0.
\]
For \(0<p\le1/3\), the first assertion is the classical binomial mean-tail estimate of Samuels and Jogdeo--Samuels; see \cite{Samuels1965,JogdeoSamuels1968}. In the form needed here, that estimate states exactly that for every \(N\ge1\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil]\ge p.
\]
Because \(X_{N,p}\) is integer-valued, the events
\[
\{X_{N,p}\ge Np\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\{X_{N,p}\ge \lceil Np\rceil\}
\]
are identical. This proves the first assertion. 


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Neither \cite{Samuels1965} nor \cite{JogdeoSamuels1968} contains this statement in the form presented here. While it is plausible that a bound of this type could be derived from the results in those papers, it is not immediately clear how such a derivation would proceed.]]

For \(p=1/2\), the binomial distribution is symmetric:
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=j]=\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=N-j]
\qquad (0\le j\le N).
\]
If \(N=2r+1\) is odd, then the values \(0,\ldots,r\) pair with the values \(2r+1,\ldots,r+1\), and exactly one member of each pair is at least \(N/2=r+\frac12\). Hence
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]=\frac12.
\]
If \(N=2r\) is even, then the values \(0,\ldots,r-1\) pair with \(2r,\ldots,r+1\), while \(r\) is the central value and is included in the event \(\{X_{N,1/2}\ge r\}\). Therefore
\[
\Pr[X_{N,1/2}\ge N/2]
=
\frac12\bigl(1-\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]\bigr)
+\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]
=
\frac12+\frac12\Pr[X_{N,1/2}=r]
\ge\frac12.
\]
This proves the second assertion.

Finally, if \(N=1\) and \(0<p\le1/3\), then
\[
\{X_{1,p}\ge p\}=\{X_{1,p}=1\},
\]
so
\[
\Pr[X_{1,p}\ge p]=p.
\]
Thus equality is possible in the first assertion.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The positive cases}

\begin{proposition}[The interval \(0\le p\le1/3\)]\label{prop:smallp}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds for every
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13].
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in[0,1/3]\). Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables.

Extend \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\), if necessary, to an infinite i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) sequence \(X_1,X_2,\ldots\) with \(X_i=v_i\) for \(1\le i\le m\). Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} with \(t=p\) gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i X_i\ge p\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge p\right].
\]
For each \(N\), the sum \(X_1+\cdots+X_N\) has binomial distribution \(\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)\). Hence, writing \(X_{N,p}\sim\operatorname{Bin}(N,p)\),
\[
\Pr\!\left[\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_N}{N}\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np].
\]
Therefore
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
\ge
\inf_{N\ge1}\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np].
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}, since \(0\le p\le1/3\),
\[
\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p
\qquad\text{for every }N\ge1.
\]
Taking the infimum over \(N\) gives
\[
\inf_{N\ge1}\Pr[X_{N,p}\ge Np]\ge p.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge p\right]\ge p.
\]
Since \(m\), the weights, and the Bernoulli\((p)\) family were arbitrary, \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The point \(p=1/2\)]\label{prop:halfp}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((1/2)\) random variables.

Let
\[
A=\{i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}: v_i=1\}.
\]
Because the \(v_i\) are independent and each is \(1\) with probability \(1/2\), the random set \(A\) is uniformly distributed over all \(2^m\) subsets of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\). For a subset \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\), write
\[
w(B)=\sum_{i\in B}w_i.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i=w(A),
\]
so the desired event is
\[
\{w(A)\ge1/2\}.
\]

Pair every subset \(B\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with its complement \(B^c\). These pairs partition the \(2^m\) subsets into \(2^{m-1}\) unordered pairs. Since
\[
w(B)+w(B^c)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
at least one of \(B\) and \(B^c\) has weight at least \(1/2\). Thus at least one subset in each complementary pair belongs to the event \(\{w(A)\ge1/2\}\).

Every subset has probability \(2^{-m}\). Since at least \(2^{m-1}\) subsets satisfy \(w(B)\ge1/2\), we obtain
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge\frac12\right]
=
\Pr[w(A)\ge1/2]
\ge
2^{m-1}\cdot 2^{-m}
=
\frac12.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[The point \(p=1\)]\label{prop:onep}
The assertion \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(m\ge1\), let
\[
w_1,\ldots,w_m\ge0,\qquad \sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i=1,
\]
and let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((1)\) random variables. A Bernoulli\((1)\) random variable equals \(1\) almost surely, so
\[
v_i=1\qquad\text{almost surely for every }i.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i
=
\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i
=
1
\]
almost surely. Hence
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{m}w_i v_i\ge1\right]=1\ge1.
\]
Thus \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Counterexamples outside the claimed set}

\begin{proposition}[Failure for \(1/3<p<1/2\)]\label{prop:countermiddle}
For every
\[
p\in\left(\frac13,\frac12\right),
\]
the assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\). Take
\[
m=3,\qquad w_1=w_2=w_3=\frac13,
\]
and let \(v_1,v_2,v_3\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables. Put
\[
N=v_1+v_2+v_3.
\]
Then \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,p)\) and
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i=\frac{N}{3}.
\]

Because \(p>1/3\), one success is not enough:
\[
\frac13<p.
\]
Because \(p<1/2<2/3\), two successes are enough:
\[
\frac23\ge p.
\]
Thus
\[
\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right\}
=
\{N\ge2\}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[N\ge2].
\]
Since \(N\sim\operatorname{Bin}(3,p)\),
\[
\Pr[N\ge2]
=
\binom{3}{2}p^2(1-p)+p^3
=
3p^2(1-p)+p^3
=
p^2(3-2p).
\]
Now
\[
p-p^2(3-2p)
=
p(1-3p+2p^2)
=
p(1-p)(1-2p).
\]
For \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), the factors \(p\), \(1-p\), and \(1-2p\) are all positive. Hence
\[
p-p^2(3-2p)>0,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
p^2(3-2p)<p.
\]
Thus this choice of weights gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{3}w_i v_i\ge p\right]<p.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Failure for \(1/2<p<1\)]\label{prop:counterlarge}
For every
\[
p\in\left(\frac12,1\right),
\]
the assertion \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(p\in(1/2,1)\). Take
\[
m=2,\qquad w_1=w_2=\frac12,
\]
and let \(v_1,v_2\) be i.i.d. Bernoulli\((p)\) random variables. Put
\[
N=v_1+v_2.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i=\frac{N}{2}.
\]
Because \(p>1/2\), one success is not enough:
\[
\frac12<p.
\]
Since \(N\) can only take the values \(0,1,2\), the event
\[
\left\{\frac{N}{2}\ge p\right\}
\]
occurs only when \(N=2\), that is, when both \(v_1\) and \(v_2\) equal \(1\). Hence
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i\ge p\right]
=
\Pr[v_1=1,\ v_2=1].
\]
By independence,
\[
\Pr[v_1=1,\ v_2=1]=p^2.
\]
Since \(0<p<1\),
\[
p^2<p.
\]
Thus this choice of weights gives
\[
\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^{2}w_i v_i\ge p\right]<p.
\]
Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) fails.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Proof of the classification}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main}]
Proposition~\ref{prop:smallp} proves that \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds for every
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13].
\]
Proposition~\ref{prop:halfp} proves that \(\mathcal P(1/2)\) holds, and Proposition~\ref{prop:onep} proves that \(\mathcal P(1)\) holds. Hence
\[
\mathcal P(p)\quad\text{holds for every}\quad
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]

It remains to show that no other probability works. Since \(p\) is a probability, \(p\in[0,1]\). The complement of
\[
[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}
\]
inside \([0,1]\) is
\[
\left(\frac13,\frac12\right)\cup\left(\frac12,1\right).
\]
For every \(p\in(1/3,1/2)\), Proposition~\ref{prop:countermiddle} gives an explicit choice of weights for which the desired inequality fails. For every \(p\in(1/2,1)\), Proposition~\ref{prop:counterlarge} gives an explicit choice of weights for which the desired inequality fails.

Therefore \(\mathcal P(p)\) holds exactly for
\[
p\in[0,\tfrac13]\cup\{\tfrac12,1\}.
\]
This proves the theorem.
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The model arrives at the conjecturally correct range of probabilities $p$, but falsely claims a complete proof. The counterexamples for $p \in (1/3,1/2)$ and $p \in (1/2, 1)$ are presented correctly. The immediate cases of $p=0,1$ and the short argument via symmetry for $p=1/2$ are also noted. However, the proof of the remaining case $p \leq 1/3$ is reduced to two lemmas, neither of which follow from the provided citations, although the reduction is given correctly. Upon further inspection, the lemmas are plausible but proofs remain open to the best of my knowledge.

## Novelty.

The novelty of the argument is limited at best. The approach taken is rather naive, and after short manipulations the conclusion is made on the basis of two falsely cited references. (In hindsight, the main connection to the Manickam-Miklos-Singhi conjecture is not made.)

## Presentation.

The presentation of the paper is very bare bones. The paper includes some citations, there is no attempt at exposition, and the paper reads like a list of lemmas and algebraic manipulations. This may be due in part to the simplicity of the argument, which requires only a sequence of routine steps.
reviews.recommendation: I recommend a decision of rejection. While the argument does reduce the problem to two concrete lemmas, it is not clear that the lemmas are more approachable than the original question. This combined with the lack of novelty in the reduction leads to my recommendation.

## Correctness.

My recommendation is that the submission should be rejected. The proof attempt relies on two key inequalities, Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} and Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}. The main flaw lies precisely in these lemmas: the cited sources either do not contain the claimed statements, or it is not clear how the statements are meant to be derived from them.

Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} seems especially problematic. Neither of the two cited sources appears to contain a result resembling the claimed lemma. In fact, a quick search suggests that if the strict inequality in the lemma were replaced by a weak inequality, the statement would become a version of Cs{\'o}ka's conjecture (see \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06804}), which, to the best of my knowledge, remains open. This is the major flaw in the proof attempt.

Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial} is also not stated in the cited sources. The solution claims that it is classical and can be proved using Jogdeo and Samuels~\cite{JogdeoSamuels1968}. This is plausible, but it is not obvious how to obtain the lemma from that paper, and no explanation is provided.

The remaining argument, which reduces the problem to these two lemmas, appears to be correct.

## Novelty.

I would say that the novelty of this solution is low. Assuming the two lemmas, the reduction is immediate and should be regarded as the main contribution. Since the lemmas themselves already work with the same objects as the target statement, there does not seem to be much new content beyond this reduction.
inline_comments: It does not appear to me that either Hoeffding \cite{Hoeffding1956} or Pinelis \cite{Pinelis2016} implies Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding}. Moreover, \cite{Pinelis2016} does not contain a Corollary 3.7. In fact, a quick search suggests that Lemma~\ref{lem:hoeffding} is equivalent to Cs{\'o}ka's conjecture (see \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06804v4}). To the best of my knowledge this is still open. This is a major flaw of the attempt.

Jogdeo and Samuels \cite{JogdeoSamuels1968} prove a stronger result only in the special case where $n\theta$ is an integer. As stated, their paper does not contain Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}. It would not be surprising if the lemma could be derived, with additional work, from \cite[Theorem~2.1]{JogdeoSamuels1968} via monotonicty; however, no such derivation is provided and it remains unclear what is the source of Lemma~\ref{lem:binomial}.

\title{Submission D solution to Problem 3}
\date{}
\maketitle


\section*{Problem Statement}

Let $w_1, \ldots, w_m$ be non-negative real numbers such that $\sum_{i=1}^m w_i=1$, and let $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ be i.i.d.\ Bernoulli$(p)$ random variables. For which values of probability $p$ is it true that
\[\Pr\Big[\sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i\geq p\Big]\geq p?\]

\section*{Partial Solution}

\textit{Note: The following represents a partial solution to the problem. As noted at the end of the proof, sufficiency is fully established, but there remains a structural gap in proving the necessity for non-reciprocal values of $p$.}

\begin{theorem}
Let $w_1, \ldots, w_m$ be non-negative real numbers such that $\sum_{i=1}^m w_i = 1$, and let $v_1, \ldots, v_m$ be i.i.d.\ Bernoulli$(p)$ random variables. The inequality 
\[\Pr\Big[\sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i\geq p\Big]\geq p\]
holds for all valid weight distributions if and only if $p = 1/k$ for some integer $k \ge 1$ (or $p=0$).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For $p = 0$, the condition reduces to $\Pr[0 \ge 0] \ge 0$, which evaluates to $1 \ge 0$ and is trivially true.

Assume $p = 1/k$ for some integer $k \ge 1$. 
We construct $k$ coupled sequences of random variables $v_i^{(j)}$ for indices $i \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ and $j \in \{1, \dots, k\}$ as follows:
For each $i$, select an index $J_i$ uniformly at random from the set $\{1, \dots, k\}$, such that the choices $J_1, \ldots, J_m$ are mutually independent. 
Set $v_i^{(J_i)} = 1$, and set $v_i^{(j)} = 0$ for all $j \neq J_i$.

By this construction, for any fixed sequence index $j$, the variables $v_1^{(j)}, \ldots, v_m^{(j)}$ are independent Bernoulli$(1/k)$ random variables. 
Define $X^{(j)} = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i^{(j)}$. 
For each $j$, the random variable $X^{(j)}$ has the exact same distribution as the original sum $\sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i$.

Summing across all $k$ sequences yields:
\[\sum_{j=1}^k X^{(j)} = \sum_{j=1}^k \sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i^{(j)} = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \sum_{j=1}^k v_i^{(j)}\]
Since exactly one $v_i^{(j)} = 1$ for each $i$ (specifically when $j = J_i$), the inner sum $\sum_{j=1}^k v_i^{(j)}$ equals $1$ deterministically.
Thus,
\[\sum_{j=1}^k X^{(j)} = \sum_{i=1}^m w_i (1) = 1\]

Because the $k$ identically distributed random variables $X^{(j)}$ sum to exactly $1$, at least one of them must evaluate to $1/k$ or greater. 
Let $A_j$ be the event that $X^{(j)} \ge 1/k$. We have $\Pr\Big[\bigcup_{j=1}^k A_j\Big] = 1$.
By the union bound:
\[ 1 = \Pr\Big[\bigcup_{j=1}^k A_j\Big] \le \sum_{j=1}^k \Pr[A_j] = k \Pr\Big[X^{(1)} \ge \frac{1}{k}\Big] \]
Dividing by $k$ gives:
\[ \Pr\Big[\sum_{i=1}^m w_i v_i \ge \frac{1}{k}\Big] \ge \frac{1}{k} \]
This establishes sufficiency.

For values of $p \notin \{0\} \cup \{1/k \mid k \in \mathbb{Z}^+\}$, the inequality does not universally hold.

\vspace{\baselineskip}
\noindent\textbf{[Gap: The explicit construction of pathological weight distributions providing counterexamples for all non-reciprocal values of $p$ is structurally omitted.]}
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
The submission proves that the inequality holds for $p = 1/k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}$. The argument is the same as the argument of N. Alon, Y. Emek, M. Feldman, and M. Tennenholtz in their paper \textit{Adversarial Leakage in Games}. 

## Correctness.

The submission correctly proves the inequality for $p = 1/k$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}_{> 0}$ using a well-known proof without proper citation. The submission does not consider other values of $p$. 

## Novelty.

The presented argument appears in other work and is not cited.
reviews.recommendation: This submission should be rejected. It repeats a known argument without citation, and does not attempt to answer the question beyond this point.
inline_comments: This argument appears in work of N. Alon, Y. Emek, M. Feldman, and M. Tennenholtz.
There are more values of $p$ which satisfy the inequality universally.

## Correctness.

I recommend rejecting this submission. The proof of Theorem 1 is correct. However, it is essentially a direct replication of the simple coupling argument from the paper by Alon, Emek, Feldman, and Tennenholtz (see Remark on page 7 of \url{https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nalon/PDFS/leakage7.pdf}). The argument is not developed any further to yield meaningful progress on the problem. In particular, it does not rule out any values of $p$, and the submission ultimately arrives at an incorrect conjecture for the answer.

## Novelty.

None. The main argument is the same as the coupling argument in the paper cited above and does not contain any new ideas or insights.

\title{Submission A solution to Problem 4}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{center}
{\bf Partial proof: the first alternative and the remaining hard estimate}
\end{center}

\section*{Problem statement and interpretation}

I write the small universal constant in the problem as \(\kappa\), reserving
\(k\) for \(k\)-dilation.  Rectangles are oriented Euclidean products and
degree \(1\) means relative degree \(1\) on
\(H_4(R,\partial R;\mathbb Z)\to H_4(S,\partial S;\mathbb Z)\).

The current proof is complete through the first alternative and through a
conditional reduction of the hard case.  It is not a complete proof of the
stated dichotomy, because the averaged tightening estimate \((\mathrm{EAT})\)
below remains unproved.  The arguments are written for smooth transverse maps;
piecewise smooth maps may be treated by the same current-slicing argument, or
by smoothing on strata with an arbitrarily small \(C^1\)-loss and then
absorbing that loss into the universal constants.

\section*{Standard inputs}

All constants are positive and universal.  If \(\Dil_2(f)\le1\), then
\(\Dil_3(f),\Dil_4(f)\le1\): for singular values
\(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_4\), the inequality
\(\sigma_1\sigma_2\le1\) implies \(\sigma_2\le1\) and
\(\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_j\le\sigma_1\sigma_2\) for \(j\ge2\).

We use Guth's map-of-pairs estimate \cite[Estimate 1]{GuthExpanding}.  For
\(n=4,k=2,j=1,l=4\) it gives
\begin{equation}\label{guth14}
        R_1^2\,\Vol(R)\ge c_0\,S_1^3S_2S_3S_4 .
\end{equation}
We also use the small-volume relative isoperimetric estimate in rectangles
\cite[Theorem 3]{GuthExpanding}: if \(Z\) is a relative \(2\)-cycle in \(R\)
with \(A=\Mass Z\le c_*R_1R_2\), then
\[
        \Fill_R(Z)\le C_*\max\{A^{3/2},A^2/R_1\}.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{profile-inverse}
\Fill_R(Z)\ge L\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Mass Z\ge c\min\{R_1R_2,L^{2/3},(R_1L)^{1/2}\},
\end{equation}
and, after decreasing \(c_*\),
\begin{equation}\label{iso}
        \Mass Z<c_*R_1R_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
        \Fill_R(Z)\le C R_1R_2^2 .
\end{equation}

\section*{The first alternative}

Let \(Q\) be the concentric subrectangle of the \((x_3,x_4)\)-face of \(S\)
with side lengths \(S_3/2,S_4/2\), and set
\[
        P_y=[0,S_1]\times[0,S_2]\times\{y\},\qquad y\in Q.
\]

\begin{lemma}[central target plane]\label{central}
Every relative \(3\)-chain in \(S\) with boundary \(P_y\), \(y\in Q\), has
mass at least \(cS_1S_2S_3\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Choose a \(1\)-Lipschitz function \(\psi\) on the
\((x_3,x_4)\)-rectangle which vanishes on its boundary and satisfies
\(\psi\ge cS_3\) on \(Q\).  Put \(\beta=\psi\,dx_1\wedge dx_2\).  Then
\(d\beta\) has comass at most \(1\), and Stokes' theorem gives
\[
\Mass Y\ge\left|\int_Yd\beta\right|
 =\left|\int_{P_y}\beta\right|\ge cS_1S_2S_3 .
\]
The relative boundary terms vanish because \(dx_1\wedge dx_2=0\) on the
\(x_1,x_2\)-faces and \(\psi=0\) on the \(x_3,x_4\)-faces.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{firstalt}
There is \(c_2>0\) such that, under the hypotheses of the problem, if
\[
        R_1R_2^2\le c_2S_1S_2S_3 ,
\]
then \(R_3R_4\ge c_2S_3S_4\).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(T=[[R]]\) be the fundamental relative current and put \(F=(f_3,f_4)\).
Since \(f\) has relative degree \(1\), \(f_\#T=[[S]]\) as a relative
\(4\)-current.  For a.e. \(y\in Q\), slicing naturality gives
\[
        f_\#\langle T,F,y\rangle
        =\langle [[S]],(x_3,x_4),y\rangle=\pm P_y .
\]
Write \(Z_y=\langle T,F,y\rangle\).  Any relative filling of \(Z_y\) in \(R\)
pushes forward, using \(\Dil_3(f)\le1\), to a filling of \(P_y\) in \(S\).
Lemma \ref{central} therefore gives
\[
        \Fill_R(Z_y)\ge cS_1S_2S_3 .
\]
If \(c_2\) is sufficiently small, \eqref{iso} forces
\(\Mass Z_y\ge c_*R_1R_2\).  Since \(J_2F\le\Dil_2(f)\le1\), the coarea
formula yields
\[
 \Vol(R)\ge\int_Q\Mass Z_y\,dy
        \ge cR_1R_2S_3S_4 .
\]
Cancelling \(R_1R_2\) proves the proposition.
\end{proof}

\section*{The unconditional partial hard-case bound}

Assume \(R_1=\alpha S_1\le S_1\) and that the first conclusion fails with a
small constant.  Proposition \ref{firstalt} gives
\begin{equation}\label{r12large}
        R_1R_2^2\ge cS_1S_2S_3 .
\end{equation}
For the slices above, \eqref{profile-inverse} with
\(L=cS_1S_2S_3\) gives
\[
\Mass Z_y\ge c\min\{R_1R_2,(S_1S_2S_3)^{2/3},
                         (R_1S_1S_2S_3)^{1/2}\}.
\]
Using \eqref{r12large} and \(R_1=\alpha S_1\), every term in the minimum is
at least \(c\alpha^{1/2}S_1(S_2S_3)^{1/2}\).  Hence
\begin{equation}\label{slicevol}
        \Vol(R)\ge
        c\alpha^{1/2}S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4 .
\end{equation}
On the other hand, \eqref{guth14} gives
\begin{equation}\label{monovol}
        \Vol(R)\ge
        c\alpha^{-2}S_1S_2S_3S_4 .
\end{equation}
Optimizing between \eqref{slicevol} and \eqref{monovol} gives
\[
        \Vol(R)\ge cS_1S_2^{3/5}S_3^{7/5}S_4 .
\]
Thus the remaining gap is exactly the high-aspect factor
\((S_3/S_2)^{1/10}\).

\section*{A sufficient averaged hard-case estimate}

Let \(G=(f_1,f_2)\), keep \(F=(f_3,f_4)\), and define
\[
E_y=\int_{Z_y}\|dG|_{TZ_y}\|_{HS}^2\,d\|Z_y\|,\qquad
I=\int_QE_y\,dy,\qquad q=|Q|.
\]
At a regular point of \(F\), let \(K=\ker dF\), and let \(a\ge b\) be the
singular values of \(dF|_{K^\perp}\); then \(ab=J_2F\).  For any unit

unit vector with \(|dF(v)|=a\), has a component of norm
\(|dG(w)|a\).  Since \(\Dil_2(f)\le1\), \(|dG(w)|a\le1\), and hence
\(|dG(w)|^2J_2F\le b/a\le1\).  Summing over an orthonormal basis of \(K\)
gives
\[
        \|dG|_{\ker dF}\|_{HS}^2J_2F\le2 .
\]
By coarea,
\begin{equation}\label{Icoarea}
        I\le C\Vol(R).
\end{equation}
Let \(\Omega=\{y\in Q:E_y\le4I/q\}\), so \(|\Omega|\ge3q/4\).

For real normal currents define
\[
\EFill_f(y)=\inf\{\Mass C:\ C\in N_3(R,\partial R;\mathbb R),\
        f_\#(\partial C)=\pm P_y\}.
\]
This class is nonempty by filling the actual slice \(Z_y\).  If \(C\) is
admissible, then \(f_\#C\) fills \(P_y\) and \(\Mass(f_\#C)\le\Mass C\);
Lemma \ref{central} gives
\begin{equation}\label{EFilllower}
        \EFill_f(y)\ge cS_1S_2S_3 .
\end{equation}
Therefore
\begin{equation}\label{AElower}
A_\Omega:=\int_\Omega\EFill_f(y)\,dy
        \ge cS_1S_2S_3\,q
        \ge cS_1S_2S_3^2S_4 .
\end{equation}

\(z\) belongs to the \(F\)-image of at least one coordinate \(2\)-plaque

and \(J_2F\le1\) on each plaque.  Hence, for every normal \(3\)-current \(B\),

\end{equation}

near-minimizers \(C_y^0\) with
\(\Mass C_y^0\le2\EFill_f(y)\); standard measurable selection in the
separable flat topology, or equivalently outer integration with
\(\varepsilon\)-minimizers, is enough for this formal step.  One needs
\begin{equation}\tag{EAT}\label{EAT}
 A_\Omega
 \le C\left(R_1I+\frac{I^2}{S_1q}\right)
 +\frac{C}{q}\int_Q\int_\Omega
       \Mass(C_y^0\llcorner{\mathcal B}_z)\,dy\,dz .
\end{equation}

\(\Mass C_y^0\le2\EFill_f(y)\) give
\[
A_\Omega\le C\left(R_1I+\frac{I^2}{S_1q}\right)
  +C\frac{R_3R_4}{S_3S_4}A_\Omega .
\]

\(\kappa\) small.  If also \(R_1\le\kappa S_1\) and
\(I\le\delta S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4\), then, since \(q\sim S_3S_4\),
\[
R_1I\le C\kappa\delta S_1S_2S_3^2S_4,\qquad
\frac{I^2}{S_1q}\le C\delta^2S_1S_2S_3^2S_4 .
\]
For small \(\delta,\kappa\) this contradicts \eqref{AElower}.  Thus
\(I\ge cS_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4\), and \eqref{Icoarea} gives the desired
second alternative.

\section*{Why the remaining estimate is non-routine}

The estimate \eqref{EAT} cannot be obtained by a standard source-local
cellular deformation in the quotient by \(f\)-null chains without a new idea.
The obstruction is already visible in a two-cell model.  Let \(A,A'\) be two
oriented \(2\)-cells with \(f_\#A=f_\#A'=P\).  Then \(N=A-A'\in\ker f_\#\).
If an exact-plaque bad set contains \(A\) but not \(A'\), the source-local
projection \(P_{\rm bad}\) with \(P_{\rm bad}A=A\), \(P_{\rm bad}A'=0\) gives
\(f_\#P_{\rm bad}N=P\ne0\).  Dually, a quotient cochain has equal values on
\(A\) and \(A'\), but restricting it to the nonsaturated bad set destroys that
property.  Thus exact source localization and quotient invariance are in
tension.

This does not disprove \eqref{EAT}; it identifies what is missing.  A proof

cochain homotopy whose residual term is nevertheless controlled by the
unsaturated exact-plaque mass in \eqref{badfubini}.

\item The essential mathematical gap is \eqref{EAT}, an averaged tightening
estimate for the degree-carrying part of the slices \(Z_y\).  It is used only
in the last section, but it is indispensable for the high-aspect hard case.

\item The first alternative, the single-slice bound, the weighted coarea
estimate, the essential filling lower bound, the exact-plaque Fubini estimate,
and the absorption algebra are proved above.

\item Standard approaches tried so far do not close the gap: monomial

reviews.review_summary:
This submission makes some partial progress on the question. 
It divides the original problem into an `easy' case and a `hard' case and proves the easy case. It also proves a weaker estimate in the hard case. 

## Correctness.
 The proofs in this submission are correct. There is one place where there is either a small error or bad writing, but it can be fixed easily. 

## Novelty.

I think there is some novelty in the submission. The paper uses tools and ideas from the paper ``Area-expanding embeddings of rectangles,'' which it cites. It also adapts some of the proof ideas from that paper to a somewhat different situation. In the original paper, the argument pushes forward chains from the domain to the range, and uses the isoperimetric inequality in the range. In this submission, the argument pulls back chains from the range to the domain and uses the isoperimetric inequality in the domain. This is the most novel ingredient in the submission. It also gathers together a few known results from the literature and combines the information from these known results.

This submission contains some of the ideas in the author's solution, but not the most novel idea in the solution.
reviews.recommendation:
I don't think that this submission fits cleanly into the four categories provided. It does not claim to solve the whole problem but only to make partial progress. The proofs here are correct and could be published with minor clarification.

The partial work here makes some progress towards answering the question, but on the other hand, the most novel and important idea in the solution is missing.

On this basis, I recommend `major revisions', because some meaningful progress has been made, but it would still require major additional work to answer the question posed.

conditional reduction of the hard case.  It is not a complete proof of the

\(\sigma_1\cdots\sigma_j\le\sigma_1\sigma_2\) for \(j\ge2\).

\]

\begin{equation}\label{profile-inverse}
\Fill_R(Z)\ge L\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\Mass Z\ge c\min\{R_1R_2,L^{2/3},(R_1L)^{1/2}\},
\end{equation}
and, after decreasing \(c_*\),
\begin{equation}\label{iso}
        \Mass Z<c_*R_1R_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
        \Fill_R(Z)\le C R_1R_2^2 .
\end{equation}

mass at least \(cS_1S_2S_3\).
\end{lemma}

Choose a \(1\)-Lipschitz function \(\psi\) on the
\((x_3,x_4)\)-rectangle which vanishes on its boundary and satisfies
\(\psi\ge cS_3\) on \(Q\).  Put \(\beta=\psi\,dx_1\wedge dx_2\).  Then
\(d\beta\) has comass at most \(1\), and Stokes' theorem gives
\[
\Mass Y\ge\left|\int_Yd\beta\right|
 =\left|\int_{P_y}\beta\right|\ge cS_1S_2S_3 .
\]
The relative boundary terms vanish because \(dx_1\wedge dx_2=0\) on the
\(x_1,x_2\)-faces and \(\psi=0\) on the \(x_3,x_4\)-faces.

[Reviewer comment: The last justification is either a small error or bad writing, though it is easily fixed.  The form \(dx_1 \wedge dx_2\) vanishes on all faces except those in the \(x_1, x_2\) direction, and \(\psi\) vanishes on those faces.  Possibly it writes $x_1$-face to mean a face where $x_1$ is constant, but this is unclear writing and not consistent with the convention above, where it says that $Q$ is in the \((x_3,x_4)\) face of S.]
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{firstalt}
There is \(c_2>0\) such that, under the hypotheses of the problem, if
\[
        R_1R_2^2\le c_2S_1S_2S_3 ,
\]
then \(R_3R_4\ge c_2S_3S_4\).
\end{proposition}

Let \(T=[[R]]\) be the fundamental relative current and put \(F=(f_3,f_4)\).
Since \(f\) has relative degree \(1\), \(f_\#T=[[S]]\) as a relative
\(4\)-current.  For a.e. \(y\in Q\), slicing naturality gives
\[

        =\langle [[S]],(x_3,x_4),y\rangle=\pm P_y .
\]
Write \(Z_y=\langle T,F,y\rangle\).  Any relative filling of \(Z_y\) in \(R\)

\[

\end{equation}

Thus the remaining gap is exactly the high-aspect factor

## Correctness.

The argument solves a special case of the problem, (Proposition 1) showing that there is a $c_2$ such that if $R_1R_2^2 \le c_2 S_1 S_2 S_3$, then $R_3 R_4 \ge c_2 S_3 S_4$. This is a good start and seems to be correct. The argument goes on to show a weaker bound that's off by a factor of $(S_3/S_2)^{\frac{1}{10}}$. It tries to prove the full bound, but I don't think it makes much progress. Ultimately, it states an inequality (EAT) which would solve the problem if it were true, but it doesn't give any justification for why this inequality should be true or should be easier to prove. 

## Novelty.

The first part of the argument (the proof of Proposition 1) uses an isoperimetric inequality of Guth to derive lower bounds on the mass of some fibers of $F$. This is similar to arguments in Guth's paper ``Area-expanding embeddings of rectangles.'' 

The second part of the argument (``A sufficient averaged hard-case estimate'') introduces some new ideas (the integrals $E_y$ and $I$ and the set $\mathcal{B}_z$) but it doesn't get far enough to demonstrate that these ideas are useful or explain how they are relevant to the problem.

\section*{Theorem (fiber-filling and coarea reduction)}

Let
\[
R=\prod_{i=1}^4[0,R_i],\qquad S=\prod_{i=1}^4[0,S_i],
\]
with \(0<R_1\le R_2\le R_3\le R_4\) and \(0<S_1\le S_2\le S_3\le S_4\). Orient \(S\) by
\[
dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3\wedge dx_4.
\]
Write
\[
Q=[0,S_1]\times[0,S_2],\qquad B=[0,S_3]\times[0,S_4],
\]
so \(S=Q\times B\), and orient \(Q\) and \(B\) by \(dx_1\wedge dx_2\) and \(dx_3\wedge dx_4\), respectively. Let
\[
\pi:S\to B,\qquad \pi(x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(x_3,x_4),
\]
and suppose
\[
f:(R,\partial R)\to(S,\partial S)
\]
is a Lipschitz finite piecewise smooth map of degree \(1\) with \(\operatorname{Dil}_2(f)\le 1\). Put
\[
F=\pi\circ f=(f_3,f_4),\qquad G=(f_1,f_2).
\]

For \(y\in B\), set
\[
P_y=Q\times\{y\}.
\]
Use the slicing convention normalized by
\[
\langle \llbracket Q\times B\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle
=
\llbracket Q\times\{y\}\rrbracket .
\]

Then for a.e. \(y\in \operatorname{int}B\), the slice
\[
z_y=\langle \llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle
\]
is a relative integral \(2\)-cycle in \((R,\partial R)\), and
\[
f_\# z_y=\llbracket P_y\rrbracket .
\]
Consequently,
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)
=S_1S_2\,\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]

Moreover,
\[
\int_B \operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy\le \operatorname{Vol}(R).
\]

Finally, let
\[
B_0=\left[\frac{S_3}{3},\frac{2S_3}{3}\right]\times
\left[\frac{S_4}{3},\frac{2S_4}{3}\right].
\]
At points where \(dF\) has rank \(2\), let
\[
\sigma_1(x)\ge \sigma_2(x)>0
\]
be the two nonzero singular values of \(dF_x\). Define the measure
\[
d\mu=\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\,dx
\]
on the rank-two set of \(dF\), and \(d\mu=0\) where \(\operatorname{rank}dF<2\). Then
\[
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))\ge \frac19 S_1S_2S_3S_4
\]
and
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu.
\]

Thus, if in addition one has an estimate
\[
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\]
for some constant \(c_d>0\), then
\[
R_1R_2R_3R_4
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]

\subsection*{Proof}

Write \(\mathbf M(T)\) for the mass of an integral current \(T\), and write \(\llbracket X\rrbracket\) for the integral current associated to an oriented Lipschitz manifold or rectangle \(X\).

For a compact rectangle \(X\), if \(Z\in \mathbf I_m(X)\) satisfies \(\operatorname{spt}\partial Z\subset \partial X\), define its relative filling volume by
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_X(Z)
=
\inf\left\{
\mathbf M(Y):
Y\in \mathbf I_{m+1}(X),\
\operatorname{spt}(\partial Y-Z)\subset \partial X
\right\}.
\]

We use the standard slicing theorem for integral currents: if \(T\in \mathbf I_m\) and \(\Phi\) is Lipschitz into \(\mathbb R^k\), then for a.e. \(a\), the slice \(\langle T,\Phi,a\rangle\in \mathbf I_{m-k}\) exists and
\[
\partial\langle T,\Phi,a\rangle
=
\pm \langle \partial T,\Phi,a\rangle.
\]
We also use slicing naturality: for Lipschitz \(H\),
\[
H_\#\langle T,\Phi\circ H,a\rangle
=
\langle H_\#T,\Phi,a\rangle
\]
for a.e. \(a\). Finally, we use the rectifiable-current area inequality
\[
\mathbf M(H_\#T)
\le
\int J_k(dH|_{\operatorname{Tan}T})\,d\|T\|
\]
for \(T\in\mathbf I_k\).

First prove the fundamental current identity
\[
f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket=\llbracket S\rrbracket .
\]
Let
\[
T=f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket.
\]
Since \(f\) is Lipschitz, \(T\in\mathbf I_4(S)\), and
\[
\partial T=f_\#\partial\llbracket R\rrbracket
\]
is supported in \(f(\partial R)\subset \partial S\). Hence, in \(\operatorname{int}S\),
\[
\partial(T\llcorner \operatorname{int}S)=0.
\]
By the constancy theorem on the connected open set \(\operatorname{int}S\),
\[
T\llcorner \operatorname{int}S
=
m\,\llbracket \operatorname{int}S\rrbracket
\]
for some \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Therefore \(T-m\llbracket S\rrbracket\) is supported in \(\partial S\). Since \(\partial S\) has \(\mathcal H^4\)-measure zero, no nonzero integral \(4\)-current can be supported there, so
\[
T=m\llbracket S\rrbracket.
\]
Because \(f\) has degree \(1\), \(T\) represents the relative fundamental class \([S,\partial S]\), hence \(m=1\). Thus
\[
f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket=\llbracket S\rrbracket .
\]

Now apply slicing to \(F=\pi\circ f\). For a.e. \(y\in\operatorname{int}B\),
\[
z_y=\langle \llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle
\]
is an integral \(2\)-current, and
\[
\partial z_y
=
\pm \langle \partial\llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle,
\]
so \(\partial z_y\) is supported in \(\partial R\). Hence \(z_y\) is a relative integral \(2\)-cycle in \((R,\partial R)\).

By slicing naturality,
\[
f_\# z_y
=
f_\#\langle \llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle
=
\langle f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle
=
\langle \llbracket S\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle .
\]
With the stated product orientation and slice convention,
\[
\langle \llbracket S\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle
=
\llbracket Q\times\{y\}\rrbracket
=
\llbracket P_y\rrbracket.
\]
Thus
\[
f_\#z_y=\llbracket P_y\rrbracket.
\]

Next, \(\operatorname{Dil}_2(f)\le 1\) implies \(\operatorname{Dil}_3(f)\le 1\). Indeed, at a differentiability point of \(f\), let
\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge a_3\ge a_4\ge 0
\]
be the singular values of \(df\). The hypothesis gives \(a_1a_2\le 1\). Hence \(a_2\le 1\), so \(a_3\le 1\), and therefore
\[
a_1a_2a_3\le a_1a_2\le 1.
\]
Thus \(\|\Lambda^3df\|\le 1\) a.e.

Let \(Y\in \mathbf I_3(R)\) be a relative filling of \(z_y\), so
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\partial Y-z_y)\subset \partial R.
\]
Then
\[
\partial(f_\#Y)-f_\#z_y
=
f_\#(\partial Y-z_y)
\]
is supported in \(f(\partial R)\subset \partial S\). Since \(f_\#z_y=\llbracket P_y\rrbracket\), the current \(f_\#Y\) is a relative filling of \(P_y\) in \(S\). Also,
\[
\mathbf M(f_\#Y)\le \int \|\Lambda^3df\|\,d\|Y\|\le \mathbf M(Y).
\]
Taking the infimum over all such \(Y\) gives
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y).
\]

It remains to compute \(\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\). Let
\[
\delta(y)=\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]
For the upper bound, choose a shortest segment \(\gamma\subset B\) from \(\partial B\) to \(y\), oriented toward \(y\). Then
\[
C=\llbracket Q\rrbracket\times \llbracket \gamma\rrbracket
\]
is a relative filling of \(P_y\) in \(S\), and
\[
\mathbf M(C)=S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Hence
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\le S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]

For the lower bound, define
\[
\delta(q)=\operatorname{dist}(q,\partial B)
=
\min\{q_3,S_3-q_3,q_4,S_4-q_4\}.
\]
For \(\eta>0\), set
\[
m_\eta(q)
=
-\eta\log\left(
e^{-q_3/\eta}
+
e^{-(S_3-q_3)/\eta}
+
e^{-q_4/\eta}
+
e^{-(S_4-q_4)/\eta}
\right).
\]
Then
\[
\delta(q)-\eta\log 4\le m_\eta(q)\le \delta(q),
\qquad
|\nabla m_\eta(q)|\le 1.
\]
Choose a smooth function \(\chi_\eta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\chi_\eta(t)=0\quad\text{for }t\le 0,\qquad
0\le \chi_\eta'(t)\le 1,\qquad
\chi_\eta(t)\ge t-\eta\quad\text{for }t\ge 0.
\]
Set
\[
\rho_\eta(q)=\chi_\eta(m_\eta(q)).
\]
Then \(\rho_\eta\) is smooth,
\[
\rho_\eta=0\quad\text{on }\partial B,\qquad |d\rho_\eta|\le 1,
\]
and for every fixed \(y\in\operatorname{int}B\),
\[
\rho_\eta(y)\to \delta(y)
\qquad\text{as }\eta\to 0.
\]

Define the smooth \(2\)-form
\[
\alpha_\eta=\rho_\eta(x_3,x_4)\,dx_1\wedge dx_2.
\]
It restricts to zero on \(\partial S\): on the \(x_1\)- and \(x_2\)-faces because \(dx_1\wedge dx_2\) vanishes there, and on the \(x_3\)- and \(x_4\)-faces because \(\rho_\eta=0\) on \(\partial B\).

Let \(Y\in\mathbf I_3(S)\) be any relative filling of \(P_y\), so
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\partial Y-\llbracket P_y\rrbracket)\subset \partial S.
\]
Since \(\alpha_\eta\) vanishes on \(\partial S\),
\[
\partial Y(\alpha_\eta)
=
\llbracket P_y\rrbracket(\alpha_\eta)
=
\rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
By Stokes’ theorem for currents,
\[
Y(d\alpha_\eta)=\rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
But
\[
d\alpha_\eta=d\rho_\eta\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2,
\]
whose comass is at most \(|d\rho_\eta|\le 1\). Therefore
\[
\mathbf M(Y)\ge \rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
Letting \(\eta\to 0\) gives
\[
\mathbf M(Y)\ge S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Taking the infimum over \(Y\),
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\ge S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)=S_1S_2\,\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]

In particular, for \(y\in B_0\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B)\ge \frac{S_3}{3},
\]
because \(S_4\ge S_3\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \frac13 S_1S_2S_3.
\]

Now apply the coarea formula to the Lipschitz map \(F:R\to B\). For every nonnegative Borel function \(g\),
\[
\int_B\int_{F^{-1}(y)} g\,d\mathcal H^2\,dy
=
\int_R g\,J_2F\,dx,
\]
where
\[
J_2F=\|\Lambda^2 dF\|.
\]
For a.e. \(y\), the mass of the slice \(z_y\) is \(\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\), so with \(g=1\),
\[
\int_B \operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_R J_2F\,dx.
\]
Since \(F=\pi\circ f\) and \(\pi\) is an orthogonal projection,
\[
J_2F\le \|\Lambda^2df\|\le 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_B \operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\le
\operatorname{Vol}(R).
\]

It remains to prove the two estimates involving \(\mu\). Fix a regular value \(y\in B_0\), and let \(x\in z_y\) be a point where \(f\) is differentiable and \(dF_x\) has rank \(2\). Then
\[
T_xz_y=\ker dF_x.
\]
Let
\[
N_x=(T_xz_y)^\perp.
\]
The restriction \(dF_x|_{N_x}:N_x\to\mathbb R^2\) has singular values \(\sigma_1(x)\ge \sigma_2(x)>0\).

Choose a unit vector \(n\in N_x\) such that
\[
|dF_x(n)|=\sigma_1(x).
\]
For any unit vector \(v\in T_xz_y\), one has \(dF_x(v)=0\). Since
\[
df_x=(dG_x,dF_x),
\]
we get
\[
df_x(v)=(dG_x(v),0),
\qquad
df_x(n)=(dG_x(n),dF_x(n)).
\]
In the orthogonal splitting \(\mathbb R^4=\mathbb R^2_Q\oplus\mathbb R^2_B\), the mixed \(Q\wedge B\) component of
\[
df_x(v)\wedge df_x(n)
\]
is
\[
dG_x(v)\wedge dF_x(n),
\]
whose norm is
\[
|dG_x(v)|\,|dF_x(n)|
=
|dG_x(v)|\,\sigma_1(x).
\]
This mixed component has norm at most the norm of the full wedge. Therefore, using \(\operatorname{Dil}_2(f)\le 1\),
\[
|dG_x(v)|\,\sigma_1(x)
\le
|df_x(v)\wedge df_x(n)|
\le 1.
\]
Hence
\[
|dG_x(v)|\le \sigma_1(x)^{-1}.
\]
Taking the supremum over unit \(v\in T_xz_y\),
\[
\|dG_x|_{T_xz_y}\|\le \sigma_1(x)^{-1}.
\]
Since \(T_xz_y\) is two-dimensional,
\[
J_2(G|_{T_xz_y})\le \sigma_1(x)^{-2}.
\]

Let \(p_Q:S\to Q\) be the projection onto the first two coordinates. Since \(G=p_Q\circ f\), for a.e. \(y\in B_0\),
\[
G_\#z_y
=
(p_Q)_\# f_\#z_y
=
(p_Q)_\#\llbracket P_y\rrbracket
=
\llbracket Q\rrbracket.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_1S_2
=
\mathbf M(\llbracket Q\rrbracket)
=
\mathbf M(G_\#z_y)
\le
\int_{z_y}J_2(G|_{Tz_y})\,dA
\le
\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA.
\]
Integrating over \(B_0\),
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
\ge
S_1S_2\,|B_0|
=
\frac19 S_1S_2S_3S_4.
\]

Now define
\[
\widetilde g(x)
=
\sigma_1(x)^{-2}\,
\mathbf 1_{F^{-1}(B_0)\cap\{\operatorname{rank}dF=2\}}(x).
\]
For \(M>0\), set \(g_M=\min\{\widetilde g,M\}\). By the coarea formula,
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y} g_M\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}g_M\,J_2F\,dx.
\]
Letting \(M\to\infty\) and using monotone convergence,
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)\cap\{\operatorname{rank}dF=2\}}
\sigma_1^{-2}J_2F\,dx.
\]
On the rank-two set,
\[
J_2F=\sigma_1\sigma_2.
\]
Thus
\[
\sigma_1^{-2}J_2F
=
\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\,dx
=
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0)).
\]
Combining this with the previous inequality gives
\[
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\ge
\frac19 S_1S_2S_3S_4.
\]

Finally, applying the ordinary coarea formula over \(B_0\),
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}J_2F\,dx.
\]
On the rank-two set,
\[
J_2F=\sigma_1\sigma_2
=
\sigma_1^2\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1},
\]
while both sides vanish on the rank \(<2\) set. Therefore
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu.
\]

Assume now that
\[
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0)).
\]
Then
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2S_3S_4
\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}.
\]
Since
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(R)
\ge
\int_B\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\ge
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy,
\]
we obtain
\[
R_1R_2R_3R_4
=
\operatorname{Vol}(R)
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]

This completes the proof.

{ Instead of the theorem in the problem, this submission wrote down a different theorem and then proved it. This different theorem follows from standard facts in a fairly easy way. It does not require the main mathematical ideas in the solution of the actual problem.

The submission does correctly explain some standard facts that are relevant to the problem. But it does not make real progress on the question asked.

}

## Correctness.
 The submission states a different theorem than the one in the problem. The proof of the different theorem is correct. There is one place where there is either a small error or some bad writing, but it can be fixed easily.

There are also some issues with the organization of the writing. The statement of the theorem is very long, and some of the statement should really be moved to the proof. Some parts of the argument are never used and could be omitted. On the other hand, on a line-by-line basis, the writing is clear.

## Novelty.
 
I don't see anything novel in the proof. The ingredients are standard.

\partial(T\llcorner \operatorname{int}S)=0.
\]
By the constancy theorem on the connected open set \(\operatorname{int}S\),
\[
T\llcorner \operatorname{int}S
=
m\,\llbracket \operatorname{int}S\rrbracket
\]
for some \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Therefore \(T-m\llbracket S\rrbracket\) is supported in \(\partial S\). Since \(\partial S\) has \(\mathcal H^4\)-measure zero, no nonzero integral \(4\)-current can be supported there, so
\[
T=m\llbracket S\rrbracket.
\]
Because \(f\) has degree \(1\), \(T\) represents the relative fundamental class \([S,\partial S]\), hence \(m=1\). Thus
\[
f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket=\llbracket S\rrbracket .
\]

Now apply slicing to \(F=\pi\circ f\). For a.e. \(y\in\operatorname{int}B\),
\[
z_y=\langle \llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle
\]
is an integral \(2\)-current, and
\[
\partial z_y
=
\pm \langle \partial\llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle,
\]
so \(\partial z_y\) is supported in \(\partial R\). Hence \(z_y\) is a relative integral \(2\)-cycle in \((R,\partial R)\).

By slicing naturality,
\[
f_\# z_y
=
f_\#\langle \llbracket R\rrbracket,F,y\rangle
=
\langle f_\#\llbracket R\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle
=
\langle \llbracket S\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle .
\]
With the stated product orientation and slice convention,
\[
\langle \llbracket S\rrbracket,\pi,y\rangle
=
\llbracket Q\times\{y\}\rrbracket
=
\llbracket P_y\rrbracket.
\]
Thus
\[
f_\#z_y=\llbracket P_y\rrbracket.
\]

Next, \(\operatorname{Dil}_2(f)\le 1\) implies \(\operatorname{Dil}_3(f)\le 1\). Indeed, at a differentiability point of \(f\), let
\[
a_1\ge a_2\ge a_3\ge a_4\ge 0
\]
be the singular values of \(df\). The hypothesis gives \(a_1a_2\le 1\). Hence \(a_2\le 1\), so \(a_3\le 1\), and therefore
\[
a_1a_2a_3\le a_1a_2\le 1.
\]
Thus \(\|\Lambda^3df\|\le 1\) a.e.

Let \(Y\in \mathbf I_3(R)\) be a relative filling of \(z_y\), so
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\partial Y-z_y)\subset \partial R.
\]
Then
\[
\partial(f_\#Y)-f_\#z_y
=
f_\#(\partial Y-z_y)
\]
is supported in \(f(\partial R)\subset \partial S\). Since \(f_\#z_y=\llbracket P_y\rrbracket\), the current \(f_\#Y\) is a relative filling of \(P_y\) in \(S\). Also,
\[
\mathbf M(f_\#Y)\le \int \|\Lambda^3df\|\,d\|Y\|\le \mathbf M(Y).
\]
Taking the infimum over all such \(Y\) gives
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y).
\]

It remains to compute \(\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\). Let
\[
\delta(y)=\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]
For the upper bound, choose a shortest segment \(\gamma\subset B\) from \(\partial B\) to \(y\), oriented toward \(y\). Then
\[
C=\llbracket Q\rrbracket\times \llbracket \gamma\rrbracket
\]
is a relative filling of \(P_y\) in \(S\), and
\[
\mathbf M(C)=S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Hence
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\le S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]

For the lower bound, define
\[
\delta(q)=\operatorname{dist}(q,\partial B)
=
\min\{q_3,S_3-q_3,q_4,S_4-q_4\}.
\]
For \(\eta>0\), set
\[
m_\eta(q)
=
-\eta\log\left(
e^{-q_3/\eta}
+
e^{-(S_3-q_3)/\eta}
+
e^{-q_4/\eta}
+
e^{-(S_4-q_4)/\eta}
\right).
\]
Then
\[
\delta(q)-\eta\log 4\le m_\eta(q)\le \delta(q),
\qquad
|\nabla m_\eta(q)|\le 1.
\]
Choose a smooth function \(\chi_\eta:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) such that
\[
\chi_\eta(t)=0\quad\text{for }t\le 0,\qquad
0\le \chi_\eta'(t)\le 1,\qquad
\chi_\eta(t)\ge t-\eta\quad\text{for }t\ge 0.
\]
Set
\[
\rho_\eta(q)=\chi_\eta(m_\eta(q)).
\]
Then \(\rho_\eta\) is smooth,
\[
\rho_\eta=0\quad\text{on }\partial B,\qquad |d\rho_\eta|\le 1,
\]
and for every fixed \(y\in\operatorname{int}B\),
\[
\rho_\eta(y)\to \delta(y)
\qquad\text{as }\eta\to 0.
\]

Define the smooth \(2\)-form
\[
\alpha_\eta=\rho_\eta(x_3,x_4)\,dx_1\wedge dx_2.
\]
It restricts to zero on \(\partial S\): on the \(x_1\)- and \(x_2\)-faces because \(dx_1\wedge dx_2\) vanishes there, and on the \(x_3\)- and \(x_4\)-faces because \(\rho_\eta=0\) on \(\partial B\).

Let \(Y\in\mathbf I_3(S)\) be any relative filling of \(P_y\), so
\[
\operatorname{spt}(\partial Y-\llbracket P_y\rrbracket)\subset \partial S.
\]
Since \(\alpha_\eta\) vanishes on \(\partial S\),
\[
\partial Y(\alpha_\eta)
=
\llbracket P_y\rrbracket(\alpha_\eta)
=
\rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
By Stokes’ theorem for currents,
\[
Y(d\alpha_\eta)=\rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
But
\[
d\alpha_\eta=d\rho_\eta\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2,
\]
whose comass is at most \(|d\rho_\eta|\le 1\). Therefore
\[
\mathbf M(Y)\ge \rho_\eta(y)S_1S_2.
\]
Letting \(\eta\to 0\) gives
\[
\mathbf M(Y)\ge S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Taking the infimum over \(Y\),
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)\ge S_1S_2\,\delta(y).
\]
Thus
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)=S_1S_2\,\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]

In particular, for \(y\in B_0\),
\[
\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B)\ge \frac{S_3}{3},
\]
because \(S_4\ge S_3\). Hence
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \frac13 S_1S_2S_3.
\]

Now apply the coarea formula to the Lipschitz map \(F:R\to B\). For every nonnegative Borel function \(g\),
\[
\int_B\int_{F^{-1}(y)} g\,d\mathcal H^2\,dy
=
\int_R g\,J_2F\,dx,
\]
where
\[
J_2F=\|\Lambda^2 dF\|.
\]
For a.e. \(y\), the mass of the slice \(z_y\) is \(\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\), so with \(g=1\),
\[
\int_B \operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_R J_2F\,dx.
\]
Since \(F=\pi\circ f\) and \(\pi\) is an orthogonal projection,
\[
J_2F\le \|\Lambda^2df\|\le 1.
\]
Therefore
\[
\int_B \operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\le
\operatorname{Vol}(R).
\]

It remains to prove the two estimates involving \(\mu\). Fix a regular value \(y\in B_0\), and let \(x\in z_y\) be a point where \(f\) is differentiable and \(dF_x\) has rank \(2\). Then
\[
T_xz_y=\ker dF_x.
\]
Let
\[
N_x=(T_xz_y)^\perp.
\]
The restriction \(dF_x|_{N_x}:N_x\to\mathbb R^2\) has singular values \(\sigma_1(x)\ge \sigma_2(x)>0\).

Choose a unit vector \(n\in N_x\) such that
\[
|dF_x(n)|=\sigma_1(x).
\]
For any unit vector \(v\in T_xz_y\), one has \(dF_x(v)=0\). Since
\[
df_x=(dG_x,dF_x),
\]
we get
\[
df_x(v)=(dG_x(v),0),
\qquad
df_x(n)=(dG_x(n),dF_x(n)).
\]
In the orthogonal splitting \(\mathbb R^4=\mathbb R^2_Q\oplus\mathbb R^2_B\), the mixed \(Q\wedge B\) component of
\[
df_x(v)\wedge df_x(n)
\]
is
\[
dG_x(v)\wedge dF_x(n),
\]
whose norm is
\[
|dG_x(v)|\,|dF_x(n)|
=
|dG_x(v)|\,\sigma_1(x).
\]
This mixed component has norm at most the norm of the full wedge. Therefore, using \(\operatorname{Dil}_2(f)\le 1\),
\[
|dG_x(v)|\,\sigma_1(x)
\le
|df_x(v)\wedge df_x(n)|
\le 1.
\]
Hence
\[
|dG_x(v)|\le \sigma_1(x)^{-1}.
\]
Taking the supremum over unit \(v\in T_xz_y\),
\[
\|dG_x|_{T_xz_y}\|\le \sigma_1(x)^{-1}.
\]
Since \(T_xz_y\) is two-dimensional,
\[
J_2(G|_{T_xz_y})\le \sigma_1(x)^{-2}.
\]

Let \(p_Q:S\to Q\) be the projection onto the first two coordinates. Since \(G=p_Q\circ f\), for a.e. \(y\in B_0\),
\[
G_\#z_y
=
(p_Q)_\# f_\#z_y
=
(p_Q)_\#\llbracket P_y\rrbracket
=
\llbracket Q\rrbracket.
\]
Therefore
\[
S_1S_2
=
\mathbf M(\llbracket Q\rrbracket)
=
\mathbf M(G_\#z_y)
\le
\int_{z_y}J_2(G|_{Tz_y})\,dA
\le
\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA.
\]
Integrating over \(B_0\),
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
\ge
S_1S_2\,|B_0|
=
\frac19 S_1S_2S_3S_4.
\]

Now define
\[
\widetilde g(x)
=
\sigma_1(x)^{-2}\,
\mathbf 1_{F^{-1}(B_0)\cap\{\operatorname{rank}dF=2\}}(x).
\]
For \(M>0\), set \(g_M=\min\{\widetilde g,M\}\). By the coarea formula,
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y} g_M\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}g_M\,J_2F\,dx.
\]
Letting \(M\to\infty\) and using monotone convergence,
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)\cap\{\operatorname{rank}dF=2\}}
\sigma_1^{-2}J_2F\,dx.
\]
On the rank-two set,
\[
J_2F=\sigma_1\sigma_2.
\]
Thus
\[
\sigma_1^{-2}J_2F
=
\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}.
\]
Hence
\[
\int_{B_0}\int_{z_y}\sigma_1^{-2}\,dA\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}\,dx
=
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0)).
\]
Combining this with the previous inequality gives
\[
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\ge
\frac19 S_1S_2S_3S_4.
\]

Finally, applying the ordinary coarea formula over \(B_0\),
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}J_2F\,dx.
\]
On the rank-two set,
\[
J_2F=\sigma_1\sigma_2
=
\sigma_1^2\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1},
\]
while both sides vanish on the rank \(<2\) set. Therefore
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
=
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu.
\]

Assume now that
\[
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0)).
\]
Then
\[
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2S_3S_4
\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}.
\]
Since
\[
\operatorname{Vol}(R)
\ge
\int_B\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy
\ge
\int_{B_0}\operatorname{Area}(z_y)\,dy,
\]
we obtain
\[
R_1R_2R_3R_4
=
\operatorname{Vol}(R)
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}
S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]

This completes the proof.

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

This is a little difficult to read - the statement of the ``Theorem'' is spread out over two pages and makes a lot of disconnected claims.

The key part of the statement is: 

\begin{quote}
[I]f in addition one has an estimate
\[
\int_{F^{-1}(B_0)}\sigma_1^2\,d\mu
\ge
c_d\sqrt{\frac{S_3}{S_2}}\,
\mu(F^{-1}(B_0))
\]
for some constant \(c_d>0\), then
\[
R_1R_2R_3R_4
\ge
\frac{c_d}{9}S_1S_2^{1/2}S_3^{3/2}S_4.
\]
\end{quote}

That is, the argument proves that the problem is solvable given a substantial additional assumption. 

Overall, the argument is a little verbose, but it seems to be essentially correct. There are two main problems: first, as noted above, the argument needs an additional assumption. Second, in the original problem, there are two cases: that $R_3 R_4 > k S_3 S_4$ or that $R_1 R_2 R_3 R_4 > k S_1 S_2^{1/2} S_3^{3/2} S_4$. The argument aims to show that if the additional condition holds, then the second inequality is true, but that leaves out one of the cases. 

This is a strange submission. It spends most of its space proving that 
\[
\operatorname{FillVol}_R(z_y)\ge \operatorname{FillVol}_S(P_y)
=S_1S_2\,\operatorname{dist}(y,\partial B).
\]
This is an intermediate result that shows up in other submissions and in the problem solution, but this submission doesn't use it to prove anything -- it just states it and moves on. 

## Novelty.
reviews.recommendation: Reject
inline_comments: In most arguments, the next step would be to use the relative isoperimetric inequality to prove a lower bound on $\operatorname{Area}(z_y)$, but this is the last place that this argument mentions $\operatorname{FillVol}$.
