reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.
 After checking this proof carefully, I believe it to be correct. It handles the singularity of the delta function forcing by using the linear part of the equation to in some sense lower bound the size of the (space--time--probability) set at which the solution is equal to zero (although it is not phrased in exactly this way). This allows it to show that the contribution of the singular drift to the solution is in $L^2$, so the Girsanov theorem can be used to show absolute continuity with respect to the Gaussian invariant measure. From here, standard techniques in infinite-dimensional ergodic theory allow it to show that the explicitly-constructed invariant measure is unique.

The approximation of the equation by its linearization on short time intervals introduces some error, which is bounded via the stochastic sewing lemma of Khoa Lê. There are some notational issues in the proofs that create some ambiguity and impede understanding to some degree but for an expert reader these issues are not serious.

## Novelty.
 
I rate the novelty of the solution as rather high. The use of stochastic sewing to control the difference between the solution to the linear and nonlinear problems on short time scales is very clean. To write such a solution, one would need to have expertise in ergodic theory, infinite-dimensional stochastic analysis, and the theory of rough stochastic equations. The proof actually proves a somewhat stronger statement than the human-generated solution (a finite-time absolute continuity result rather than the asymptotic strong Feller property).

## Exposition

The exposition could use some work. In particular, the importance of Lemma~1 should be signposted before it is proved. The reviewers agreed that it was easier to read the submission starting at the end and proceeding towards the beginning.
reviews.recommendation: I rate the solution as essentially flawless. All of the mathematical arguments are present and are presented rather cleanly. An important issue that needs to be addressed, though, is that paper of Khoa Lê needs to be cited for the stochastic sewing lemma: in the submission, although the paper is mentioned in the bibliography, it is not cited in-text when the stochastic sewing lemma is presented. A reader could be led to be believe that the stochastic sewing lemma is due to this proposition, which is not the case.

\date{}

\begin{center}
{\bf Uniqueness of the invariant measure}
\end{center}

\subsection*{Problem statement and interpretation}

Put \(E=C_0([0,1])\), \(H=L^2(0,1)\), and let \(S_t\) be the Dirichlet heat
semigroup generated by \(\frac12\Delta\).  I use the Dirichlet version of the
Athreya--Butkovsky--L\^e--Mytnik approximation assumption in the following
form.  For each deterministic initial condition \(x\in E\), if \(b_n=G_{1/n}\),
then the regularized equation has the mild solution
\[
  u_t^n=S_t x+V_t+K_t^n,\qquad
  K_t^n=\int_0^tS_{t-r}b_n(u_r^n)\,dr,\qquad
  V_t=\int_0^tS_{t-r}\,dW_r ,
\]
and, for every \(t>0\) and every \(\Phi\in C_b(E)\),
\[
        P_t^n\Phi(x):=\E\Phi(u_t^n)\longrightarrow P_t\Phi(x).
        \tag{1}
\]
Thus I interpret the stated weak convergence of \(u^n(t)\) to \(u(t)\) as
holding for all deterministic starting points; this is the form needed for a
statement about invariant measures of the whole Markov semigroup.

\begin{lemma}[Uniform estimate on the regularized drift]\label{lem:Hestimate}
For each \(T<\infty\) there is \(C_T<\infty\), independent of \(n\) and
\(x\in E\), such that
\[
 \|K_t^n-S_{t-s}K_s^n\|_{L^2(\Omega;H)}
      \le C_T |t-s|^{3/4},\qquad 0\le s<t\le T .             \tag{2}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(p_t\) be the Dirichlet kernel and \(d(y)=y\wedge(1-y)\).  For
\(0<a\le 2T\), the reflection formula for the interval and comparison with
the two half-lines at the nearer boundary give
\[
p_a(z,y)\le Ca^{-1/2}e^{-|z-y|^2/(Ca)},\qquad
p_a(y,y)\asymp a^{-1/2}\bigl(1\wedge d(y)^2/a\bigr).          \tag{3}
\]
For example, if \(d(y)\le\sqrt a\), the half-line expression
\((2\pi a)^{-1/2}(1-e^{-2d(y)^2/a})\) is comparable to \(d(y)^2a^{-3/2}\);
if \(d(y)\ge\sqrt a\), the reflected terms are exponentially smaller than
the free diagonal term.  The finitely many remaining images are absorbed in a
constant depending only on \(T\).  Hence, for
\(\rho_\tau(y)=\int_0^\tau p_{2r}(y,y)\,dr\),
\[
        \rho_\tau(y)\asymp \sqrt{\tau}\wedge d(y),\qquad
        \int_0^1\rho_\tau(y)^{-1/2}dy\le C_T\tau^{-1/4}.      \tag{4}
\]
Indeed the integral of \(r^{-1/2}(1\wedge d^2/r)\) is comparable to
\(\sqrt\tau\) when \(d\ge\sqrt\tau\), and to \(d\) otherwise.  Also
\[
 \sup_z\int_0^1p_a(z,y)\rho_\tau(y)^{-1/2}dy
 \le C_T(a^{-1/4}+\tau^{-1/4}).                              \tag{5}
\]
To see this, use \(\rho_\tau^{-1/2}\le C(\tau^{-1/4}+d^{-1/2})\).  The first
part integrates to \(C\tau^{-1/4}\).  For the second, bound
\(d(y)^{-1/2}\le y^{-1/2}+(1-y)^{-1/2}\) and use
\(y=\sqrt a\,r\) near the left boundary (similarly near the right) to get
\(Ca^{-1/4}\sup_{\alpha\ge0}\int_0^\infty
e^{-(r-\alpha)^2/C}r^{-1/2}dr<\infty\).  Finally, for \(0<\tau\le T\),
\[
        \|\rho_\tau^{-1}S_\tau f\|_2\le C_T\tau^{-1/2}\|f\|_2. \tag{6}
\]
Here \(\rho_\tau^{-1}\le C(\tau^{-1/2}+d^{-1})\); \(S_\tau f\in H^1_0\);
Hardy's inequality gives \(\|S_\tau f/d\|_2\le C\|\partial_xS_\tau f\|_2\);
and \(\|\partial_xS_\tau f\|_2\le C\tau^{-1/2}\|f\|_2\).

Write \(D^n_{s,t}=K_t^n-S_{t-s}K_s^n\).  Freeze the equation at time \(s\):
\[
 A^n_{s,t}=\int_s^tS_{t-r}
 b_n\!\left(S_{r-s}u_s^n+V_r-S_{r-s}V_s\right)\,dr .          \tag{7}
\]
For fixed \(n\), if \(\Pi\) is a partition of \([s,t]\), then
\[
 \sum_{[a,b]\in\Pi}S_{t-b}A^n_{a,b}\to D^n_{s,t}\quad\hbox{in }L^2(H).
 \tag{8}
\]
Indeed the summand differs from
\(\int_a^bS_{b-r}b_n(u_r^n)\,dr\) by at most
\(C_n(b-a)^2\) in \(L^2(H)\), because \(b_n\) is Lipschitz and the two
arguments differ only by the drift accumulated on \([a,r]\), whose \(H\)-norm
is at most \(C_n(r-a)\).  After applying \(S_{t-b}\) and summing, the error is
\(O_n((t-s)|\Pi|)\).

The estimates below are uniform in \(n\).  Given \(\calF_s\),

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The notation should indicate the dependence on $s$, e.g. $Z_{s,r}$.]]

\[
Z_r(y):=S_{r-s}u_s^n(y)+V_r(y)-S_{r-s}V_s(y)
\]
is Gaussian with variance \(\rho_{r-s}(y)\).  Since \(b_n\) is a probability
density, \(\sup_m\E b_n(m+N(0,\sigma^2))\le C\sigma^{-1}\).  Moreover, given
\(\calF_r\), the future part of \(Z_q(z)\), \(q>r\), has variance
\[
 \int_r^q\!\!\int_0^1p_{q-\ell}(z,\xi)^2\,d\xi d\ell
 =\int_0^{q-r}p_{2a}(z,z)\,da=\rho_{q-r}(z).
\]
Thus, for \(s<r<q\),

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The notation $\mathbb{E}_s$ needs to be defined as $\mathbb{E}[\cdot\mid \mathcal{F}_s]$ since this is not standard notation.]]

\[
 \E_s\,b_n(Z_r(y))b_n(Z_q(z))
 \le C\rho_{r-s}(y)^{-1/2}\rho_{q-r}(z)^{-1/2}.              \tag{9}
\]
Using
\(\int p_{t-r}(x,y)p_{t-q}(x,z)dx=p_{2t-r-q}(y,z)\), then (5) in \(y\) and
(4) in \(z\), we obtain

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The notation $\|\cdot\|_2$ needs to be defined.]]

\[
 \E_s\|A^n_{s,t}\|_2^2
 \le C\!\int_s^t\!\!\int_r^t
      \bigl((2t-r-q)^{-1/4}+(r-s)^{-1/4}\bigr)(q-r)^{-1/4}\,dq\,dr
 \le C|t-s|^{3/2}.                                          \tag{10}
\]
The last inequality is just scaling on the triangle
\(0\le r-s\le q-s\le t-s\).  Hence
\(\|A^n_{s,t}\|_{L^2H}\le C|t-s|^{3/4}\).


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The statements in the following paragraph are vague. The reviewers wrote them out and believe that they are correct but they need to be explained more carefully.]]

For \(s<u<t\), let
\(\delta A^n_{s,u,t}=A^n_{s,t}-S_{t-u}A^n_{s,u}-A^n_{u,t}\).  The pieces before
\(u\) cancel.  For \(r>u\), the two frozen arguments differ by
\(S_{r-u}D^n_{s,u}\).  Conditional on \(\calF_u\), the remaining noise at
space point \(y\) has variance \(\rho_{r-u}(y)\), and
\(\|(b_n*\varphi_\sigma)'\|_\infty\le C\sigma^{-2}\), uniformly in \(n\).
Therefore
\[
 \left|\E_u\{b_n(Z_r(y))-b_n(Z_r(y)+h(y))\}\right|
      \le C\rho_{r-u}(y)^{-1}|h(y)|.
\]
With \(h=S_{r-u}D^n_{s,u}\), (6) and contraction of \(S_t\) imply
\[
        \|\E_u\delta A^n_{s,u,t}\|_2
        \le C(t-u)^{1/2}\|D^n_{s,u}\|_2 .                    \tag{11}
\]
Taking \(\E_s\) and using Jensen gives the same estimate with \(\E_s\) in
place of \(\E_u\).

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The above statement is difficult to interpret because we don't know what $\|\cdot\|_2$ is exactly supposed to mean. It is essentially true, however.]]



[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The following paragraph needs to cite the work of Khoa Lê referenced in the bibliography.]]

We need only the following dyadic sewing fact.  Suppose \(A_{s,t}\) is
\(H\)-valued and \(\calF_t\)-measurable, and for every dyadic interval
\([a,b]\) with midpoint \(u\),
\[
\|\E_a\delta A_{a,u,b}\|_{L^2H}\le \Gamma_1(b-a)^{1+\varepsilon_1},\quad
\|\delta A_{a,u,b}-\E_a\delta A_{a,u,b}\|_{L^2H}
        \le \Gamma_2(b-a)^{1/2+\varepsilon_2}.
\]
If \(J_m=\sum_iS_{t-t_{i+1}}A_{t_i,t_{i+1}}\) over the \(2^m\) equal
subintervals of \([s,t]\), then \(J_m\) converges and
\[
 \|{\cal A}_{s,t}-A_{s,t}\|_{L^2H}
 \le C(\Gamma_1|t-s|^{1+\varepsilon_1}
       +\Gamma_2|t-s|^{1/2+\varepsilon_2}).                 \tag{12}
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: $\mathcal{A}_{s,t}$ needs to be defined.]]

Indeed, \(J_{m+1}-J_m\) is the sum of
\(-S_{t-b}\delta A_{a,u,b}\).  The conditional-mean parts are bounded by the
triangle inequality, giving a factor
\(2^m(|t-s|2^{-m})^{1+\varepsilon_1}\).  The centered parts are orthogonal:
for two level-\(m\) intervals with the first lying earlier, the earlier
summand is \(\calF_a\)-measurable for the later one, while the later summand
has conditional mean zero given \(\calF_a\).  Thus the square norm is the sum
of the square norms.  Summing the resulting geometric series proves (12).

For fixed \(n\), \(Y_n(h)=\sup_{0<t-s\le h}\|D^n_{s,t}\|_{L^2H}/|t-s|^{3/4}\)
is finite, because \(b_n\) is bounded.  On intervals of length at most \(h\),
(11) gives
\[
 \|\E_a\delta A^n_{a,u,b}\|_{L^2H}\le C Y_n(h)(b-a)^{5/4}.
\]
Also
\[
\|\delta A^n_{a,u,b}-\E_a\delta A^n_{a,u,b}\|_{L^2H}
 \le 2\|\delta A^n_{a,u,b}\|_{L^2H}
 \le C(b-a)^{3/4},
\]
because \(\delta A\) is a sum of three \(A\)-terms and (10) applies to each.
The dyadic sewing limit is \(D^n_{s,t}\) by (8).
[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The explicit limit should be written out instead of calling it the ``dyadic sewing limit,'' which is vague.]]
  Combining (10) and (12),
\[
 \|D^n_{s,t}\|_{L^2H}\le C|t-s|^{3/4}
        +C Y_n(h)|t-s|^{5/4}.
\]
Thus \(Y_n(h)\le C+Ch^{1/2}Y_n(h)\).  Choose \(h_0>0\), depending only on
\(T\), so that \(Ch_0^{1/2}\le1/2\); then \(Y_n(h_0)\le2C\), uniformly in
\(n\).  For longer intervals use the additivity
\(D^n_{s,t}=S_{t-r}D^n_{s,r}+D^n_{r,t}\) and split into pieces of length at
most \(h_0\).  This gives a linear bound \(C_T|t-s|\), which is bounded by
\(C_T|t-s|^{3/4}\) on \(0\le t-s\le T\).  The lemma follows.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{The reversible reference measure and its gap}

Let \(\gamma\) be Brownian bridge measure on \(E\), the centered Gaussian
measure with covariance \((-\Delta_D)^{-1}\).  Define
\[
  \Lambda(v)=\int_0^1\1_{\{v(r)>0\}}\,dr,\qquad
  \pi(dv)=Z^{-1}e^{2\Lambda(v)}\,\gamma(dv).                 \tag{13}
\]
For \(B_n'=b_n\), \(B_n(a)=\int_{-\infty}^ab_n(r)dr\), put
\[
   \pi_n(dv)=Z_n^{-1}\exp\left(2\int_0^1B_n(v(r))\,dr\right)\gamma(dv).
\]
Since \(0\le B_n\le1\), \(B_n(a)\to\1_{\{a>0\}}\) for \(a\ne0\), and a
Brownian bridge spends zero Lebesgue time at a fixed level,
\[
        \|\pi_n-\pi\|_{\TV}\to0 .                            \tag{14}
\]
All densities \(d\pi_n/d\gamma\) and \(d\pi/d\gamma\) are bounded above and
below by deterministic positive constants.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:reggap}
There are constants \(C,c>0\), independent of \(n\), such that for every
bounded continuous \(f,g\) and every \(t\ge0\),
\[
 \int P_t^n f\,d\pi_n=\int f\,d\pi_n,\qquad
 \int gP_t^n f\,d\pi_n=\int fP_t^n g\,d\pi_n,                \tag{15}
\]
and
\[
        \Var_{\pi_n}(P_t^n f)\le e^{-ct}\Var_{\pi_n}(f).      \tag{16}
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\Pi_m\) be projection onto the first \(m\) Dirichlet modes and set
\[
        U_{n,m}(v)=\int_0^1B_n(\Pi_m v(r))\,dr .
\]
Its \(H\)-gradient is \(\nabla_HU_{n,m}(v)=\Pi_m b_n(\Pi_m v)\).  Let
\(P_t^{n,m}\) be the semigroup of
\[
u_t^{n,m}=S_t x+V_t+\int_0^tS_{t-r}\Pi_m b_n(\Pi_m u_r^{n,m})\,dr .
\]
The first \(m\) Fourier coordinates solve the finite-dimensional Langevin
diffusion
\[
dX_j=-(\lambda_j/2)X_j\,dt+\partial_j U_{n,m}(X)\,dt+d\beta_j,
\qquad j\le m,
\]
and the tail is an independent OU process.  Hence, by finite-dimensional
integration by parts and the standard OU integration by parts in the tail,
\(P_t^{n,m}\) is reversible with respect to
\(\pi_{n,m}=Z_{n,m}^{-1}e^{2U_{n,m}}\gamma\), and its Dirichlet form is
\(\calE_{n,m}(F,F)=\frac12\int\|\nabla_HF\|_2^2\,d\pi_{n,m}\) on smooth
cylinder functions.

The measures \(\pi_{n,m}\) converge to \(\pi_n\) in total variation: \(\Pi_m
v\to v\) in \(H\), \(\gamma\)-a.s., and \(B_n\) is bounded and Lipschitz.  For
fixed \(n\), \(u_t^{n,m}\to u_t^n\) in probability in \(E\).  In \(H\), this
follows from Gronwall, since \(\Pi_m b_n(\Pi_m z)\) is uniformly Lipschitz in
\(z\) for fixed \(n\), and for each \(H\)-valued \(y\),
\(\Pi_m b_n(\Pi_m y)\to b_n(y)\) in \(H\), dominated by \(2\|b_n\|_\infty\).
For convergence in \(E\) at a fixed \(t>0\), split the drift convolution into
\([0,t-\varepsilon]\) and \([t-\varepsilon,t]\).  On the first part,
\(S_{t-r}:H\to H^\alpha_0\subset E\), \(\alpha>1/2\), is bounded.  On the
short terminal part,
\[
 \int_{t-\varepsilon}^t\|S_{t-r}F_r\|_\infty dr
 \le C\|b_n\|_\infty\int_0^\varepsilon a^{-1/4}da,
\]
for both \(F_r=\Pi_m b_n(\Pi_mu_r^{n,m})\) and \(F_r=b_n(u_r^n)\), because
\(\Pi_m\) is an \(L^2\)-contraction and \(S_a:H\to E\) has norm \(Ca^{-1/4}\).
This tends to zero with \(\varepsilon\), uniformly in \(m\).

Consequently the reversible identities pass to \(m=\infty\).  For instance,
if \(h_m=d\pi_{n,m}/d\gamma\), then \(h_m\to h_n=d\pi_n/d\gamma\) in
\(L^1(\gamma)\) and the \(h_m\)'s are uniformly bounded; together with
\(P_t^{n,m}f(x)\to P_t^nf(x)\) and bounded convergence this gives (15).

It remains to record the gap uniformly.  The Gaussian Poincare inequality for
\(\gamma\) in \(H\)-gradient form is
\[
        \Var_\gamma(F)\le \lambda_1^{-1}\int\|\nabla_HF\|_2^2\,d\gamma
\]
on smooth cylinder functions.  Since all densities
\(d\pi_{n,m}/d\gamma\) lie in a fixed interval \([a_0,a_0^{-1}]\), the
Holley--Stroock bounded perturbation argument gives
\[
        \Var_{\pi_{n,m}}(F)\le C\,\calE_{n,m}(F,F),
\]
with \(C\) independent of \(n,m\).  For a symmetric Markov semigroup this
Poincare inequality is equivalent to exponential \(L^2\)-decay, so
\[
 \Var_{\pi_{n,m}}(P_t^{n,m}f)\le e^{-ct}\Var_{\pi_{n,m}}(f).
\]
Letting \(m\to\infty\), using the convergence just proved and the uniformly
bounded densities, yields (16).
\end{proof}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The following proposition should be cited to the work of Bounebache--Zambotti (2014).]]

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:gap}
The measure \(\pi\) is \(P_t\)-invariant, \(P_t\) is symmetric on
\(L^2(\pi)\), and
\[
       \Var_\pi(P_t f)\le e^{-ct}\Var_\pi(f),
       \qquad f\in L^2(\pi),\ t\ge0 .                       \tag{17}
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For \(f,g\in C_b(E)\), (1), (14), (15), and the uniform boundedness of the
densities imply, by dominated convergence with respect to \(\gamma\),
\[
 \int P_tf\,d\pi=\lim_n\int P_t^nf\,d\pi_n=\int f\,d\pi,\qquad
 \int gP_tf\,d\pi=\int fP_tg\,d\pi .
\]
On the Polish space \(E\), these identities identify the measure
\(\int\pi(dx)P_t(x,\cdot)\) with \(\pi\), and the measure
\(\pi(dx)P_t(x,dy)\) with its transpose; hence invariance and detailed balance
hold for all bounded Borel functions.  Similarly, (16) passes to the limit for
bounded continuous \(f\).  Finally \(C_b(E)\) is dense in \(L^2(\pi)\), and an
invariant Markov operator is an \(L^2\)-contraction, so symmetry and (17)
extend to all \(L^2(\pi)\).
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Fixed-time absolute continuity}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:control}
For every deterministic \(x\in E\) and every \(t>0\),
\[
        P_t(x,\cdot)\ll \gamma ,
\]
and hence \(P_t(x,\cdot)\ll\pi\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\nu_t^x=\Law(S_tx+V_t)\).  We first bound
\(\Ent(P_t^n(x,\cdot)\mid\nu_t^x)\) uniformly in \(n\).  Put
\(r_k=t(1-2^{-k})\), \(\Delta_k=r_{k+1}-r_k\), and
\(D_k^n=K^n_{r_{k+1}}-S_{\Delta_k}K^n_{r_k}\).  Define
\[
 F_s^n=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\1_{(r_{k+1},r_{k+2}]}(s)}{\Delta_{k+1}}\,
        S_{s-r_{k+1}}D_k^n .                                \tag{18}
\]
The process is predictable because \(D_k^n\) is \(\calF_{r_{k+1}}\)-measurable.
Lemma \ref{lem:Hestimate} and contraction of \(S_t\) give
\[
 \E\int_0^t\|F_s^n\|_2^2ds
 \le C_t\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{\Delta_k^{3/2}}{\Delta_{k+1}}<\infty, \tag{19}
\]
uniformly in \(n\).  For partial sums,
\[
 \int_0^tS_{t-s}F_s^{n,N}ds
 =\sum_{k=0}^NS_{t-r_{k+1}}D_k^n
 =S_{t-r_{N+1}}K^n_{r_{N+1}},
\]
where \(F^{n,N}\) denotes the sum in (18) up to \(k=N\).  Since
\(r_{N+1}\uparrow t\), the regularized mild solution gives \(K^n\) continuous
with values in \(E\), and \(S_a\to I\) strongly on \(E\),
\[
        \int_0^tS_{t-s}F_s^n\,ds=K_t^n                       \tag{20}
\]
in probability in \(E\) (and hence in \(H\)).  The state space assertion is
legitimate because, for every deterministic \(F\in L^2(0,t;H)\),
\[
 \sum_j\lambda_j^\alpha\Big|\int_0^te^{-\lambda_j(t-s)/2}F_j(s)ds\Big|^2
 \le \sum_j\lambda_j^{\alpha-1}\int_0^t|F_j(s)|^2ds
 \le C\|F\|_{L^2(0,t;H)}^2
\]
for \(0<\alpha<1\); choosing \(\alpha>1/2\) gives an element of
\(H^\alpha_0(0,1)\subset E\).

We use the following standard entropy form of Girsanov, and recall its proof.
If \(F\) is predictable, \(H\)-valued, and has bounded energy, then
\[
 X^F=S_tx+V_t+\int_0^tS_{t-s}F_sds
\]
satisfies
\[
        \Ent(\Law(X^F)\mid\nu_t^x)
        \le \frac12\,\E\int_0^t\|F_s\|_2^2ds .               \tag{21}
\]
For the first \(M\) Brownian coordinates this is finite-dimensional
Girsanov: under the tilted measure, the shifted coordinates
\(\beta_j+\int_0^\cdot F_j(s)ds\), \(j\le M\), are Brownian, and the entropy
cost is \(\frac12\E\int_0^t\sum_{j\le M}F_j(s)^2ds\).  
[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Should say ``applying the data processing inequality'']]
 Applying data
processing to the deterministic-kernel stochastic convolution gives the same
bound for the first \(M\) terminal Fourier coordinates.  Since the Borel
sigma-field of \(E\) is generated by these coordinates and relative entropy
is the supremum over increasing finite-coordinate sigma-fields, (21) follows.

Localize \(F^n\) by
\(\tau_R=\inf\{s:\int_0^s\|F_r^n\|_2^2dr>R\}\) and
\(\widehat F^{\,n,R}=F^n\1_{[0,\tau_R]}\).  Let
\[
 X_R=S_tx+V_t+\int_0^tS_{t-s}\widehat F^{\,n,R}_sds .
\]
Then (21) and (19) give
\[
 \Ent(\Law(X_R)\mid\nu_t^x)
 \le \frac12\,\E\int_0^t\|F_s^n\|_2^2ds .                   \tag{22}
\]
On \(\{\tau_R>t\}\), (20) gives \(X_R=u_t^n\), while
\(\mathbb P(\tau_R\le t)\le R^{-1}\E\int_0^t\|F_s^n\|_2^2ds\to0\).  Hence
\(X_R\to u_t^n\) in probability in \(E\).  Lower semicontinuity of relative
entropy on the Polish space \(E\), then (19) and (22), yield
\[
        \sup_n\Ent(P_t^n(x,\cdot)\mid\nu_t^x)<\infty .       \tag{23}
\]
By the assumed weak convergence (1) and lower semicontinuity again,
\(\Ent(P_t(x,\cdot)\mid\nu_t^x)<\infty\).  Thus
\(P_t(x,\cdot)\ll\nu_t^x\).

It remains only to compare Gaussian measures.  In the basis
\(e_j(r)=\sqrt2\sin(j\pi r)\), \(\lambda_j=j^2\pi^2\), the covariance of
\(\nu_t^x\) has eigenvalues
\[
        q_j(t)=\frac{1-e^{-\lambda_jt}}{\lambda_j},
\]
whereas \(\gamma\) has eigenvalues \(\lambda_j^{-1}\).  The ratios
\(1-e^{-\lambda_jt}\) are bounded away from zero and differ from \(1\) by a
square-summable sequence.  The Cameron--Martin spaces are therefore both
\(H^1_0(0,1)\), and \(S_tx\in H^1_0\).  Feldman--Hajek gives
\(\nu_t^x\sim\gamma\).
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Conclusion}

Let \(\eta\) be an invariant probability measure.  If \(\pi(A)=0\), then
Lemma \ref{lem:control} gives \(P_t(y,A)=0\) for every \(y\in E\), and hence
\[
        \eta(A)=\int_E P_t(y,A)\,\eta(dy)=0.
\]
Thus \(\eta\ll\pi\); write \(d\eta=h\,d\pi\).  Detailed balance gives the
\(L^1\)-duality
\[
        \int f\,P_t g\,d\pi=\int P_t f\,g\,d\pi
\]
for bounded Borel \(f\) and \(g\in L^1(\pi)\), by truncating \(g\).  Therefore
\[
 \int f h\,d\pi=\int P_tf\,d\eta
      =\int P_tf\,h\,d\pi=\int f\,P_t h\,d\pi ,
\]
so \(P_t h=h\) in \(L^1(\pi)\).  For \(a>0\), let \(h_a=h\wedge a\).  Since
\(r\mapsto r\wedge a\) is concave,
\[
        P_t h_a\le (P_t h)\wedge a=h_a .
\]
The two sides have the same \(\pi\)-integral; therefore \(P_t h_a=h_a\).
Now \(h_a\in L^2(\pi)\), and the spectral gap (17) implies
\(\Var_\pi(h_a)=0\).  Thus \(h_a\) is constant for every \(a\).  Letting
\(a\uparrow\infty\) and using \(\int h\,d\pi=1\), we obtain \(h=1\)
\(\pi\)-a.s.  Hence \(\eta=\pi\).

Therefore \(P_t\) has at most one invariant probability measure on
\(C_0([0,1])\).  In fact, if an invariant probability exists, it is the Gibbs
measure \(\pi\) in (13).

\title{Submission B solution to Problem 5}
\date{}
\maketitle

\section*{Overview / Strategy}

The original target is to decide whether the Markov semigroup \(P_t\) of the
Dirichlet stochastic heat equation with distributional drift \(\delta_0\) has
at most one invariant probability measure.  The first part of the argument
constructs the natural Gibbs measure
\[
\nu(\dd v)=Z^{-1}\exp\!\left(2\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x\right)\gamma(\dd v),
\]
where \(\gamma\) is Brownian-bridge law, and proves that \(\nu\) is invariant by
passing to the limit from the smooth mollified equations.  This is carried out
in Theorem \ref{thm:invariance}.

Uniqueness requires more than this invariant-measure construction.  The clean
abstract mechanism is that pairwise non-singularity of one transition skeleton
implies uniqueness; see Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise}.  A compact-local Hellinger
overlap estimate for the mollified last-step kernels would imply such
non-singularity in the limit; see Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger}.  A second route is
to prove that every invariant measure is absolutely continuous with respect to
\(\nu\); see Theorem \ref{thm:uac} and Proposition \ref{prop:resolvent}.  The
stated ABLM-type assumptions provide existence, uniqueness in law, and weak
convergence of the mollified equations, but they do not themselves provide any
of these deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimates.  Thus the
unconditional conclusion proved here is invariance of \(\nu\), together with
precise conditional criteria under which the desired uniqueness follows.

\section{Standing assumptions, notation, and the target statement}

Let
\[
E:=C_0([0,1])
=\{v\in C([0,1],\R):v(0)=v(1)=0\},
\qquad H:=L^2(0,1),
\]
with \(E\) equipped with the supremum norm.  Let
\[
e_k(x):=\sqrt2\sin(k\pi x),\qquad \lambda_k:=\pi^2k^2,\qquad k\ge1,
\]
be the Dirichlet eigenbasis of \(-\partial_{xx}\).  Let \(\gamma\) denote
Brownian-bridge law on \(E\), equivalently the centered Gaussian measure with
covariance \((-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\):
\[
\E_\gamma[(v,e_k)_H(v,e_\ell)_H]=\frac{\delta_{k\ell}}{\lambda_k}.
\]

The SPDE from the original problem is
\begin{align}
\tag{\(*\)}\label{eq:spde}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x,t)
&=\frac12\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,t)
+\delta_0(u(x,t))+\dot W(x,t),\qquad t\ge0,\\
u(x,0)&=u_0(x)\in E,\nonumber\\
u(0,t)&=u(1,t)=0.\nonumber
\end{align}

\begin{assumption}[ABLM-type input on the bounded interval]\label{ass:ablm}
For every \(u_0\in E\) and \(T>0\), there is a unique-in-law adapted mild
solution \(u\in C([0,T],E)\) to \eqref{eq:spde}, and the solutions define a
Markov semigroup \((P_t)_{t\ge0}\) on \(E\).  For
\[
b_n(r):=G_{1/n}(r)=\sqrt{\frac n{2\pi}}e^{-nr^2/2},
\]
let \(P_t^n\) be the semigroup of the mollified equation obtained by replacing
\(\delta_0\) with \(b_n\).  For every \(t>0\), \(v\in E\), and \(f\in C_b(E)\),
\[
P_t^n f(v)\longrightarrow P_tf(v),
\]
or equivalently \(P_t^n(v,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_t(v,\cdot)\).
\end{assumption}

Define
\[
F_n(r):=\int_{-\infty}^r b_n(s)\dd s,\qquad
\Phi_n(v):=\int_0^1F_n(v(x))\dd x,\qquad
\Phi(v):=\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x.
\]
Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gibbs}
\nu_n(\dd v):=Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n(v)}\gamma(\dd v),
\qquad
\nu(\dd v):=Z^{-1}e^{2\Phi(v)}\gamma(\dd v),
\end{equation}
where \(Z_n\) and \(Z\) are the normalizing constants.  Since
\(0\le\Phi_n,\Phi\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-bounds}
1\le Z_n,Z\le e^2,
\qquad
e^{-2}\le \frac{\dd\nu_n}{\dd\gamma},\frac{\dd\nu}{\dd\gamma}\le e^2.
\end{equation}

For a Markov kernel \(K\) and a probability measure \(\mu\), write
\(\mu K(A):=\int_EK(x,A)\mu(\dd x)\).  A probability measure \(\mu\) is invariant
for a semigroup \((P_t)\) if \(\mu P_t=\mu\) for all \(t\ge0\).

\begin{theorem}[Original problem: target and established claim]\label{thm:headline}
The target assertion from the original problem is
\[
\tag{U}\label{eq:target}
\text{\((P_t)\) has at most one invariant probability measure on \(E\).}
\]
Under Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}, the Gibbs measure \(\nu\) in
\eqref{eq:gibbs} is invariant.  Moreover, \eqref{eq:target} follows if one adds
any of the deterministic-start smoothing or overlap hypotheses in Theorem
\ref{thm:hellinger}, Theorem \ref{thm:uac}, or Proposition
\ref{prop:resolvent} together with Proposition \ref{prop:acunique}.  In that
case the unique invariant probability measure is \(\nu\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The invariance statement is Theorem \ref{thm:invariance}.  The Hellinger
overlap hypothesis of Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger} implies pairwise
non-singularity of one skeleton, and Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise} then gives
uniqueness.  The compact-local uniform absolute-continuity hypothesis of
Theorem \ref{thm:uac} gives \(\mu\ll\nu\) for every invariant \(\mu\), and its
third hypothesis, supplied for instance by Proposition \ref{prop:acunique},
then gives \(\mu=\nu\).  Finally, Proposition \ref{prop:resolvent} is a
resolvent version of the same absolute-continuity route.  Since
Theorem \ref{thm:invariance} supplies an invariant measure, any ``at most one''
conclusion identifies the invariant law with \(\nu\).
\end{proof}

\section{The Gibbs invariant measure}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance of the Gibbs measure]\label{thm:invariance}
Under Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}, the measure
\[
\nu(\dd v)
=
Z^{-1}\exp\!\left(2\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x\right)\gamma(\dd v)
\]
is invariant for \((P_t)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We prove this by approximation.

\emph{Step 1: \(\nu_n\to\nu\) in total variation.}
For each \(r\ne0\), \(F_n(r)\to\1_{\{r>0\}}\).  Let \(B\sim\gamma\).  For
\(x\in(0,1)\), \(B(x)\) is a nondegenerate centered Gaussian, hence
\(\gamma(B(x)=0)=0\).  Therefore, by Fubini,
\[
\E_\gamma\bigl|\{x\in[0,1]:B(x)=0\}\bigr|
=\int_0^1\gamma(B(x)=0)\dd x=0,
\]
where the endpoints do not matter.  Thus \(|\{x:B(x)=0\}|=0\) for
\(\gamma\)-a.e. \(B\).  For such \(B\),
\[
\Phi_n(B)=\int_0^1F_n(B(x))\dd x
\longrightarrow
\int_0^1\1_{\{B(x)>0\}}\dd x=\Phi(B)
\]
by dominated convergence in \(x\).  Since \(0\le\Phi_n,\Phi\le1\), dominated
convergence in \(\gamma\) gives \(Z_n\to Z\) and
\[
\int_E\left|
Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n(v)}-Z^{-1}e^{2\Phi(v)}
\right|\gamma(\dd v)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hence \(\|\nu_n-\nu\|_{\TV}\to0\).

\emph{Step 2: \(\nu_n\) is invariant for \(P_t^n\).}
For fixed \(n\), the drift \(b_n\) is bounded and Lipschitz.  Also
\(\Phi_n\) has \(H\)-gradient \(D\Phi_n(v)=b_n(v)\), because for
\(h\in H\),
\[
D\Phi_n(v)[h]=\int_0^1b_n(v(x))h(x)\dd x=\ip{b_n(v)}{h}_H.
\]
On smooth cylinder functions the formal generator is
\[
L_nF(v)=\frac12\operatorname{Tr}D^2F(v)
-\frac12\ip{-\partial_{xx}v}{DF(v)}_H
+\ip{D\Phi_n(v)}{DF(v)}_H.
\]
The Gaussian integration-by-parts formula for \(\gamma\), together with
\(\dd\nu_n=Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n}\dd\gamma\), gives for smooth cylinder \(F,G\)
\[
\int_EG\,L_nF\,\dd\nu_n
=
-\frac12\int_E\ip{DG}{DF}_H\dd\nu_n.
\]
Indeed, the derivative of \(e^{2\Phi_n}\) contributes
\(2e^{2\Phi_n}D\Phi_n\), which cancels exactly the added drift term
\(\ip{D\Phi_n}{DF}_H\).  Taking \(G\equiv1\) gives
\[
\int_EL_nF\,\dd\nu_n=0.
\]
For bounded Lipschitz gradient drifts, the standard martingale-problem or
symmetric-Dirichlet-form construction of the stochastic heat equation identifies
\(P_t^n\) with the Markov semigroup generated by the closure of \(L_n\); see,
for example, \cite{DPZ14,MR92}.  Infinitesimal invariance on the cylinder core
therefore implies
\[
\nu_nP_t^n=\nu_n,\qquad t\ge0.
\]

\emph{Step 3: pass to the singular limit.}
Let \(f\in C_b(E)\) and \(t>0\).  By Assumption \ref{ass:ablm},
\(P_t^nf(v)\to P_tf(v)\) for every \(v\in E\).  Using
\(\dd\nu_n/\dd\gamma\le e^2\), dominated convergence gives
\[
\int_E|P_t^nf-P_tf|\dd\nu_n
\le
e^2\int_E|P_t^nf-P_tf|\dd\gamma
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Also, \(\nu_n\to\nu\) in total variation and \(P_tf\) is bounded, so
\[
\int_EP_tf\dd\nu_n\longrightarrow\int_EP_tf\dd\nu,
\qquad
\int_Ef\dd\nu_n\longrightarrow\int_Ef\dd\nu.
\]
Since \(\nu_nP_t^n=\nu_n\),
\[
\int_EP_tf\dd\nu
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_EP_t^nf\dd\nu_n
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_Ef\dd\nu_n
=
\int_Ef\dd\nu.
\]
Thus \(\nu P_t=\nu\) for all \(t>0\), and the case \(t=0\) is trivial.
\end{proof}

\section{Pairwise overlap and Hellinger criteria}

\begin{theorem}[Pairwise non-singularity of one skeleton implies uniqueness]\label{thm:pairwise}
Let \(E\) be Polish and \(K\) a Markov kernel on \(E\).  If
\[
K(x,\cdot)\not\perp K(y,\cdot)\qquad\forall x,y\in E,
\]
then \(K\) has at most one invariant probability measure.  Consequently, if a
semigroup \((P_t)\) has some \(t_0>0\) such that
\(P_{t_0}(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_{t_0}(y,\cdot)\) for all \(x,y\), then
\((P_t)\) has at most one invariant probability measure.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume that \(\mu_1\ne\mu_2\) are invariant for \(K\).  Let
\(\sigma:=\mu_1-\mu_2\), and write its Jordan decomposition
\(\sigma=\sigma^+-\sigma^-\).  Since \(\sigma(E)=0\),
\(m:=\sigma^+(E)=\sigma^-(E)>0\).

For every finite signed measure \(\eta\),
\[
|\eta K|\le |\eta|K.
\]
Indeed, for Borel \(A\), taking the supremum over finite measurable partitions
\(\{A_i\}\) of \(A\),
\[
|\eta K|(A)
\le
\sup_{\{A_i\}}\sum_i\int_EK(x,A_i)|\eta|(\dd x)
=
\int_EK(x,A)|\eta|(\dd x).
\]
Since \(\sigma K=\sigma\), we get \(|\sigma|\le|\sigma|K\).  The two measures
have equal total mass, so \(|\sigma|K=|\sigma|\).  Hence
\[
\sigma^+K=\frac12(|\sigma|K+\sigma K)=\sigma^+,
\qquad
\sigma^-K=\frac12(|\sigma|K-\sigma K)=\sigma^-.
\]
Thus \(\alpha:=\sigma^+/m\) and \(\beta:=\sigma^-/m\) are invariant
probabilities, and \(\alpha\perp\beta\).  Choose a Borel set \(A\) with
\(\alpha(A)=1\) and \(\beta(A)=0\).  Invariance gives
\[
1=\int_EK(x,A)\alpha(\dd x),\qquad
0=\int_EK(y,A)\beta(\dd y).
\]
Therefore \(K(x,A)=1\) for \(\alpha\)-a.e. \(x\) and \(K(y,A)=0\) for
\(\beta\)-a.e. \(y\).  Choosing such \(x,y\), \(K(x,\cdot)\) is concentrated on
\(A\) while \(K(y,\cdot)\) is concentrated on \(A^c\), so
\(K(x,\cdot)\perp K(y,\cdot)\), a contradiction.  The semigroup assertion
follows because every invariant measure for \((P_t)\) is invariant for the
skeleton \(P_{t_0}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Hellinger affinity]
For probability measures \(\mu,\rho\) on \(E\), define
\[
\Aff(\mu,\rho)
:=
\int_E\sqrt{\frac{\dd\mu}{\dd\lambda}\frac{\dd\rho}{\dd\lambda}}\,\dd\lambda,
\]
where \(\lambda\) is any finite measure dominating both \(\mu\) and \(\rho\).
The value is independent of \(\lambda\).  We use the normalized total variation
norm
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}:=\sup_{A\in\cB(E)}|\mu(A)-\rho(A)|.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary Hellinger facts]\label{lem:hellfacts}
For probability measures \(\mu,\rho\),
\[
\mu\perp\rho
\iff
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}=1
\iff
\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0,
\]
and
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
\le
\sqrt{1-\Aff(\mu,\rho)^2}.
\]
Moreover, if \(\mathcal P\) ranges over finite measurable partitions of \(E\),
then
\[
\Aff(\mu,\rho)
=
\inf_{\mathcal P}\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{\mu(B)\rho(B)}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take \(\lambda=\mu+\rho\), and write \(f=\dd\mu/\dd\lambda\),
\(g=\dd\rho/\dd\lambda\).  The definition is independent of \(\lambda\) because
changing the dominating measure multiplies both densities by the same
Radon--Nikodym factor.  If \(\mu\perp\rho\), then \(fg=0\) \(\lambda\)-a.e., so
\(\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0\).  Conversely, if \(\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0\), then
\(\sqrt{fg}=0\) \(\lambda\)-a.e.; the sets \(\{f>0\}\) and \(\{g>0\}\) separate
\(\mu\) and \(\rho\), so \(\mu\perp\rho\).  The equivalence with
\(\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}=1\) is the standard characterization of singularity for
probability measures.

Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
&=\frac12\int_E|f-g|\dd\lambda                                      \\
&=\frac12\int_E|\sqrt f-\sqrt g|(\sqrt f+\sqrt g)\dd\lambda          \\
&\le \frac12
\left(\int_E(\sqrt f-\sqrt g)^2\dd\lambda\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int_E(\sqrt f+\sqrt g)^2\dd\lambda\right)^{1/2}               \\
&=\sqrt{1-\Aff(\mu,\rho)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the partition formula, let \(\mathcal P\) be finite.  On each atom \(B\),
\[
\int_B\sqrt{\E_\lambda(f\mid\mathcal P)\E_\lambda(g\mid\mathcal P)}\dd\lambda
=
\sqrt{\mu(B)\rho(B)}.
\]
Conditional Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\E_\lambda(\sqrt{fg}\mid\mathcal P)
\le
\sqrt{\E_\lambda(f\mid\mathcal P)\E_\lambda(g\mid\mathcal P)},
\]
so every partition sum is at least \(\Aff(\mu,\rho)\).  Since \(E\) is Polish,
\(\cB(E)\) is countably generated.  Choosing finite partitions increasing to a
countable generating algebra, the bounded martingale convergence theorem
(applied with \(\lambda=\mu+\rho\), so \(0\le f,g\le1\)) gives partition sums
converging down to \(\int\sqrt{fg}\dd\lambda\).  Hence the infimum equals
\(\Aff(\mu,\rho)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mixture lower bound]\label{lem:mixture}
Let \(K\) be a Markov kernel on \(E\).  Suppose \(C\subset E\) is measurable and
there is \(a>0\) such that
\[
\Aff(K(v,\cdot),K(w,\cdot))\ge a\qquad\forall v,w\in C.
\]
Then, for all probability measures \(\alpha,\beta\),
\[
\Aff(\alpha K,\beta K)\ge a\,\alpha(C)\beta(C).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a finite partition.  For each atom \(B\),
\[
\sqrt{(\alpha K)(B)(\beta K)(B)}
\ge
\int_C\int_C\sqrt{K(v,B)K(w,B)}\,\alpha(\dd v)\beta(\dd w),
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the functions \(\sqrt{K(v,B)}\) and
\(\sqrt{K(w,B)}\).  Summing over \(B\in\mathcal P\) gives
\[
\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{(\alpha K)(B)(\beta K)(B)}
\ge
\int_C\int_C
\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{K(v,B)K(w,B)}
\,\alpha(\dd v)\beta(\dd w).
\]
The inner sum is at least
\(\Aff(K(v,\cdot),K(w,\cdot))\) by Lemma \ref{lem:hellfacts}; hence the last
display is at least \(a\alpha(C)\beta(C)\).  Taking the infimum over
\(\mathcal P\) and using the partition formula proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Lower semicontinuity of total variation]\label{lem:tv-lsc}
If \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\) and \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\rho\) weakly on a Polish
space, then
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
\le
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|\mu_n-\rho_n\|_{\TV}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(\eta=\mu-\rho\), regularity of the finite signed measure \(\eta\) implies
\[
\|\eta\|_{\TV}
=
\sup_{\substack{f\in C_b(E)\\0\le f\le1}}
\left|\int_Ef\dd\eta\right|.
\]
Indeed, indicators of Borel sets are approximated from inside and outside by
continuous functions using regularity of \(|\eta|\) and Urysohn's lemma.  For
each such \(f\),
\[
\int_Ef\dd(\mu_n-\rho_n)\longrightarrow\int_Ef\dd(\mu-\rho),
\]
so
\[
\left|\int_Ef\dd(\mu-\rho)\right|
\le
\liminf_n\|\mu_n-\rho_n\|_{\TV}.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(f\) proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional uniqueness from compact-local Hellinger overlap]\label{thm:hellinger}
Let \(E\) be Polish.  Let \((P_s)\) and \((P_s^n)\) be Markov semigroups on
\(E\).  Fix \(0<\varepsilon<t\).  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every \(x\in E\),
\[
P_t^n(x,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_t(x,\cdot),
\qquad
P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(x,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_{t-\varepsilon}(x,\cdot);
\]
\item for every compact \(C\subset E\), there is \(a(C)>0\) such that
\[
\Aff(P_\varepsilon^n(v,\cdot),P_\varepsilon^n(w,\cdot))\ge a(C)
\]
for all \(n\ge1\) and all \(v,w\in C\).
\end{enumerate}
Then \(P_t(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_t(y,\cdot)\) for all \(x,y\in E\).  Consequently,
if this holds for some \(t>0\), then \((P_s)\) has at most one invariant
probability measure.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(x,y\in E\), and set
\[
\alpha_n:=P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(x,\cdot),\qquad
\beta_n:=P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(y,\cdot).
\]
The two sequences are tight, because they are weakly convergent.  Hence there
is a compact \(C\subset E\) such that
\(\alpha_n(C)\ge1/2\) and \(\beta_n(C)\ge1/2\) for all \(n\).  By hypothesis 2,
\[
\Aff(P_\varepsilon^n(v,\cdot),P_\varepsilon^n(w,\cdot))\ge a(C),
\qquad v,w\in C.
\]
Using the semigroup property and Lemma \ref{lem:mixture},
\[
\Aff(P_t^n(x,\cdot),P_t^n(y,\cdot))
=
\Aff(\alpha_nP_\varepsilon^n,\beta_nP_\varepsilon^n)
\ge
a(C)\alpha_n(C)\beta_n(C)\ge \frac{a(C)}4.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:hellfacts},
\[
\|P_t^n(x,\cdot)-P_t^n(y,\cdot)\|_{\TV}
\le
\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{a(C)}4\right)^2}
=:\rho<1.
\]
Weak convergence at time \(t\), followed by Lemma \ref{lem:tv-lsc}, yields
\[
\|P_t(x,\cdot)-P_t(y,\cdot)\|_{\TV}\le\rho<1.
\]
Thus the two limiting transition probabilities are not singular.  The final
claim follows from Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise}.
\end{proof}

\section{Absolute continuity routes and the Dirichlet-form limitation}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional uniqueness from compact-local uniform absolute continuity]\label{thm:uac}
Let \(E=C_0([0,1])\), and let \(\nu\) be the Gibbs measure in
\eqref{eq:gibbs}.  Fix \(t_0>0\).  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every \(x\in E\) and \(f\in C_b(E)\),
\[
P_{t_0}^nf(x)\to P_{t_0}f(x);
\]
\item for every compact \(K\subset E\), the family
\[
\{P_{t_0}^n(x,\cdot): n\ge1,\ x\in K\}
\]
is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\);
\item every \(P_t\)-invariant probability measure that is absolutely continuous
with respect to \(\nu\) equals \(\nu\).
\end{enumerate}
Then \(\nu\) is the unique invariant probability measure of \((P_t)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mu\) be invariant for \((P_t)\), and set
\(\rho_n:=\mu P_{t_0}^n\).  For \(f\in C_b(E)\), dominated convergence and
hypothesis 1 give
\[
\int_Ef\dd\rho_n
=
\int_EP_{t_0}^nf(x)\mu(\dd x)
\longrightarrow
\int_EP_{t_0}f(x)\mu(\dd x)
=
\int_Ef\dd\mu,
\]
so \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\mu\).

Let \(B\) be Borel with \(\nu(B)=0\).  Fix \(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  By tightness
of \(\mu\), choose compact \(K\) with \(\mu(K^c)<\eta\).  By uniform absolute
continuity on \(K\), choose \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\nu(A)<\delta
\implies
\sup_{n\ge1}\sup_{x\in K}P_{t_0}^n(x,A)<\varepsilon.
\]
By outer regularity, choose open \(O\supset B\) with \(\nu(O)<\delta\).  Then
for every \(n\),
\[
\rho_n(O)
=
\int_EP_{t_0}^n(x,O)\mu(\dd x)
\le
\varepsilon+\eta.
\]
Since \(O\) is open and \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\mu\), Portmanteau gives
\[
\mu(O)\le\liminf_n\rho_n(O)\le\varepsilon+\eta.
\]
Thus \(\mu(B)\le\varepsilon+\eta\).  Letting \(\varepsilon,\eta\downarrow0\)
shows \(\mu\ll\nu\).  Hypothesis 3 gives \(\mu=\nu\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A simple sufficient condition for uniform absolute continuity]
Hypothesis 2 of Theorem \ref{thm:uac} follows if, for every compact
\(K\subset E\), there are \(p>1\) and \(C_K<\infty\) such that
\(P_{t_0}^n(x,\cdot)=r_{n,x}\nu\) and
\[
\sup_{n\ge1}\sup_{x\in K}\|r_{n,x}\|_{L^p(\nu)}\le C_K.
\]
Indeed, with \(q=p/(p-1)\), Holder's inequality gives
\(P_{t_0}^n(x,A)\le C_K\nu(A)^{1/q}\).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Pointwise resolvent absolute continuity]\label{prop:resolvent}
Assume that \(\nu\) is invariant and that every invariant probability measure
absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\) equals \(\nu\).  If, for some
\(\lambda>0\),
\[
R_\lambda(x,\cdot)
:=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}P_t(x,\cdot)\dd t
\ll\nu
\qquad\forall x\in E,
\]
then \(\nu\) is the unique invariant probability measure.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mu\) be invariant and let \(B\) be Borel with \(\nu(B)=0\).  Then
\(R_\lambda(x,B)=0\) for every \(x\), and therefore
\[
0
=
\int_ER_\lambda(x,B)\mu(\dd x)
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\mu P_t(B)\dd t
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\mu(B)\dd t
=
\frac1\lambda\mu(B).
\]
Thus \(\mu\ll\nu\), and by the assumed uniqueness among \(\nu\)-absolutely
continuous invariant measures, \(\mu=\nu\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[What the Gibbs Dirichlet form proves]\label{prop:acunique}
Let \((T_t)\) be a \(\nu\)-symmetric Markov semigroup on \(L^2(\nu)\), and let
\(\mathcal E\) be its closed Dirichlet form.  Assume that the only
zero-energy functions in the domain of \(\mathcal E\) are constants.  Then every
\(T_t\)-invariant probability measure \(\mu\) with \(\mu\ll\nu\) equals \(\nu\).

For the Gibbs measure above, the zero-energy condition holds for the gradient
form
\[
\mathcal E(F,G)=\frac12\int_E\ip{DF}{DG}_H\dd\nu
\]
provided the limiting semigroup is indeed the symmetric semigroup associated
with this form.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(h=\dd\mu/\dd\nu\).  Invariance gives, for bounded \(f\),
\[
\int_ET_tf\,h\dd\nu=\int_Ef\,h\dd\nu.
\]
By symmetry and the \(L^1\)-extension of \(T_t\), this says \(T_th=h\) in
\(L^1(\nu)\).  For \(m\ge1\), let \(h_m=h\wedge m\).  Since
\(r\mapsto r\wedge m\) is concave and \(T_t\) is Markov,
\[
T_th_m\le (T_th)\wedge m=h_m.
\]
Integrating both sides against the invariant measure \(\nu\) gives equality,
hence \(T_th_m=h_m\).  Now \(h_m\in L^2(\nu)\), and a fixed \(L^2\)-function has
zero energy:
\[
\mathcal E(h_m,h_m)
=
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac1t\ip{h_m-T_th_m}{h_m}_{L^2(\nu)}
=0.
\]
Thus \(h_m\) is constant.  By monotone convergence,
\(\int h_m\dd\nu\to\int h\dd\nu=1\), so \(h_m\to1\) and \(h=1\) \(\nu\)-a.e.

For the displayed Gibbs gradient form, the density bounds \eqref{eq:density-bounds}
make \(\nu\) equivalent to \(\gamma\) with bounded density above and below.
The Gaussian Poincare inequality for the Brownian-bridge measure,
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(F)
\le
\frac1{\pi^2}\int_E\|DF\|_H^2\dd\gamma
\]
on cylinder functions, extends by closure.  Hence zero \(\nu\)-energy implies
zero \(\gamma\)-energy and therefore constancy.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Irreducibility in \(L^2(\nu)\) does not rule out singular invariant laws]\label{ex:nullmod}
Let \(E=[0,1]\), let \(\nu\) be Lebesgue measure, and define a Markov kernel
\[
K(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\nu(\cdot),&x\ne0,\\
\delta_0(\cdot),&x=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\nu K=\nu\) because \(\nu(\{0\})=0\), and \(\delta_0K=\delta_0\).  On
\(L^2(\nu)\), however, \(Kf=\int f\dd\nu\) \(\nu\)-a.e.; hence the \(L^2(\nu)\)
operator is symmetric and has only constant fixed functions.  The extra
invariant measure \(\delta_0\) is invisible to the \(L^2(\nu)\) theory because
it is supported on a \(\nu\)-null point.
\end{example}

\section{What is missing from the stated assumptions}

The preceding results identify exactly what would close the uniqueness proof.
One needs a deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimate, such as:
\[
P_{t_0}(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_{t_0}(y,\cdot)\quad\forall x,y,
\]
or the compact-local Hellinger estimate of Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger}, or
compact-local uniform \(\nu\)-absolute continuity as in Theorem
\ref{thm:uac}, or pointwise resolvent absolute continuity as in Proposition
\ref{prop:resolvent}.  These are not consequences of weak convergence alone.

\begin{example}[Weak convergence can destroy absolute continuity and overlap]
On \(\R\), each Gaussian law \(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) is absolutely continuous with
respect to Lebesgue measure, but
\[
\mathcal N(0,1/n)\Rightarrow\delta_0,
\]
and \(\delta_0\) is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.  Likewise,
\(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) and \(\mathcal N(1,1/n)\) have positive Hellinger affinity
for each \(n\), but their affinities tend to \(0\), and the weak limits
\(\delta_0\) and \(\delta_1\) are singular.  Thus weak convergence of kernels
does not by itself preserve absolute continuity, uniform integrability, or a
positive overlap lower bound.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Finite-dimensional domination as a possible missing theorem]
A convenient way to prove the compact-local Hellinger input would be a uniform
finite-dimensional heat-kernel domination theorem.  Let \(P_t^{n,m}\) be the
\(m\)-mode Galerkin approximation of the mollified equation and \(Q_t^m\) the
\(m\)-dimensional Dirichlet Ornstein--Uhlenbeck kernel.  A bound of the form
\[
P_t^{n,m}(a,\cdot)\ge c\,Q_t^m(a,\cdot),
\]
with \(c>0\) independent of \(n,m,a\), together with a passage from Galerkin
kernels to the infinite-dimensional kernels, would yield overlap.  For the
Galerkin potential
\[
\Psi_{n,m}(a)
=
\int_0^1F_n\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^ma_ke_k(x)\right)\dd x,
\]
one has the layer-cake representation, with
\(e(x)=(e_1(x),\ldots,e_m(x))\),
\[
\Psi_{n,m}(a)
=
\int_0^1\int_{\R}
\1_{\{\ip{e(x)}{a}>s\}}\,b_n(s)\dd s\,\dd x.
\]
This displays \(\Psi_{n,m}\) as an average of affine half-space membrane
potentials of total mass \(1\).  Proving the domination estimate is, however,
an additional finite-dimensional heat-kernel theorem; it is not part of
Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}.
\end{remark}

\section*{Final conclusion}

The natural Gibbs measure \(\nu\) is rigorously proved invariant for the
limiting singular semigroup.  The desired uniqueness statement follows from
any of the deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimates isolated above.
Under only the assumptions explicitly stated in the original problem---namely
well-posedness and weak convergence of the mollified equations---the argument
does not rule out invariant measures singular with respect to \(\nu\).  Thus the
candidate proof establishes invariance and conditional uniqueness, but an
additional smoothing or overlap theorem is needed for an unconditional proof of
\eqref{eq:target}.

## Correctness.

The AI has proved the existence of an invariant measure for the SPDE. It does it by studying the invariant measures of the approximate equations and passing to the limit. However, no proof is provided that the invariant measure is unique. The AI states and proves several seemingly standard results from stochastic analysis. Using these results, it formulates a list of conditions that imply uniqueness of the invariant measure. However, it does not prove that any of these conditions hold for the given SPDE.

## Novelty.

The provided solution does not contain any novelty. The existence argument follows a standard approach, and the uniqueness result—which would require additional ideas—has not been proved.

\subsection*{Overview / Strategy}

The original target is to decide whether the Markov semigroup \(P_t\) of the
Dirichlet stochastic heat equation with distributional drift \(\delta_0\) has
at most one invariant probability measure.  The first part of the argument
constructs the natural Gibbs measure
\[
\nu(\dd v)=Z^{-1}\exp\!\left(2\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x\right)\gamma(\dd v),
\]
where \(\gamma\) is Brownian-bridge law, and proves that \(\nu\) is invariant by
passing to the limit from the smooth mollified equations.  This is carried out
in Theorem \ref{thm:invariance}.

Uniqueness requires more than this invariant-measure construction.  The clean
abstract mechanism is that pairwise non-singularity of one transition skeleton
implies uniqueness; see Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise}.  A compact-local Hellinger
overlap estimate for the mollified last-step kernels would imply such
non-singularity in the limit; see Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger}.  A second route is
to prove that every invariant measure is absolutely continuous with respect to
\(\nu\); see Theorem \ref{thm:uac} and Proposition \ref{prop:resolvent}.  The
stated ABLM-type assumptions provide existence, uniqueness in law, and weak
convergence of the mollified equations, but they do not themselves provide any
of these deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimates.  Thus the
unconditional conclusion proved here is invariance of \(\nu\), together with
precise conditional criteria under which the desired uniqueness follows.

\subsection{Standing assumptions, notation, and the target statement}

Let
\[
E:=C_0([0,1])
=\{v\in C([0,1],\R):v(0)=v(1)=0\},
\qquad H:=L^2(0,1),
\]
with \(E\) equipped with the supremum norm.  Let
\[
e_k(x):=\sqrt2\sin(k\pi x),\qquad \lambda_k:=\pi^2k^2,\qquad k\ge1,
\]
be the Dirichlet eigenbasis of \(-\partial_{xx}\).  Let \(\gamma\) denote
Brownian-bridge law on \(E\), equivalently the centered Gaussian measure with
covariance \((-\partial_{xx})^{-1}\):
\[
\E_\gamma[(v,e_k)_H(v,e_\ell)_H]=\frac{\delta_{k\ell}}{\lambda_k}.
\]

The SPDE from the original problem is
\begin{align}
\tag{\(*\)}\label{eq:spde}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial t}(x,t)
&=\frac12\frac{\partial^2u}{\partial x^2}(x,t)
+\delta_0(u(x,t))+\dot W(x,t),\qquad t\ge0,\\
u(x,0)&=u_0(x)\in E,\nonumber\\
u(0,t)&=u(1,t)=0.\nonumber
\end{align}

\begin{assumption}[ABLM-type input on the bounded interval]\label{ass:ablm}
For every \(u_0\in E\) and \(T>0\), there is a unique-in-law adapted mild
solution \(u\in C([0,T],E)\) to \eqref{eq:spde}, and the solutions define a
Markov semigroup \((P_t)_{t\ge0}\) on \(E\).  For
\[
b_n(r):=G_{1/n}(r)=\sqrt{\frac n{2\pi}}e^{-nr^2/2},
\]
let \(P_t^n\) be the semigroup of the mollified equation obtained by replacing
\(\delta_0\) with \(b_n\).  For every \(t>0\), \(v\in E\), and \(f\in C_b(E)\),
\[
P_t^n f(v)\longrightarrow P_tf(v),
\]
or equivalently \(P_t^n(v,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_t(v,\cdot)\).
\end{assumption}

Define
\[
F_n(r):=\int_{-\infty}^r b_n(s)\dd s,\qquad
\Phi_n(v):=\int_0^1F_n(v(x))\dd x,\qquad
\Phi(v):=\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x.
\]
Set
\begin{equation}\label{eq:gibbs}
\nu_n(\dd v):=Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n(v)}\gamma(\dd v),
\qquad
\nu(\dd v):=Z^{-1}e^{2\Phi(v)}\gamma(\dd v),
\end{equation}
where \(Z_n\) and \(Z\) are the normalizing constants.  Since
\(0\le\Phi_n,\Phi\le1\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:density-bounds}
1\le Z_n,Z\le e^2,
\qquad
e^{-2}\le \frac{\dd\nu_n}{\dd\gamma},\frac{\dd\nu}{\dd\gamma}\le e^2.
\end{equation}

For a Markov kernel \(K\) and a probability measure \(\mu\), write
\(\mu K(A):=\int_EK(x,A)\mu(\dd x)\).  A probability measure \(\mu\) is invariant
for a semigroup \((P_t)\) if \(\mu P_t=\mu\) for all \(t\ge0\).

\begin{theorem}[Original problem: target and established claim]\label{thm:headline}
The target assertion from the original problem is
\[
\tag{U}\label{eq:target}
\text{\((P_t)\) has at most one invariant probability measure on \(E\).}
\]
Under Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}, the Gibbs measure \(\nu\) in
\eqref{eq:gibbs} is invariant.  Moreover, \eqref{eq:target} follows if one adds
any of the deterministic-start smoothing or overlap hypotheses in Theorem
\ref{thm:hellinger}, Theorem \ref{thm:uac}, or Proposition
\ref{prop:resolvent} together with Proposition \ref{prop:acunique}.  In that
case the unique invariant probability measure is \(\nu\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The invariance statement is Theorem \ref{thm:invariance}.  The Hellinger
overlap hypothesis of Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger} implies pairwise
non-singularity of one skeleton, and Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise} then gives
uniqueness.  The compact-local uniform absolute-continuity hypothesis of
Theorem \ref{thm:uac} gives \(\mu\ll\nu\) for every invariant \(\mu\), and its
third hypothesis, supplied for instance by Proposition \ref{prop:acunique},
then gives \(\mu=\nu\).  Finally, Proposition \ref{prop:resolvent} is a
resolvent version of the same absolute-continuity route.  Since
Theorem \ref{thm:invariance} supplies an invariant measure, any ``at most one''
conclusion identifies the invariant law with \(\nu\).
\end{proof}

\subsection{The Gibbs invariant measure}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance of the Gibbs measure]\label{thm:invariance}
Under Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}, the measure
\[
\nu(\dd v)
=
Z^{-1}\exp\!\left(2\int_0^1\1_{\{v(x)>0\}}\dd x\right)\gamma(\dd v)
\]
is invariant for \((P_t)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We prove this by approximation.

\emph{Step 1: \(\nu_n\to\nu\) in total variation.}
For each \(r\ne0\), \(F_n(r)\to\1_{\{r>0\}}\).  Let \(B\sim\gamma\).  For
\(x\in(0,1)\), \(B(x)\) is a nondegenerate centered Gaussian, hence
\(\gamma(B(x)=0)=0\).  Therefore, by Fubini,
\[
\E_\gamma\bigl|\{x\in[0,1]:B(x)=0\}\bigr|
=\int_0^1\gamma(B(x)=0)\dd x=0,
\]
where the endpoints do not matter.  Thus \(|\{x:B(x)=0\}|=0\) for
\(\gamma\)-a.e. \(B\).  For such \(B\),
\[
\Phi_n(B)=\int_0^1F_n(B(x))\dd x
\longrightarrow
\int_0^1\1_{\{B(x)>0\}}\dd x=\Phi(B)
\]
by dominated convergence in \(x\).  Since \(0\le\Phi_n,\Phi\le1\), dominated
convergence in \(\gamma\) gives \(Z_n\to Z\) and
\[
\int_E\left|
Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n(v)}-Z^{-1}e^{2\Phi(v)}
\right|\gamma(\dd v)\longrightarrow0.
\]
Hence \(\|\nu_n-\nu\|_{\TV}\to0\).

\emph{Step 2: \(\nu_n\) is invariant for \(P_t^n\).}
For fixed \(n\), the drift \(b_n\) is bounded and Lipschitz.  Also
\(\Phi_n\) has \(H\)-gradient \(D\Phi_n(v)=b_n(v)\), because for
\(h\in H\),
\[
D\Phi_n(v)[h]=\int_0^1b_n(v(x))h(x)\dd x=\ip{b_n(v)}{h}_H.
\]
On smooth cylinder functions the formal generator is
\[
L_nF(v)=\frac12\operatorname{Tr}D^2F(v)
-\frac12\ip{-\partial_{xx}v}{DF(v)}_H
+\ip{D\Phi_n(v)}{DF(v)}_H.
\]
The Gaussian integration-by-parts formula for \(\gamma\), together with
\(\dd\nu_n=Z_n^{-1}e^{2\Phi_n}\dd\gamma\), gives for smooth cylinder \(F,G\)
\[
\int_EG\,L_nF\,\dd\nu_n
=
-\frac12\int_E\ip{DG}{DF}_H\dd\nu_n.
\]
Indeed, the derivative of \(e^{2\Phi_n}\) contributes
\(2e^{2\Phi_n}D\Phi_n\), which cancels exactly the added drift term
\(\ip{D\Phi_n}{DF}_H\).  Taking \(G\equiv1\) gives
\[
\int_EL_nF\,\dd\nu_n=0.
\]
For bounded Lipschitz gradient drifts, the standard martingale-problem or
symmetric-Dirichlet-form construction of the stochastic heat equation identifies
\(P_t^n\) with the Markov semigroup generated by the closure of \(L_n\); see,
for example, \cite{DPZ14,MR92}.  Infinitesimal invariance on the cylinder core
therefore implies
\[
\nu_nP_t^n=\nu_n,\qquad t\ge0.
\]

\emph{Step 3: pass to the singular limit.}
Let \(f\in C_b(E)\) and \(t>0\).  By Assumption \ref{ass:ablm},
\(P_t^nf(v)\to P_tf(v)\) for every \(v\in E\).  Using
\(\dd\nu_n/\dd\gamma\le e^2\), dominated convergence gives
\[
\int_E|P_t^nf-P_tf|\dd\nu_n
\le
e^2\int_E|P_t^nf-P_tf|\dd\gamma
\longrightarrow0.
\]
Also, \(\nu_n\to\nu\) in total variation and \(P_tf\) is bounded, so
\[
\int_EP_tf\dd\nu_n\longrightarrow\int_EP_tf\dd\nu,
\qquad
\int_Ef\dd\nu_n\longrightarrow\int_Ef\dd\nu.
\]
Since \(\nu_nP_t^n=\nu_n\),
\[
\int_EP_tf\dd\nu
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_EP_t^nf\dd\nu_n
=
\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_Ef\dd\nu_n
=
\int_Ef\dd\nu.
\]
Thus \(\nu P_t=\nu\) for all \(t>0\), and the case \(t=0\) is trivial.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Pairwise overlap and Hellinger criteria}

\begin{theorem}[Pairwise non-singularity of one skeleton implies uniqueness]\label{thm:pairwise}
Let \(E\) be Polish and \(K\) a Markov kernel on \(E\).  If
\[
K(x,\cdot)\not\perp K(y,\cdot)\qquad\forall x,y\in E,
\]
then \(K\) has at most one invariant probability measure.  Consequently, if a
semigroup \((P_t)\) has some \(t_0>0\) such that
\(P_{t_0}(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_{t_0}(y,\cdot)\) for all \(x,y\), then
\((P_t)\) has at most one invariant probability measure.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Assume that \(\mu_1\ne\mu_2\) are invariant for \(K\).  Let
\(\sigma:=\mu_1-\mu_2\), and write its Jordan decomposition
\(\sigma=\sigma^+-\sigma^-\).  Since \(\sigma(E)=0\),
\(m:=\sigma^+(E)=\sigma^-(E)>0\).

For every finite signed measure \(\eta\),
\[
|\eta K|\le |\eta|K.
\]
Indeed, for Borel \(A\), taking the supremum over finite measurable partitions
\(\{A_i\}\) of \(A\),
\[
|\eta K|(A)
\le
\sup_{\{A_i\}}\sum_i\int_EK(x,A_i)|\eta|(\dd x)
=
\int_EK(x,A)|\eta|(\dd x).
\]
Since \(\sigma K=\sigma\), we get \(|\sigma|\le|\sigma|K\).  The two measures
have equal total mass, so \(|\sigma|K=|\sigma|\).  Hence
\[
\sigma^+K=\frac12(|\sigma|K+\sigma K)=\sigma^+,
\qquad
\sigma^-K=\frac12(|\sigma|K-\sigma K)=\sigma^-.
\]
Thus \(\alpha:=\sigma^+/m\) and \(\beta:=\sigma^-/m\) are invariant
probabilities, and \(\alpha\perp\beta\).  Choose a Borel set \(A\) with
\(\alpha(A)=1\) and \(\beta(A)=0\).  Invariance gives
\[
1=\int_EK(x,A)\alpha(\dd x),\qquad
0=\int_EK(y,A)\beta(\dd y).
\]
Therefore \(K(x,A)=1\) for \(\alpha\)-a.e. \(x\) and \(K(y,A)=0\) for
\(\beta\)-a.e. \(y\).  Choosing such \(x,y\), \(K(x,\cdot)\) is concentrated on
\(A\) while \(K(y,\cdot)\) is concentrated on \(A^c\), so
\(K(x,\cdot)\perp K(y,\cdot)\), a contradiction.  The semigroup assertion
follows because every invariant measure for \((P_t)\) is invariant for the
skeleton \(P_{t_0}\).
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Hellinger affinity]
For probability measures \(\mu,\rho\) on \(E\), define
\[
\Aff(\mu,\rho)
:=
\int_E\sqrt{\frac{\dd\mu}{\dd\lambda}\frac{\dd\rho}{\dd\lambda}}\,\dd\lambda,
\]
where \(\lambda\) is any finite measure dominating both \(\mu\) and \(\rho\).
The value is independent of \(\lambda\).  We use the normalized total variation
norm
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}:=\sup_{A\in\cB(E)}|\mu(A)-\rho(A)|.
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Elementary Hellinger facts]\label{lem:hellfacts}
For probability measures \(\mu,\rho\),
\[
\mu\perp\rho
\iff
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}=1
\iff
\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0,
\]
and
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
\le
\sqrt{1-\Aff(\mu,\rho)^2}.
\]
Moreover, if \(\mathcal P\) ranges over finite measurable partitions of \(E\),
then
\[
\Aff(\mu,\rho)
=
\inf_{\mathcal P}\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{\mu(B)\rho(B)}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take \(\lambda=\mu+\rho\), and write \(f=\dd\mu/\dd\lambda\),
\(g=\dd\rho/\dd\lambda\).  The definition is independent of \(\lambda\) because
changing the dominating measure multiplies both densities by the same
Radon--Nikodym factor.  If \(\mu\perp\rho\), then \(fg=0\) \(\lambda\)-a.e., so
\(\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0\).  Conversely, if \(\Aff(\mu,\rho)=0\), then
\(\sqrt{fg}=0\) \(\lambda\)-a.e.; the sets \(\{f>0\}\) and \(\{g>0\}\) separate
\(\mu\) and \(\rho\), so \(\mu\perp\rho\).  The equivalence with
\(\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}=1\) is the standard characterization of singularity for
probability measures.

Also,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
&=\frac12\int_E|f-g|\dd\lambda                                      \\
&=\frac12\int_E|\sqrt f-\sqrt g|(\sqrt f+\sqrt g)\dd\lambda          \\
&\le \frac12
\left(\int_E(\sqrt f-\sqrt g)^2\dd\lambda\right)^{1/2}
\left(\int_E(\sqrt f+\sqrt g)^2\dd\lambda\right)^{1/2}               \\
&=\sqrt{1-\Aff(\mu,\rho)^2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For the partition formula, let \(\mathcal P\) be finite.  On each atom \(B\),
\[
\int_B\sqrt{\E_\lambda(f\mid\mathcal P)\E_\lambda(g\mid\mathcal P)}\dd\lambda
=
\sqrt{\mu(B)\rho(B)}.
\]
Conditional Cauchy--Schwarz gives
\[
\E_\lambda(\sqrt{fg}\mid\mathcal P)
\le
\sqrt{\E_\lambda(f\mid\mathcal P)\E_\lambda(g\mid\mathcal P)},
\]
so every partition sum is at least \(\Aff(\mu,\rho)\).  Since \(E\) is Polish,
\(\cB(E)\) is countably generated.  Choosing finite partitions increasing to a
countable generating algebra, the bounded martingale convergence theorem
(applied with \(\lambda=\mu+\rho\), so \(0\le f,g\le1\)) gives partition sums
converging down to \(\int\sqrt{fg}\dd\lambda\).  Hence the infimum equals
\(\Aff(\mu,\rho)\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Mixture lower bound]\label{lem:mixture}
Let \(K\) be a Markov kernel on \(E\).  Suppose \(C\subset E\) is measurable and
there is \(a>0\) such that
\[
\Aff(K(v,\cdot),K(w,\cdot))\ge a\qquad\forall v,w\in C.
\]
Then, for all probability measures \(\alpha,\beta\),
\[
\Aff(\alpha K,\beta K)\ge a\,\alpha(C)\beta(C).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mathcal P\) be a finite partition.  For each atom \(B\),
\[
\sqrt{(\alpha K)(B)(\beta K)(B)}
\ge
\int_C\int_C\sqrt{K(v,B)K(w,B)}\,\alpha(\dd v)\beta(\dd w),
\]
by Cauchy--Schwarz applied to the functions \(\sqrt{K(v,B)}\) and
\(\sqrt{K(w,B)}\).  Summing over \(B\in\mathcal P\) gives
\[
\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{(\alpha K)(B)(\beta K)(B)}
\ge
\int_C\int_C
\sum_{B\in\mathcal P}\sqrt{K(v,B)K(w,B)}
\,\alpha(\dd v)\beta(\dd w).
\]
The inner sum is at least
\(\Aff(K(v,\cdot),K(w,\cdot))\) by Lemma \ref{lem:hellfacts}; hence the last
display is at least \(a\alpha(C)\beta(C)\).  Taking the infimum over
\(\mathcal P\) and using the partition formula proves the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Lower semicontinuity of total variation]\label{lem:tv-lsc}
If \(\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\) and \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\rho\) weakly on a Polish
space, then
\[
\|\mu-\rho\|_{\TV}
\le
\liminf_{n\to\infty}\|\mu_n-\rho_n\|_{\TV}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For \(\eta=\mu-\rho\), regularity of the finite signed measure \(\eta\) implies
\[
\|\eta\|_{\TV}
=
\sup_{\substack{f\in C_b(E)\\0\le f\le1}}
\left|\int_Ef\dd\eta\right|.
\]
Indeed, indicators of Borel sets are approximated from inside and outside by
continuous functions using regularity of \(|\eta|\) and Urysohn's lemma.  For
each such \(f\),
\[
\int_Ef\dd(\mu_n-\rho_n)\longrightarrow\int_Ef\dd(\mu-\rho),
\]
so
\[
\left|\int_Ef\dd(\mu-\rho)\right|
\le
\liminf_n\|\mu_n-\rho_n\|_{\TV}.
\]
Taking the supremum over \(f\) proves the result.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional uniqueness from compact-local Hellinger overlap]\label{thm:hellinger}
Let \(E\) be Polish.  Let \((P_s)\) and \((P_s^n)\) be Markov semigroups on
\(E\).  Fix \(0<\varepsilon<t\).  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every \(x\in E\),
\[
P_t^n(x,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_t(x,\cdot),
\qquad
P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(x,\cdot)\Rightarrow P_{t-\varepsilon}(x,\cdot);
\]
\item for every compact \(C\subset E\), there is \(a(C)>0\) such that
\[
\Aff(P_\varepsilon^n(v,\cdot),P_\varepsilon^n(w,\cdot))\ge a(C)
\]
for all \(n\ge1\) and all \(v,w\in C\).
\end{enumerate}
Then \(P_t(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_t(y,\cdot)\) for all \(x,y\in E\).  Consequently,
if this holds for some \(t>0\), then \((P_s)\) has at most one invariant
probability measure.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Fix \(x,y\in E\), and set
\[
\alpha_n:=P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(x,\cdot),\qquad
\beta_n:=P_{t-\varepsilon}^n(y,\cdot).
\]
The two sequences are tight, because they are weakly convergent.  Hence there
is a compact \(C\subset E\) such that
\(\alpha_n(C)\ge1/2\) and \(\beta_n(C)\ge1/2\) for all \(n\).  By hypothesis 2,
\[
\Aff(P_\varepsilon^n(v,\cdot),P_\varepsilon^n(w,\cdot))\ge a(C),
\qquad v,w\in C.
\]
Using the semigroup property and Lemma \ref{lem:mixture},
\[
\Aff(P_t^n(x,\cdot),P_t^n(y,\cdot))
=
\Aff(\alpha_nP_\varepsilon^n,\beta_nP_\varepsilon^n)
\ge
a(C)\alpha_n(C)\beta_n(C)\ge \frac{a(C)}4.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:hellfacts},
\[
\|P_t^n(x,\cdot)-P_t^n(y,\cdot)\|_{\TV}
\le
\sqrt{1-\left(\frac{a(C)}4\right)^2}
=:\rho<1.
\]
Weak convergence at time \(t\), followed by Lemma \ref{lem:tv-lsc}, yields
\[
\|P_t(x,\cdot)-P_t(y,\cdot)\|_{\TV}\le\rho<1.
\]
Thus the two limiting transition probabilities are not singular.  The final
claim follows from Theorem \ref{thm:pairwise}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Absolute continuity routes and the Dirichlet-form limitation}

\begin{theorem}[Conditional uniqueness from compact-local uniform absolute continuity]\label{thm:uac}
Let \(E=C_0([0,1])\), and let \(\nu\) be the Gibbs measure in
\eqref{eq:gibbs}.  Fix \(t_0>0\).  Assume:
\begin{enumerate}
\item for every \(x\in E\) and \(f\in C_b(E)\),
\[
P_{t_0}^nf(x)\to P_{t_0}f(x);
\]
\item for every compact \(K\subset E\), the family
\[
\{P_{t_0}^n(x,\cdot): n\ge1,\ x\in K\}
\]
is uniformly absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\);
\item every \(P_t\)-invariant probability measure that is absolutely continuous
with respect to \(\nu\) equals \(\nu\).
\end{enumerate}
Then \(\nu\) is the unique invariant probability measure of \((P_t)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mu\) be invariant for \((P_t)\), and set
\(\rho_n:=\mu P_{t_0}^n\).  For \(f\in C_b(E)\), dominated convergence and
hypothesis 1 give
\[
\int_Ef\dd\rho_n
=
\int_EP_{t_0}^nf(x)\mu(\dd x)
\longrightarrow
\int_EP_{t_0}f(x)\mu(\dd x)
=
\int_Ef\dd\mu,
\]
so \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\mu\).

Let \(B\) be Borel with \(\nu(B)=0\).  Fix \(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  By tightness
of \(\mu\), choose compact \(K\) with \(\mu(K^c)<\eta\).  By uniform absolute
continuity on \(K\), choose \(\delta>0\) such that
\[
\nu(A)<\delta
\implies
\sup_{n\ge1}\sup_{x\in K}P_{t_0}^n(x,A)<\varepsilon.
\]
By outer regularity, choose open \(O\supset B\) with \(\nu(O)<\delta\).  Then
for every \(n\),
\[
\rho_n(O)
=
\int_EP_{t_0}^n(x,O)\mu(\dd x)
\le
\varepsilon+\eta.
\]
Since \(O\) is open and \(\rho_n\Rightarrow\mu\), Portmanteau gives
\[
\mu(O)\le\liminf_n\rho_n(O)\le\varepsilon+\eta.
\]
Thus \(\mu(B)\le\varepsilon+\eta\).  Letting \(\varepsilon,\eta\downarrow0\)
shows \(\mu\ll\nu\).  Hypothesis 3 gives \(\mu=\nu\).
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[A simple sufficient condition for uniform absolute continuity]
Hypothesis 2 of Theorem \ref{thm:uac} follows if, for every compact
\(K\subset E\), there are \(p>1\) and \(C_K<\infty\) such that
\(P_{t_0}^n(x,\cdot)=r_{n,x}\nu\) and
\[
\sup_{n\ge1}\sup_{x\in K}\|r_{n,x}\|_{L^p(\nu)}\le C_K.
\]
Indeed, with \(q=p/(p-1)\), Holder's inequality gives
\(P_{t_0}^n(x,A)\le C_K\nu(A)^{1/q}\).
\end{remark}

\begin{proposition}[Pointwise resolvent absolute continuity]\label{prop:resolvent}
Assume that \(\nu\) is invariant and that every invariant probability measure
absolutely continuous with respect to \(\nu\) equals \(\nu\).  If, for some
\(\lambda>0\),
\[
R_\lambda(x,\cdot)
:=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}P_t(x,\cdot)\dd t
\ll\nu
\qquad\forall x\in E,
\]
then \(\nu\) is the unique invariant probability measure.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\mu\) be invariant and let \(B\) be Borel with \(\nu(B)=0\).  Then
\(R_\lambda(x,B)=0\) for every \(x\), and therefore
\[
0
=
\int_ER_\lambda(x,B)\mu(\dd x)
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\mu P_t(B)\dd t
=
\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\mu(B)\dd t
=
\frac1\lambda\mu(B).
\]
Thus \(\mu\ll\nu\), and by the assumed uniqueness among \(\nu\)-absolutely
continuous invariant measures, \(\mu=\nu\).
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[What the Gibbs Dirichlet form proves]\label{prop:acunique}
Let \((T_t)\) be a \(\nu\)-symmetric Markov semigroup on \(L^2(\nu)\), and let
\(\mathcal E\) be its closed Dirichlet form.  Assume that the only
zero-energy functions in the domain of \(\mathcal E\) are constants.  Then every
\(T_t\)-invariant probability measure \(\mu\) with \(\mu\ll\nu\) equals \(\nu\).

For the Gibbs measure above, the zero-energy condition holds for the gradient
form
\[
\mathcal E(F,G)=\frac12\int_E\ip{DF}{DG}_H\dd\nu
\]
provided the limiting semigroup is indeed the symmetric semigroup associated
with this form.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Let \(h=\dd\mu/\dd\nu\).  Invariance gives, for bounded \(f\),
\[
\int_ET_tf\,h\dd\nu=\int_Ef\,h\dd\nu.
\]
By symmetry and the \(L^1\)-extension of \(T_t\), this says \(T_th=h\) in
\(L^1(\nu)\).  For \(m\ge1\), let \(h_m=h\wedge m\).  Since
\(r\mapsto r\wedge m\) is concave and \(T_t\) is Markov,
\[
T_th_m\le (T_th)\wedge m=h_m.
\]
Integrating both sides against the invariant measure \(\nu\) gives equality,
hence \(T_th_m=h_m\).  Now \(h_m\in L^2(\nu)\), and a fixed \(L^2\)-function has
zero energy:
\[
\mathcal E(h_m,h_m)
=
\lim_{t\downarrow0}\frac1t\ip{h_m-T_th_m}{h_m}_{L^2(\nu)}
=0.
\]
Thus \(h_m\) is constant.  By monotone convergence,
\(\int h_m\dd\nu\to\int h\dd\nu=1\), so \(h_m\to1\) and \(h=1\) \(\nu\)-a.e.

For the displayed Gibbs gradient form, the density bounds \eqref{eq:density-bounds}
make \(\nu\) equivalent to \(\gamma\) with bounded density above and below.
The Gaussian Poincare inequality for the Brownian-bridge measure,
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\gamma(F)
\le
\frac1{\pi^2}\int_E\|DF\|_H^2\dd\gamma
\]
on cylinder functions, extends by closure.  Hence zero \(\nu\)-energy implies
zero \(\gamma\)-energy and therefore constancy.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Irreducibility in \(L^2(\nu)\) does not rule out singular invariant laws]\label{ex:nullmod}
Let \(E=[0,1]\), let \(\nu\) be Lebesgue measure, and define a Markov kernel
\[
K(x,\cdot)=
\begin{cases}
\nu(\cdot),&x\ne0,\\
\delta_0(\cdot),&x=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then \(\nu K=\nu\) because \(\nu(\{0\})=0\), and \(\delta_0K=\delta_0\).  On
\(L^2(\nu)\), however, \(Kf=\int f\dd\nu\) \(\nu\)-a.e.; hence the \(L^2(\nu)\)
operator is symmetric and has only constant fixed functions.  The extra
invariant measure \(\delta_0\) is invisible to the \(L^2(\nu)\) theory because
it is supported on a \(\nu\)-null point.
\end{example}

\subsection{What is missing from the stated assumptions}

The preceding results identify exactly what would close the uniqueness proof.
One needs a deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimate, such as:
\[
P_{t_0}(x,\cdot)\not\perp P_{t_0}(y,\cdot)\quad\forall x,y,
\]
or the compact-local Hellinger estimate of Theorem \ref{thm:hellinger}, or
compact-local uniform \(\nu\)-absolute continuity as in Theorem
\ref{thm:uac}, or pointwise resolvent absolute continuity as in Proposition
\ref{prop:resolvent}.  These are not consequences of weak convergence alone.

\begin{example}[Weak convergence can destroy absolute continuity and overlap]
On \(\R\), each Gaussian law \(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) is absolutely continuous with
respect to Lebesgue measure, but
\[
\mathcal N(0,1/n)\Rightarrow\delta_0,
\]
and \(\delta_0\) is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure.  Likewise,
\(\mathcal N(0,1/n)\) and \(\mathcal N(1,1/n)\) have positive Hellinger affinity
for each \(n\), but their affinities tend to \(0\), and the weak limits
\(\delta_0\) and \(\delta_1\) are singular.  Thus weak convergence of kernels
does not by itself preserve absolute continuity, uniform integrability, or a
positive overlap lower bound.
\end{example}

\begin{remark}[Finite-dimensional domination as a possible missing theorem]
A convenient way to prove the compact-local Hellinger input would be a uniform
finite-dimensional heat-kernel domination theorem.  Let \(P_t^{n,m}\) be the
\(m\)-mode Galerkin approximation of the mollified equation and \(Q_t^m\) the
\(m\)-dimensional Dirichlet Ornstein--Uhlenbeck kernel.  A bound of the form
\[
P_t^{n,m}(a,\cdot)\ge c\,Q_t^m(a,\cdot),
\]
with \(c>0\) independent of \(n,m,a\), together with a passage from Galerkin
kernels to the infinite-dimensional kernels, would yield overlap.  For the
Galerkin potential
\[
\Psi_{n,m}(a)
=
\int_0^1F_n\!\left(\sum_{k=1}^ma_ke_k(x)\right)\dd x,
\]
one has the layer-cake representation, with
\(e(x)=(e_1(x),\ldots,e_m(x))\),
\[
\Psi_{n,m}(a)
=
\int_0^1\int_{\R}
\1_{\{\ip{e(x)}{a}>s\}}\,b_n(s)\dd s\,\dd x.
\]
This displays \(\Psi_{n,m}\) as an average of affine half-space membrane
potentials of total mass \(1\).  Proving the domination estimate is, however,
an additional finite-dimensional heat-kernel theorem; it is not part of
Assumption \ref{ass:ablm}.
\end{remark}

\subsection*{Final conclusion}

The natural Gibbs measure \(\nu\) is rigorously proved invariant for the
limiting singular semigroup.  The desired uniqueness statement follows from
any of the deterministic-start smoothing or overlap estimates isolated above.
Under only the assumptions explicitly stated in the original problem---namely
well-posedness and weak convergence of the mollified equations---the argument
does not rule out invariant measures singular with respect to \(\nu\).  Thus the
candidate proof establishes invariance and conditional uniqueness, but an
additional smoothing or overlap theorem is needed for an unconditional proof of
\eqref{eq:target}.

## Correctness.
 The solution is explicitly partial. The invariance of the explicit Gibbs measure is proved (but should be cited to the literature, as it was already known). The submission claims to provide a number of results towards uniqueness conditional on various assumptions, which are essentially standard in the literature. None of these parts of the submission engage at all with the specific form of the equation under consideration, which is required for a proof. In other words, these are abstract criteria for the uniqueness of an invariant measure, and no progress is made towards checking the conditions in the specific situation under consideration.

## Novelty.
 I do not believe that any of the criteria for uniqueness are novel.
