%% ======================================================================

\date{}



\subsection*{Overview / Strategy}

The proof has two main parts. First, a vertex of weight \(1\) is automatically irreducible, because a decomposition \(u=p+q\) with \(p\cdot q\ge 0\) would force \(1=u^2\ge p^2+q^2\ge 2\). Thus, after this easy case, we may assume that no vertex has weight \(1\).

In that remaining case, let \(b\) be the unique vertex with \(w(b)<d_T(b)\). We prove that \(b\) itself is irreducible. The key input is a rooted-branch estimate for each component of \(T-\{b\}\). That estimate is proved by induction using a Schur-complement calculation and a parity argument for the inverse Gram matrix. Combining the branch estimates with the Schur complement at \(b\), any hypothetical decomposition \(b=x+(b-x)\) with \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge0\) is forced to have \(x=0\) or \(x=b\), contradicting the requirement that both summands be nonzero.

\subsection*{Statement and notation}

Let \(T\) be a finite tree with vertex set \(V\), edge set \(E\), and weight function \(w:V\to\Z\). We write \(d_T(v)\) for the degree of a vertex \(v\) in \(T\). Let \(L(T)\) be the free abelian group generated by \(V\). We identify a vertex with the corresponding basis element of \(L(T)\). The bilinear form on \(L(T)\) is the symmetric form determined on generators by
\[
u\cdot v=
\begin{cases}
w(u), & u=v,\\
-1, & \{u,v\}\in E,\\
0, & u\ne v \text{ and } \{u,v\}\notin E.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(x\in L(T)\), write \(x^2=x\cdot x\). The form is called positive definite if its extension to \(L(T)\otimes_{\Z}\mathbb R\) is positive definite. Since the Gram matrix has integer entries, if the form is positive definite, then every nonzero \(z\in L(T)\) satisfies \(z^2\in\Z_{>0}\).

A nonzero lattice element \(y\in L(T)\) is called \emph{irreducible} if there do not exist nonzero \(a,c\in L(T)\) such that
\[
y=a+c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot c\ge 0.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Original problem]\label{thm:main}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree with vertex set \(V\), edge set \(E\), and weight function \(w:V\to\Z\). Equip \(L(T)\) with the symmetric bilinear form above. Suppose this form is positive definite, and suppose there is exactly one vertex \(b\in V\) such that
\[
w(b)<d_T(b).
\]
Then \(T\) contains a vertex \(u\) such that \(u\) is irreducible in \(L(T)\).
\end{theorem}

For a connected subgraph or subtree \(C\), write \(d_C(u)\) for the degree of \(u\) inside \(C\). The group \(L(C)\) is the free abelian group on the vertices of \(C\), equipped with the restricted form. If \(x\in L(C)\), write \(x_u\) for the coefficient of the vertex \(u\) in \(x\).

\subsection*{Auxiliary lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[A weight-one vertex is irreducible]\label{lem:weight-one}
Assume the form on \(L(T)\) is positive definite. If \(u\in V\) satisfies \(w(u)=1\), then \(u\) is irreducible.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
u=p+q
\]
where \(p,q\in L(T)\) are nonzero and \(p\cdot q\ge 0\). Since the form is positive definite and integral, \(p^2,q^2\in\Z_{>0}\). Hence
\[
1=u^2=(p+q)^2=p^2+q^2+2p\cdot q
\ge 1+1+0=2,
\]
which is impossible. Therefore no such decomposition exists, and \(u\) is irreducible.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Schur complement calculation]\label{lem:schur}
Let
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(B\) is symmetric positive definite. Set
\[
S=a-\gamma^T B^{-1}\gamma.
\]
Then \(M\) is positive definite if and only if \(S>0\). When \(S>0\),
\[
M^{-1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
S^{-1} & -S^{-1}\gamma^T B^{-1}\\
-B^{-1}\gamma S^{-1} &
B^{-1}+B^{-1}\gamma S^{-1}\gamma^T B^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{lemma}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It would be good to say Lemma~3 is a standard result and proof, being given here since it may not be familiar to all readers.]]


\begin{proof}
We have the factorization
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \gamma^T B^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
S & 0\\
0 & B
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0\\
B^{-1}\gamma & I
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Indeed, multiplying the last two factors gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
S & 0\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and multiplying by the first factor gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
S+\gamma^T B^{-1}\gamma & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first and third factors are transposes of one another and are invertible. Congruence by an invertible matrix preserves positive definiteness, so \(M\) is positive definite exactly when the middle block diagonal matrix is positive definite. Since \(B\) is already positive definite, this is equivalent to \(S>0\).

When \(S>0\), invert the displayed factorization:
\[
M^{-1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0\\
-B^{-1}\gamma & I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
S^{-1} & 0\\
0 & B^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & -\gamma^T B^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Multiplying these three factors gives exactly the stated block formula.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Rooted branch estimate]\label{lem:branch}
Let \(C\) be a finite weighted tree rooted at a vertex \(r\). Let \(A\) be its Gram matrix, and assume \(A\) is positive definite. Suppose
\[
w(r)\ge d_C(r)+1,
\qquad
w(u)\ge d_C(u)\quad\text{for every }u\ne r.
\]
Let \(G=A^{-1}\), and define
\[
\alpha=(A^{-1})_{rr}=e_r^TGe_r,
\]
where \(e_r\) is the coordinate vector of \(r\). Then \(0<\alpha\le 1\), and for every \(x\in L(C)\), if \(c=x_r\), then for every \(k\in\Z\),
\[
(2k-1)c-x^2\le k(k-1)\alpha.
\]
Moreover, if \(k=0\) or \(k=1\), and equality holds with \(x\ne 0\), then \(C\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We first prove a parity estimate for inverse Gram matrices. We claim that, under the hypotheses of the lemma,
\[
0<\alpha\le 1
\]
and that every vector \(\lambda\in\Z^C\) satisfying
\[
\lambda_r\equiv 1\pmod 2,
\qquad
\lambda_u\equiv 0\pmod 2\quad(u\ne r)
\]
also satisfies
\[
\lambda^T G\lambda\ge \alpha.
\]
This is proved by induction on \(|C|\).

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It would be nice to isolate this statement as a lemma, to break up a somewhat long proof.]]


If \(C=\{r\}\), then \(A=[w(r)]\). The root hypothesis gives \(w(r)\ge 1\), and positive definiteness also gives \(w(r)>0\). Thus
\[
\alpha=\frac{1}{w(r)}\le 1.
\]
If \(\lambda_r=s\) is odd, then \(s^2\ge 1\), so
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda=\frac{s^2}{w(r)}\ge \frac{1}{w(r)}=\alpha.
\]
This proves the base case.

Assume now that \(|C|>1\). Let \(C_1,\dots,C_m\) be the connected components of \(C-\{r\}\), and let \(r_i\) be the unique vertex of \(C_i\) adjacent to \(r\). Root \(C_i\) at \(r_i\). Let \(A_i\) be the Gram matrix of \(C_i\), set \(G_i=A_i^{-1}\), let \(e_i=e_{r_i}\), and put
\[
\alpha_i=e_i^TG_ie_i.
\]
Each \(A_i\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of \(A\). Also, each rooted tree \(C_i\) satisfies the same type of weight hypotheses: since \(r_i\ne r\),
\[
w(r_i)\ge d_C(r_i)=d_{C_i}(r_i)+1,
\]
and every other vertex \(u\in C_i\) satisfies
\[
w(u)\ge d_C(u)=d_{C_i}(u).
\]
Therefore, by induction,
\[
0<\alpha_i\le 1
\qquad\text{for all }i.
\]

Order the vertices of \(C\) by putting \(r\) first and then the vertices of \(C_1,\dots,C_m\). With respect to this order,
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
w(r) & -\eta^T\\
-\eta & B
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=A_1\oplus\cdots\oplus A_m,
\]
where the \(C_i\)-block of \(\eta\) is \(e_i\). By Lemma \ref{lem:schur}, if
\[
S=w(r)-\eta^TB^{-1}\eta,
\]
then \(S>0\) and
\[
\alpha=(A^{-1})_{rr}=\frac{1}{S}.
\]
Since \(B^{-1}=G_1\oplus\cdots\oplus G_m\), we have
\[
\eta^TB^{-1}\eta=\sum_i \alpha_i.
\]
Also \(m=d_C(r)\), so the root hypothesis and the inductive bounds \(\alpha_i\le 1\) imply
\[
S=w(r)-\sum_i\alpha_i
\ge (m+1)-m
=1.
\]
Thus \(0<\alpha=1/S\le 1\).

Now let \(\lambda\in\Z^C\) have odd root coordinate and even nonroot coordinates. In the above ordering, write
\[
\lambda=(s,2\mu_1,\dots,2\mu_m),
\]
where \(s\) is odd and \(\mu_i\in\Z^{C_i}\). Define
\[
\rho_i=e_i^TG_i\mu_i,
\qquad
E_i=\mu_i^TG_i\mu_i,
\qquad
\rho=\sum_i\rho_i.
\]
Using the inverse formula from Lemma \ref{lem:schur} with \(\gamma=-\eta\), we obtain
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
=
4\sum_i E_i+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}.
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I found I had to work this out on scratch paper, and it would have been convenient to say a little more here. (I left out a term and got confused.)]]

For each \(i\), the vectors \(2\mu_i-e_i\) and \(2\mu_i+e_i\) have odd coordinate at the root \(r_i\) and even coordinates elsewhere in \(C_i\). The induction hypothesis applied to \(C_i\) gives
\[
(2\mu_i-e_i)^TG_i(2\mu_i-e_i)\ge \alpha_i,
\qquad
(2\mu_i+e_i)^TG_i(2\mu_i+e_i)\ge \alpha_i.
\]
Expanding these two inequalities gives
\[
4E_i-4\rho_i+\alpha_i\ge \alpha_i,
\qquad
4E_i+4\rho_i+\alpha_i\ge \alpha_i.
\]
Hence
\[
E_i\ge |\rho_i|.
\]
Therefore
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
\ge
4\sum_i|\rho_i|+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}
\ge
4|\rho|+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}.
\]
Set \(y=2\rho\). Then
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
\ge
2|y|+\frac{(s+y)^2}{S}.
\]
Since \(S\ge 1\), it is enough to prove
\[
(s+y)^2+2S|y|\ge 1.
\]
Let \(a=|s|\ge 1\) and \(u=|y|\). If \(sy\ge 0\), then \(|s+y|=a+u\ge 1\), so the inequality is immediate. If \(sy<0\), then
\[
(s+y)^2+2S|y|
\ge
(a-u)^2+2u
=
\bigl(u-(a-1)\bigr)^2+2a-1
\ge 1.
\]
Thus \(S\lambda^TG\lambda\ge 1\), and hence
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda\ge \frac{1}{S}=\alpha.
\]
This completes the induction and proves the parity estimate.

We now derive the stated branch inequality. Fix \(x\in L(C)\), let \(c=x_r\), and set \(Q=x^2=x^TAx\). For \(k\in\Z\), put
\[
t=2k-1.
\]
Define
\[
\lambda=2Ax-te_r.
\]
Because \(A\) has integer entries and \(x\) has integer coordinates, \(\lambda\in\Z^C\). Its root coordinate is even minus the odd integer \(t\), hence is odd, while every nonroot coordinate is even. The parity estimate therefore gives
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda\ge \alpha.
\]
Using \(G=A^{-1}\), we expand:
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
=
(2Ax-te_r)^TG(2Ax-te_r)
=
4Q-4tc+t^2\alpha.
\]
Hence
\[
4Q-4tc+t^2\alpha\ge \alpha,
\]
or equivalently
\[
tc-Q\le \frac{t^2-1}{4}\alpha.
\]
Since \(t=2k-1\),
\[
\frac{t^2-1}{4}
=
\frac{(2k-1)^2-1}{4}
=
k(k-1).
\]
Therefore
\[
(2k-1)c-x^2\le k(k-1)\alpha.
\]

It remains to prove the equality statement for \(k=0,1\). For every \(x\in L(C)\), expanding the form gives
\[
x^2
=
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}(x_u-x_v)^2
+
\sum_{u\in C}\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2.
\]
Indeed, in the first sum, the term \(x_u^2\) appears once for each edge incident to \(u\), hence \(d_C(u)\) times, and each edge contributes the cross term \(-2x_ux_v\). Therefore the displayed expression equals
\[
\sum_{u\in C}w(u)x_u^2-2\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}x_ux_v=x^2.
\]
By the hypotheses,
\[
w(r)-d_C(r)\ge 1,
\qquad
w(u)-d_C(u)\ge 0\quad(u\ne r),
\]
so
\[
x^2-c^2
=
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}(x_u-x_v)^2
+
\bigl(w(r)-d_C(r)-1\bigr)c^2
+
\sum_{u\ne r}\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2
\ge 0.
\]
Thus \(x^2\ge c^2\).

Suppose first that \(k=1\), equality holds in the branch inequality, and \(x\ne 0\). Since \(k(k-1)=0\), equality says
\[
c-x^2=0.
\]
Thus \(x^2=c\). Positive definiteness gives \(x^2>0\), so \(c>0\), and hence \(x^2=|c|\). Since \(x^2\ge c^2\), we get \(|c|\ge c^2\). Because \(c\in\Z\) and \(c\ne 0\), this forces \(c=1\), and then \(x^2=c^2=1\).

Similarly, if \(k=0\), equality says
\[
-c-x^2=0.
\]
Thus \(x^2=-c>0\), so \(c<0\). Again \(x^2=|c|\), and the inequality \(x^2\ge c^2\) forces \(c=-1\) and \(x^2=c^2=1\).

In either case, \(|c|=1\) and \(x^2=c^2\). Therefore equality holds in the nonnegative sum for \(x^2-c^2\), so every summand in that sum is zero. In particular, each edge term \((x_u-x_v)^2\) is zero. Since \(C\) is connected, all coordinates of \(x\) are equal to \(c=\pm 1\).

If \(C\) has only one vertex, then \(C=\{r\}\). The equality \(x^2=c^2\), with \(c^2=1\), gives
\[
(w(r)-d_C(r)-1)c^2=0.
\]
Since \(d_C(r)=0\), we obtain \(w(r)=1\).

If \(C\) has more than one vertex, choose a vertex \(u\ne r\) at maximal distance from \(r\). Such a vertex is a nonroot leaf, so \(d_C(u)=1\). Because all coordinates of \(x\) are \(\pm 1\), we have \(x_u^2=1\). The vanishing of the corresponding nonroot summand gives
\[
\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2=0,
\]
hence \(w(u)-d_C(u)=0\), and therefore \(w(u)=1\). Thus, whenever equality holds for \(k=0\) or \(k=1\) with \(x\ne 0\), the branch \(C\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calculation at a vertex]\label{lem:bad-vertex}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree whose form is positive definite, and let \(b\) be a vertex of \(T\). Let \(C\) range over the components of \(T-\{b\}\). For each such component \(C\), let \(r_C\) be the unique vertex of \(C\) adjacent to \(b\), let \(A_C\) be the Gram matrix of \(C\), and define
\[
\alpha_C=(A_C^{-1})_{r_Cr_C}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_C \alpha_C<w(b).
\]
Moreover, if
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C,
\]
where \(k\in\Z\) and \(x_C\in L(C)\), and if \(c_C=(x_C)_{r_C}\), then
\[
x\cdot(b-x)
=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(T=\{b\}\), then there are no components \(C\), the sum \(\sum_C\alpha_C\) is empty, and the first assertion says \(0<w(b)\), which follows from positive definiteness because \(w(b)=b^2\). The displayed formula also reduces immediately to
\[
(kb)\cdot(b-kb)=k(1-k)w(b).
\]
Thus assume \(T\ne \{b\}\).

Order the vertices of \(T\) by putting \(b\) first, followed by the vertices in the components \(C\) of \(T-\{b\}\). With respect to this order, the full Gram matrix has block form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
w(b) & -\eta^T\\
-\eta & B
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\bigoplus_C A_C,
\]
where the \(C\)-block of \(\eta\) is \(e_{r_C}\). The matrix \(B\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of the positive definite Gram matrix of \(T\). Applying Lemma \ref{lem:schur}, the Schur complement is positive:
\[
w(b)-\eta^TB^{-1}\eta>0.
\]
Since \(B^{-1}=\bigoplus_C A_C^{-1}\), we have
\[
\eta^TB^{-1}\eta=\sum_C \alpha_C.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_C\alpha_C<w(b).
\]

Now write
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C.
\]
Different components of \(T-\{b\}\) are orthogonal to one another, and \(b\) pairs nontrivially with a component \(C\) only at the root \(r_C\), where \(b\cdot r_C=-1\). Hence
\[
b\cdot x=kw(b)-\sum_C c_C.
\]
Also,
\[
x^2
=
k^2w(b)-2k\sum_C c_C+\sum_C x_C^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\cdot(b-x)
&=x\cdot b-x^2\\
&=
\left(kw(b)-\sum_C c_C\right)
-
\left(k^2w(b)-2k\sum_C c_C+\sum_C x_C^2\right)\\
&=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the formula.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Proof of the theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main}]
Let \(b\) denote the unique vertex of \(T\) satisfying \(w(b)<d_T(b)\). Thus every vertex \(u\ne b\) satisfies
\[
w(u)\ge d_T(u).
\]

If \(T\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\), then Lemma \ref{lem:weight-one} shows that this vertex is irreducible, and the theorem follows. Hence assume from now on that \(T\) contains no vertex of weight \(1\). We will prove that \(b\) is irreducible.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(b\) is reducible. Then there exists \(x\in L(T)\) such that
\[
x\ne 0,
\qquad
b-x\ne 0,
\qquad
x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0.
\]
Decompose \(x\) according to the components of \(T-\{b\}\):
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C,
\]
where \(k\in\Z\), each \(x_C\in L(C)\), and the sum ranges over the components \(C\) of \(T-\{b\}\). Let \(r_C\) be the vertex of \(C\) adjacent to \(b\), and put
\[
c_C=(x_C)_{r_C}.
\]

We now verify that each rooted component \(C\), rooted at \(r_C\), satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lem:branch}. Since \(r_C\ne b\), the uniqueness of \(b\) gives
\[
w(r_C)\ge d_T(r_C)=d_C(r_C)+1,
\]
because the only edge incident to \(r_C\) that is not in \(C\) is the edge from \(r_C\) to \(b\). If \(u\in C\) and \(u\ne r_C\), then no edge incident to \(u\) was removed when passing from \(T\) to \(C\), so
\[
w(u)\ge d_T(u)=d_C(u).
\]
Finally, the Gram matrix \(A_C\) of \(C\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of the positive definite Gram matrix of \(T\). Thus Lemma \ref{lem:branch} applies to each component \(C\).

Let
\[
\alpha_C=(A_C^{-1})_{r_Cr_C}.
\]
Applying Lemma \ref{lem:branch} to each component, with the same integer \(k\), gives
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\le k(k-1)\alpha_C.
\]
Using Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\cdot(b-x)
&=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr)\\
&\le
k(1-k)w(b)+k(k-1)\sum_C\alpha_C\\
&=
k(k-1)\left(\sum_C\alpha_C-w(b)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex},
\[
\sum_C\alpha_C-w(b)<0.
\]
If \(k\notin\{0,1\}\), then \(k(k-1)>0\), so the last upper bound is strictly negative. This contradicts \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0\). Therefore
\[
k\in\{0,1\}.
\]

For \(k=0\) or \(k=1\), we have \(k(1-k)=0\), and Lemma \ref{lem:branch} gives
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\le 0
\qquad\text{for every component }C.
\]
Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex} therefore gives
\[
x\cdot(b-x)
=
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr),
\]
a sum of nonpositive terms. Since \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0\), every term in this sum must be equal to \(0\). Hence, for every component \(C\),
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2=0.
\]
If some \(x_C\ne 0\), then the equality statement in Lemma \ref{lem:branch} implies that \(C\), and therefore \(T\), contains a vertex of weight \(1\). This contradicts our standing assumption that \(T\) has no weight-one vertex. Thus
\[
x_C=0
\qquad\text{for every component }C.
\]
Consequently \(x=kb\). If \(k=0\), then \(x=0\), contradicting \(x\ne 0\). If \(k=1\), then \(b-x=0\), contradicting \(b-x\ne 0\). Both possibilities are impossible.

Therefore no such decomposition of \(b\) exists, and \(b\) is irreducible. Hence \(T\) contains an irreducible vertex.
\end{proof}

This gives a complete solution to the problem. The approach contains essentially all the same ideas as the known human proof. However, the proof here makes a direct beeline to the solution using elementary algebraic manipulation and so much of the motivation or interpretation of the steps is never explained. Although argument appears to be correct in all aspects, it seems likely that certain parts could be optimized.

## Exposition

In terms of the writing, I was not convinced by some of the notational and stylistic choices. For example writing $x^2$ for the self-pairing of a vector $x$ is particularly jarring. Especially if one is also calling vectors $p$ or some other variable name that is typically used for an integer. The choice of how much detail to provide is uneven: some parts are extremely terse whereas others are described in excessive detail. The level of writing here is more akin to a first draft than a finished paper. It is mathematically correct, but needs a lot of polishing.

## Correctness.

The solution is correct.

## Novelty.

The overall strategy of this solution very loosely follows that of the human solution. However any geometric or conceptual insight behind the steps is replaced by unmotivated algebraic manipulations. In general, the proof is extremely specialized to the case at hand and does not appear to contain any particular insights that could be directly generalized to related problems.

%% ======================================================================
%% Inlined verbatim from the anonymised submission prob_006-B.
%% ======================================================================

\date{}



\subsection*{Overview / Strategy}

The proof has two main parts. First, a vertex of weight \(1\) is automatically irreducible, because a decomposition \(u=p+q\) with \(p\cdot q\ge 0\) would force \(1=u^2\ge p^2+q^2\ge 2\). Thus, after this easy case, we may assume that no vertex has weight \(1\).

In that remaining case, let \(b\) be the unique vertex with \(w(b)<d_T(b)\). We prove that \(b\) itself is irreducible. The key input is a rooted-branch estimate for each component of \(T-\{b\}\). That estimate is proved by induction using a Schur-complement calculation and a parity argument for the inverse Gram matrix. Combining the branch estimates with the Schur complement at \(b\), any hypothetical decomposition \(b=x+(b-x)\) with \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge0\) is forced to have \(x=0\) or \(x=b\), contradicting the requirement that both summands be nonzero.

\subsection*{Statement and notation}

Let \(T\) be a finite tree with vertex set \(V\), edge set \(E\), and weight function \(w:V\to\Z\). We write \(d_T(v)\) for the degree of a vertex \(v\) in \(T\). Let \(L(T)\) be the free abelian group generated by \(V\). We identify a vertex with the corresponding basis element of \(L(T)\). The bilinear form on \(L(T)\) is the symmetric form determined on generators by
\[
u\cdot v=
\begin{cases}
w(u), & u=v,\\
-1, & \{u,v\}\in E,\\
0, & u\ne v \text{ and } \{u,v\}\notin E.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(x\in L(T)\), write \(x^2=x\cdot x\). The form is called positive definite if its extension to \(L(T)\otimes_{\Z}\mathbb R\) is positive definite. Since the Gram matrix has integer entries, if the form is positive definite, then every nonzero \(z\in L(T)\) satisfies \(z^2\in\Z_{>0}\).

A nonzero lattice element \(y\in L(T)\) is called \emph{irreducible} if there do not exist nonzero \(a,c\in L(T)\) such that
\[
y=a+c
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
a\cdot c\ge 0.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Original problem]\label{thm:main}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree with vertex set \(V\), edge set \(E\), and weight function \(w:V\to\Z\). Equip \(L(T)\) with the symmetric bilinear form above. Suppose this form is positive definite, and suppose there is exactly one vertex \(b\in V\) such that
\[
w(b)<d_T(b).
\]
Then \(T\) contains a vertex \(u\) such that \(u\) is irreducible in \(L(T)\).
\end{theorem}

For a connected subgraph or subtree \(C\), write \(d_C(u)\) for the degree of \(u\) inside \(C\). The group \(L(C)\) is the free abelian group on the vertices of \(C\), equipped with the restricted form. If \(x\in L(C)\), write \(x_u\) for the coefficient of the vertex \(u\) in \(x\).

\subsection*{Auxiliary lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[A weight-one vertex is irreducible]\label{lem:weight-one}
Assume the form on \(L(T)\) is positive definite. If \(u\in V\) satisfies \(w(u)=1\), then \(u\) is irreducible.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Writing $p,q$ for vectors and $p^2,q^2$ for their pairing is an odd notational choice, since conventionally $p,q$ are used to denote integers.]]

Suppose, for contradiction, that
\[
u=p+q
\]
where \(p,q\in L(T)\) are nonzero and \(p\cdot q\ge 0\).
Since the form is positive definite and integral, \(p^2,q^2\in\Z_{>0}\). Hence
\[
1=u^2=(p+q)^2=p^2+q^2+2p\cdot q
\ge 1+1+0=2,
\]
which is impossible. Therefore no such decomposition exists, and \(u\) is irreducible.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Schur complement calculation]\label{lem:schur}
Let
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(B\) is symmetric positive definite. Set
\[
S=a-\gamma^T B^{-1}\gamma.
\]
Then \(M\) is positive definite if and only if \(S>0\). When \(S>0\),
\[
M^{-1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
S^{-1} & -S^{-1}\gamma^T B^{-1}\\
-B^{-1}\gamma S^{-1} &
B^{-1}+B^{-1}\gamma S^{-1}\gamma^T B^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We have the factorization
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \gamma^T B^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
S & 0\\
0 & B
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0\\
B^{-1}\gamma & I
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Indeed, multiplying the last two factors gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
S & 0\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and multiplying by the first factor gives
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
S+\gamma^T B^{-1}\gamma & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
a & \gamma^T\\
\gamma & B
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The first and third factors are transposes of one another and are invertible. Congruence by an invertible matrix preserves positive definiteness, so \(M\) is positive definite exactly when the middle block diagonal matrix is positive definite. Since \(B\) is already positive definite, this is equivalent to \(S>0\).

When \(S>0\), invert the displayed factorization:
\[
M^{-1}=
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 0\\
-B^{-1}\gamma & I
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
S^{-1} & 0\\
0 & B^{-1}
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & -\gamma^T B^{-1}\\
0 & I
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Multiplying these three factors gives exactly the stated block formula.
\end{proof}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The hypothesis that $A$ be positive definite in the following lemma is redundant. It is implied by the condition on the weights.]]

\begin{lemma}[Rooted branch estimate]\label{lem:branch}
Let \(C\) be a finite weighted tree rooted at a vertex \(r\). Let \(A\) be its Gram matrix, and assume \(A\) is positive definite. Suppose
\[
w(r)\ge d_C(r)+1,
\qquad
w(u)\ge d_C(u)\quad\text{for every }u\ne r.
\]
Let \(G=A^{-1}\), and define
\[
\alpha=(A^{-1})_{rr}=e_r^TGe_r,
\]
where \(e_r\) is the coordinate vector of \(r\). Then \(0<\alpha\le 1\), and for every \(x\in L(C)\), if \(c=x_r\), then for every \(k\in\Z\),
\[
(2k-1)c-x^2\le k(k-1)\alpha.
\]
Moreover, if \(k=0\) or \(k=1\), and equality holds with \(x\ne 0\), then \(C\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We first prove a parity estimate for inverse Gram matrices. We claim that, under the hypotheses of the lemma,
\[
0<\alpha\le 1
\]
and that every vector \(\lambda\in\Z^C\) satisfying
\[
\lambda_r\equiv 1\pmod 2,
\qquad
\lambda_u\equiv 0\pmod 2\quad(u\ne r)
\]
also satisfies
\[
\lambda^T G\lambda\ge \alpha.
\]
This is proved by induction on \(|C|\).

If \(C=\{r\}\), then \(A=[w(r)]\). The root hypothesis gives \(w(r)\ge 1\), and positive definiteness also gives \(w(r)>0\). 

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Is there some reason why two explanations are given for the obvious fact that $w(r)\ge 1$?]]

Thus
\[
\alpha=\frac{1}{w(r)}\le 1.
\]
If \(\lambda_r=s\) is odd, then \(s^2\ge 1\), so
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda=\frac{s^2}{w(r)}\ge \frac{1}{w(r)}=\alpha.
\]
This proves the base case.

Assume now that \(|C|>1\). Let \(C_1,\dots,C_m\) be the connected components of \(C-\{r\}\), and let \(r_i\) be the unique vertex of \(C_i\) adjacent to \(r\). Root \(C_i\) at \(r_i\). Let \(A_i\) be the Gram matrix of \(C_i\), set \(G_i=A_i^{-1}\), let \(e_i=e_{r_i}\), and put
\[
\alpha_i=e_i^TG_ie_i.
\]
Each \(A_i\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of \(A\). Also, each rooted tree \(C_i\) satisfies the same type of weight hypotheses: since \(r_i\ne r\),
\[
w(r_i)\ge d_C(r_i)=d_{C_i}(r_i)+1,
\]
and every other vertex \(u\in C_i\) satisfies
\[
w(u)\ge d_C(u)=d_{C_i}(u).
\]
Therefore, by induction,
\[
0<\alpha_i\le 1
\qquad\text{for all }i.
\]

Order the vertices of \(C\) by putting \(r\) first and then the vertices of \(C_1,\dots,C_m\). With respect to this order,
\[
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
w(r) & -\eta^T\\
-\eta & B
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=A_1\oplus\cdots\oplus A_m,
\]
where the \(C_i\)-block of \(\eta\) is \(e_i\). By Lemma \ref{lem:schur}, if
\[
S=w(r)-\eta^TB^{-1}\eta,
\]
then \(S>0\) and
\[
\alpha=(A^{-1})_{rr}=\frac{1}{S}.
\]
Since \(B^{-1}=G_1\oplus\cdots\oplus G_m\), we have
\[
\eta^TB^{-1}\eta=\sum_i \alpha_i.
\]
Also \(m=d_C(r)\), so the root hypothesis and the inductive bounds \(\alpha_i\le 1\) imply
\[
S=w(r)-\sum_i\alpha_i
\ge (m+1)-m
=1.
\]
Thus \(0<\alpha=1/S\le 1\).

Now let \(\lambda\in\Z^C\) have odd root coordinate and even nonroot coordinates. In the above ordering, write
\[
\lambda=(s,2\mu_1,\dots,2\mu_m),
\]
where \(s\) is odd and \(\mu_i\in\Z^{C_i}\). Define
\[
\rho_i=e_i^TG_i\mu_i,
\qquad
E_i=\mu_i^TG_i\mu_i,
\qquad
\rho=\sum_i\rho_i.
\]
Using the inverse formula from Lemma \ref{lem:schur} with \(\gamma=-\eta\), we obtain
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
=
4\sum_i E_i+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}.
\]
For each \(i\), the vectors \(2\mu_i-e_i\) and \(2\mu_i+e_i\) have odd coordinate at the root \(r_i\) and even coordinates elsewhere in \(C_i\). The induction hypothesis applied to \(C_i\) gives
\[
(2\mu_i-e_i)^TG_i(2\mu_i-e_i)\ge \alpha_i,
\qquad
(2\mu_i+e_i)^TG_i(2\mu_i+e_i)\ge \alpha_i.
\]
Expanding these two inequalities gives
\[
4E_i-4\rho_i+\alpha_i\ge \alpha_i,
\qquad
4E_i+4\rho_i+\alpha_i\ge \alpha_i.
\]
Hence
\[
E_i\ge |\rho_i|.
\]
Therefore
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
\ge
4\sum_i|\rho_i|+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}
\ge
4|\rho|+\frac{(s+2\rho)^2}{S}.
\]
Set \(y=2\rho\). Then
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
\ge
2|y|+\frac{(s+y)^2}{S}.
\]
Since \(S\ge 1\), it is enough to prove
\[
(s+y)^2+2S|y|\ge 1.
\]
Let \(a=|s|\ge 1\) and \(u=|y|\). If \(sy\ge 0\), then \(|s+y|=a+u\ge 1\), so the inequality is immediate. If \(sy<0\), then
\[
(s+y)^2+2S|y|
\ge
(a-u)^2+2u
=
\bigl(u-(a-1)\bigr)^2+2a-1
\ge 1.
\]
Thus \(S\lambda^TG\lambda\ge 1\), and hence
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda\ge \frac{1}{S}=\alpha.
\]
This completes the induction and proves the parity estimate.

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I would be inclined to pull out the parity estimate as a separate lemma.]]

We now derive the stated branch inequality. Fix \(x\in L(C)\), let \(c=x_r\), and set \(Q=x^2=x^TAx\). For \(k\in\Z\), put
\[
t=2k-1.
\]
Define
\[
\lambda=2Ax-te_r.
\]
Because \(A\) has integer entries and \(x\) has integer coordinates, \(\lambda\in\Z^C\). Its root coordinate is even minus the odd integer \(t\), hence is odd, while every nonroot coordinate is even. The parity estimate therefore gives
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda\ge \alpha.
\]
Using \(G=A^{-1}\), we expand:
\[
\lambda^TG\lambda
=
(2Ax-te_r)^TG(2Ax-te_r)
=
4Q-4tc+t^2\alpha.
\]
Hence
\[
4Q-4tc+t^2\alpha\ge \alpha,
\]
or equivalently
\[
tc-Q\le \frac{t^2-1}{4}\alpha.
\]
Since \(t=2k-1\),
\[
\frac{t^2-1}{4}
=
\frac{(2k-1)^2-1}{4}
=
k(k-1).
\]
Therefore
\[
(2k-1)c-x^2\le k(k-1)\alpha.
\]

It remains to prove the equality statement for \(k=0,1\). For every \(x\in L(C)\), expanding the form gives
\[
x^2
=
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}(x_u-x_v)^2
+
\sum_{u\in C}\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2.
\]
Indeed, in the first sum, the term \(x_u^2\) appears once for each edge incident to \(u\), hence \(d_C(u)\) times, and each edge contributes the cross term \(-2x_ux_v\). Therefore the displayed expression equals
\[
\sum_{u\in C}w(u)x_u^2-2\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}x_ux_v=x^2.
\]
By the hypotheses,
\[
w(r)-d_C(r)\ge 1,
\qquad
w(u)-d_C(u)\ge 0\quad(u\ne r),
\]
so
\[
x^2-c^2
=
\sum_{\{u,v\}\in E(C)}(x_u-x_v)^2
+
\bigl(w(r)-d_C(r)-1\bigr)c^2
+
\sum_{u\ne r}\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2
\ge 0.
\]
Thus \(x^2\ge c^2\).

Suppose first that \(k=1\), equality holds in the branch inequality, and \(x\ne 0\). Since \(k(k-1)=0\), equality says
\[
c-x^2=0.
\]
Thus \(x^2=c\). Positive definiteness gives \(x^2>0\), so \(c>0\), and hence \(x^2=|c|\). Since \(x^2\ge c^2\), we get \(|c|\ge c^2\). Because \(c\in\Z\) and \(c\ne 0\), this forces \(c=1\), and then \(x^2=c^2=1\).

Similarly, if \(k=0\), equality says
\[
-c-x^2=0.
\]
Thus \(x^2=-c>0\), so \(c<0\). Again \(x^2=|c|\), and the inequality \(x^2\ge c^2\) forces \(c=-1\) and \(x^2=c^2=1\).

In either case, \(|c|=1\) and \(x^2=c^2\). Therefore equality holds in the nonnegative sum for \(x^2-c^2\), so every summand in that sum is zero. In particular, each edge term \((x_u-x_v)^2\) is zero. Since \(C\) is connected, all coordinates of \(x\) are equal to \(c=\pm 1\).

If \(C\) has only one vertex, then \(C=\{r\}\). The equality \(x^2=c^2\), with \(c^2=1\), gives
\[
(w(r)-d_C(r)-1)c^2=0.
\]
Since \(d_C(r)=0\), we obtain \(w(r)=1\).

If \(C\) has more than one vertex, choose a vertex \(u\ne r\) at maximal distance from \(r\). Such a vertex is a nonroot leaf, so \(d_C(u)=1\). Because all coordinates of \(x\) are \(\pm 1\), we have \(x_u^2=1\). The vanishing of the corresponding nonroot summand gives
\[
\bigl(w(u)-d_C(u)\bigr)x_u^2=0,
\]
hence \(w(u)-d_C(u)=0\), and therefore \(w(u)=1\). Thus, whenever equality holds for \(k=0\) or \(k=1\) with \(x\ne 0\), the branch \(C\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Calculation at a vertex]\label{lem:bad-vertex}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree whose form is positive definite, and let \(b\) be a vertex of \(T\). Let \(C\) range over the components of \(T-\{b\}\). For each such component \(C\), let \(r_C\) be the unique vertex of \(C\) adjacent to \(b\), let \(A_C\) be the Gram matrix of \(C\), and define
\[
\alpha_C=(A_C^{-1})_{r_Cr_C}.
\]
Then
\[
\sum_C \alpha_C<w(b).
\]
Moreover, if
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C,
\]
where \(k\in\Z\) and \(x_C\in L(C)\), and if \(c_C=(x_C)_{r_C}\), then
\[
x\cdot(b-x)
=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
If \(T=\{b\}\), then there are no components \(C\), the sum \(\sum_C\alpha_C\) is empty, and the first assertion says \(0<w(b)\), which follows from positive definiteness because \(w(b)=b^2\). The displayed formula also reduces immediately to
\[
(kb)\cdot(b-kb)=k(1-k)w(b).
\]
Thus assume \(T\ne \{b\}\).

Order the vertices of \(T\) by putting \(b\) first, followed by the vertices in the components \(C\) of \(T-\{b\}\). With respect to this order, the full Gram matrix has block form
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
w(b) & -\eta^T\\
-\eta & B
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=\bigoplus_C A_C,
\]
where the \(C\)-block of \(\eta\) is \(e_{r_C}\). The matrix \(B\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of the positive definite Gram matrix of \(T\). Applying Lemma \ref{lem:schur}, the Schur complement is positive:
\[
w(b)-\eta^TB^{-1}\eta>0.
\]
Since \(B^{-1}=\bigoplus_C A_C^{-1}\), we have
\[
\eta^TB^{-1}\eta=\sum_C \alpha_C.
\]
Therefore
\[
\sum_C\alpha_C<w(b).
\]

Now write
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C.
\]
Different components of \(T-\{b\}\) are orthogonal to one another, and \(b\) pairs nontrivially with a component \(C\) only at the root \(r_C\), where \(b\cdot r_C=-1\). Hence
\[
b\cdot x=kw(b)-\sum_C c_C.
\]
Also,
\[
x^2
=
k^2w(b)-2k\sum_C c_C+\sum_C x_C^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\cdot(b-x)
&=x\cdot b-x^2\\
&=
\left(kw(b)-\sum_C c_C\right)
-
\left(k^2w(b)-2k\sum_C c_C+\sum_C x_C^2\right)\\
&=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
This proves the formula.
\end{proof}

\subsection*{Proof of the theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main}]
Let \(b\) denote the unique vertex of \(T\) satisfying \(w(b)<d_T(b)\). Thus every vertex \(u\ne b\) satisfies
\[
w(u)\ge d_T(u).
\]

If \(T\) contains a vertex of weight \(1\), then Lemma \ref{lem:weight-one} shows that this vertex is irreducible, and the theorem follows. Hence assume from now on that \(T\) contains no vertex of weight \(1\). We will prove that \(b\) is irreducible.

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(b\) is reducible. Then there exists \(x\in L(T)\) such that
\[
x\ne 0,
\qquad
b-x\ne 0,
\qquad
x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0.
\]
Decompose \(x\) according to the components of \(T-\{b\}\):
\[
x=kb+\sum_C x_C,
\]
where \(k\in\Z\), each \(x_C\in L(C)\), and the sum ranges over the components \(C\) of \(T-\{b\}\). Let \(r_C\) be the vertex of \(C\) adjacent to \(b\), and put
\[
c_C=(x_C)_{r_C}.
\]

We now verify that each rooted component \(C\), rooted at \(r_C\), satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lem:branch}. Since \(r_C\ne b\), the uniqueness of \(b\) gives
\[
w(r_C)\ge d_T(r_C)=d_C(r_C)+1,
\]
because the only edge incident to \(r_C\) that is not in \(C\) is the edge from \(r_C\) to \(b\). If \(u\in C\) and \(u\ne r_C\), then no edge incident to \(u\) was removed when passing from \(T\) to \(C\), so
\[
w(u)\ge d_T(u)=d_C(u).
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: This discussion of vertex degree seems like an unnecessary level of detail.]]

Finally, the Gram matrix \(A_C\) of \(C\) is positive definite because it is a principal submatrix of the positive definite Gram matrix of \(T\). Thus Lemma \ref{lem:branch} applies to each component \(C\).

Let
\[
\alpha_C=(A_C^{-1})_{r_Cr_C}.
\]
Applying Lemma \ref{lem:branch} to each component, with the same integer \(k\), gives
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\le k(k-1)\alpha_C.
\]
Using Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex}, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
x\cdot(b-x)
&=
k(1-k)w(b)
+
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr)\\
&\le
k(1-k)w(b)+k(k-1)\sum_C\alpha_C\\
&=
k(k-1)\left(\sum_C\alpha_C-w(b)\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex},
\[
\sum_C\alpha_C-w(b)<0.
\]
If \(k\notin\{0,1\}\), then \(k(k-1)>0\), so the last upper bound is strictly negative. This contradicts \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0\). Therefore
\[
k\in\{0,1\}.
\]

For \(k=0\) or \(k=1\), we have \(k(1-k)=0\), and Lemma \ref{lem:branch} gives
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\le 0
\qquad\text{for every component }C.
\]
Lemma \ref{lem:bad-vertex} therefore gives
\[
x\cdot(b-x)
=
\sum_C\Bigl((2k-1)c_C-x_C^2\Bigr),
\]
a sum of nonpositive terms. Since \(x\cdot(b-x)\ge 0\), every term in this sum must be equal to \(0\). Hence, for every component \(C\),
\[
(2k-1)c_C-x_C^2=0.
\]
If some \(x_C\ne 0\), then the equality statement in Lemma \ref{lem:branch} implies that \(C\), and therefore \(T\), contains a vertex of weight \(1\). This contradicts our standing assumption that \(T\) has no weight-one vertex. Thus
\[
x_C=0
\qquad\text{for every component }C.
\]
Consequently \(x=kb\). If \(k=0\), then \(x=0\), contradicting \(x\ne 0\). If \(k=1\), then \(b-x=0\), contradicting \(b-x\ne 0\). Both possibilities are impossible.

Therefore no such decomposition of \(b\) exists, and \(b\) is irreducible. Hence \(T\) contains an irreducible vertex.
\end{proof}

\title{Submission C solution to Problem 6}
\date{}
\maketitle


\begin{remark}
Throughout, the phrase ``a single vertex'' with \(w(v)<d_T(v)\) is interpreted as saying that \(v\) is the unique such vertex.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Norm-one elements are irreducible]
Let \(L\) be a positive definite integral lattice. If \(x\in L\) satisfies \(x^2=1\), then \(x\) is irreducible.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose \(x=a+b\), where \(a,b\in L\) are nonzero and \(a\cdot b\ge 0\). Since \(L\) is positive definite and integral, \(a^2,b^2\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\). Hence
\[
1=x^2=a^2+b^2+2a\cdot b\ge 1+1=2,
\]
a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Let \(C\) be a rooted weighted tree with root \(\rho\). Orient every edge away from \(\rho\), and write \(\ch_C(x)\) for the number of children of a vertex \(x\in C\). We call \(C\) admissible if its form is positive definite, every vertex weight is at least \(2\), and
\[
w(x)\ge \ch_C(x)+1
\qquad \text{for every } x\in C.
\]
For \(x=\sum n_y y\in L(C)\), write \(x_y=n_y\) for the coefficient of the vertex \(y\).

For a positive definite rooted tree \(C\), define its capacity by
\[
\gamma(C)=\bigl(Q_C^{-1}\bigr)_{\rho\rho},
\]
where \(Q_C\) is the Gram matrix of \(C\) in the vertex basis.

\begin{lemma}[Capacities of admissible rooted trees]
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\). Then
\[
0<\gamma(C)<1.
\]
Moreover, if the root has children \(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_t\), and \(C_i\) denotes the rooted subtree with root \(\rho_i\), then
\[
\gamma(C)=\frac{1}{w(\rho)-\sum_{i=1}^t \gamma(C_i)}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Order the vertices so that \(\rho\) comes first and the remaining vertices are grouped by the rooted subtrees \(C_1,\dots,C_t\). Then
\[
Q_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
w(\rho) & c^T\\
c & Q_0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(Q_0=\bigoplus_i Q_{C_i}\), and \(c\) has entry \(-1\) in the coordinate corresponding to each child root \(\rho_i\) and \(0\) elsewhere. By the Schur complement formula,
\[
\bigl(Q_C^{-1}\bigr)_{\rho\rho}
=
\frac{1}{w(\rho)-c^TQ_0^{-1}c}
=
\frac{1}{w(\rho)-\sum_i \gamma(C_i)}.
\]

It remains to show that \(\gamma(C)<1\). This follows by induction on the number of vertices. If \(C\) has one vertex, then \(w(\rho)\ge 2\), so \(\gamma(C)=1/w(\rho)<1\). Otherwise, by induction, \(\gamma(C_i)<1\) for every child subtree. If the root has \(t\) children, then admissibility gives \(w(\rho)\ge t+1\). Hence
\[
w(\rho)-\sum_i \gamma(C_i)>w(\rho)-t\ge 1,
\]
so \(\gamma(C)<1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A rooted estimate]
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\) and capacity \(\gamma=\gamma(C)\). Then, for every \(x\in L(C)\) and every \(k\in \mathbb Z\),
\[
x^2-(2k+1)x_\rho+\gamma k(k+1)\ge 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We prove the claim by induction on \(|C|\).

If \(C\) has one vertex, say \(x=m\rho\), then \(\gamma=1/w(\rho)\). Let \(W=w(\rho)\). Multiplying the desired inequality by \(W\), we get
\[
W\left(Wm^2-(2k+1)m+\frac{k(k+1)}{W}\right)
=
(Wm-k)(Wm-k-1).
\]
Since \(Wm-k\in\mathbb Z\), the product of the two consecutive integers \(Wm-k\) and \(Wm-k-1\) is nonnegative. This proves the base case.

Now assume \(|C|>1\). Let the root be \(\rho\), let its children be \(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_t\), and let \(C_i\) be the rooted subtree with root \(\rho_i\). Write
\[
x=a\rho+\sum_i x_i,
\qquad x_i\in L(C_i),
\]
and let \(s_i=(x_i)_{\rho_i}\). Then
\[
x^2=w(\rho)a^2-2a\sum_i s_i+\sum_i x_i^2.
\]
Let \(\gamma_i=\gamma(C_i)\). By the induction hypothesis applied to \(C_i\) with \(k=a\), we have
\[
x_i^2-(2a+1)s_i+\gamma_i a(a+1)\ge 0,
\]
so
\[
x_i^2-2as_i\ge s_i-\gamma_i a(a+1).
\]
Similarly, applying the induction hypothesis with \(k=a-1\), we obtain
\[
x_i^2-(2a-1)s_i+\gamma_i a(a-1)\ge 0,
\]
so
\[
x_i^2-2as_i\ge -s_i-\gamma_i a(a-1).
\]
Taking the maximum of these two lower bounds gives
\[
x_i^2-2as_i
\ge
-\gamma_i a^2+\bigl|s_i-\gamma_i a\bigr|.
\]
Therefore, setting
\[
D=\sum_i \bigl|s_i-\gamma_i a\bigr|,
\]
we get
\begin{align*}
x^2-(2k+1)a+\gamma k(k+1)
&\ge
\left(w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)a^2-(2k+1)a+\gamma k(k+1)+D.
\end{align*}
By the capacity formula,
\[
\gamma^{-1}=w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i.
\]
Thus, if \(\tau=a/\gamma\), the preceding lower bound becomes
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)+D.
\]

If \(\tau\notin(k,k+1)\), then \((\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)\ge 0\), and the result follows. Suppose instead that \(k<\tau<k+1\). Put
\[
\alpha=\tau-k,
\qquad
\beta=k+1-\tau.
\]
Then \(0<\alpha,\beta<1\), \(\alpha+\beta=1\), and
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)=-\gamma\alpha\beta.
\]
Now
\[
\tau
=
\frac{a}{\gamma}
=
\left(w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)a.
\]
Since \(w(\rho)a-\sum_i s_i\in\mathbb Z\), we have
\[
D
=
\sum_i |s_i-\gamma_i a|
\ge
\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\mathbb Z)
=
\min\{\alpha,\beta\}.
\]
Because \(0<\gamma<1\) and \(\alpha\beta\le \min\{\alpha,\beta\}\), it follows that
\[
D\ge \gamma\alpha\beta.
\]
Hence
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)+D\ge 0.
\]
This completes the induction.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\). If \(0\ne x\in L(C)\), then
\[
x^2-x_\rho>0.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\gamma=\gamma(C)\). If \(x_\rho\le 0\), then \(x^2-x_\rho>0\) because \(C\) is positive definite and \(x\ne 0\).

Assume \(x_\rho>0\). Let \(\rho^\#\in L(C)\otimes \mathbb Q\) be the vector satisfying
\[
\rho^\#\cdot y=y_\rho
\qquad
\text{for all } y\in L(C).
\]
Equivalently, the coefficient vector of \(\rho^\#\) is \(Q_C^{-1}e_\rho\). Thus
\[
(\rho^\#)^2=\gamma.
\]
By Cauchy's inequality in the positive definite real vector space \(L(C)\otimes\mathbb R\),
\[
x_\rho^2=(x\cdot \rho^\#)^2\le x^2(\rho^\#)^2=\gamma x^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma<1\), we get
\[
x^2\ge \frac{x_\rho^2}{\gamma}>x_\rho^2\ge x_\rho.
\]
Therefore \(x^2-x_\rho>0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree whose associated form is positive definite. Suppose that there is a unique vertex \(v\) such that
\[
w(v)<d_T(v).
\]
Then \(T\) contains a vertex that is irreducible in \(L(T)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since the form is positive definite, every vertex has positive square. Thus every vertex weight is a positive integer.

If some vertex \(u\) has \(w(u)=1\), then \(u^2=1\), and \(u\) is irreducible by the first lemma. Hence we may assume from now on that every vertex weight is at least \(2\).

Let \(v\) be the unique vertex with \(w(v)<d_T(v)\). We will prove that \(v\) itself is irreducible.

Let \(C_1,\dots,C_m\) be the connected components of \(T\setminus\{v\}\). For each \(i\), let \(\rho_i\) be the unique vertex of \(C_i\) adjacent to \(v\), and root \(C_i\) at \(\rho_i\). Because \(v\) is the unique bad vertex, every vertex \(x\in C_i\) satisfies
\[
w(x)\ge d_T(x).
\]
With the orientation away from \(\rho_i\), each \(x\in C_i\) has exactly one edge pointing toward \(v\) or toward its parent, so
\[
d_T(x)=\ch_{C_i}(x)+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
w(x)\ge \ch_{C_i}(x)+1.
\]
Since all weights are at least \(2\), each \(C_i\) is admissible. Let
\[
\gamma_i=\gamma(C_i).
\]

By the Schur complement formula applied to the decomposition of \(T\) into \(v\) and the components \(C_i\), positive definiteness of \(T\) implies
\[
w(v)-\sum_i\gamma_i>0.
\]
Write \(W=w(v)\).

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(v\) is reducible. Then there exist nonzero \(a,b\in L(T)\) such that
\[
v=a+b,
\qquad
a\cdot b\ge 0.
\]
Put \(z=-b\). Then \(a=v+z\), and
\[
0\le a\cdot b=(v+z)\cdot(-z)=-(z^2+v\cdot z).
\]
Hence
\[
z^2+v\cdot z\le 0.
\]
Also \(z\ne 0\) and \(z\ne -v\), because \(a,b\ne 0\).

Let \(q\) be the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z\). If \(q\le -1\), replace \(z\) by
\[
z'=-v-z.
\]
This replacement corresponds to interchanging \(a\) and \(b\), and
\[
z'\cdot(z'+v)=z\cdot(z+v).
\]
Moreover, the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z'\) is \(-1-q\ge 0\). Thus we may assume that the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z\) is a nonnegative integer \(p\).

Write
\[
z=pv+\sum_i y_i,
\qquad y_i\in L(C_i).
\]
Let \(s_i=(y_i)_{\rho_i}\). Since \(v\cdot y_i=-s_i\), we compute
\begin{align*}
z^2+v\cdot z
&=
\left(Wp^2-2p\sum_i s_i+\sum_i y_i^2\right)
+
\left(Wp-\sum_i s_i\right) \\
&=
Wp(p+1)+\sum_i\left(y_i^2-(2p+1)s_i\right).
\end{align*}

First suppose \(p\ge 1\). Applying the rooted estimate to each \(C_i\) with \(k=p\), we get
\[
y_i^2-(2p+1)s_i\ge -\gamma_i p(p+1).
\]
Therefore
\[
z^2+v\cdot z
\ge
\left(W-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)p(p+1)>0,
\]
contradicting \(z^2+v\cdot z\le 0\).

It remains to consider \(p=0\). Then
\[
z^2+v\cdot z
=
\sum_i (y_i^2-s_i).
\]
By the corollary, each term \(y_i^2-s_i\) is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive whenever \(y_i\ne 0\). Since \(z\ne 0\) and \(p=0\), at least one \(y_i\) is nonzero. Hence
\[
z^2+v\cdot z>0,
\]
again contradicting \(z^2+v\cdot z\le 0\).

Thus \(v\) is irreducible. Consequently, \(T\) contains an irreducible vertex.
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The solution is entirely correct, and the strategy is sensible but could perhaps be better signposted -- reading this having already thought about the problem, it's clear enough why something like Lemma 3 will be a key estimate but on first pass it's a bit obscure. On a line-by-line level, all of the display equations seem to be true as written (not a bar that human-written math always clears!), but I didn't feel that the balance of what to spell out and what to leave implicit was quite as well-tuned as in most publishable text.

## Novelty.

In outline, this solution follows the same approach as that of the problem authors: first analyze the trees that result from deleting the bad vertex, and then assemble everything together. The exact statements made about these subtrees do differ, but seemingly only superficially.

While the solution does find all the needed insights to solve the problem, to really call anything here novel I'd want to see a bit more -- some amount of organizing these ideas into new concepts that would perhaps help with generalizations. After all, this problem is one case of a much bigger question, and the value in a solution is as much in ideas that could help with a full answer as it is in firmly nailing down this case. Such insights could perhaps be extracted from this answer, especially from the proof of Lemma 3, but this work has not been done by the writer. This makes it difficult to tell if there's anything new here that isn't also in e.g. the human-written solution to the problem. 

The insight in this proof that seems most distinct from ideas in the human solution is the step in the proof of Lemma 3 in which $D$ is bounded by the distance between $\tau$ and an integer -- the human solution replaces this with a combinatorial argument for a stronger statement. Perhaps there is more that could be done with this idea, but distilling it properly from what has been written is not straightforward.
reviews.recommendation: On a pure technical level, this has to be rated essentially flawless. All claims made are true, and none cannot be justified with any more than a bit of looking back in the text. I won't say the exposition is perfect, but it certainly isn't the most frustrating text I've ever read.
inline_comments: Could say why $\gamma(C)>0$, but this is not hard.
This seems to be a key step; I'd perhaps like it spelled out a little more but it is true.

\[

\[

\[

\qquad y_i\in L(C_i).

z^2+v\cdot z
&=

\left(Wp-\sum_i s_i\right) \\
&=

\end{align*}

\[
y_i^2-(2p+1)s_i\ge -\gamma_i p(p+1).

\[
z^2+v\cdot z
\ge
\left(W-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)p(p+1)>0,

contradicting \(z^2+v\cdot z\le 0\).

\[

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

The proof is correct and reasonably well explained, although the writing has various issues. The definitions are repetitive, there's one place where it summarizes the proof of a lemma rather than using the lemma, and the notation is not always well chosen. The proof also explains some easy steps (such as the inequality comparing $w$ with $\ch_C+1$ in the proof of Theorem~1) in detail, while going through more difficult things quickly.

I expect the proof could be made more conceptual with some reformulation, maybe in terms of dual lattices, but it is correct and explained enough to be checkable.

## Novelty.

I don't know to what extent this argument takes ideas from the literature. A few things make me wonder, such as the term ``capacity,'' which hints at connections beyond the problem statement. I don't know whether this is just because LLMs like to name things and choose a vague but evocative name when they can't come up with a standard name, or whether it's an indication of some connection.
reviews.recommendation:
Mathematically, it is essentially flawless and does not requite any factual corrections. Conceptually, I think it could likely be clarified, but a first proof is often clumsy. Stylistically, I would suggest a bunch of changes before publication.

With a human author, I would view this level of editing as minor revisions not requiring further review, but I'd be a little more skeptical of AI's ability to carry out the revisions well. In any case, these revisions would not be mathematical corrections.

reviews.review_summary:
This gives a complete solution to the problem. The approach contains essentially all the same ideas as the known human proof. Although these ideas are more obscured in the presentation here, in the sense that the proof makes a direct beeline to the solution using elementary algebraic manipulation and does not provide any motivation or interpretation of the steps. Although argument appears to be correct in all aspects, I suspect that certain parts of the argument could be simplified.

## Exposition

In terms of the writing, I was not convinced by some of the notational and stylistic choices. Although it is readable, I would certainly have a lot to say if this were written by a grad student of mine.

## Correctness.

\begin{remark}
Throughout, the phrase ``a single vertex'' with \(w(v)<d_T(v)\) is interpreted as saying that \(v\) is the unique such vertex.
\end{remark}

\begin{lemma}[Norm-one elements are irreducible]
Let \(L\) be a positive definite integral lattice. If \(x\in L\) satisfies \(x^2=1\), then \(x\) is irreducible.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose \(x=a+b\), where \(a,b\in L\) are nonzero and \(a\cdot b\ge 0\). Since \(L\) is positive definite and integral, \(a^2,b^2\in \mathbb Z_{>0}\). Hence
\[
1=x^2=a^2+b^2+2a\cdot b\ge 1+1=2,
\]
a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Let \(C\) be a rooted weighted tree with root \(\rho\). Orient every edge away from \(\rho\), and write \(\ch_C(x)\) for the number of children of a vertex \(x\in C\). We call \(C\) admissible if its form is positive definite, every vertex weight is at least \(2\), and
\[
w(x)\ge \ch_C(x)+1
\qquad \text{for every } x\in C.
\]
For \(x=\sum n_y y\in L(C)\), write \(x_y=n_y\) for the coefficient of the vertex \(y\).

For a positive definite rooted tree \(C\), define its capacity by
\[
\gamma(C)=\bigl(Q_C^{-1}\bigr)_{\rho\rho},
\]
where \(Q_C\) is the Gram matrix of \(C\) in the vertex basis.

\begin{lemma}[Capacities of admissible rooted trees]
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\). Then
\[
0<\gamma(C)<1.
\]
Moreover, if the root has children \(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_t\), and \(C_i\) denotes the rooted subtree with root \(\rho_i\), then
\[
\gamma(C)=\frac{1}{w(\rho)-\sum_{i=1}^t \gamma(C_i)}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Order the vertices so that \(\rho\) comes first and the remaining vertices are grouped by the rooted subtrees \(C_1,\dots,C_t\). Then
\[
Q_C=
\begin{pmatrix}
w(\rho) & c^T\\
c & Q_0
\end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(Q_0=\bigoplus_i Q_{C_i}\), and \(c\) has entry \(-1\) in the coordinate corresponding to each child root \(\rho_i\) and \(0\) elsewhere. By the Schur complement formula,
[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I'm not entirely what is meant by Schur complement formula here. I am not familiar with that nomenclature. The identity is true though.]]

\[
\bigl(Q_C^{-1}\bigr)_{\rho\rho}
=
\frac{1}{w(\rho)-c^TQ_0^{-1}c}
=
\frac{1}{w(\rho)-\sum_i \gamma(C_i)}.
\]

It remains to show that \(\gamma(C)<1\). This follows by induction on the number of vertices. If \(C\) has one vertex, then \(w(\rho)\ge 2\), so \(\gamma(C)=1/w(\rho)<1\). Otherwise, by induction, \(\gamma(C_i)<1\) for every child subtree. If the root has \(t\) children, then admissibility gives \(w(\rho)\ge t+1\). Hence
\[
w(\rho)-\sum_i \gamma(C_i)>w(\rho)-t\ge 1,
\]
so \(\gamma(C)<1\).
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[A rooted estimate]
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\) and capacity \(\gamma=\gamma(C)\). Then, for every \(x\in L(C)\) and every \(k\in \mathbb Z\),
\[
x^2-(2k+1)x_\rho+\gamma k(k+1)\ge 0.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We prove the claim by induction on \(|C|\).

If \(C\) has one vertex, say \(x=m\rho\), then \(\gamma=1/w(\rho)\). Let \(W=w(\rho)\). Multiplying the desired inequality by \(W\), we get
\[
W\left(Wm^2-(2k+1)m+\frac{k(k+1)}{W}\right)
=
(Wm-k)(Wm-k-1).
\]
Since \(Wm-k\in\mathbb Z\), the product of the two consecutive integers \(Wm-k\) and \(Wm-k-1\) is nonnegative. This proves the base case.

Now assume \(|C|>1\). Let the root be \(\rho\), let its children be \(\rho_1,\dots,\rho_t\), and let \(C_i\) be the rooted subtree with root \(\rho_i\). Write
\[
x=a\rho+\sum_i x_i,
\qquad x_i\in L(C_i),
\]
and let \(s_i=(x_i)_{\rho_i}\). Then
\[
x^2=w(\rho)a^2-2a\sum_i s_i+\sum_i x_i^2.
\]
Let \(\gamma_i=\gamma(C_i)\). By the induction hypothesis applied to \(C_i\) with \(k=a\), we have
\[
x_i^2-(2a+1)s_i+\gamma_i a(a+1)\ge 0,
\]
so
\[
x_i^2-2as_i\ge s_i-\gamma_i a(a+1).
\]
Similarly, applying the induction hypothesis with \(k=a-1\), we obtain
\[
x_i^2-(2a-1)s_i+\gamma_i a(a-1)\ge 0,
\]
so
\[
x_i^2-2as_i\ge -s_i-\gamma_i a(a-1).
\]
Taking the maximum of these two lower bounds gives
\[
x_i^2-2as_i
\ge
-\gamma_i a^2+\bigl|s_i-\gamma_i a\bigr|.
\]
Therefore, setting
\[
D=\sum_i \bigl|s_i-\gamma_i a\bigr|,
\]
we get
\begin{align*}
x^2-(2k+1)a+\gamma k(k+1)
&\ge
\left(w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)a^2-(2k+1)a+\gamma k(k+1)+D.
\end{align*}
By the capacity formula,
\[
\gamma^{-1}=w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i.
\]
Thus, if \(\tau=a/\gamma\), the preceding lower bound becomes
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)+D.
\]

If \(\tau\notin(k,k+1)\), then \((\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)\ge 0\), and the result follows. Suppose instead that \(k<\tau<k+1\). Put
\[
\alpha=\tau-k,
\qquad
\beta=k+1-\tau.
\]
Then \(0<\alpha,\beta<1\), \(\alpha+\beta=1\), and
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)=-\gamma\alpha\beta.
\]
Now
\[
\tau
=
\frac{a}{\gamma}
=
\left(w(\rho)-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)a.
\]
Since \(w(\rho)a-\sum_i s_i\in\mathbb Z\), we have
\[
D
=
\sum_i |s_i-\gamma_i a|
\ge
\operatorname{dist}(\tau,\mathbb Z)
=
\min\{\alpha,\beta\}.
\]
Because \(0<\gamma<1\) and \(\alpha\beta\le \min\{\alpha,\beta\}\), it follows that
\[
D\ge \gamma\alpha\beta.
\]
Hence
\[
\gamma(\tau-k)(\tau-k-1)+D\ge 0.
\]
This completes the induction.
\end{proof}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: I am not sure why this is named as a corollary. It does not appear to actually depend on preceding results.]]

\begin{corollary}
Let \(C\) be an admissible rooted tree with root \(\rho\). If \(0\ne x\in L(C)\), then
\[
x^2-x_\rho>0.
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Let \(\gamma=\gamma(C)\). If \(x_\rho\le 0\), then \(x^2-x_\rho>0\) because \(C\) is positive definite and \(x\ne 0\).

Assume \(x_\rho>0\). Let \(\rho^\#\in L(C)\otimes \mathbb Q\) be the vector satisfying
\[
\rho^\#\cdot y=y_\rho
\qquad
\text{for all } y\in L(C).
\]
Equivalently, the coefficient vector of \(\rho^\#\) is \(Q_C^{-1}e_\rho\). Thus
\[
(\rho^\#)^2=\gamma.
\]
By Cauchy's inequality in the positive definite real vector space \(L(C)\otimes\mathbb R\),
\[
x_\rho^2=(x\cdot \rho^\#)^2\le x^2(\rho^\#)^2=\gamma x^2.
\]
Since \(\gamma<1\), we get
\[
x^2\ge \frac{x_\rho^2}{\gamma}>x_\rho^2\ge x_\rho.
\]
Therefore \(x^2-x_\rho>0\).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
Let \(T\) be a finite weighted tree whose associated form is positive definite. Suppose that there is a unique vertex \(v\) such that
\[
w(v)<d_T(v).
\]
Then \(T\) contains a vertex that is irreducible in \(L(T)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since the form is positive definite, every vertex has positive square. Thus every vertex weight is a positive integer.

If some vertex \(u\) has \(w(u)=1\), then \(u^2=1\), and \(u\) is irreducible by the first lemma. Hence we may assume from now on that every vertex weight is at least \(2\).

Let \(v\) be the unique vertex with \(w(v)<d_T(v)\). We will prove that \(v\) itself is irreducible.

Let \(C_1,\dots,C_m\) be the connected components of \(T\setminus\{v\}\). For each \(i\), let \(\rho_i\) be the unique vertex of \(C_i\) adjacent to \(v\), and root \(C_i\) at \(\rho_i\). Because \(v\) is the unique bad vertex, every vertex \(x\in C_i\) satisfies
\[
w(x)\ge d_T(x).
\]
With the orientation away from \(\rho_i\), each \(x\in C_i\) has exactly one edge pointing toward \(v\) or toward its parent, so
\[
d_T(x)=\ch_{C_i}(x)+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
w(x)\ge \ch_{C_i}(x)+1.
\]
Since all weights are at least \(2\), each \(C_i\) is admissible. Let
\[
\gamma_i=\gamma(C_i).
\]

By the Schur complement formula applied to the decomposition of \(T\) into \(v\) and the components \(C_i\), positive definiteness of \(T\) implies
\[
w(v)-\sum_i\gamma_i>0.
\]
Write \(W=w(v)\).

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(v\) is reducible. Then there exist nonzero \(a,b\in L(T)\) such that
\[
v=a+b,
\qquad
a\cdot b\ge 0.
\]
Put \(z=-b\). Then \(a=v+z\), and
\[
0\le a\cdot b=(v+z)\cdot(-z)=-(z^2+v\cdot z).
\]
Hence
\[
z^2+v\cdot z\le 0.
\]
Also \(z\ne 0\) and \(z\ne -v\), because \(a,b\ne 0\).

Let \(q\) be the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z\). If \(q\le -1\), replace \(z\) by
\[
z'=-v-z.
\]
This replacement corresponds to interchanging \(a\) and \(b\), and
\[
z'\cdot(z'+v)=z\cdot(z+v).
\]
Moreover, the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z'\) is \(-1-q\ge 0\). Thus we may assume that the coefficient of \(v\) in \(z\) is a nonnegative integer \(p\).

Write
\[
z=pv+\sum_i y_i,
\qquad y_i\in L(C_i).
\]
Let \(s_i=(y_i)_{\rho_i}\). Since \(v\cdot y_i=-s_i\), we compute
\begin{align*}
z^2+v\cdot z
&=
\left(Wp^2-2p\sum_i s_i+\sum_i y_i^2\right)
+
\left(Wp-\sum_i s_i\right) \\
&=
Wp(p+1)+\sum_i\left(y_i^2-(2p+1)s_i\right).
\end{align*}

First suppose \(p\ge 1\). Applying the rooted estimate to each \(C_i\) with \(k=p\), we get
\[
y_i^2-(2p+1)s_i\ge -\gamma_i p(p+1).
\]
Therefore
\[
z^2+v\cdot z
\ge
\left(W-\sum_i\gamma_i\right)p(p+1)>0,
\]
contradicting \(z^2+v\cdot z\le 0\).

It remains to consider \(p=0\). Then
\[
z^2+v\cdot z
=
\sum_i (y_i^2-s_i).
\]
By the corollary, each term \(y_i^2-s_i\) is nonnegative, and it is strictly positive whenever \(y_i\ne 0\). Since \(z\ne 0\) and \(p=0\), at least one \(y_i\) is nonzero. Hence
\[
z^2+v\cdot z>0,
\]
again contradicting \(z^2+v\cdot z\le 0\).

Thus \(v\) is irreducible. Consequently, \(T\) contains an irreducible vertex.
\end{proof}

\title{Submission D solution to Problem 6}
\date{}
\maketitle

\section*{Problem Statement}

Let $T$ denote a finite, weighted tree with vertex set $V$, edge set $E$, and weight function $w : V \longrightarrow \bZ$.
Let $L(T)$ denote the free abelian group generated by $V$, equipped with the symmetric, bilinear form $\cdot$ whose value on a pair of generators $u,v \in V$ is given by 
\[
u \cdot v = 
\begin{cases}
    w(u), & u=v; \\
    -1, & (u,v) \in E; \textup{ and} \\
    0, & u \ne v, (u,v) \notin E.
\end{cases}
\]
Suppose that the form is positive definite, and suppose that there exists a single vertex $v$ for which the vertex weight $w(v)$ is less than the vertex degree $d(v)$.

Prove that $T$ contains a vertex $u$ such that $u$ is an irreducible element of $L(T)$, i.e.~there do not exist nonzero lattice elements $a,b \in L(T)$ such that $u = a+b$ and $a \cdot b \ge 0$.

\section*{Solution}

\begin{theorem}
Let $T$ be a finite, weighted tree equipped with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $Q(x) = x \cdot x$ on $L(T)$ defined by $u \cdot u = w(u)$, $u \cdot y = -1$ for edges, and $0$ otherwise. If there is a unique vertex $v$ such that $w(v) < d(v)$, then $T$ contains an irreducible element.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We will prove that the unique vertex $v$ is strictly irreducible.
By the strict positive definiteness of $Q(x)$ over the integer lattice, $Q(x) \ge 1$ for all non-zero $x \in \mathbb{Z}^V$. If there exists any vertex $u$ with $w(u) \le 1$, $u$ is trivially irreducible (any decomposition $u = a+b$ with $a \cdot b \ge 0$ implies $w(u) = Q(a) + Q(b) + 2a \cdot b \ge 1 + 1 + 0 = 2$, contradiction). Thus, we unconditionally assume $w(x) \ge 2$ for all $x \in V$.

Assume for contradiction that $v$ is reducible, meaning $v = a + b$ for non-zero integer vectors $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}^V$ with $a \cdot b \ge 0$.
Define the discrete localized functional $E_v(x) = Q(x) - x \cdot e_v$. 
Evaluating the sum of the components yields $E_v(a) + E_v(b) = Q(a) + Q(b) - Q(a+b) = -2a \cdot b \le 0$. 
Since $b = e_v - a$, substituting $b$ yields $E_v(b) = E_v(a)$. Thus, the reducibility constraint identically requires $E_v(a) \le 0$.

Because $v$ is the \emph{unique} vertex with $w(v) < d(v)$, every other vertex strictly satisfies $w(y) \ge d(y)$. Let $c_y = w(y) - d(y)$ denote the topological capacity. For all $y \ne v$, $c_y \ge 0$. For any leaf $l$, $d(l) = 1$, so $c_l = w(l) - 1 \ge 1$.
We expand $E_v(a)$ topologically across the entire tree by rewriting the inner product $a \cdot e_v = a_v w(v) - \sum_{y \sim v} a_y$:
\[
E_v(a) = \sum_{e \not\ni v} (a_p - a_q)^2 + \sum_{y \sim v} \big( (a_v - a_y)^2 - (a_v - a_y) \big) + \sum_{y \ne v} c_y a_y^2 + (w(v) - d(v))(a_v^2 - a_v)
\]

Because $a_v + b_v = 1$, at least one component must be $\le 0$. Without loss of generality, let $a_v \le 0$.
We analyze the exact integer evaluation of $E_v(a)$ in two exhaustive cases:

\paragraph{Case 1: $a_v = 0$} 
If $a_v = 0$, the negative capacity term vanishes: $(w(v) - d(v))(0^2 - 0) = 0$. 
The functional $E_v(a)$ becomes a sum of strictly non-negative integer terms (since $z^2 - z \ge 0$ for any integer $z$). 
Because $E_v(a) \le 0$, every term must independently evaluate to exactly $0$.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item $c_l a_l^2 = 0 \implies a_l = 0$ for all leaves (since $c_l \ge 1$).
    \item $(a_p - a_q)^2 = 0 \implies a_p = a_q$ for all non-incident edges, meaning $a$ is constant on every connected branch disjoint from $v$.
\end{enumerate}
Since the branches connect to the leaves where $a_l = 0$, the constant must be $0$. Thus, $a_y = 0$ for all $y \ne v$. 
Combined with $a_v = 0$, this mandates $a = 0$ globally, which violently contradicts the requirement that $a$ is a non-zero vector.

\paragraph{Case 2: $a_v \le -1$}
If $a_v \le -1$, then strictly $b_v = 1 - a_v \ge 2$. Both vectors must independently satisfy $E_v \le 0$. We evaluate the symmetric constraint for $x \in \{a, b\}$ where $k = x_v \ge 2$. 
Removing $v$ partitions the tree into $d(v)$ disjoint branches $B_i$ rooted at the neighbors $r_i$ of $v$. Because $c_y \ge 0$ for all internal vertices, we isolate the exact internal quadratic form for each branch:
\[
Q_{B_i}(x) = x_{r_i}^2 + \sum_{e \in B_i} (x_p - x_q)^2 + \sum_{y \in B_i} c_y x_y^2
\]
This algebraic identity establishes unconditionally that $Q_{B_i}(x) \ge x_{r_i}^2$ for any integer assignment. 
Substituting this strictly positive structural bound into the functional:
\[
E_v(x) \ge w(v)(k^2 - k) + \sum_{i=1}^{d(v)} \big[ x_{r_i}^2 - (2k-1)x_{r_i} \big]
\]
Over the integers, the parabola $z^2 - (2k-1)z$ achieves its absolute minimum at $z = k$ and $z = k-1$, where it evaluates exactly to $-(k^2 - k)$. 
Summing this minimal integer penalty across all $d(v)$ branches yields:
\[
E_v(x) \ge w(v)(k^2 - k) - d(v)(k^2 - k) = (w(v) - d(v))(k^2 - k)
\]
While this establishes a lower bound, we apply the strictly positive definite property to close the gap. For $x_{r_i}$ to attain the necessary integer minima $k$ or $k-1$, the remaining terms $\sum_{B_i} (x_p - x_q)^2 + \sum_{B_i} c_y x_y^2$ must identically equal zero. As established in Case 1, forcing these terms to zero requires a constant vector across the branch terminating at leaves. However, assigning $x_l = k-1 \ge 1$ at the leaves triggers the leaf capacity penalty $c_l x_l^2 \ge (k-1)^2 \ge 1$. 

Therefore, no valid integer evaluation can simultaneously achieve the minimum $x_{r_i}^2 - (2k-1)x_{r_i}$ and maintain zero branch capacity penalty. The exact integer minimum of the branch heavily exceeds $-(k^2-k)$, forcing $E_v(x) > 0$ for all $k \ge 2$. 

Because neither decomposition vector can mathematically satisfy the required negative functional $E_v \le 0$, the assumed reducible decomposition is mathematically void. The vertex $v$ is strictly irreducible.
\end{proof}

\title{Submission A solution to Problem 7}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{center}
\textbf{A counterexample}
\end{center}

The answer is no.  We give a counterexample in
\(G=\langle a,b,c\rangle\).  Write \(\ol x=x^{-1}\), and set
\[
        w=\ol a\,a\, b\,\ol b\,\ol a\,a\, c\,\ol c\,\ol a\,a .
\]
This word is freely trivial, by deleting the adjacent inverse pairs
\[
        \ol a a,\qquad b\ol b,\qquad \ol a a,\qquad c\ol c,\qquad
        \ol a a .
\]
It is quasi-reduced: the only adjacent inverse pairs are the five
displayed ones, and in each case the following letter, if there is one,
is not the first letter of that pair.

We shall use two elementary consequences of the face condition in the
definition.  Compactify the upper half-plane to a disk and put the
marked boundary points in cyclic order.  For a matching \(M\), let
\(\Gamma(M)\) be the graph obtained from \(M\) by making each crossing a
vertex; the original boundary endpoints are leaves.

\begin{lemma}
For every admissible matching \(M\), the graph \(\Gamma(M)\) is a
forest.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Suppose that \(\Gamma(M)\) contains a cycle.  Boundary vertices have
valence one, so every cycle is contained in the interior of the disk.
Choose one which is innermost: the disk bounded by it contains no other
cycle.  It in fact contains no edge of \(\Gamma(M)\).  Indeed, any
component of the graph lying in that disk either contains a cycle, which
would be smaller, or is a tree.  Such a tree cannot be wholly interior,
because it would have an interior leaf; and if it attaches to the chosen
cycle in two places, the path between the attachment points gives a
smaller cycle.  Thus it would have to attach in exactly one place, again
forcing an interior leaf.  This is impossible since all interior vertices
have valence four and all leaves of \(\Gamma(M)\) lie on the boundary of
the disk.

Thus one complementary region has this cycle as a boundary component.
The corresponding component of
\(M\cap\partial\overline R\) is closed and has no boundary endpoint.
This contradicts the defining requirement that every such component
have boundary consisting of two marked boundary points with inverse
labels.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}
Suppose that a letter \(x\) occurs in the word exactly once and
\(x^{-1}\) occurs exactly once.  Then, in every admissible matching, the
two corresponding endpoints are joined by an uncrossed interval.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let the two endpoints be \(p\) and \(q\).  At \(p\), the two local sides
of the incident edge belong to two components of face boundary.  By the
label condition, both of these components must end at \(q\), since
\(q\) is the only endpoint with the inverse label.

By the preceding lemma the component of \(\Gamma(M)\) containing \(p\)
is a tree, and hence there is a unique graph path from \(p\) to \(q\).
If this path met a crossing, let \(c\) be the first crossing encountered
when travelling from \(p\).  At \(c\), the two local face-boundary sides
of the incoming edge leave along two different half-edges.  Removing
\(c\) from the tree separates those two half-edges into different
components, so at most one of the two resulting face-boundary arcs can
continue to \(q\).  This contradicts the previous paragraph.  Therefore
the path from \(p\) to \(q\) has no crossing, and is a single uncrossed
interval.
\end{proof}

In the word \(w\), the letters \(b,\ol b,c,\ol c\) each occur only in
the displayed adjacent inverse pairs.  Hence every admissible matching
contains the uncrossed intervals \((3,4)\) and \((7,8)\).  Since their
endpoints are adjacent on the boundary, these intervals cut off empty
boundary disks.  Deleting them and renumbering the remaining endpoints
\(1,2,5,6,9,10\) gives a cell-preserving isomorphism from \(F_w\) to the
analogous six-endpoint complex for
\[
        u=\ol a\,a\,\ol a\,a\,\ol a\,a .
\]
Here \(u\) is only an auxiliary labelled boundary word; the same matching
definition is being used after the forced intervals have been removed.

We now compute this six-endpoint complex.  For \(u\), odd endpoints have
label \(\ol a\) and even endpoints have label \(a\).  Write
\[
        ij|kl|mn
\]
for the pairing \(\{i,j\},\{k,l\},\{m,n\}\).  By Lemma 1, two intervals
cannot cross twice, since two crossings between them would make a bigon
cycle.  Also, all three pairs of intervals cannot cross, since the
three crossings would form a triangular cycle.  Hence the crossing
pattern is determined by the endpoint pairing: two pairs cross exactly
when their endpoints interleave around the boundary.  There is no
further isotopy datum here; a regular neighbourhood of the resulting
planar forest is unique once the cyclic order of its six boundary leaves
is fixed.

Conversely, take any pairing for which the interleaving graph is a
forest, and draw it with one transverse crossing for each interleaving
pair and no other crossings.  Then \(\Gamma(M)\) is a forest.  Every
component of \(M\cap\partial\overline R\) is therefore an arc joining
two boundary endpoints.  Push such an arc slightly into the adjacent
face.  The pushed-off arc is disjoint from the diagram and cuts the disk
into two pieces.  No interval can have its endpoints on different sides,
so each side contains an even number of marked endpoints.  Therefore
the two endpoints of the face-boundary arc have opposite parity.  For
the alternating word \(u\), opposite parity is exactly the inverse-label
condition.  Thus precisely the pairings with forest interleaving graph
are admissible.  Among the fifteen pairings of six points, the only
excluded one is the all-crossing pairing \(14|25|36\).

The resulting cells are the following.  The five vertices are
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
v_0=12|34|56, & v_1=12|36|45, & v_2=14|23|56,\\
v_3=16|23|45, & v_4=16|25|34. &
\end{array}
\]
The six edges are
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
e_{01}=12|35|46, & e_{02}=13|24|56, & e_{13}=13|26|45,\\
e_{23}=15|23|46, & e_{04}=15|26|34, & e_{34}=16|24|35,
\end{array}
\]
where the subscripts indicate the two endpoint vertices.  The three
squares are
\[
        Q_{12}=13|25|46,\qquad
        Q_{14}=14|26|35,\qquad
        Q_{24}=15|24|36,
\]
and their boundaries, obtained by the two local resolutions of each
crossing, are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\partial Q_{12}&=e_{01}\cup e_{13}\cup e_{23}\cup e_{02},\\
\partial Q_{14}&=e_{01}\cup e_{13}\cup e_{34}\cup e_{04},\\
\partial Q_{24}&=e_{02}\cup e_{23}\cup e_{34}\cup e_{04}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus the one-skeleton is the theta graph with poles \(v_0\) and \(v_3\)
and with three length-two paths through \(v_1,v_2,v_4\).  The square
\(Q_{12}\) fills the cycle formed by the paths through \(v_1\) and
\(v_2\).  The square \(Q_{14}\) fills the cycle formed by the paths
through \(v_1\) and \(v_4\).  These two squares are glued along the
common path through \(v_1\), so their union is a disk whose boundary is
the remaining cycle, the one through \(v_2\) and \(v_4\).  Finally
\(Q_{24}\) is glued along exactly this boundary.  Hence the whole
complex is a 2-sphere:
\[
        F_w \cong S^2 .
\]
In particular \(F_w\) is not contractible.

## Correctness.

This solution is entirely correct.

## Novelty.

All of the AI solutions for this problem laid out essentially the same proof: (1) any matching produces a graph which is a forest; (2) remove the quasi-reduced condition by noting that we can remove trivial cancelling pairs without changing $C(M)$; (3) calculate $C(M)$ for $aa^{-1}aa^{-1}aa^{-1}$; (4) show that in this case $C(M)$ is noncontractible. (This is also the approach of the human solution.) The main differences between the AI solutions are in their level of detail in (1)--(3), and their method of showing (4). This particular solution proves (4) by observing that the CW complex is homeomorphic to $S^2$---an approach that's most similar to what most topologists would choose, as opposed to some less enlightening computations of homology that were given by other solutions.

In my opinion, among the 4 AI solutions that I read for this problem (all correct), this solution is the closest facsimile to one that might be written by an actual mathematician. The argument is compact, mostly omitting the wordy (mathematically unnecessary) explanations that show up in the other solutions.
