\begin{abstract}
We prove that if the lattice of flats of a finite matroid \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\), then the relative Dressian
\[
   \Dr(M)=\{\text{tropical linear subspaces of }\Trop(M)\}
\]
admits an order-reversing involution extending \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) under the natural embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   F\longmapsto \Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}).
\]
The main point is that an order-reversing involution of a geometric lattice forces the lattice to be modular.  For modular matroids, valuated quotients are naturally valuated matroids on the modular lattice of flats, and the desired involution is obtained by pulling back along the lattice polarity.
\end{abstract}

\section{Conventions and background}

Let \(M\) be a finite matroid of rank \(d\) on ground set \(E\).  We write
\[
  \cL(M)
\]
for its lattice of flats, ordered by inclusion.  If \(F\in \cL(M)\), then
\[
  X_F:=\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
\]
is a tropical linear subspace of \(\Trop(M)\).  The assignment \(F\mapsto X_F\) is order-reversing, hence gives an embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M).
\]

We use the valuated-matroid model of tropical linear spaces.  A valuated matroid \(p\) of rank \(s\) on \(E\) determines a tropical linear space \(\Trop(p)\) of dimension \(s-1\), and tropical linear spaces are identified up to adding a global scalar to \(p\).  If \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated matroids of ranks \(t\ge s\), then
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
\]
if and only if \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(q\), equivalently \((q,p)\) satisfies the tropical incidence--Plucker relations.  This is the valuated flag matroid correspondence; see Speyer \cite{SpeyerTLS}, Maclagan--Sturmfels \cite[Ch.~4]{MS}, and Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

For a flat \(F\), the corresponding valuated quotient \(p_F\) of rank \(d-\rk(F)\) is the trivial valuation on the matroid \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\).  Thus, if \(B\subseteq E\) has size \(d-\rk(F)\), then
\[
   p_F(B)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & \text{if } B \text{ is a basis of }M/F,\\
   \infty, & \text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, for an independent set \(B\) of \(M\),
\[
   p_F(B)<\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \cl_M(B)\vee F=E.
\]

\section{A lattice-theoretic consequence of polarity}

We first record the key structural consequence of the existence of an order-reversing involution on the lattice of flats.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}
Let \(L\) be a finite ranked semimodular lattice of rank \(d\).  Suppose that \(L\) admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   \alpha:L\longrightarrow L,\qquad x\longmapsto x^\perp .
\]
Then \(L\) is modular.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(\alpha\) is an order-reversing involution, it sends maximal chains to maximal chains with the order reversed.  Hence
\[
   \rk(x^\perp)=d-\rk(x)
\]
for all \(x\in L\).

Because \(L\) is semimodular, for all \(x,y\in L\) we have
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\ge \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Apply semimodularity to \(x^\perp\) and \(y^\perp\).  Using
\[
   x^\perp\wedge y^\perp=(x\vee y)^\perp,
   \qquad
   x^\perp\vee y^\perp=(x\wedge y)^\perp,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \rk(x^\perp)+\rk(y^\perp)
  &\ge
  \rk((x\vee y)^\perp)+\rk((x\wedge y)^\perp)\\
  (d-\rk(x))+(d-\rk(y))
  &\ge
  (d-\rk(x\vee y))+(d-\rk(x\wedge y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Cancelling \(2d\) gives
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\le \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Together with semimodularity, equality holds:
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)=\rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
This is precisely the rank form of modularity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:M-modular}
If \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\), then \(\cL(M)\) is modular.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lattice of flats of a matroid is a finite geometric lattice, hence finite, ranked, atomic, and semimodular.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}.
\end{proof}

\section{Valuated quotients of modular matroids}

We now use the standard modular-lattice form of valuated matroids.

Let \(M\) be modular of rank \(d\).  For \(0\le s\le d\), write
\[
   \cL_s(M):=\{F\in \cL(M):\rk(F)=s\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:flat-invariance}
Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of the trivial valuated matroid of \(M\).  If \(B,B'\subseteq E\) are bases of the same rank-\(s\) flat of \(M\), then
\[
   p(B)=p(B').
\]
Hence \(p\) descends to a function
\[
   \bar p:\cL_s(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T,\qquad
   \bar p(F)=p(B)
\]
for any basis \(B\) of \(F\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
It is enough to prove the claim when \(B\) and \(B'\) differ by one element.  Let
\[
   B=S\cup\{i\},\qquad B'=S\cup\{j\},
\]
where \(|S|=s-1\), and assume
\[
   \cl_M(S\cup\{i\})=\cl_M(S\cup\{j\})=:F.
\]
Extend \(S\cup\{i\}\), equivalently \(S\cup\{j\}\), to a basis of \(M\) by choosing a set \(C\) of size \(d-s\) such that
\[
   S\cup\{i\}\cup C
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   S\cup\{j\}\cup C
\]
are both bases of \(M\).

Let
\[
   J:=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup C.
\]
Then \(|J|=d+1\).  Consider the tropical incidence relation for the valuated quotient \(p\), indexed by \(S\) and \(J\):
\[
   \min_{e\in J\setminus S}\{p(S\cup\{e\})+\mu(J\setminus\{e\})\}
\]
must attain its minimum at least twice, where \(\mu\) is the trivial valuation of \(M\).  For \(e=i\) and \(e=j\), the terms are respectively
\[
   p(S\cup\{i\})+\mu(S\cup\{j\}\cup C)=p(B),
\]
and
\[
   p(S\cup\{j\})+\mu(S\cup\{i\}\cup C)=p(B').
\]
For \(e\in C\), the set
\[
   J\setminus\{e\}=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup(C\setminus\{e\})
\]
is dependent in \(M\), because \(i\) and \(j\) are dependent over \(S\).  Hence
\[
   \mu(J\setminus\{e\})=\infty.
\]
Thus the incidence relation reduces to saying that the minimum of the two values \(p(B)\) and \(p(B')\) is attained twice.  Therefore \(p(B)=p(B')\).

Since the basis graph of a matroid restriction \(M|F\) is connected, any two bases of \(F\) are connected by such single-element exchanges.  The result follows.
\end{proof}

We will use the following standard form of valuated matroid duality on modular geometric lattices.  It is the modular-lattice version of ordinary valuated-matroid duality.  In the Boolean case it is exactly the usual operation
\[
   p^*(A)=p(E\setminus A).
\]
For modular lattices, the same construction is obtained by replacing set-complement by the lattice anti-isomorphism.  See Dress--Wenzel \cite{DW}, Murota \cite[Ch.~4]{Murota}, and the flag version in Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

\begin{theorem}[Modular-lattice valuated duality]\label{thm:modular-duality}
Let \(M\) be a modular matroid of rank \(d\), and let
\[
   \alpha:\cL(M)\longrightarrow \cL(M),\qquad F\longmapsto F^\perp
\]
be an order-reversing involution.  Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of \(M\), and let \(\bar p:\cL_s(M)\to \mathbb T\) be the descended function from Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}.  Define a function
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}:\cL_{d-s}(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T
\]
by
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}(G):=\bar p(G^\perp).
\]
Then \(\bar p^{\,\perp}\) is the flat-valued form of a rank-\((d-s)\) valuated quotient \(p^\perp\) of \(M\).

Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \((p^\perp)^\perp=p\) up to tropical scalar;
\item if \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated quotients of \(M\) with \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\), then
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp;
\]
\item the construction is compatible with tropical linear spaces:
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp).
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We recall the argument.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}, every valuated quotient \(p\) of a modular matroid \(M\) is equivalently a valuated matroid on the modular lattice \(\cL(M)\), with coordinates indexed by rank-\(s\) flats.  The tropical Plucker relations are local relations in length-four intervals of \(\cL(M)\), and the tropical incidence relations for a pair of quotients are the corresponding local flag-Plucker relations.  An order-reversing lattice isomorphism sends length-four intervals to length-four intervals and interchanges rank \(s\) with rank \(d-s\).  Therefore pulling the flat-valued Plucker coordinates back along \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) preserves the tropical Plucker relations and reverses the flag incidence relations.

Thus \(\bar p^\perp\) is again a valuated quotient of \(M\), now of rank \(d-s\).  Since \(\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), applying the construction twice gives back \(\bar p\).  Finally, the valuated flag relation \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\) is carried to \(p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp\), which is precisely the asserted reversal of containment of tropical linear spaces.
\end{proof}

\section{Construction of the involution}

Let \(L=\Trop(p)\in \Dr(M)\), where \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(M\) of rank \(s\).  Define
\[
   \Phi(L):=\Trop(p^\perp),
\]
where \(p^\perp\) is the rank-\((d-s)\) quotient supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality}.

Equivalently, if \(A\subseteq E\) is independent of size \(d-s\), then
\[
   p^\perp(A)=\bar p(\cl_M(A)^\perp),
\]
and if \(A\) is dependent in \(M\), then \(p^\perp(A)=\infty\).

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid whose lattice of flats admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   F\longmapsto F^\perp.
\]
Then the map
\[
   \Phi:\Dr(M)\longrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   \Trop(p)\longmapsto \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
is an order-reversing involution.  Moreover, for every flat \(F\in \cL(M)\),
\[
   \Phi\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
   =
   \Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) extends the given involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) on \(\cL(M)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:M-modular}, \(M\) is modular.  Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} applies.

First, \(\Phi\) is well-defined because tropical linear spaces are identified with valuated matroids up to tropical scalar, and the construction \(p\mapsto p^\perp\) is unchanged by adding a global scalar to \(p\).

Second, since \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} gives
\[
   (p^\perp)^\perp=p
\]
up to tropical scalar.  Therefore
\[
   \Phi^2=\operatorname{id}_{\Dr(M)}.
\]

Third, suppose
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q).
\]
Equivalently, \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\).  By Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality},
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
which is precisely
\[
   \Phi(\Trop(q))\subseteq \Phi(\Trop(p)).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) is order-reversing.

It remains to check that \(\Phi\) extends the given flat involution.  Let \(F\in\cL(M)\), and put \(f=\rk(F)\).  Let \(p_F\) be the trivial valuation of the quotient \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\), so \(p_F\) has rank \(d-f\).  In flat-valued form,
\[
   \bar p_F(H)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & H\vee F=E,\\
   \infty, & H\vee F\ne E,
   \end{cases}
   \qquad H\in \cL_{d-f}(M).
\]
Let \(G\in\cL_f(M)\).  Then
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)
   =
   \bar p_F(G^\perp).
\]
Thus
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G^\perp\vee F=E.
\]
Applying the order-reversing involution gives
\[
   G^\perp\vee F=E
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0.
\]
Because \(\cL(M)\) is modular and
\[
   \rk(G)+\rk(F^\perp)=f+(d-f)=d,
\]
the condition \(G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0\) is equivalent to
\[
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
But this is exactly the flat-valued trivial valuation of the quotient
\[
   M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}.
\]
Hence
\[
   p_F^\perp=p_{F^\perp},
\]
and consequently
\[
   \Phi(X_F)=X_{F^\perp}.
\]
This proves the claimed extension property.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The answer to the question is affirmative: every order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\) extends to an order-reversing involution on \(\Dr(M)\).
\end{corollary}

reviews.review_summary:
## Correctness.

This submission found a few of the ingredients needed for the proof, and correctly proves some minor lemmas. However, the submission gives too many details for easier lemmas and does not supply the needed detail in its main theorem. In particular, it places all the essential claims into Theorem \ref{thm:modular-duality} and only gestures at what one would have to do to prove it. While the claims of this theorem statement are made to appear sufficient to prove the result, there is not nearly enough detail to constitute a proof (and parts of the proof are too imprecise to have much meaning). The submission thinks that Theorem 3.4 is in the literature but its citations are hallucinations (they do not contain Theorem 3.4). 

## Novelty.

Lemma 3.3 is a reasonable start. The suggestions in this submission could potentially be a useful road-map, but reaching each claim of the main theorem is still a non-trivial undertaking from this point.
reviews.recommendation: The submission should be rejected. The problem is that the difficult claims are squished into the statement of Theorem \ref{thm:modular-duality} and the only justifications for the claims are reasonable-sounding statements which don't show much of anything. Part of the problem is that the submission is convinced (or perhaps trying to convince the reader) that Theorem 3.4 is a standard argument (which it is not).

In the remainder, the submission repeatedly references the unjustified claims collected in the main theorem that allow it to continue.

\date{}


\begin{abstract}
We prove that if the lattice of flats of a finite matroid \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\), then the relative Dressian
\[
   \Dr(M)=\{\text{tropical linear subspaces of }\Trop(M)\}
\]
admits an order-reversing involution extending \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) under the natural embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   F\longmapsto \Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}).
\]
The main point is that an order-reversing involution of a geometric lattice forces the lattice to be modular.  For modular matroids, valuated quotients are naturally valuated matroids on the modular lattice of flats, and the desired involution is obtained by pulling back along the lattice polarity.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Conventions and background}

Let \(M\) be a finite matroid of rank \(d\) on ground set \(E\).  We write
\[
  \cL(M)
\]
for its lattice of flats, ordered by inclusion.  If \(F\in \cL(M)\), then
\[
  X_F:=\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
\]
is a tropical linear subspace of \(\Trop(M)\).  The assignment \(F\mapsto X_F\) is order-reversing, hence gives an embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M).
\]

We use the valuated-matroid model of tropical linear spaces.  A valuated matroid \(p\) of rank \(s\) on \(E\) determines a tropical linear space \(\Trop(p)\) of dimension \(s-1\), and tropical linear spaces are identified up to adding a global scalar to \(p\).  If \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated matroids of ranks \(t\ge s\), then
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
\]
if and only if \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(q\), equivalently \((q,p)\) satisfies the tropical incidence--Plucker relations.  This is the valuated flag matroid correspondence; see Speyer \cite{SpeyerTLS}, Maclagan--Sturmfels \cite[Ch.~4]{MS}, and Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Wrong reference \cite{SpeyerTLS}, Maclagan--Sturmfels \cite[Ch.~4]{MS}.]]



For a flat \(F\), the corresponding valuated quotient \(p_F\) of rank \(d-\rk(F)\) is the trivial valuation on the matroid \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\).  Thus, if \(B\subseteq E\) has size \(d-\rk(F)\), then
\[
   p_F(B)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & \text{if } B \text{ is a basis of }M/F,\\
   \infty, & \text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, for an independent set \(B\) of \(M\),
\[
   p_F(B)<\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \cl_M(B)\vee F=E.
\]

\subsection{A lattice-theoretic consequence of polarity}

We first record the key structural consequence of the existence of an order-reversing involution on the lattice of flats.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}
Let \(L\) be a finite ranked semimodular lattice of rank \(d\).  Suppose that \(L\) admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   \alpha:L\longrightarrow L,\qquad x\longmapsto x^\perp .
\]
Then \(L\) is modular.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(\alpha\) is an order-reversing involution, it sends maximal chains to maximal chains with the order reversed.  Hence
\[
   \rk(x^\perp)=d-\rk(x)
\]
for all \(x\in L\).

Because \(L\) is semimodular, for all \(x,y\in L\) we have
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\ge \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Apply semimodularity to \(x^\perp\) and \(y^\perp\).  Using
\[
   x^\perp\wedge y^\perp=(x\vee y)^\perp,
   \qquad
   x^\perp\vee y^\perp=(x\wedge y)^\perp,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \rk(x^\perp)+\rk(y^\perp)
  &\ge
  \rk((x\vee y)^\perp)+\rk((x\wedge y)^\perp)\\
  (d-\rk(x))+(d-\rk(y))
  &\ge
  (d-\rk(x\vee y))+(d-\rk(x\wedge y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Cancelling \(2d\) gives
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\le \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Together with semimodularity, equality holds:
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)=\rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
This is precisely the rank form of modularity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:M-modular}
If \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\), then \(\cL(M)\) is modular.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lattice of flats of a matroid is a finite geometric lattice, hence finite, ranked, atomic, and semimodular.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}.
\end{proof}

But this is exactly the flat-valued trivial valuation of the quotient
\[
   M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}.
\]
Hence
\[
   p_F^\perp=p_{F^\perp},
\]
and consequently
\[
   \Phi(X_F)=X_{F^\perp}.
\]
This proves the claimed extension property.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The answer to the question is affirmative: every order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\) extends to an order-reversing involution on \(\Dr(M)\).
\end{corollary}

%% ======================================================================
%% Inlined verbatim from the anonymised submission prob_008-C.
%% ======================================================================

\date{}


\begin{abstract}
We prove that if the lattice of flats of a finite matroid \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\), then the relative Dressian
\[
   \Dr(M)=\{\text{tropical linear subspaces of }\Trop(M)\}
\]
admits an order-reversing involution extending \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) under the natural embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   F\longmapsto \Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}).
\]
The main point is that an order-reversing involution of a geometric lattice forces the lattice to be modular.  For modular matroids, valuated quotients are naturally valuated matroids on the modular lattice of flats, and the desired involution is obtained by pulling back along the lattice polarity.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Conventions and background}

Let \(M\) be a finite matroid of rank \(d\) on ground set \(E\).  We write
\[
  \cL(M)
\]
for its lattice of flats, ordered by inclusion.  If \(F\in \cL(M)\), then
\[
  X_F:=\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})
\]
is a tropical linear subspace of \(\Trop(M)\).  The assignment \(F\mapsto X_F\) is order-reversing, hence gives an embedding
\[
   \cL(M)^{\operatorname{op}}\hookrightarrow \Dr(M).
\]

We use the valuated-matroid model of tropical linear spaces.  A valuated matroid \(p\) of rank \(s\) on \(E\) determines a tropical linear space \(\Trop(p)\) of dimension \(s-1\), and tropical linear spaces are identified up to adding a global scalar to \(p\).  If \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated matroids of ranks \(t\ge s\), then
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
\]
if and only if \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(q\), equivalently \((q,p)\) satisfies the tropical incidence--Plucker relations.  This is the valuated flag matroid correspondence; see Speyer \cite{SpeyerTLS}, Maclagan--Sturmfels \cite[Ch.~4]{MS}, and Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

For a flat \(F\), the corresponding valuated quotient \(p_F\) of rank \(d-\rk(F)\) is the trivial valuation on the matroid \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\).  Thus, if \(B\subseteq E\) has size \(d-\rk(F)\), then
\[
   p_F(B)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & \text{if } B \text{ is a basis of }M/F,\\
   \infty, & \text{otherwise}.
   \end{cases}
\]
Equivalently, for an independent set \(B\) of \(M\),
\[
   p_F(B)<\infty
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \cl_M(B)\vee F=E.
\]

\subsection{A lattice-theoretic consequence of polarity}

We first record the key structural consequence of the existence of an order-reversing involution on the lattice of flats.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}
Let \(L\) be a finite ranked semimodular lattice of rank \(d\).  Suppose that \(L\) admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   \alpha:L\longrightarrow L,\qquad x\longmapsto x^\perp .
\]
Then \(L\) is modular.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since \(\alpha\) is an order-reversing involution, it sends maximal chains to maximal chains with the order reversed.  Hence
\[
   \rk(x^\perp)=d-\rk(x)
\]
for all \(x\in L\).

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: At this point, one should immediately conclude that $-\rk$ is semimodular and thus $\rk$ is modular.
The remainder of this proof is superfluous. In fact, the mere assertion that the order-reversing involution implies modularity would have been sufficient.]]


Because \(L\) is semimodular, for all \(x,y\in L\) we have
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\ge \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Apply semimodularity to \(x^\perp\) and \(y^\perp\).  Using
\[
   x^\perp\wedge y^\perp=(x\vee y)^\perp,
   \qquad
   x^\perp\vee y^\perp=(x\wedge y)^\perp,
\]
we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \rk(x^\perp)+\rk(y^\perp)
  &\ge
  \rk((x\vee y)^\perp)+\rk((x\wedge y)^\perp)\\
  (d-\rk(x))+(d-\rk(y))
  &\ge
  (d-\rk(x\vee y))+(d-\rk(x\wedge y)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Cancelling \(2d\) gives
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)\le \rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
Together with semimodularity, equality holds:
\[
   \rk(x)+\rk(y)=\rk(x\wedge y)+\rk(x\vee y).
\]
This is precisely the rank form of modularity.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:M-modular}
If \(M\) admits an order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\), then \(\cL(M)\) is modular.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
The lattice of flats of a matroid is a finite geometric lattice, hence finite, ranked, atomic, and semimodular.  Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:selfdual-implies-modular}.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Valuated quotients of modular matroids}

We now use the standard modular-lattice form of valuated matroids.

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The lemmas in this section do not appear to be standard at all. Nor is there a ``modular-lattice'' form of valuated matroids.]]


Let \(M\) be modular of rank \(d\).  For \(0\le s\le d\), write
\[
   \cL_s(M):=\{F\in \cL(M):\rk(F)=s\}.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:flat-invariance}
Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of the trivial valuated matroid of \(M\).  If \(B,B'\subseteq E\) are bases of the same rank-\(s\) flat of \(M\), then
\[
   p(B)=p(B').
\]
Hence \(p\) descends to a function
\[
   \bar p:\cL_s(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T,\qquad
   \bar p(F)=p(B)
\]
for any basis \(B\) of \(F\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
It is enough to prove the claim when \(B\) and \(B'\) differ by one element.  Let
\[
   B=S\cup\{i\},\qquad B'=S\cup\{j\},
\]
where \(|S|=s-1\), and assume
\[
   \cl_M(S\cup\{i\})=\cl_M(S\cup\{j\})=:F.
\]
Extend \(S\cup\{i\}\), equivalently \(S\cup\{j\}\), to a basis of \(M\) by choosing a set \(C\) of size \(d-s\) such that
\[
   S\cup\{i\}\cup C
   \quad\text{and}\quad
   S\cup\{j\}\cup C
\]
are both bases of \(M\).

Let
\[
   J:=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup C.
\]
Then \(|J|=d+1\).  Consider the tropical incidence relation for the valuated quotient \(p\), indexed by \(S\) and \(J\):
\[
   \min_{e\in J\setminus S}\{p(S\cup\{e\})+\mu(J\setminus\{e\})\}
\]
must attain its minimum at least twice, where \(\mu\) is the trivial valuation of \(M\).  For \(e=i\) and \(e=j\), the terms are respectively
\[
   p(S\cup\{i\})+\mu(S\cup\{j\}\cup C)=p(B),
\]
and
\[
   p(S\cup\{j\})+\mu(S\cup\{i\}\cup C)=p(B').
\]
For \(e\in C\), the set
\[
   J\setminus\{e\}=S\cup\{i,j\}\cup(C\setminus\{e\})
\]
is dependent in \(M\), because \(i\) and \(j\) are dependent over \(S\).  Hence
\[
   \mu(J\setminus\{e\})=\infty.
\]
Thus the incidence relation reduces to saying that the minimum of the two values \(p(B)\) and \(p(B')\) is attained twice.  Therefore \(p(B)=p(B')\).

Since the basis graph of a matroid restriction \(M|F\) is connected, any two bases of \(F\) are connected by such single-element exchanges.  The result follows.

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The proof of this lemma is rather wordy. An expert reader would expect a more concise formulation. A novice would however appreciate the simplicity and clarity of it.]]

\end{proof}

We will use the following standard form of valuated matroid duality on modular geometric lattices.  It is the modular-lattice version of ordinary valuated-matroid duality.  In the Boolean case it is exactly the usual operation
\[
   p^*(A)=p(E\setminus A).
\]
For modular lattices, the same construction is obtained by replacing set-complement by the lattice anti-isomorphism.  See Dress--Wenzel \cite{DW}, Murota \cite[Ch.~4]{Murota}, and the flag version in Brandt--Eur--Zhang \cite{BEZ}.

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: This part misleadingly suggests that these sources contain statements about relative duality operations in the relative Dressians of modular matroids. No such statements can be found in these sources.]]


\begin{theorem}[Modular-lattice valuated duality]\label{thm:modular-duality}
Let \(M\) be a modular matroid of rank \(d\), and let
\[
   \alpha:\cL(M)\longrightarrow \cL(M),\qquad F\longmapsto F^\perp
\]
be an order-reversing involution.  Let \(p\) be a rank-\(s\) valuated quotient of \(M\), and let \(\bar p:\cL_s(M)\to \mathbb T\) be the descended function from Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}.  Define a function
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}:\cL_{d-s}(M)\longrightarrow \mathbb T
\]
by
\[
   \bar p^{\,\perp}(G):=\bar p(G^\perp).
\]
Then \(\bar p^{\,\perp}\) is the flat-valued form of a rank-\((d-s)\) valuated quotient \(p^\perp\) of \(M\).

Moreover:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item \((p^\perp)^\perp=p\) up to tropical scalar;
\item if \(q\) and \(p\) are valuated quotients of \(M\) with \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\), then
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp;
\]
\item the construction is compatible with tropical linear spaces:
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q)
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp).
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Point (iii) is redundant. It follows trivially from (i) and (ii) and standard facts about valuated matroid quotients.]]

\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We recall the argument.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:flat-invariance}, every valuated quotient \(p\) of a modular matroid \(M\) is equivalently a valuated matroid on the modular lattice \(\cL(M)\), with coordinates indexed by rank-\(s\) flats.  The tropical Plucker relations are local relations in length-four intervals of \(\cL(M)\), and the tropical incidence relations for a pair of quotients are the corresponding local flag-Plucker relations.  An order-reversing lattice isomorphism sends length-four intervals to length-four intervals and interchanges rank \(s\) with rank \(d-s\).  Therefore pulling the flat-valued Plucker coordinates back along \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) preserves the tropical Plucker relations and reverses the flag incidence relations.

Thus \(\bar p^\perp\) is again a valuated quotient of \(M\), now of rank \(d-s\).  Since \(\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), applying the construction twice gives back \(\bar p\).  Finally, the valuated flag relation \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\) is carried to \(p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp\), which is precisely the asserted reversal of containment of tropical linear spaces.
\end{proof}

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: This single lemma crams in essentially all the difficult statements needed for the proof of the main result. Part (i) is trivial. The non-trivial aspects are (a) the proof that $\overline{p}^{\perp}$ is the flat-valued form of a valuated quotient of $M$, and (b) a proof of compatibility with quotients, i.e.\ (ii).

Only the slightest hint is given about how (a) should be approached. Namely, it is suggested that it is enough to check the local-exchange relations for valuated matroids, and that this follows straightforwardly by looking at the corresponding relations for $p$. This is not quite correct. One must accompany the local-exchange relations with a verification that the support of $p^{\perp}$ is a matroid. This local-global condition suffices by standard results in the literature (e.g.\ Murota's work). The absent support condition is in general the more difficult and more substantial of the two. A lesser but still significant problem is that the proof of the validity of local-exchange relations is not given, only hinted at in vague terms. It is not only length-four intervals that have to be examined. The more ``degenerate'' cases must be dealt with also.

As for part (b), its validity is asserted with no justification whatsoever.]]


\subsection{Construction of the involution}

Let \(L=\Trop(p)\in \Dr(M)\), where \(p\) is a valuated quotient of \(M\) of rank \(s\).  Define
\[
   \Phi(L):=\Trop(p^\perp),
\]
where \(p^\perp\) is the rank-\((d-s)\) quotient supplied by Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality}.

Equivalently, if \(A\subseteq E\) is independent of size \(d-s\), then
\[
   p^\perp(A)=\bar p(\cl_M(A)^\perp),
\]
and if \(A\) is dependent in \(M\), then \(p^\perp(A)=\infty\).

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:main}
Let \(M\) be a finite matroid whose lattice of flats admits an order-reversing involution
\[
   F\longmapsto F^\perp.
\]
Then the map
\[
   \Phi:\Dr(M)\longrightarrow \Dr(M),\qquad
   \Trop(p)\longmapsto \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
is an order-reversing involution.  Moreover, for every flat \(F\in \cL(M)\),
\[
   \Phi\!\left(\Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})\right)
   =
   \Trop(M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) extends the given involution \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) on \(\cL(M)\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:M-modular}, \(M\) is modular.  Hence Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} applies.

First, \(\Phi\) is well-defined because tropical linear spaces are identified with valuated matroids up to tropical scalar, and the construction \(p\mapsto p^\perp\) is unchanged by adding a global scalar to \(p\).

Second, since \(F\mapsto F^\perp\) is an involution on \(\cL(M)\), Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality} gives
\[
   (p^\perp)^\perp=p
\]
up to tropical scalar.  Therefore
\[
   \Phi^2=\operatorname{id}_{\Dr(M)}.
\]

Third, suppose
\[
   \Trop(p)\subseteq \Trop(q).
\]
Equivalently, \(q\twoheadrightarrow p\).  By Theorem~\ref{thm:modular-duality},
\[
   p^\perp\twoheadrightarrow q^\perp.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \Trop(q^\perp)\subseteq \Trop(p^\perp),
\]
which is precisely
\[
   \Phi(\Trop(q))\subseteq \Phi(\Trop(p)).
\]
Thus \(\Phi\) is order-reversing.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The first part of this proof is just a trivial translation of the unproven Theorem 3.4. Only the latter half is non-trivial (though still straightforward).]]


It remains to check that \(\Phi\) extends the given flat involution.  Let \(F\in\cL(M)\), and put \(f=\rk(F)\).  Let \(p_F\) be the trivial valuation of the quotient \(M/F\oplus U_{0,F}\), so \(p_F\) has rank \(d-f\).  In flat-valued form,
\[
   \bar p_F(H)=
   \begin{cases}
   0, & H\vee F=E,\\
   \infty, & H\vee F\ne E,
   \end{cases}
   \qquad H\in \cL_{d-f}(M).
\]
Let \(G\in\cL_f(M)\).  Then
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)
   =
   \bar p_F(G^\perp).
\]
Thus
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G^\perp\vee F=E.
\]
Applying the order-reversing involution gives
\[
   G^\perp\vee F=E
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0.
\]
Because \(\cL(M)\) is modular and
\[
   \rk(G)+\rk(F^\perp)=f+(d-f)=d,
\]
the condition \(G\wedge F^\perp=\hat 0\) is equivalent to
\[
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
Therefore
\[
   \bar p_F^{\,\perp}(G)=0
   \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
   G\vee F^\perp=E.
\]
But this is exactly the flat-valued trivial valuation of the quotient
\[
   M/F^\perp\oplus U_{0,F^\perp}.
\]
Hence
\[
   p_F^\perp=p_{F^\perp},
\]
and consequently
\[
   \Phi(X_F)=X_{F^\perp}.
\]
This proves the claimed extension property.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
The answer to the question is affirmative: every order-reversing involution on \(\cL(M)\) extends to an order-reversing involution on \(\Dr(M)\).
\end{corollary}

## Correctness.

This submission incorrectly claims that there is not an order-reversing involution of $Dr(M)$ extending the assumed involution of the flats. Many of the claims are not clearly interpretable as anything mathematically meaningful. For instance, it hallucinates ``Prior misconceptions regarding deformations" and ``unvaluated topologies." The submission does not get beyond trying to apply a cardinality augment to rule out a bijection (which was not going to work since the duality claim is true). 

## Novelty.

This submission does not contribute any ideas toward proving duality for tropical linear subspaces (and claims it is false). I was unable to find any interesting ideas in its attempt to disprove the result.
reviews.recommendation: This submission should be rejected. It does not have any strategy to prove the claim since it attempted to disprove a true statement.

It should do more than claim existence of an involution here.
``principal ideal of points" is very weird terminology here
I cannot make sense of the preceding sentence. In the following sentence, it is unclear what ``initial matroid at infinity" means. Ideally this would be defined, since it does not seem standard.
It starts talking about topologies here which is not relevant.
It is unclear what the prior misconceptions are and what deformations it is referring to.

%% ======================================================================

%% ======================================================================
%
\date{}



\noindent \textbf{Problem Statement.} Let $M$ be a matroid, and let $\Trop(M)$ be the corresponding tropical linear space, i.e., the closure of the Bergman fan of $M$ in tropical projective space. The relative Dressian of $M$ is 
\[ \Dr(M) :=\{\text{ tropical linear subspaces of $\Trop M$ }\}, \]
which is partially ordered by inclusion of tropical linear spaces. 

Suppose $M$ admits an order-reversing involution $F\mapsto F^\perp$ on the lattice of flats $\cLL(M)$. Note that there is a natural inclusion $\cLL(M)^{\op} \subset \Dr(M)$ given by $F\mapsto \Trop(M/F\oplus U_{0,F})$.

\medskip
\noindent \textbf{Question.} Is there an order-reversing involution $\Phi$ on $\Dr(M)$ that extends the involution $F\mapsto F^\perp$?

\bigskip

\begin{proof}[Solution]
\textbf{Answer:} No. We construct a rigorous counterexample using the Fano matroid $M = F_7$.


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: The claim is true, so the rest cannot be good.]]

\medskip
\noindent \textbf{Step 1: The Poset Structure and the Assumed Involution}


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It should do more than claim existence of an involution here.]]

Let $M = F_7$ be the Fano matroid on $E = \{1, \dots, 7\}$. A standard polarity of the Fano plane induces an incidence-reversing bijection between its points (rank $1$ flats) and lines (rank $2$ flats), yielding an order-reversing involution $F \mapsto F^\perp$ on the lattice of flats $\cLL(F_7)$. For instance, we may map the point $F = \{1\}$ to the line $F^\perp = L_1 = \{1,2,3\}$.

The relative Dressian $\Dr(F_7)$ is the poset of tropical linear subspaces of $\Trop(F_7)$ graded by rank. 
\begin{itemize}
    \item The rank $1$ elements ($\Dr_1$) are the points of $\Trop(F_7)$.
    \item The rank $2$ elements ($\Dr_2$) are the tropical lines contained in $\Trop(F_7)$.
\end{itemize}
Since points are the atoms of $\Dr(F_7)$ (covering only the empty set), any inclusion-reversing involution $\Phi$ on $\Dr(F_7)$ must map atoms to coatoms. As $\Trop(F_7)$ has rank $3$, the coatoms are precisely the rank $2$ spaces. Thus, $\Phi$ strictly restricts to a bijection between $\Dr_1$ and $\Dr_2$.

\medskip
\noindent \textbf{Step 2: The Boundary Elements and the Cardinality Contradiction Strategy}

The problem supplies an embedding $F \mapsto V_F := \Trop(F_7/F \oplus U_{0,F})$.
\begin{itemize}
    \item Let $F = \{1\}$. The quotient $F_7/\{1\}$ has rank $2$, and $U_{0,\{1\}}$ has rank $0$. Their direct sum has rank $2$, so $V_{\{1\}} \in \Dr_2$ is a tropical line. Geometrically, it is a $1$-dimensional metric tree with a loop at $1$ (forcing coordinate $x_1 = \infty$ globally, under the max-plus convention) and rays corresponding to parallel classes $\{2,3\}$, $\{4,5\}$, and $\{6,7\}$. Being a $1$-dimensional continuous complex, $V_{\{1\}}$ contains uncountably many points.
    
[[REVIEWER COMMENT: ``principal ideal of points" is very weird terminology here]]

    Thus, its principal ideal of points $I(V_{\{1\}}) = \{ x \in \Dr_1 \mid x \subset V_{\{1\}} \}$ has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$.
    \item Let $L_1 = \{1,2,3\}$. The sum $F_7/L_1 \oplus U_{0,L_1}$ has rank $1$. Thus $V_{L_1} \in \Dr_1$ is a single infinite point. Because $\{1,2,3\}$ evaluates as loops and $\{4,5,6,7\}$ evaluates as a parallel class, this point uniquely occurs where coordinates $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = \infty$ simultaneously, and the others remain finite.
\end{itemize}

Because $\Phi$ extends the flat involution, we strictly have $\Phi(V_{\{1\}}) = V_{L_1}$. Because $\Phi$ reverses inclusion, $x \subset V_{\{1\}} \iff \Phi(x) \supset \Phi(V_{\{1\}})$. Thus, $\Phi$ must map the uncountable set $I(V_{\{1\}})$ bijectively onto the principal filter $F(V_{L_1}) = \{ T \in \Dr_2 \mid V_{L_1} \subset T \}$.

This structural limit mandates that in the initial matroid of $T$ at infinity, the subset $\{1,2,3\}$ must act globally as a single parallel class, or contain loops alongside a parallel class. We exhaustively classify all valid rank $2$ valuated matroid quotients of $F_7$ satisfying this:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Loopless Quotients:} If $T$ has no loops, $\{1,2,3\}$ must form a parallel class. The remaining elements $\{4,5,6,7\}$ must partition into valid rank $1$ flats of $F_7$. The only flats of $F_7$ fully contained within $\{4,5,6,7\}$ are singletons. Thus, they must partition exclusively into $\{4\}, \{5\}, \{6\}, \{7\}$. This uniquely isolates the degenerate star tree $S_{L_1}$.
    \item \textbf{Quotients with Loops:} If $T$ contains loops, their union must form a valid flat of $F_7$ (sizes $0, 1, 3, 7$). 
    \begin{itemize}
        \item A flat of $3$ loops (e.g., $\{1,2,3\}$) leaves a rank $2$ matroid on $\{4,5,6,7\}$. As proven above, its rank $1$ flats must be the $4$ singletons, forcing the underlying matroid to be $U_{0,\{1,2,3\}} \oplus U_{2,4}$. However, this matroid contains the closed flat $\{1,2,3,4\}$, which is not a flat of $F_7$. Thus, $3$ loops strictly fail the strong map condition.
        \item A flat of $1$ loop must be chosen from $\{1,2,3\}$ to maintain the necessary ray direction. If $1$ is a loop, $\{2,3\}$ must act as a parallel class. The remaining elements must partition such that $\{1\} \cup P_i$ form valid lines of $F_7$. The only lines containing $1$ are $\{1,2,3\}, \{1,4,5\}, \{1,6,7\}$. This uniquely forces the remaining parallel classes to be $\{4,5\}$ and $\{6,7\}$, isolating the tree $V_{\{1\}}$. Repeating this exact flat-matching calculation for loops at $2$ and $3$ uniquely isolates the boundary trees $V_{\{2\}}$ and $V_{\{3\}}$.
    \end{itemize}
\end{enumerate}

This explicitly exhausts the unvaluated topologies. None of these four topologies ($S_{L_1}, V_{\{1\}}, V_{\{2\}}, V_{\{3\}}$) admit internal valuated edges that maintain the $e_{123}$ ray, because any internal split would necessitate intermediate parallel groupings (e.g., size $2$ subsets of $\{4,5,6,7\}$) which do not correspond to valid flats of $F_7$. Consequently, they exist precisely as four isolated, rigid trees.

\noindent \textbf{Step 4: Defusing Prior Misconceptions Regarding Deformations}


[[REVIEWER COMMENT: It is unclear what the prior misconceptions are and what deformations it is referring to.]]


A known theoretical failure mode involves assuming that continuous $1$-parameter families of trees (such as $T_{L_1, l}$, which locally splits $\{1,2,3\}$ from $\{4,5,6,7\}$ along an internal edge) contain $V_{L_1}$, thereby generating $\mathfrak{c}$ elements and dissolving the contradiction. In the split family $T_{L_1, l}$, the leaves $1$, $2$, and $3$ are separated by the internal vertex and diverge along independent infinite rays $e_1, e_2, e_3$. Consequently, their geometric limits trace to the three distinct boundary points where exactly \emph{one} coordinate is infinite (i.e., $V_{\{1\}}, V_{\{2\}}, V_{\{3\}}$). The strict boundary point $V_{L_1}$ is never reached by this family.

Because all continuous families structurally miss $V_{L_1}$, the count is strictly locked at $|F(V_{L_1})| = 4$. \title{Submission A solution to Problem 9}
\date{}
\maketitle

\begin{center}
{\bf Hook coefficients in the universal Hilbert series of diagonal coinvariants}
\end{center}

\section*{Problem statement and interpretation}

I interpret \(R_n^{(m)}\) as the diagonal coinvariant algebra
\[
 R_n^{(m)}=\mathbb C[x_i^{(r)}:1\le i\le n,\ 1\le r\le m]\,
/\,\langle \mathbb C[x_i^{(r)}]^{\mathfrak S_n}_{+}\rangle,
\]
where \(\mathfrak S_n\) acts by simultaneously permuting the subscript \(i\) in all
\(m\) sets of variables.  Thus the coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) are the stable
multiplicities of the polynomial \(GL_m\)-irreducibles \(S_\lambda(\mathbb C^m)\).

\section*{The combinatorial model}

For \(r,k\ge 1\), let \(\OP_{r,k}\) be the set of ordered set partitions
\(\sigma=(B_1|\cdots|B_k)\) of \([r]\) into \(k\) nonempty blocks.  An inversion of
\(\sigma\) is a pair \((i,j)\) such that
\[
        i<j,\qquad i=\min B_m,\qquad j\in B_\ell,\qquad \ell<m .
\]
Let \(\inv(\sigma)\) be the number of such pairs.  When \(k=r\), this is the
usual inversion number of the permutation obtained by reading the singleton
blocks from left to right.

\begin{theorem}
Let \(\lambda=(a,1^b)\) be a hook, with \(a\ge 1\) and \(b\ge 0\).  Then
\(c_{(a,1^b)}(n)\) is the number of ordered set partitions
\(\sigma=(B_1|\cdots|B_k)\) of \([r]\), for some \(2\le r\le n\), such that
\[
        r-k=b+1,\qquad r\hbox{ is not a singleton block of }\sigma,\qquad
        \inv(\sigma)=a-1 .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0} c_{(a,1^b)}(n)\,q^{a-1}z^b
=
\sum_{\substack{2\le r\le n\\1\le k\le r-1}}
\ \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in \OP_{r,k}\\
                  r\text{ not singleton in }\sigma}}
        q^{\inv(\sigma)}z^{r-k-1}.
\]
The empty partition coefficient is \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We use two standard inputs.  First, diagonal supersymmetry says that the
universal Schur coefficients for diagonal coinvariants can be read from the
coinvariant ring with one bosonic alphabet and one fermionic alphabet,
\[
 SR_n=\bigl(\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\otimes
          \bigwedge(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\bigr)
/\langle(\mathbb C[x]\otimes\bigwedge\theta)^{\mathfrak S_n}_{+}\rangle .
\]
More explicitly, the supersymmetric Frobenius/character expansion has the same
universal multiplicity modules as the purely bosonic expansion; after applying
the dimension map to the \(\mathfrak S_n\)-Frobenius factor one obtains exactly
the Hilbert coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) appearing in the question.  Therefore
\[
        \Hilb(SR_n;q,z)=\sum_\lambda c_\lambda(n)s_\lambda(q/z),
\]
where \(s_\lambda(q/z)\) denotes the super Schur polynomial in one even variable
\(q\) and one odd variable \(z\).  With one even and one odd variable,
\(s_\lambda(q/z)\) vanishes unless \(\lambda\) lies in the \((1,1)\)-hook, i.e.
unless \(\lambda\) is a hook, and
\[
        s_{(a,1^b)}(q/z)=q^a z^b+q^{a-1}z^{b+1}
        =q^{a-1}z^b(q+z).
\]
Thus
\[
        \Hilb(SR_n;q,z)
        =1+(q+z)\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0}
              c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^{a-1}z^b .          \tag{1}
\]

Second, the Hilbert series of \(SR_n\), due to Rhoades--Wilson, is
\[
        H_n(q,z):=\Hilb(SR_n;q,z)
        =\sum_{k=1}^{n} z^{\,n-k}[k]!_q\,\Stir_q(n,k),                 \tag{2}
\]
where \([k]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{k-1}\), \([k]!_q=[k]_q[k-1]_q\cdots[1]_q\), and
\[
        \Stir_q(r,k)=\Stir_q(r-1,k-1)+[k]_q\Stir_q(r-1,k).
\]
The boundary conditions are
\(\Stir_q(0,0)=1\), \(\Stir_q(r,0)=0\) for \(r>0\), and
\(\Stir_q(r,k)=0\) outside \(0\le k\le r\).  Put
\(F_{r,k}=[k]!_q\Stir_q(r,k)\).  Then \(F_{r,k}=0\) outside
\(1\le k\le r\), except for the harmless convention \(F_{0,0}=1\), and
\[
        F_{r,k}=[k]_qF_{r-1,k-1}+[k]_qF_{r-1,k}.
\]
Using \([k+1]_q=1+q[k]_q\) in (2), we get, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_n(q,z)
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}z^{n-k}\bigl([k]_qF_{n-1,k-1}
                         +[k]_qF_{n-1,k}\bigr)\\
&=H_{n-1}(q,z)
 +(q+z)\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}[k]_qF_{n-1,k}z^{n-1-k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(H_1(q,z)=1\), iteration gives
\[
        \frac{H_n(q,z)-1}{q+z}
        =
        \sum_{r=1}^{n-1}\sum_{k=1}^{r}
             [k]_q\,F_{r,k}\,z^{r-k}.                    \tag{3}
\]

It remains to identify the right side of (3).  The polynomial \(F_{r,k}\) is
the inversion enumerator of ordered set partitions:
\[
        F_{r,k}=\sum_{\tau\in \OP_{r,k}}q^{\inv(\tau)}.                \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, both sides satisfy the same recurrence.  To see this directly, insert
the largest letter \(r\) into an ordered partition of \([r-1]\).  To obtain
\(k\) final blocks, either insert \(r\) as a singleton block into one of the
\(k\) possible final block positions, or insert \(r\) into one of the \(k\)
existing blocks.  If the final position is \(i\) from the left, the new
inversions involving \(r\) are exactly the minima of the blocks to its right, so
their number is \(k-i\).  Summing over \(i=1,\ldots,k\) contributes
\([k]_q\) in each of the two cases, giving the recurrence above and the initial
condition.

Now restrict this insertion argument to insertions of \(r+1\) into an existing
block of an ordered partition \(\tau\in\OP_{r,k}\).  The result is precisely an
ordered partition \(\sigma\in\OP_{r+1,k}\) in which \(r+1\) is not a singleton,
and the extra inversion contribution is again one of \(0,1,\ldots,k-1\).
Hence
\[
 [k]_qF_{r,k}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\OP_{r+1,k}\\ r+1\text{ not singleton}}}
      q^{\inv(\sigma)} .
\]
Substituting this into (3), and replacing \(r+1\) by \(r\), gives exactly
\[
\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0}c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^{a-1}z^b
=
\sum_{\substack{2\le r\le n\\1\le k\le r-1}}
\sum_{\substack{\sigma\in \OP_{r,k}\\r\text{ not singleton}}}
q^{\inv(\sigma)}z^{r-k-1}.
\]
Extracting the coefficient of \(q^{a-1}z^b\) proves the claimed interpretation.
\end{proof}

\begin{thebibliography}{9}

\bibitem{Bergeron}
F. Bergeron,
\emph{Multivariate diagonal coinvariant spaces for complex reflection groups},
Adv. Math. 239 (2013), 97--108.

\bibitem{Lentfer}
J. Lentfer,
\emph{Diagonal supersymmetry for coinvariant rings},
arXiv:2505.14885 (2025).

\bibitem{RhoadesWilson}
B. Rhoades and A. T. Wilson,
\emph{The Hilbert series of the superspace coinvariant ring},
Forum Math. Pi 12 (2024), e16.

\end{thebibliography}

reviews.review_summary:
The solution gives a combinatorial formula for the coefficients $c_{(a,1^b)}(n)$ in terms of ordered set partitions.

The proof starts from the diagonal supersymmetry result of \cite{Lentfer} to relate the coefficients in question to the Hilbert series of the super coinvariant ring $SR_n$.
It then uses the formula established in \cite{RhoadesWilson} for this Hilbert series to express the coefficients using $q$-Stirling numbers. Finally, some $q$-series manipulations are then used to obtain the combinatorial formula.

Here are some comments:
\begin{itemize}
 \item The correct references are used, but they are not cited in the text. 
 \item The presentation is quite dense; all the steps are included in the same proof. I recommend first recalling, in separate theorem environments, Lentfer's result on the universality of the coefficients $c_\lambda(n)$, and Rhoades–Wilson's formula for the Hilbert series. This would make the argument easier to follow.
\end{itemize}

## Correctness.

The formula is correct, as is the proof.

## Novelty.

The two first steps of the proof are standard. The trick used to factorize the series $H_n(q,z)$ (see Eq. (3)) simplifies the last step of the proof. The combinatorial formula is quite nice.
reviews.recommendation: I recommend publication after minor revisions.

\(m\) sets of variables.  Thus the coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) are the stable
multiplicities of the polynomial \(GL_m\)-irreducibles \(S_\lambda(\mathbb C^m)\).

\subsection*{The combinatorial model}

For \(r,k\ge 1\), let \(\OP_{r,k}\) be the set of ordered set partitions
\(\sigma=(B_1|\cdots|B_k)\) of \([r]\) into \(k\) nonempty blocks.  An inversion of
\(\sigma\) is a pair \((i,j)\) such that
\[
        i<j,\qquad i=\min B_m,\qquad j\in B_\ell,\qquad \ell<m .
\]
Let \(\inv(\sigma)\) be the number of such pairs.  When \(k=r\), this is the
usual inversion number of the permutation obtained by reading the singleton
blocks from left to right.

\begin{theorem}
Let \(\lambda=(a,1^b)\) be a hook, with \(a\ge 1\) and \(b\ge 0\).  Then
\(c_{(a,1^b)}(n)\) is the number of ordered set partitions
\(\sigma=(B_1|\cdots|B_k)\) of \([r]\), for some \(2\le r\le n\), such that
\[
        r-k=b+1,\qquad r\hbox{ is not a singleton block of }\sigma,\qquad
        \inv(\sigma)=a-1 .
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0} c_{(a,1^b)}(n)\,q^{a-1}z^b
=
\sum_{\substack{2\le r\le n\\1\le k\le r-1}}
\ \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in \OP_{r,k}\\
                  r\text{ not singleton in }\sigma}}
        q^{\inv(\sigma)}z^{r-k-1}.
\]
The empty partition coefficient is \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
We use two standard inputs.  First, diagonal supersymmetry says that the
universal Schur coefficients for diagonal coinvariants can be read from the
coinvariant ring with one bosonic alphabet and one fermionic alphabet,
\[
 SR_n=\bigl(\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\otimes
          \bigwedge(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\bigr)
/\langle(\mathbb C[x]\otimes\bigwedge\theta)^{\mathfrak S_n}_{+}\rangle .
\]
More explicitly, the supersymmetric Frobenius/character expansion has the same
universal multiplicity modules as the purely bosonic expansion; after applying
the dimension map to the \(\mathfrak S_n\)-Frobenius factor one obtains exactly
the Hilbert coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) appearing in the question.  Therefore
\[
        \Hilb(SR_n;q,z)=\sum_\lambda c_\lambda(n)s_\lambda(q/z),
\]
where \(s_\lambda(q/z)\) denotes the super Schur polynomial in one even variable
\(q\) and one odd variable \(z\).  With one even and one odd variable,
\(s_\lambda(q/z)\) vanishes unless \(\lambda\) lies in the \((1,1)\)-hook, i.e.
unless \(\lambda\) is a hook, and
\[
        s_{(a,1^b)}(q/z)=q^a z^b+q^{a-1}z^{b+1}
        =q^{a-1}z^b(q+z).
\]

[[REVIEWER COMMENT: Add a reference for this formula.]]

Thus
\[
        \Hilb(SR_n;q,z)
        =1+(q+z)\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0}
              c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^{a-1}z^b .          \tag{1}
\]

Second, the Hilbert series of \(SR_n\), due to Rhoades--Wilson, is
\[
        H_n(q,z):=\Hilb(SR_n;q,z)
        =\sum_{k=1}^{n} z^{\,n-k}[k]!_q\,\Stir_q(n,k),                 \tag{2}
\]
where \([k]_q=1+q+\cdots+q^{k-1}\), \([k]!_q=[k]_q[k-1]_q\cdots[1]_q\), and
\[
        \Stir_q(r,k)=\Stir_q(r-1,k-1)+[k]_q\Stir_q(r-1,k).
\]
The boundary conditions are
\(\Stir_q(0,0)=1\), \(\Stir_q(r,0)=0\) for \(r>0\), and
\(\Stir_q(r,k)=0\) outside \(0\le k\le r\).  Put
\(F_{r,k}=[k]!_q\Stir_q(r,k)\).  Then \(F_{r,k}=0\) outside
\(1\le k\le r\), except for the harmless convention \(F_{0,0}=1\), and
\[
        F_{r,k}=[k]_qF_{r-1,k-1}+[k]_qF_{r-1,k}.
\]
Using \([k+1]_q=1+q[k]_q\) in (2), we get, for \(n\ge2\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_n(q,z)
&=\sum_{k=1}^{n}z^{n-k}\bigl([k]_qF_{n-1,k-1}
                         +[k]_qF_{n-1,k}\bigr)\\
&=H_{n-1}(q,z)
 +(q+z)\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}[k]_qF_{n-1,k}z^{n-1-k}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(H_1(q,z)=1\), iteration gives
\[
        \frac{H_n(q,z)-1}{q+z}
        =
        \sum_{r=1}^{n-1}\sum_{k=1}^{r}
             [k]_q\,F_{r,k}\,z^{r-k}.                    \tag{3}
\]

It remains to identify the right side of (3).  The polynomial \(F_{r,k}\) is
the inversion enumerator of ordered set partitions:
\[
        F_{r,k}=\sum_{\tau\in \OP_{r,k}}q^{\inv(\tau)}.                \tag{4}
\]
Indeed, both sides satisfy the same recurrence.  To see this directly, insert
the largest letter \(r\) into an ordered partition of \([r-1]\).  To obtain
\(k\) final blocks, either insert \(r\) as a singleton block into one of the
\(k\) possible final block positions, or insert \(r\) into one of the \(k\)
existing blocks.  If the final position is \(i\) from the left, the new
inversions involving \(r\) are exactly the minima of the blocks to its right, so
their number is \(k-i\).  Summing over \(i=1,\ldots,k\) contributes
\([k]_q\) in each of the two cases, giving the recurrence above and the initial
condition.

Now restrict this insertion argument to insertions of \(r+1\) into an existing
block of an ordered partition \(\tau\in\OP_{r,k}\).  The result is precisely an
ordered partition \(\sigma\in\OP_{r+1,k}\) in which \(r+1\) is not a singleton,
and the extra inversion contribution is again one of \(0,1,\ldots,k-1\).
Hence
\[
 [k]_qF_{r,k}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{\sigma\in\OP_{r+1,k}\\ r+1\text{ not singleton}}}
      q^{\inv(\sigma)} .
\]
Substituting this into (3), and replacing \(r+1\) by \(r\), gives exactly
\[
\sum_{a\ge1,\ b\ge0}c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^{a-1}z^b
=
\sum_{\substack{2\le r\le n\\1\le k\le r-1}}
\sum_{\substack{\sigma\in \OP_{r,k}\\r\text{ not singleton}}}
q^{\inv(\sigma)}z^{r-k-1}.
\]
Extracting the coefficient of \(q^{a-1}z^b\) proves the claimed interpretation.
\end{proof}

F. Bergeron,
\emph{Multivariate diagonal coinvariant spaces for complex reflection groups},
Adv. Math. 239 (2013), 97--108.

\bibitem{Lentfer}
J. Lentfer,
\emph{Diagonal supersymmetry for coinvariant rings},
arXiv:2505.14885 (2025).

\bibitem{RhoadesWilson}
B. Rhoades and A. T. Wilson,
\emph{The Hilbert series of the superspace coinvariant ring},
Forum Math. Pi 12 (2024), e16.

\end{thebibliography}

reviews.review_summary:
The proof is quite elegant and short, with the main points being:
\begin{enumerate}
 \item Use diagonal supersymmetry and the structure of super schur functions for hook shapes to show the Hilbert series of the superspace \footnote{one commuting variable, one anticommuting variable} coinvariant ring is of the form $H_n = 1 + (q + z)\sum_{a \geq 1, b \geq 0} c_{(a, 1^b)}(n)q^{a - 1}z^b$.
 \item Use the Rhoades--Wilson formula for $H_n$, which is in terms of $q$-Stirling numbers, and classical recursions of $q$-Stirling numbers to show that $H_n$ satisfies $\frac{H_n - 1}{q + z} = \sum_{r = 1}^{n - 1}\sum_{k = 1}^r[k]_q F_{r, k}z^{r - k}$, where $F_{r, k} = [k]!_q \Stir_q(r, k)$. 
 \item Show that $[k]_qF_{r, k}$ is the generating function tracking inversions of ordered set partitions of $\{1, 2, \ldots, r + 1\}$ into $k$ parts with $r + 1$ not in its own block.
 \item Finally, to prove the claimed interpretation, simply substitute (3) into (2), then extract the coefficient of $q^{a - 1}z^b$, which by (1), matches $c_{(a, 1^b)}(n)$.
\end{enumerate}

## Correctness.

This proof seems to be correct, as far as I'm able to tell. There are some incorrect (or confusing) superfluous details, and there might be a missing (but very easy) edge case (see inline comments). Otherwise, the argument seems true.

## Novelty.
 In some sense, I find this combinatorial interpretation the most natural and elegant of the four model solutions -- it is certainly the easiest formula to compute examples with! The proof is also much shorter than the others, and also much shorter than the human solution. However, given that the combinatorics of the superspace ring has a lot to do with ordered set partitions of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, it in some sense feels ``unnatural'' that this interpretation is given in terms of ordered set partitions of $\{1, \ldots, r\}$ as $r$ varies, rather than just for $r = n$. (The human solution is the only one whose combinatorial interpretation is in terms of special ordered set partitions of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}.$)

## Attributions.
 Although this submission includes all the papers it used in its final bibliography, it is missing several important in-text citations. It says some statements are ``standard'' which are actually the main results of these recent papers. The rare in-text citation does not give explicit theorem statements, putting extra work on the reader.

## Exposition.
 The claim is proven all in one theorem. It would be nicer to read if it was broken into several lemmas. There are also a couple of unnecessary/irrelevant comments which do not make sense to me, though this doesn't actually impact the argument.

\title{Submission B solution to Problem 9}
\date{}
\maketitle

\section*{Overview / Strategy}

The proof passes from the ordinary diagonal coinvariant algebra with \(m\) bosonic alphabets to the one-bosonic-one-fermionic coinvariant algebra \(SR_n\).  A diagonal supersymmetry theorem says that the same universal Schur coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) occur after replacing \(s_\lambda(q_1,\ldots,q_m)\) by the super Schur function \(s_\lambda(q/u)\).  In one bosonic and one fermionic variable, every nonempty non-hook shape vanishes, while
\[
s_{(a,1^b)}(q/u)=q^a u^b+q^{a-1}u^{b+1}.
\]
This gives a triangular relation between the hook generating functions \(C_b(q)=\sum_{a\ge 1}c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^a\) and the coefficients \(D_b(q)=[u^b]\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)\).

The second input is the Fields Frobenius formula, proved by Murai--Rhoades--Wilson.  After forgetting the \(S_n\)-module structure and using the Robinson--Schensted descent correspondence, this formula becomes a sum over permutations \(w\in S_n\).  Extracting the coefficient of \(u^b\) introduces a Gaussian binomial coefficient.  The triangular relation is then solved by induction using the \(q\)-Pascal identity, and the Gaussian binomial is finally expanded as a generating function for partitions in a rectangle.  This yields the stated counting formula for hook coefficients.

\section{Definitions and headline theorem}

For \(m,n\ge 1\), let
\[
P_n^{(m)}=\mathbb C[x_{i,j}:1\le i\le n,\ 1\le j\le m],
\]
with the diagonal action of \(S_n\) given by \(\sigma\cdot x_{i,j}=x_{\sigma(i),j}\).  The coinvariant algebra with \(m\) sets of \(n\) variables is
\[
R_n^{(m)}
=
P_n^{(m)}\big/
\left\langle \left(P_n^{(m)}\right)^{S_n}_{+}\right\rangle,
\]
where \(\left(P_n^{(m)}\right)^{S_n}_{+}\) denotes the invariant polynomials with zero constant term.  The algebra is \(m\)-multigraded by degrees in the \(m\) sets of variables, and
\[
\Hilb(R_n^{(m)};q_1,\ldots,q_m)
=
\sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_m\ge 0}
\dim\!\left(R_n^{(m)}\right)_{(i_1,\ldots,i_m)}
q_1^{i_1}\cdots q_m^{i_m}.
\]
As in the problem statement, write
\[
\Hilb(R_n^{(m)};q_1,\ldots,q_m)
=
\sum_{\lambda} c_\lambda(n)\,s_\lambda(q_1,\ldots,q_m)
\]
for the known universal Schur expansion, with coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) independent of \(m\).

For a permutation \(w=w_1\cdots w_n\in S_n\), define
\[
\Des(w)=\{\,i\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}:w_i>w_{i+1}\,\},
\qquad
\des(w)=|\Des(w)|,
\qquad
\maj(w)=\sum_{i\in\Des(w)}i.
\]
For integers \(b,r\ge 0\), the notation \(\rho\subseteq b\times r\) means that \(\rho\) is a partition with at most \(b\) parts, each at most \(r\).  Its size is \(|\rho|\).

\begin{theorem}[Original problem: hook coefficients in the universal Hilbert series]\label{thm:main}
Fix \(n\ge 1\).  Then
\[
c_{\varnothing}(n)=1.
\]
For every nonempty hook \(\lambda=(a,1^b)\), where \(a\ge 1\) and \(b\ge 0\),
\[
\boxed{
c_{(a,1^b)}(n)
=
\#\left\{
(w,\rho):
\begin{array}{l}
w\in S_n,\quad d=\des(w)\ge b+1,\\[2pt]
\rho\subseteq b\times(d-b-1),\\[2pt]
a=\maj(w)-bd+\binom{b}{2}+|\rho|
\end{array}
\right\}.
}
\]
When \(b=0\), the rectangle \(0\times(d-1)\) contains only the empty partition, and the formula becomes
\[
c_{(a)}(n)
=
\#\{\,w\in S_n:\des(w)\ge 1,\ \maj(w)=a\,\}
\qquad (a\ge 1),
\]
with the identity permutation accounted for separately by \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).  Also,
\[
c_{(a,1^b)}(n)=0
\qquad\text{whenever } b\ge n-1.
\]
\end{theorem}

The proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main} occupies the rest of the document.

\section{Cited inputs}

We use two external theorems.

First, define the one-bosonic-one-fermionic coinvariant algebra
\[
SR_n
=
\frac{\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\otimes \bigwedge(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)}
{\left\langle
\left(\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\otimes \bigwedge(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_n)\right)^{S_n}_{+}
\right\rangle},
\]
where \(S_n\) acts diagonally by permuting the \(x_i\)'s and the \(\theta_i\)'s.  The variable \(q\) records \(x\)-degree and \(u\) records \(\theta\)-degree.  The diagonal supersymmetry theorem for bosonic-fermionic coinvariant rings \cite{Lentfer2025} implies that the same universal coefficients \(c_\lambda(n)\) satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:diagonal-supersymmetry}
\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)
=
\sum_\lambda c_\lambda(n)\,s_\lambda(q/u),
\end{equation}
where \(s_\lambda(q/u)\) is the one-bosonic-one-fermionic super Schur function.

Second, the Fields Frobenius formula, proved by Murai--Rhoades--Wilson \cite{MRW2025}, gives the bigraded Frobenius characteristic of \(SR_n\).  For a standard Young tableau \(T\), let
\[
\Des(T)=\{\,i: i+1 \text{ appears in a strictly lower row of }T\text{ than }i\,\},
\]
and define \(\des(T)=|\Des(T)|\), \(\maj(T)=\sum_{i\in\Des(T)}i\).  Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fields}
\grFrob(SR_n;q,u)
=
\sum_{T\in \SYT(n)}
q^{\maj(T)-\binom{\des(T)+1}{2}}
\prod_{i=1}^{\des(T)}(q^i+u)\,
s_{\shape(T)}.
\end{equation}
Here \(\SYT(n)\) denotes the set of all standard Young tableaux with \(n\) boxes, and \(s_{\shape(T)}\) is the Schur function appearing in the Frobenius characteristic.  This is the Schur-tableau form of the \(t=0\) Delta expression; see also \cite{HRS2019}.  We also use the standard Robinson--Schensted correspondence and its descent property \(\Des(Q(w))=\Des(w)\) for the recording tableau \(Q(w)\); see Fulton \cite{Fulton1997}.

\section{Forgetting the \(S_n\)-module structure}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:permutation-hilbert}
The Hilbert series of \(SR_n\) is
\[
\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)
=
\sum_{w\in S_n}
q^{\maj(w)-\binom{\des(w)+1}{2}}
\prod_{i=1}^{\des(w)}(q^i+u).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let \(f^\mu=|\SYT(\mu)|\).  The Frobenius characteristic sends the irreducible \(S_n\)-module of shape \(\mu\) to \(s_\mu\).  Therefore applying the dimension map
\[
s_\mu\longmapsto f^\mu
\]
to a graded Frobenius characteristic gives the corresponding Hilbert series.  Applying this map to \eqref{eq:fields} gives
\[
\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)
=
\sum_{\mu\vdash n}
\sum_{T\in \SYT(\mu)}
f^\mu\,
q^{\maj(T)-\binom{\des(T)+1}{2}}
\prod_{i=1}^{\des(T)}(q^i+u).
\]
For each tableau \(T\in\SYT(\mu)\), the factor \(f^\mu\) counts a choice of another tableau \(P\in\SYT(\mu)\).  Thus the right-hand side is a sum over ordered pairs \((P,Q)\) of standard Young tableaux of the same shape, with \(Q=T\), weighted by
\[
q^{\maj(Q)-\binom{\des(Q)+1}{2}}
\prod_{i=1}^{\des(Q)}(q^i+u).
\]
By the Robinson--Schensted correspondence, such pairs \((P,Q)\) are in bijection with permutations \(w\in S_n\).  Under this bijection, \(\Des(Q(w))=\Des(w)\), hence \(\des(Q(w))=\des(w)\) and \(\maj(Q(w))=\maj(w)\).  Substituting these equalities into the preceding sum gives
\[
\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)
=
\sum_{w\in S_n}
q^{\maj(w)-\binom{\des(w)+1}{2}}
\prod_{i=1}^{\des(w)}(q^i+u),
\]
as claimed.
\end{proof}

\section{The one-bosonic-one-fermionic specialization}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:super-schur}
With the convention
\[
s_\lambda(q/u)=\sum_{\nu\subseteq\lambda}s_\nu(q)\,s_{\lambda'/\nu'}(u),
\]
one has
\[
s_{\varnothing}(q/u)=1.
\]
If \(\lambda=(a,1^b)\) is a hook with \(a\ge 1\), \(b\ge 0\), then
\[
s_{(a,1^b)}(q/u)=q^a u^b+q^{a-1}u^{b+1}.
\]
Every nonempty non-hook shape has \(s_\lambda(q/u)=0\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For an ordinary Schur function in one variable, \(s_\nu(q)\) is nonzero only when \(\nu\) has at most one row.  Indeed, in the semistandard tableau definition, only the entry \(1\) is available, and a column of length at least two would violate strict increase down columns.  Thus \(s_{(r)}(q)=q^r\), with \((0)=\varnothing\).

Similarly, a skew Schur function \(s_{\alpha/\beta}(u)\) in one variable is nonzero exactly when the skew shape \(\alpha/\beta\) has at most one cell in each column, i.e. is a horizontal strip.  In that case the unique semistandard filling uses only \(1\)'s and contributes \(u^{|\alpha/\beta|}\).

For \(\lambda=\varnothing\), the only summand is \(\nu=\varnothing\), giving \(s_{\varnothing}(q/u)=1\).

Now suppose \(\lambda\neq\varnothing\).  If \(\lambda\) is not a hook, then \(\lambda_2\ge 2\).  In any potentially nonzero summand, \(\nu\) must be a row, say \(\nu=(r)\), so \(\nu'=(1^r)\) is contained in the first column of \(\lambda'\).  Removing \(\nu'\) from \(\lambda'\) does not affect the second column of \(\lambda'\), which has length \(\lambda_2\ge 2\).  Therefore \(\lambda'/\nu'\) has at least two cells in one column and is not a horizontal strip.  Hence every summand is zero.

It remains to compute the hook case.  Let \(\lambda=(a,1^b)\), so \(\lambda'=(b+1,1^{a-1})\).  Again, \(\nu\) must be a row \((r)\) with \(0\le r\le a\).  Removing \(\nu'=(1^r)\) from the first column of \(\lambda'\), the remaining part of that first column has length \(a-r\).  The skew shape \(\lambda'/\nu'\) is a horizontal strip if and only if \(a-r\le 1\), i.e. \(r=a\) or \(r=a-1\).  For \(r=a\), the contribution is \(q^a u^b\).  For \(r=a-1\), the contribution is \(q^{a-1}u^{b+1}\).  These are the only nonzero summands, proving the formula.
\end{proof}

\section{Gaussian binomial identities}

For integers \(r,s\), define
\[
\qbinom{r}{s}
=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \sum_{\rho\subseteq s\times(r-s)}q^{|\rho|},
& 0\le s\le r,\\[1em]
0,
&\text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:gaussian}
The following identities hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(0\le b\le d\), then
\[
[u^b]\prod_{i=1}^{d}(q^i+u)
=
q^{\binom{d-b+1}{2}}\qbinom{d}{b}.
\]
If \(b>d\), both sides are \(0\), using the convention above.

\item For \(1\le b\le d\),
\[
\qbinom{d}{b}
=
\qbinom{d-1}{b}
+
q^{d-b}\qbinom{d-1}{b-1}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For the first identity, if \(b>d\), no term in the product can contribute \(u^b\), and \(\qbinom{d}{b}=0\).  Assume \(0\le b\le d\), and set \(r=d-b\).  To obtain the coefficient of \(u^b\), choose \(r\) indices
\[
1\le t_1<\cdots<t_r\le d
\]
from which the \(q^i\)-term is selected.  The corresponding contribution is \(q^{t_1+\cdots+t_r}\).  Define
\[
\rho_j=t_{r+1-j}-(r+1-j)\qquad (1\le j\le r).
\]
Then \(\rho_1\ge \cdots\ge \rho_r\ge 0\), and \(\rho_1\le d-r=b\), so \(\rho\subseteq r\times b\).  Conversely, every partition in \(r\times b\) arises uniquely in this way.  Moreover,
\[
t_1+\cdots+t_r
=
1+\cdots+r+|\rho|
=
\binom{r+1}{2}+|\rho|.
\]
Thus
\[
[u^b]\prod_{i=1}^{d}(q^i+u)
=
q^{\binom{r+1}{2}}
\sum_{\rho\subseteq r\times b}q^{|\rho|}.
\]
Conjugation of partitions is a size-preserving bijection between partitions in \(r\times b\) and partitions in \(b\times r\).  Hence
\[
\sum_{\rho\subseteq r\times b}q^{|\rho|}
=
\qbinom{d}{b},
\]
because \(r=d-b\).  This proves the first identity.

For the second identity, if \(b=d\), it reads \(1=0+1\), which is immediate.  Assume \(1\le b<d\).  Partitions in the rectangle \(b\times(d-b)\) split into two disjoint classes.  If the first part is at most \(d-b-1\), the partition lies in \(b\times(d-b-1)\), and these partitions contribute \(\qbinom{d-1}{b}\).  If the first part is exactly \(d-b\), removing that first part leaves a partition in \((b-1)\times(d-b)\), and the removed part contributes a factor \(q^{d-b}\).  These partitions therefore contribute \(q^{d-b}\qbinom{d-1}{b-1}\).  The two cases are disjoint and exhaustive, proving the \(q\)-Pascal identity.
\end{proof}

\section{The coefficients of \(u^b\)}

For \(b\ge 0\), define
\[
D_b(q)=[u^b]\Hilb(SR_n;q,u).
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:Db}
For every \(b\ge 0\),
\[
D_b(q)
=
\sum_{w\in S_n}
q^{\maj(w)-b\,\des(w)+\binom{b}{2}}
\qbinom{\des(w)}{b}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use Lemma \ref{lem:permutation-hilbert}.  Fix \(w\in S_n\), and write
\[
d=\des(w),\qquad M=\maj(w).
\]
The contribution of \(w\) to \(\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)\) is
\[
q^{M-\binom{d+1}{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{d}(q^i+u).
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:gaussian},
\[
[u^b]\prod_{i=1}^{d}(q^i+u)
=
q^{\binom{d-b+1}{2}}\qbinom{d}{b},
\]
with the understanding that the expression is zero when \(b>d\).  Multiplying by the prefactor gives
\[
q^{M-\binom{d+1}{2}}
q^{\binom{d-b+1}{2}}
\qbinom{d}{b}.
\]
Since
\[
-\binom{d+1}{2}+\binom{d-b+1}{2}
=
-bd+\binom{b}{2},
\]
this contribution equals
\[
q^{M-bd+\binom{b}{2}}\qbinom{d}{b}.
\]
Summing over all \(w\in S_n\) proves the formula.
\end{proof}

\section{Solving the triangular relation}

For \(b\ge 0\), define the hook generating polynomial
\[
C_b(q)=\sum_{a\ge 1}c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^a,
\]
and set \(C_{-1}(q)=0\).

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:Cb}
One has \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).  Moreover, for every \(b\ge 0\),
\[
C_b(q)
=
\sum_{\substack{w\in S_n\\ \des(w)\ge b+1}}
q^{\maj(w)-b\,\des(w)+\binom{b}{2}}
\qbinom{\des(w)-1}{b}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
First, the ideal defining \(R_n^{(m)}\) is homogeneous and generated by positive-degree elements, so the degree-zero component of \(R_n^{(m)}\) is \(\mathbb C\).  Hence
\[
\Hilb(R_n^{(m)};0,\ldots,0)=1.
\]
In the universal Schur expansion, \(s_{\varnothing}=1\), while every nonempty Schur polynomial has zero constant term.  Therefore \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).

By \eqref{eq:diagonal-supersymmetry} and Lemma \ref{lem:super-schur},
\[
\Hilb(SR_n;q,u)
=
1+
\sum_{b\ge 0}\sum_{a\ge 1}
c_{(a,1^b)}(n)\bigl(q^a u^b+q^{a-1}u^{b+1}\bigr),
\]
because all nonempty non-hook shapes vanish under the specialization \(q/u\).  Taking the coefficient of \(u^b\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triangular}
D_b(q)
=
\delta_{b,0}+C_b(q)+q^{-1}C_{b-1}(q),
\end{equation}
where \(\delta_{b,0}\) is the Kronecker delta and \(C_{-1}(q)=0\).

We now prove the displayed formula for \(C_b(q)\) by induction on \(b\).

For \(b=0\), equation \eqref{eq:triangular} gives
\[
C_0(q)=D_0(q)-1.
\]
By Lemma \ref{lem:Db},
\[
D_0(q)=\sum_{w\in S_n}q^{\maj(w)}.
\]
The unique permutation with no descents is \(12\cdots n\), and it contributes \(1\).  Every other permutation has at least one descent.  Therefore
\[
C_0(q)
=
\sum_{\substack{w\in S_n\\ \des(w)\ge 1}}q^{\maj(w)}.
\]
This is the required formula for \(b=0\), since \(\qbinom{\des(w)-1}{0}=1\) whenever \(\des(w)\ge 1\).

Now let \(b\ge 1\), and assume the formula is known for \(b-1\).  From \eqref{eq:triangular},
\[
C_b(q)=D_b(q)-q^{-1}C_{b-1}(q).
\]
Fix \(w\in S_n\), and write \(d=\des(w)\), \(M=\maj(w)\).  By Lemma \ref{lem:Db}, the contribution of \(w\) to \(D_b(q)\) is
\[
q^{M-bd+\binom{b}{2}}\qbinom{d}{b}.
\]
By the induction hypothesis, the contribution of \(w\) to \(q^{-1}C_{b-1}(q)\), when \(d\ge b\), is
\[
q^{-1}
q^{M-(b-1)d+\binom{b-1}{2}}
\qbinom{d-1}{b-1}.
\]
The exponent satisfies
\[
-1+M-(b-1)d+\binom{b-1}{2}
=
M-bd+\binom{b}{2}+d-b.
\]
Thus, for all \(w\) with \(d\ge b\), the difference of the two contributions is
\[
q^{M-bd+\binom{b}{2}}
\left(
\qbinom{d}{b}
-
q^{d-b}\qbinom{d-1}{b-1}
\right).
\]
If \(d<b\), both contributions are zero.  For \(d\ge b\), Lemma \ref{lem:gaussian} gives
\[
\qbinom{d}{b}
-
q^{d-b}\qbinom{d-1}{b-1}
=
\qbinom{d-1}{b}.
\]
Therefore
\[
C_b(q)
=
\sum_{w\in S_n}
q^{M-bd+\binom{b}{2}}
\qbinom{d-1}{b}.
\]
The Gaussian binomial \(\qbinom{d-1}{b}\) is zero unless \(d-1\ge b\), i.e. unless \(d\ge b+1\).  Hence
\[
C_b(q)
=
\sum_{\substack{w\in S_n\\ \des(w)\ge b+1}}
q^{\maj(w)-b\,\des(w)+\binom{b}{2}}
\qbinom{\des(w)-1}{b},
\]
which completes the induction.
\end{proof}

\section{Proof of the headline theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Theorem \ref{thm:main}]
The equality \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\) is part of Proposition \ref{prop:Cb}.

Fix \(b\ge 0\).  Proposition \ref{prop:Cb} gives
\[
C_b(q)
=
\sum_{\substack{w\in S_n\\ d=\des(w)\ge b+1}}
q^{\maj(w)-bd+\binom{b}{2}}
\qbinom{d-1}{b}.
\]
By the definition of the Gaussian binomial coefficient,
\[
\qbinom{d-1}{b}
=
\sum_{\rho\subseteq b\times(d-b-1)}q^{|\rho|},
\]
because \((d-1)-b=d-b-1\).  Therefore
\[
C_b(q)
=
\sum_{\substack{w\in S_n\\ d=\des(w)\ge b+1}}
\sum_{\rho\subseteq b\times(d-b-1)}
q^{\maj(w)-bd+\binom{b}{2}+|\rho|}.
\]
On the other hand,
\[
C_b(q)=\sum_{a\ge 1}c_{(a,1^b)}(n)q^a.
\]
Thus the coefficient of \(q^a\) in \(C_b(q)\) is exactly the number of pairs \((w,\rho)\) such that
\[
w\in S_n,\qquad d=\des(w)\ge b+1,
\]
\[
\rho\subseteq b\times(d-b-1),
\]
and
\[
a=\maj(w)-bd+\binom{b}{2}+|\rho|.
\]
This is precisely the boxed formula in the theorem.

It remains only to verify the stated edge cases.  First, the exponent just displayed is always positive under the condition \(d\ge b+1\).  Indeed, if the descent set of \(w\) has size \(d\), say
\[
\Des(w)=\{i_1<\cdots<i_d\},
\]
then \(i_j\ge j\) for every \(j\), so
\[
\maj(w)=i_1+\cdots+i_d\ge 1+\cdots+d=\binom{d+1}{2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\maj(w)-bd+\binom{b}{2}
\ge
\binom{d+1}{2}-bd+\binom{b}{2}
=
\binom{d-b+1}{2}.
\]
Since \(d\ge b+1\), the last binomial coefficient is at least \(1\), and adding \(|\rho|\ge 0\) keeps the exponent positive.

When \(b=0\), the rectangle \(0\times(d-1)\) contains only the empty partition.  The condition \(d\ge b+1\) becomes \(\des(w)\ge 1\), and the equation for \(a\) becomes \(a=\maj(w)\).  Hence
\[
c_{(a)}(n)
=
\#\{\,w\in S_n:\des(w)\ge 1,\ \maj(w)=a\,\}
\qquad (a\ge 1).
\]
The identity permutation has \(\des=0\) and \(\maj=0\), and its contribution is the separate term \(c_{\varnothing}(n)=1\).

Finally, every permutation in \(S_n\) has at most \(n-1\) descents.  If \(b\ge n-1\), then the required inequality \(d=\des(w)\ge b+1\) is impossible.  Therefore
\[
c_{(a,1^b)}(n)=0
\qquad\text{for all }b\ge n-1.
\]
The theorem is proved.
\end{proof}

reviews.review_summary:
The combinatorial formula suggested for the coefficients $c_{(a,1^b)}(n)$ involves a pair $(w,\rho)$ where $w$ is a permutation and $\rho$ is a partition.

The proof strategy starts from the result of Lentfer \cite{Lentfer2025} giving the universality of the coefficients $c_\lambda(n)$, and that in the case of partitions $\lambda$ of hook shapes, these coefficients can be extracted from the Hilbert series of the super coinvariant ring $SR_n$. 
It then uses the formula established by Murai–Rhoades–Wilson \cite{MRW2025} for the graded Frobenius series for the algebra $SR_n$. An expression for the Hilbert series is then obtained by forgetting the $S_n$-module structure. 

Here are some comments:
\begin{itemize}
 \item The extra step of forgetting the $S_n$-module could be avoided by directly using the result of Rhoades–Wilson 2024 giving a formula for the Hilbert series. 
\item The equivalence between Eq. (2) and the formula established in \cite{MRW2025} (see \cite[Eqs. (1.13) and (2.15)]{MRW2025}) which involves $q$-binomial coefficients, is not proved.
\item Using the formula given in Eq. (2) rather than the formula provided in \cite{MRW2025} seems unnecessary, since the purpose of Lemma 5 is to prove that Eq (2) can be expanded using $q$-binomial coefficients.

\end{itemize}

## Correctness.

The formula is correct, as is the proof.

## Novelty.

The solution uses the expected reference \cite{Lentfer2025} to relate the coefficients in question to the ring $SR_n$. The fact of starting from the graded Frobenius series formula rather than the known formula for the Hilbert series makes the proof longer. 

This extra step is also reflected in the combinatorial interpretation which involves a permutation $w$ and a partition $\rho$ that are not genuinely related, and which makes the formula seem slightly less ``natural''.

# Attribution

Lemma 4 is a classical result. I suggest citing standard textbooks references rather than reproving it.
